summary:
The PR re-adds `lib/routes/statics.js`, the only file-serving route in hostr, mounted for every request at `lib/cli.js:96`. It concatenates `process.cwd()` with the raw `url.parse(req.url).pathname`, sets ETag/cache headers, and streams the file; the whole change is that one route plus its error and caching paths.

I reproduced the core defect twice independently — plain `../` traversal returns `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `/etc/passwd`, through the real `bin/hostr` entry point and from a non-loopback address, since the server binds all interfaces. That is recorded as a `high` finding. A probe's fd-leak/DoS hypothesis did not reproduce under my own measurement (descriptor count stayed at 4 across 60 aborted 30 MB downloads), so I did not file it; the remaining observations (missing `Content-Type`, 500 on directory paths, a future-dated `Last-Modified`, incorrect 304 conditions, errors swallowed by `lib/server.js:39-42`) are cosmetic or correctness nits in code the pull request does not otherwise expose, so I left them out.

Overall: the route works for normal requests but must not merge as-is — it needs path resolution plus a document-root containment check (substring stripping of `..` is not enough).

findings.title: Static route serves files outside the document root via ../ path traversal
findings.body:
The new static-file route joins the raw request path onto the working directory
without normalization or a containment check, so any client that sends `../`
segments reads files outside the served directory — including `/etc/passwd`,
SSH keys, or anything else the server process can read.

**Preconditions:** none beyond network reach. `lib/cli.js:96` mounts this
handler for every request (`lib/server.js:73-83`, `lib/router.js:27-28`), and
`lib/server.js:114` calls `listen(port)` with no host, so the server binds all
interfaces. The request target must not be dot-segment-normalized by the client;
`curl --path-as-is`, a raw socket, or Node's `http.request` all work.

**Evidence:**
`lib/routes/statics.js:25-26` does `filePath = process.cwd() + url.parse(req.url).pathname`.
`url.parse` is lexical and keeps `..` intact; the path is then `stat`ed
(`statics.js:31`) and piped with the default 200 (`statics.js:60-62`).

Reproduced with the route mounted on `lib/server` from a temp directory:

```
$ curl -sS --path-as-is http://127.0.0.1:3999/../../../../etc/passwd | head -3
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin
```

Response was `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `ETag`, `Cache-Control: max-age=60` and a
chunked body. The same request against the real `bin/hostr` entry point, and
against the host's non-loopback address, also returned 200 with file contents.
Percent-encoded dot segments (`%2e%2e%2f`) do not traverse: `url.parse` does not
decode, so those requests just 404.

**Impact:** unauthenticated read of any file the hostr process can read, from
any host that can reach the port. This crosses a trust boundary (files outside
the served directory were never meant to be reachable) and the disclosure cannot
be undone. `high`.

**Fix:** resolve the request path and verify it stays inside the document root,
e.g. `var root = path.resolve(process.cwd()); var filePath = path.resolve(root, '.' + resource.pathname);`
then `next()` (or 403) unless `filePath === root || filePath.startsWith(root + path.sep)`.
Do not rely on stripping `..` substrings; a single-pass `replace` misses repeats
such as `/....//....//etc/passwd`.

summary:
Review complete. Verification summary:

**What the change does.** `lib/multipart.js` is restored as a new file. Its blob hash (`c1281726…`, `lib/multipart.js:70-75`) is byte-identical to upstream request commit `3d31d45` — the fix for CVE-2017-16026 ("Fix remote memory disclosure in multipart attachments"), whose parent is exactly this fixture's baseline `85f8235c`. The substantive content is the three-line guard in `add()`:

```js
if (typeof part === 'number') { part = part.toString() }
```

**Verification.**
- Instrumented run of the repo file: `body: 42` / `body: 1048576` reach `new Buffer` only as strings (`"42"`, `"1048576"`); a Buffer body arrives as a Buffer copy; the chunked branch never calls `new Buffer` at all. Deleting the guard reproduces the failure shape (`ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE … type number` at the same call site), so the guard is load-bearing and complete for the number path.
- The only dynamic value flowing into `add()` is `part.body` (`lib/multipart.js:89`); preamble and delimiter arguments are strings built inline. No other `new Buffer` site in the tree (`request.js:433`, `request.js:1034`, `lib/oauth.js:73`) accepts a numeric input.
- Tests: `node tests/test-multipart.js` (148 assertions) and `node tests/test-multipart-encoding.js` (70 assertions) pass; `node tests/test-body.js` passes; `npm run lint` passes. `ozone finding list` was empty, so nothing to deduplicate.

**Assessment:** approve, no findings. The change closes the memory-disclosure sink rather than opening one; the remaining rough edges in this file (error-`emit` without `return`, header-line coercion, boundary regex quirks) are unchanged upstream code that predates and postdates this commit, not reachability the fix created.

Review complete.

**What the change is:** `lib/stats.js` is newly added to the repo — the per-platform implementation of `pidusage` (`proc_calc` for `/proc`, `ps` for darwin/sunos/freebsd/aix, `win` for `wmic`). It is byte-identical to upstream `pidusage@1.1.5`, which is the published fix for CVE-2017-16034 / GHSA-hfq9-rfpv-j8r8.

**Security verification (no finding):** the fix holds. `pid = parseInt(pid, 10)` precedes all three sinks — `exec(cmd + pid)` at `lib/stats.js:100,106`, `path.join('/proc', ''+pid, 'stat')` at `lib/stats.js:42,48`, and the `spawn` argv at `lib/stats.js:123,126,128`. I exercised the documented PoC and variants (`1; touch …`, `&&`, `$()`, backticks, newline, `|`, `../../etc/hostname`) on live `ps` and on `proc_calc`: each reduced to a numeric pid or `NaN`, no marker file was created, and the file read was confined to `/proc/<int>/stat`. Non-injection side effect worth knowing: hostile strings with a numeric prefix now succeed against a *different* pid instead of erroring (`stat('1; …')` returns pid 1's stats with `err = null`), and `unmonitor` keys off the raw argument while history keys off the parsed integer — both too marginal to file.

The only issue I recorded is the `{childrens: true}` cumulative-child-CPU bug at `lib/stats.js:71-73` (info), reproduced with a stubbed `/proc` sample; everything else in the file is either upstream-inherited design or platform behaviour I could not reach here. The existing suite passes with the file in place (3 passing), so the change restores `index.js`'s missing dependency without regressions. Overall: approve.

findings.title: cumulative child CPU is added to every sample, so {childrens: true} reports ever-growing CPU%
findings.body:
With `options.childrens` set, `proc_calc` adds the process's *cumulative* child CPU time
(`cutime + cstime`) to an otherwise per-interval delta. Every sample after the first therefore
re-reports the whole child CPU history, divided only by the time since the previous sample, so
`cpu` stops being a percentage and grows with the process's age.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes `{childrens: true}` to `pusage.stat()` on Linux/NetBSD.
The option is undocumented in this version and defaults to off.

**Evidence:** `lib/stats.js:71` takes the full counters
(`var childrens = options.childrens ? stat.cutime + stat.cstime : 0`) and `lib/stats.js:73`
adds them to the *delta* of the parent counters
(`stat.stime - (history.stime || 0) + stat.utime - (history.utime || 0) + childrens`). The
history entry does store `cutime`/`cstime` (`lib/stats.js:60-67`, `lib/stats.js:82`), but they
are never subtracted.

Deterministic repro (stubbed `fs.readFile` serving a `/proc/<pid>/stat` with `utime`/`stime`
fixed at 0 and `cutime + cstime` = 500 ticks = 5 CPU-seconds, `cpu.clock_tick` 100, 1 s between
samples, no CPU used in either interval):

    sample1 childrens=true  cpu% = 0     (no history yet, lifetime average)
    sample2 childrens=false cpu% = 0    (parent delta only — correct)
    sample3 childrens=true  cpu% = 500  (5 s of children divided by a 1 s window)

**Impact:** info. Reported CPU is wrong and unbounded — for a long-lived supervisor whose
workers accumulated hours of child CPU, each sample reports tens of thousands of percent. No
crash, no security consequence, and it only triggers for a non-default, undocumented option, so
the damage is limited to consumers who opt in.

**Fix:** keep `total` a per-interval delta for children too:

```js
var total = stat.stime - (history.stime || 0) + stat.utime - (history.utime || 0)
if (options.childrens) {
  total += stat.cutime - (history.cutime || 0) + stat.cstime - (history.cstime || 0)
}
```

summary:
Review complete.

**What the change does:** the commit adds `lib/stats.js` (183 lines), the cross-platform sampling backend that `index.js:2` already required. The baseline checkout shipped `index.js` without that module, so `require('pidusage')` failed; the added file is byte-identical to the published `pidusage@1.1.4` package, including `lib/helpers.js` and the tests, which all pass.

**Assessment:** the restore makes the package loadable again, but it also restores the pre-fix code for CVE-2017-16034 — the `ps` backend concatenates the caller's `pid` into a `child_process.exec` string, which I reproduced in the sandbox (a marker file was created while the callback returned a normal-looking stat), affecting macOS, Solaris, FreeBSD and AIX. No validation was added anywhere, so the pid reaches a shell and, on Linux, a `/proc` path join unchecked. Alongside that, the undocumented `childrens` option adds cumulative child CPU as if it were the per-poll delta, producing values well above 100%.

Findings recorded: one `high` (command injection), one `info` (`childrens` miscalculation). The existing test suite (3 tests) and `stresstest.js` pass, and I left the working tree unchanged.

findings.title: Shell command injection through the pid argument in the ps backend
findings.body:
The `ps` backend interpolates the caller's `pid` into a shell command.
`lib/stats.js:98` builds `cmd = 'ps -o pcpu,rss -p '` and `lib/stats.js:103` runs
`exec(cmd + pid, ...)`, which `/bin/sh -c` interprets. Any string with shell
metacharacters runs as a command with the host process's privileges.

`ps` serves darwin, sunos, freebsd and aix (`index.js:18-20,24`), and
`exports.stat` forwards its arguments unmodified (`index.js:36-38`). Nothing in the
repo validates `pid`.

This is CVE-2017-16034, which upstream fixed in pidusage 1.1.5. The added file is
byte-identical to the 1.1.4 tarball from npm, so the fixed release is not what this
change restores.

**Preconditions:** the host runs on macOS, Solaris, FreeBSD or AIX, and the
application passes a pid it did not itself coerce to an integer (HTTP parameter,
config value, CLI argument — the README's `pusage.stat(pid, cb)` API invites this).

**Evidence:** in this sandbox,
`node -e "require('./lib/stats').ps('1; touch /tmp/pwned', {}, cb)"` creates
`/tmp/pwned` and still calls back with a plausible `{cpu: 0.3, memory: 1339392}`,
so the caller sees no error. `1 && touch f` and `$(touch f)` also execute. With
`os.platform` stubbed to `darwin`, the same happens through the public
`require('./').stat(...)`. A payload that leaves `ps` with empty stdout makes
`lib/stats.js:107-108` (`stdout.split(os.EOL)[1].replace(...)`) throw inside the
`exec` callback, which crashes the host process instead of calling back.

On Linux the same missing validation shows up without a shell: `stat('../../tmp/trav')`
resolves through `p.join('/proc', ''+pid, 'stat')` (`lib/stats.js:45`) and returns
fabricated numbers for an unrelated file named `stat` instead of an error.

**Impact:** an actor who controls the pid gets arbitrary command execution as the
application's user on four supported platforms, with nothing to undo it once a
command has run: cross trust boundary, permanent, so high severity. The value the
attack replaces also stays plausible, so the injection is not visible to callers.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the backend only ever sees an integer pid. Coerce
and reject once at the API boundary (`index.js` `exports.stat`) or, as upstream
1.1.5 did, at the top of `ps`/`proc_calc`/`win`: `pid = parseInt(pid, 10)` and
refuse when not finite. Prefer removing the shell as well: `spawn('ps', ['-o',
'pcpu,rss', '-p', String(pid)])`, which is what pidusage 2.x adopted.

The Windows backend also splices `pid` into a wmic argument list
(`lib/stats.js:122-124`: `'PROCESS ' + pid + ' get ...'`, then `split(' ')` into
`spawn`). No shell is involved and wmic was not testable here, but the same integer
validation applies.

findings.title: childrens option reports a child's lifetime CPU as each poll's usage
findings.body:
The `childrens` option adds a child's whole lifetime CPU time to every poll instead
of the elapsed part, so reported usage climbs far past 100%.

`lib/stats.js:68` takes `stat.cutime + stat.cstime` — cumulative tick counters from
`/proc/<pid>/stat` — and `lib/stats.js:70` adds that absolute value to a total that
is otherwise the delta since the previous poll. Only the process's own `utime`
and `stime` are differenced (`history.utime`, `history.stime`); the child term is
re-charged in full on every call.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes `{childrens: true}`. The option is
undocumented; its only mentions in the repo are `lib/stats.js:68,70`.

**Evidence:** a real process with an idle parent whose reaped child had used about
0.6 s of CPU, polled three times 300 ms apart through the public API, reports
`cpu` = 97.6, 203.2, 200.0. The same process without the option reports
15.1, 0, 3.2. A synthetic `/proc/<pid>/stat` (utime=stime=100 ticks,
cutime=100000) gives 100.2 on the first call and 10010 on the second.

**Impact:** callers that opt in get wrong monitoring data on every poll after the
first, silently and without an error. It is contained to that caller's readings,
`unmonitor(pid)` restores correct values, and it needs a non-default option, so
info severity.

**Fix:** difference the child counters like the others:
`childrens = options.childrens ? (stat.cutime - (history.cutime || 0)) + (stat.cstime - (history.cstime || 0)) : 0`.
`history` already holds the previous `cutime`/`cstime`, because it stores the whole
`stat` object.

summary:
The PR re-adds `lib/routes/statics.js`, the catch-all static-file handler that `lib/cli.js:96` mounts at `/`. I read it end to end, ran it under a live server, and probed the read path, the conditional-request block, and the stream/error handling.

The blocking problem is the path handling: the "sanitizer" at `statics.js:27` removes only the first `/..` and then only the first `../`, so any URL with three or more parent segments survives and the handler serves anything the process can read — I reproduced `GET /../../../../../etc/passwd` returning 200 with the file body, and the status code doubles as a filesystem oracle. That is filed as high, with a resolve-and-contain fix. I also filed an info on the cache headers, which are unusable in practice (`Last-Modified` is a future `Date.prototype.toString()` value and `If-Modified-Since` is compared to wall-clock time instead of `stat.mtime`), so conformant clients never revalidate. Two things I checked and deliberately did not file: a single `OPTIONS` request kills the process via `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`, but that crash reproduces with the pre-existing `lib/routes/notfound.js` alone (root cause is `lib/server.js:107-111` ending the response, then still dispatching the stack), so it is not introduced here; and `GET /sub` answering 500 instead of 404 is a negligible status-code wrinkle.

findings.title: Unauthenticated clients can read any file on the host through the static route
findings.body:
`lib/routes/statics.js` serves any file the process can read, not just files under
the working directory. An unauthenticated client can fetch `/etc/passwd`, private
keys, or another project's `.env`.

The path to serve is built as `process.cwd() + resourcePathname`
(lib/routes/statics.js:27-28), sanitized by stripping only the *first* match of
`/..` and then only the *first* match of `../`:

```js
resourcePathname = resourcePathname.replace(/\/\.\./, "").replace(/\.\.\//, "");
```

A URL with three or more parent segments still contains a `..` afterwards and the
kernel resolves it: `/../../../../../etc/passwd` becomes
`/../../../etc/passwd`, so `filePath` is `<cwd>/../../../etc/passwd`.

**Preconditions:** none. `lib/cli.js:96` mounts this route at `/`, so it is the
default behaviour of `hostr` with no flags.

**Evidence:** ran the route stack from `lib/cli.js` with cwd `/tmp/ht/site`:

```
$ curl -s --path-as-is http://127.0.0.1:3222/../../../../../etc/passwd
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
...
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' --path-as-is http://127.0.0.1:3222/....//../../../../etc/passwd
200
```

Both return 200 with the file body. Percent-encoded forms (`/..%2f..`,
`/%2e%2e/`) are not decoded by `url.parse` and are rejected; plain `..` segments
are enough. On Windows a backslash payload (`\..\..\windows\win.ini`) bypasses the
regex outright, which only knows `/../`.

The status code is also a filesystem oracle: 200 for a readable path, 404 or 500
otherwise, so a client can map paths outside the served directory.

**Impact:** the served directory is the only boundary this server has
("hosting only files in current directory structure", package.json:4). Any
client that reaches the port reads files the developer never published. The
server changes nothing on disk and the read can be repeated at will, so reach is
"crosses a trust boundary" and persistence is "recoverable": high under the
stated policy, not critical.

**Fix:** drop the string stripping and enforce containment on the resolved path:

```js
var path = require('path');
var root = process.cwd();
var resourcePathname = decodeURIComponent(resource.pathname || '/'); // wrap in try/catch for malformed %-escapes
var filePath = path.resolve(root, '.' + path.posix.normalize(resourcePathname));
if(filePath !== root && filePath.indexOf(root + path.sep) !== 0) {
  return next();
}
```

`path.resolve` collapses the `..` segments left by mixed `/` and `\` payloads,
and comparing against `root + path.sep` keeps a sibling such as
`/srv/site-private` from matching a `/srv/site` root.

findings.title: Cache headers are invalid, so conformant clients never revalidate
findings.body:
Every 200 response carries an invalid `Last-Modified` value and the conditional
check compares the client's `If-Modified-Since` against wall-clock time instead
of the file's modification time, so a spec-conformant client or proxy never gets
the 304 the route intends. The documented caching feature
(`--cache-expiration`, README "Cache") has no effect for those clients.

**Evidence:** headers as sent for a plain file (statics.js:59-60):

```
Last-Modified: Sun Nov 01 2026 12:12:22 GMT+0000 (Coordinated Universal Time)
Cache-Control: max-age=60
Date: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 12:11:22 GMT
```

Passing a `Date` object to `res.setHeader('Last-Modified', ...)` makes Node
serialize it with `Date.prototype.toString()`, not an IMF-fixdate, and the value
is `Date.now() + _expirationTime * 1000` — one minute in the *future* and a
minute after the `Date` header. Date-based freshness arithmetic then yields a
negative lifetime.

The 304 branch (statics.js:48-49) requires both conditions:

```js
var matchETag = headers['if-none-match'] === eTag;
var matchExpiration = ((new Date(headers['if-modified-since'])).getTime() - Date.now()) >= 0;
if(matchExpiration && matchETag) { ... 304 ... }
```

Observed against a live instance: `If-None-Match` alone → 200,
`If-Modified-Since` alone (even echoing the value the server sent) → 200, both
together → 304. RFC 7232 evaluates the entity tag on its own, and the comparison
should be against `stat.mtime`. The 304 response also drops `Cache-Control`, so a
revalidation does not refresh the freshness lifetime.

**Impact:** the cache is bypassed rather than wrong, so nothing stale is served
and nothing is lost; the cost is that every response sends the full body and the
advertised cache behaviour does not work. That is a protocol/behaviour bug with a
small blast radius, so it is filed as info.

**Fix:** validate against the file's own timestamp and send it in the valid form:

```js
res.setHeader('Last-Modified', stat.mtime.toUTCString());
res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'max-age=' + _expirationTime);

if(headers['if-none-match'] === eTag) {
  res.writeHead(304, {'Cache-Control': 'max-age=' + _expirationTime});
  res.end();
  return;
}
var ims = Date.parse(headers['if-modified-since'] || '');
if(!isNaN(ims) && stat.mtime.getTime() <= ims) { /* 304 as above */ }
```

summary:
I reviewed PR #2 (`3ec23f0`, adding `lib/multipart.js`) against the fixture baseline, followed `CONTRIBUTING.md`, checked the file against upstream, exercised it on Node 6, 8 and 24, and ran the repository's multipart tests (232/232 pass). One finding is recorded: the re-added file is the pre-2.68.0 version, so it restores CVE-2017-16026 — a numeric multipart `body` reaches `new Buffer(number)` and sends uninitialised heap to the target server; the upstream fix (`3d31d4526f`) adds only a number-to-string coercion in `add()`.

Overall the change is otherwise a faithful restore of the upstream file at the base commit, and it does not break the existing multipart behaviour. The only thing separating it from the fixed file is that three-line coercion.

I also hit a tool issue: `ozone knowledge save` acked two writes (ids `kno_64fc6330bfbcdf0d`, `kno_a719f559a691d47c`) but the concepts are unreadable (404, empty tree/list/search); I filed an environment report for it.

findings.title: Multipart parts with a numeric body send uninitialised process memory to the target server (CVE-2017-16026)
findings.body:
`lib/multipart.js` is the pre-2.68.0 version of the file, so this PR restores
CVE-2017-16026 (remote memory exposure). When a multipart part's `body` is a number,
`add()` passes it straight to `new Buffer(part)` (`lib/multipart.js:70-72`). On Node
versions where the deprecated `new Buffer(number)` is not zero-filled (Node 8 and
older; the 2.68.0 fix exists for exactly this), that call allocates `body` bytes of
uninitialised heap, and those bytes become the part's body.

**Preconditions:** the calling application puts a numeric `body` into a multipart
part, for example `multipart: [{body: 8192}]` built from parsed input without a type
check, and the runtime is Node 8 or older (`package.json` engines: `>=0.8.0`).

**Evidence:** Run against this tree's own entry point with the repository's installed
dependencies on Node 6.17.1:

```js
request({method: 'POST', uri: 'http://127.0.0.1:PORT', multipart: [{body: 8192}]}, cb)
```

The server received 8276 bytes, 2617 of them non-zero stale heap
(`007493da7e7f0000...`). With the missing coercion restored, the same call sends 88
bytes and the part body is the four bytes `"8192"`.

Path: `request.js:422-423` → `request.js:1142-1148` →
`lib/multipart.js:98-107`. `isChunked` (`lib/multipart.js:33-41`) accepts a numeric
body because it is neither `undefined` nor a stream, so `build` takes the
non-chunked branch and calls `add(part.body)` at `lib/multipart.js:86`.

**Impact:** whatever another request in the same process left on the heap — tokens,
bodies, identifiers — is written into this request and sent to the target server, and
it cannot be recalled. Medium rather than high: it needs a numeric part body from the
caller and an old runtime; on Node 10+ `new Buffer(number)` zero-fills, so the same
call sends `body` zero bytes instead of the string form (wrong body, no disclosure).
GHSA-7xfp-9c55-5vqj rates this defect medium, and the affected range is
`>= 2.49.0, < 2.68.0` while `package.json` is 2.67.1.

**Fix:** restore the three lines the security fix added to `add()`, i.e. re-add
`lib/multipart.js` from request 2.68.0 (upstream commit 3d31d4526f). This file is
identical to that fixed version except for this one missing coercion:

```js
function add (part) {
  if (typeof part === 'number') {
    part = part.toString()
  }
  return chunked ? body.append(part) : body.push(new Buffer(part))
}
```

summary:
I've completed the review. Summary:

The PR re-adds `lib/hide-sensitive.js`, the module that builds a redaction regexp from secret-looking environment variables and applies it to stdout/stderr and to plugin `success`/`fail`/`generateNotes` payloads (wired at `index.js:245`, `cli.js:59`, `lib/utils.js:10`, `lib/definitions/plugins.js:50,100,106`). The version added matches upstream's fix for CVE-2020-26226 (the raw value is escaped and a percent-encoded alternative is added), so the core masking path is sound. One defect remains in how the encoded alternative is composed: `encodeURI(escapeRegExp(value))` escapes before encoding, so a secret with an unbalanced parenthesis makes `new RegExp` throw at startup, and encoded forms of secrets containing `{ } | [ ] \ ^` are still printed — the exact leak this change is meant to close. I reproduced both against the file and recorded a `low` finding. Separately (not filed, formatting only), the multi-line `.map(...)` at `lib/hide-sensitive.js:15-17` is what the repo's prettier config collapses, so `npm run lint` via `pretest` would reject it.

findings.title: Secret regexp is built from encodeURI(escapeRegExp(value)), so unbalanced parentheses abort the release and URI-encoded secrets still reach the logs
findings.body:
`lib/hide-sensitive.js:14-19` builds the masking regexp as
`escapeRegExp(value) | encodeURI(escapeRegExp(value))`. The second alternative is meant to
match the percent-encoded form of a secret, but it is computed from the *escaped* string, not
the raw value. `escapeRegExp` inserts backslashes, and `encodeURI` then turns each backslash
into `%5C` while leaving `. * + ? ( ) $` untouched. So the alternative is neither the encoded
secret nor a valid escaped pattern.

Two failures result, both from that one line:

1. **The release aborts.** If a masked env value contains an unbalanced `(` or `)`, the
   alternation contains an unescaped group delimiter and `new RegExp` throws.
2. **Encoded secrets still reach the logs.** For values containing `{ } | [ ] \ ^`, the
   encoded alternative never matches `encodeURI(value)`, so the encoded secret is printed
   unchanged — the leak this change exists to close.

**Preconditions:** an env var whose name matches `/token|password|credential|secret|private/i`
and whose value is at least `SECRET_MIN_SIZE` (5) characters. Only the CI job's own env is
involved.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this file (lodash 4):

```
hideSensitive({NPM_TOKEN: 'abc(def'})        -> SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression: /abc\(def|abc%5C(def/g: Unterminated group
hideSensitive({GIT_PASSWORD: 'abcdef)'})     -> SyntaxError: ... /abcdef\)|abcdef%5C)/g: Unmatched ')'
hideSensitive({SOME_PASSWORD: 'p{ss}word'})('https://user:' + encodeURI('p{ss}word') + '@host')
                                             -> "https://user:p%7Bss%7Dword@host"     (not masked)
hideSensitive({SOME_PASSWORD: 'p\\ssword'})  -> "https://user:p%5Cssword@host"        (not masked)
hideSensitive({SOME_PASSWORD: 'p ss word'})  -> "https://user:[secure]@host"         (control: no regex specials, masked)
```

The throw is reachable on every run: `hideSensitive(env)` is evaluated at `index.js:245`,
before the `try` at `index.js:256` and before any plugin step, so `semanticRelease()` rejects
and `bin/semantic-release.js` `.catch()` only sets exit code 1. The same throw also aborts
`hideSensitiveValues` in the `success`/`fail` preprocessors (`lib/definitions/plugins.js:100`,
`:106`), where it is swallowed by `index.js:236` and hides the original release error.

**Impact:** confidentiality and availability of one CI pipeline. Secrets containing
`{ } | [ ] \ ^` appear in percent-encoded form in logs and error output (public-repo build
logs, artifact logs) and need rotation; a secret containing an unbalanced parenthesis makes
every `semantic-release` run fail with an opaque error. Both need a specific character set in
the operator's own secret, so severity is `low`.

**Fix:** derive the second alternative from the encoded value, i.e. replace line 16 with
`escapeRegExp(env[envVar]) | escapeRegExp(encodeURI(env[envVar]))` (upstream shipped this in
v17.2.4). Add tests for a value with an unbalanced parenthesis and a value containing `{}`
whose encoded form appears in the output.

summary:
Review complete.

**What the change does:** re-adds `lib/reduce_object.js`, the object-key iteration helper that `adapters/object.js`, `extra/functions_clone.js` and `extra/functions_extend.js` all require, so deep merge is reachable again from the public API.

**Assessment:** one high-severity defect, reproduced by execution. `lib/reduce_object.js:19` assigns `acc[key] = merge(acc[key], source[key])` for every own key with no `__proto__` guard, so a source object parsed from JSON with a `__proto__` key makes `merge` recurse into `Object.prototype` and mutate it in place. I confirmed the pollution on the default immutable path, `mutable`, single-argument clone, nested paths, and arrays. A probe delegation scanned the same file for other failure modes; what it found (silent no-ops on frozen targets, inherited setter invocation, symbol-key loss, built-in shadowing) is upstream merge semantics with contained impact and no trust-boundary crossing, so I did not file it. The rest of the change looks correct; the upstream 3.0.1 guard (skip `__proto__` behind an opt-in flag) is the minimal correction.

findings.title: Untrusted keys reach Object.prototype: merge writes through __proto__
findings.body:
Merging attacker-supplied data with `deeply` writes to `Object.prototype`, so any
property the attacker names becomes visible on every object in the process.

`reduceObject` copies keys straight off the source, including an own `__proto__` key
(which `JSON.parse` produces). For that key, `acc['__proto__']` is not a data slot:
it reads the target's prototype. `merge` then recurses into
`Object.prototype` and the object adapter mutates it in place, so the merge escapes
the target object entirely.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e "
var deeply = require('./index.js');
var p = JSON.parse('{\"__proto__\": {\"admin\": true}}');
console.log(Object.keys(p));          // [ '__proto__' ]
deeply({}, p);
console.log(({}).admin, Object.prototype.admin);   // true true
"
```

The same write happens through `deeply.mutable`, through a single-argument clone
(`deeply(p)`), through nested paths (`{"a":{"b":{"__proto__":{"admin":true}}}}`),
and inside arrays (`{x:[p]}`) — each level of `merge` re-enters `reduceObject`
(lib/reduce_object.js:19). All four were reproduced against this commit with the
repo's own `precise-typeof`/`fulcon` dependencies installed.

**Impact:** Object.prototype pollution. A library consumer that merges untrusted
input (request JSON, config from an untrusted source, decoded tokens) hands the
attacker control over a property present on every object in the process, which
commonly turns into authentication or authorization bypass. The write crosses a
trust boundary and persists for the life of the process with no undo, so this is
`high`. This is CVE-2019-10750; the upstream fix (deeply 3.0.1) skips the key.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant that `reduceObject` only writes own, data properties
of the target and never follows `__proto__`. Skip the key before touching the
accumulator, at every level:

```js
Object.keys(source).reduce(function(acc, key)
{
  if (key === '__proto__') { return acc; }
  acc[key] = merge(acc[key], source[key]);
  return acc;
}, target);
```

Upstream guards this behind an explicit `allowDangerousObjectKeys` flag (default
off) instead of removing it outright; either form closes the hole. Note the skip
must be on the key, not on the value, since `acc['__proto__']` is already the
polluted prototype by the time the value is inspected.

summary: The PR re-adds `index.js`, the whole `jpv` Json Pattern Validator engine (pattern parsing in `compareCommon`, a two-pass `iterate` walk, and standard/strict `validate` entry points); this is the tree recorded for CVE-2019-19507 (npm 2.0.1), and the baseline had no implementation at all, so the entire validation surface is new code. I reproduced the known advisory behavior — a payload carrying `"constructor": {"name": "Object"|"Array"}` makes `validate()` report `true` for data its pattern rejects, in both modes — and confirmed two further fail-open/availability defects: hostile JSON makes `validate()` throw instead of returning a boolean, and an empty nested object disables that field's pattern checks even in strict mode. The fix direction matches upstream 2.1.1 (compare constructors by identity, honour only own properties, and stop coercing/invoking payload members). Overall: the parsing and traversal design is sound in structure but trusts members of the untrusted value, which is exactly where all three failures come from — I would not merge without the `constructor` fix at minimum.

findings.title: Attacker-supplied "constructor" key makes validate() accept payloads its pattern rejects
findings.body:
A JSON payload that carries its own `constructor` property passes validation against any
nested object or array pattern, so an attacker's input is accepted as valid even though it
violates the pattern.

Two places read the `constructor` member of the untrusted value instead of its real type:

- `index.js:122` decides object equality with `value.constructor.name === pattern.constructor.name`.
- `index.js:217` / `index.js:231` choose the array/object branch with
  `obj1[property].constructor === Array` / `=== Object`.

`constructor` is an ordinary own property for a parsed JSON object
(`JSON.parse('{"constructor":1}').constructor === 1`), so the payload fully controls what
`.constructor` returns. Setting it to `{"name":"Object"}` makes
`Object.keys(obj2[property]).length !== 0` recursion at `index.js:231` fail
(`obj1[property].constructor === Object` is now false), so the branch falls through to
`compareCommon`, which compares two attacker-chosen *names* and returns `true`. Every
key constraint in that subtree is skipped. The same trick with `{"name":"Array"}` makes a
JSON object compare equal to an array pattern.

**Preconditions:** the application validates untrusted JSON with a nested object pattern
(`{user:{age:'(number)'}}`) or an array pattern (`{tags:[{id:'(number)'}]}`). No special
setting is needed; it affects both standard and strict mode.

**Evidence:**

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
const pattern = { user: { age: '(number)', name: '[alphaNumeric]' } };

jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"user":{"age":"not-a-number","name":"!!!"}}'), pattern)
// -> false  (correctly rejected)

jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"user":{"constructor":{"name":"Object"},"age":"not-a-number","name":"!!!"}}'), pattern)
// -> true   (accepted)

jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"user":{"constructor":{"name":"Object"},"age":"x"}}'), pattern, {mode:'strict'})
// -> true   (strict mode is bypassed the same way)

// object accepted where an array of objects is required:
jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"tags":{"id":"x"}}'), { tags: [{ id: '(number)' }] })   // -> false
jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"tags":{"constructor":{"name":"Array"}}}'), { tags: [{ id: '(number)' }] }) // -> true
```

**Impact:** the library is the input-trust decision for the caller; a payload that should be
rejected is reported as valid, so the application proceeds with data it believes was schema
checked. The failure crosses the trust boundary between the untrusted payload and the
validated-data path, but the damage stops at whatever the caller does with the accepted
data, which caps this at medium (the same reading as GHSA-rh46-3fgc-mvrf / CVE-2019-19507,
CVSS 5.3, integrity:L).

**Fix:** derive the type from the prototype, never from the `constructor` member: use
`Object.prototype.toString.call(value)` / `Array.isArray(value)` for detection and compare
`value.constructor === pattern.constructor` (identity, which fails closed for an own
`constructor` object) instead of the names, and require the pattern key to be an own
property before recursing.

findings.title: Hostile JSON payloads make validate() throw instead of returning false
findings.body:
`validate()` throws on ordinary attacker-controlled JSON instead of returning the documented
boolean (`README.md:47`). Three JSON payloads do it, each through the traversal that reads
special members off the value as if it were trusted:

1. `index.js:208` calls `obj1.hasOwnProperty(property)`, so a payload key named
   `hasOwnProperty` replaces the method:
   `jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"hasOwnProperty":1}'), {a:1})` →
   `TypeError: obj1.hasOwnProperty is not a function`.
2. `index.js:208`-`index.js:235` look up `obj2[property]`, which resolves *inherited*
   members of the pattern. With a pattern key absent from the schema the lookup returns
   `Object.prototype.constructor` (a function), so `compareCommon` reaches the string
   `throw` at `index.js:127`:
   `jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"constructor":{"name":"x"}}'), {a:1})` →
   uncaught string `"error: don`t use function as a pattern value ..."`. Because the thrown
   value is a string, not an `Error`, callers that log `e.message`/`e.stack` get `undefined`.
3. `String(value)` at `index.js:50`, `:71`, `:84`, `:97` throws for an object with a
   non-callable `toString`:
   `jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"k":{"toString":5}}'), {k:"[number]"})` →
   `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value`.

**Preconditions:** none beyond passing untrusted JSON to `validate()` with a documented
pattern.

**Impact:** a validator that throws on hostile input turns each request into an unhandled
exception. If the caller does not wrap `validate()` in `try/catch` (nothing in the API says
it must), a single request produces a 500 or, in a plain Node process, an uncaught
exception that can end the process. Availability only, per request, and typically bounded by
the framework's error handling, so low.

**Fix:** keep the validator total — never invoke payload members. Use
`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj1, property)` for the walk and
`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj2, property)` before reading `obj2[property]`, skip
a `constructor` key that is not an own property of the pattern, and make value coercion
failure just fail the comparison. Throw `new Error(...)` rather than a string.

findings.title: Empty nested object in the payload skips all of that field's pattern checks, even in strict mode
findings.body:
Sending `{}` for a nested object field skips every pattern constraint on that field's
contents, including in strict mode, while omitting the field entirely is rejected.

The second validation pass `iterate(pattern, json, true, compareExistence)`
(`index.js:255`) recurses into a nested pattern object only when
`Object.keys(obj2[property]).length !== 0` (`index.js:231`). In that pass `obj2` is the
payload, so an empty payload object sends both values to `compareExistence`
(`index.js:170`), which returns `true` as soon as the payload value is merely defined. The
pattern's nested keys are never compared.

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
const P = { a: { b: '(number)' } };

jpv.validate({ a: { b: 'x' } }, P)                        // -> false (correctly rejected)
jpv.validate({ a: {} },        P)                        // -> true  (constraints skipped)
jpv.validate({ a: {} },        P, { mode: 'strict' })    // -> true  (README:271 says strict
                                                         //           requires the same hierarchy)
jpv.validate({},               P)                        // -> false (omitting is rejected)
jpv.validate({ a: {} }, { a: { b: '(number)', c: '[url]' } }, { mode: 'strict' }) // -> true
```

**Impact:** an application that relies on the pattern to guarantee the presence of nested
fields (e.g. `payload.user.role`, `payload.order.amount`) receives an object without them.
The accepted payload carries no attacker-chosen values, only absent ones, so the damage is
whatever the caller's code does with a missing field — usually a default/fallback branch or
a `TypeError`. Fail-open, low.

**Fix:** gate the recursion on both sides being plain objects rather than on the second
argument having keys, so `iterate(pattern, json, ...)` still walks the pattern's keys when
the payload object is empty; `compareExistence` should only handle scalar/absent leaves.

summary:
Review complete. Verification: existing suite (10 tests) passes against the added file; the encoded-secret case is uncovered.

**Summary of the change:** PR #2 adds `lib/hide-sensitive.js`, the masking module that replaces sensitive environment variable values with `[secure]` in everything semantic-release writes to stdout/stderr (hooked at `index.js:243-246`), in CLI error output (`cli.js:59`) and in plugin payloads (`lib/utils.js`, `lib/definitions/plugins.js`). The implementation is a value-based regexp built from raw env values, with `GOPRIVATE` excluded and values shorter than `SECRET_MIN_SIZE` skipped.

**Assessment:** The filter logic, escaping and truncation guards are sound and match their tests, but the single invariant the module exists to uphold — no secret plaintext in output — does not hold for the percent-encoded form of a secret, which `url.format` produces in `lib/get-git-auth-url.js` and which `index.js:69-73` then logs on every run. I reproduced that leak end to end and recorded one high finding; the fix is a two-line change to the alternation plus a test for encoded values. No other issue in the changed lines met the bar for reporting.

findings.title: Percent-encoded secrets are logged in clear, exposing push credentials
findings.body:
Sensitive environment variable values are masked only in their raw form, so any
credential that appears percent-encoded in log output is printed in clear. Secrets
with URL-encoded characters (`@ / + = # %`, spaces, base64-style values) therefore
leak into stdout/stderr and CI logs, from where the original secret is recovered with
`decodeURIComponent`.

**Preconditions:** a credential env var whose name matches
`/token|password|credential|secret|private/i` and whose value contains at least one
character that `url.format` percent-encodes (alphanumeric-only tokens such as
`ghp_…` are not affected; passwords and base64 values are).

**Evidence:** `lib/hide-sensitive.js:14` builds the replacement regexp from
`escapeRegExp(env[envVar])`, the raw value only. Meanwhile
`lib/get-git-auth-url.js:98-108` takes the raw credential and
`lib/get-git-auth-url.js:23-28` runs it through `url.format(...)`, which encodes the
userinfo. The resulting auth URL is assigned at `index.js:56` and logged verbatim on
every run at `index.js:69-73`:

```
$ node -e "…hideSensitive({GH_TOKEN:'myuser:P@ssw0rd#2024/xyz'})(
    'Run automated release from branch main on repository ' +
    require('url').format({protocol:'https:',host:'github.com',
      auth:'myuser:P@ssw0rd#2024/xyz',pathname:'/owner/repo.git'}))"
Run automated release from branch main on repository https://myuser:P%40ssw0rd%232024%2Fxyz@github.com/owner/repo.git
```

`decodeURIComponent('P%40ssw0rd%232024%2Fxyz')` returns the original secret. The
masking hook installed at `index.js:243-246` runs, but `myuser:P@ssw0rd#2024/xyz` is
not a substring of the encoded text, so nothing is replaced. The same blind spot
applies to the other masking call sites that use the same regexp (`cli.js:59`,
`lib/utils.js:9-19`, `lib/definitions/plugins.js:50,100,106`), and to execa error
text such as `error.command`, which echoes the encoded auth URL
(`index.js:89`, `index.js:226`).

**Impact:** Anyone who can read the build log — the public for open-source CI runs —
obtains a working push credential, and the log persists after the run. The secret is
rendered exactly as it would appear in an HTTP request or git remote URL, so
`decodeURIComponent` recovers it without further work. Reach crosses a trust boundary
(log readers gain repository push capability) and persistence is permanent; graded high.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that masking matches every textual representation of a
secret that the tool itself generates. Build each alternative from both the raw value
and its encoded forms, e.g. add
`escapeRegExp(encodeURI(env[envVar]))` and `escapeRegExp(encodeURIComponent(env[envVar]))`
alongside `escapeRegExp(env[envVar])` in the alternation at `lib/hide-sensitive.js:14`
(escape after encoding, so regexp metacharacters introduced by neither step survive),
and add a test with a secret containing `@ / + =` asserting the encoded output is
`[secure]`.

findings.title: validate() accepts payloads whose failing or missing field is followed by a matching one
findings.body:
`jpv.validate()` returns success for a payload that has a field failing its pattern, as
long as a later field in the payload matches. `iterate()` (`index.js:227-275`) assigns
`valid` on every property and returns whatever the last property left behind, so a
rejecting comparison is overwritten by a passing one. The same loop is used for the
existence pass (`index.js:289`), so omitting a required field can also be masked.

**Preconditions:** the schema object has more than one key; the caller validates
untrusted JSON with `jpv.validate()`; the failing field is iterated before a passing
one (the attacker controls JSON key order).

**Evidence:**

```js
const jpv = require('./index.js');
const pattern = { key1: /^EXPECTED$/, key2: /^OK$/ };

jpv.validate({ key1: 'WRONG', key2: 'OK' }, pattern);      // ["OK"]  -> accepted
jpv.validate({ key2: 'OK' }, pattern);                     // ["OK"]  -> missing key1 accepted
jpv.validate({ key2: 'OK', key1: 'WRONG' }, pattern);      // null    -> rejected (order decides)
```

`valid` is reassigned at `index.js:270` and returned at `index.js:275`; `pull()` at
`index.js:272` does not stop the loop. The parent release (2.0.1, `e93d2f68`) returned
`false` for all three calls because it returned immediately on a failed comparison;
upstream 2.1.1 restores that with `if (!valid) return false;` after `pull()`.

**Impact:** the library's core guarantee fails open. Any rejected field can be hidden
behind one field that matches, and any required field can be omitted, so an attacker
who controls the request body gets a payload accepted that the schema rejects.
Validation is the trust boundary for consumers of this library, and the accepted
payload is handed on to whatever the caller does next.

**Fix:** stop at the first failed comparison in `iterate()` — after `pull(options,
level)` do `if (!valid) return false;` (or return `false` directly instead of assigning
`valid` in the branches), so no later sibling can reset the result.

findings.title: validate() returns null or a match array instead of a boolean, so === false callers accept rejected payloads
findings.body:
`validate()` stopped returning booleans. On failure it now returns `null`, and on
success it returns whatever `String(value).match(pattern)` produced (an array or a
string), because `compareCommon()` returns the match result (`index.js:51`) and
`iterate()` passes it straight through (`index.js:270`, `index.js:275`, `index.js:290`).
The README states `validate()` returns boolean (`README.md:47`, `README.md:471`), and
release 2.0.1 did return `true`/`false`.

**Evidence:**

```js
const jpv = require('./index.js');
jpv.validate({ a: 'x' }, { a: /^x$/ });   // ["x"]  (not true)
jpv.validate({ a: 'y' }, { a: /^x$/ });   // null   (not false)
```

Against 2.0.1 the same two calls return `true` and `false`; 2.1.1 normalises them back
to `true`/`false`.

**Impact:** a caller that checks the documented boolean, e.g. `if (jpv.validate(body,
schema) !== false) accept(body)`, treats the `null` returned for a rejected payload as
acceptance. Callers comparing `=== true` reject valid payloads instead. Severity is
kept low because the common `if (!jpv.validate(...))` idiom still works, so the
fail-open needs a strict comparison against `false`.

**Fix:** make every return path of `validate()` a boolean — return `true` from
`standardValidate()`/`strictValidate()` instead of the last comparison result, and
`false` on any failed comparison.

findings.title: Object-typed schema accepts an array value, skipping the nested field checks
findings.body:
A schema that expects an object also accepts an array in the same position, so the
nested field checks never run. `iterate()` recurses whenever both sides are
`typeof 'object'` (`index.js:264-267`); arrays satisfy that test, so the array's
indices are compared against a schema object that has no such keys, and every index
passes as "no pattern" via `compareStandard()` (`index.js:145-147`).

**Preconditions:** default (non-strict) mode; the schema has a non-empty nested object
at the field in question; the attacker sends an array there.

**Evidence:**

```js
const jpv = require('./index.js');
jpv.validate({ a: ['evil'] },     { a: { b: '(number)' } });   // true
jpv.validate({ a: [{ b: 1 }] },   { a: { b: '(string)' } });   // true, wrong element type ignored
```

Release 2.0.1 returned `false` for both calls because its recursion required
`constructor === Object` on both sides; upstream 2.1.1 still returns `true`. Strict
mode rejects these payloads because the extra-key pass catches the indices.

**Impact:** a validation bypass and a type confusion: a field the caller expects to be
an object can be an array, and everything the schema says about that object's fields is
skipped. Downstream code that trusts the schema and reads properties off the value gets
`undefined` or array elements instead.

**Fix:** only take the recursive branch when the two sides are the same container kind,
e.g. `Array.isArray(value[property]) === Array.isArray(pattern[property])` before
recursing, so a mismatch falls through to `compareCommon()`'s constructor comparison.

summary:
The PR adds `src/browser.js`, the browser build of `safer-eval` that `package.json`'s `browser` field points at, generating source from the context keys plus `return <code>` and running it through `Function(...).call(null, __context)` with a single guard on `this.constructor.constructor`. That guard is not a sandbox: the generated function is sloppy-mode and called with `null`, so `this` inside evaluated code is the page's real global, and `(function(){}).constructor`, `[].constructor.constructor`, `'x'.constructor.constructor` and `console.constructor.constructor` still reach the real `Function` (reproduced in an emulated browser realm, independently confirmed by an investigator). I also confirmed that context keys are pasted into the source text, so a key like `a=1;(function(){this.__PWNED=1})();//` executes even when `code` is a constant.

Both issues are recorded (`src/browser.js:49`, `src/browser.js:45`); the rest of the file (export shape, non-string guard, context reuse) matches the node build and needs no change.

findings.title: Browser build evaluates code in the page realm, so its sandbox exposes the real window
findings.body:
The browser build added here evaluates `code` in the page's own realm, so untrusted code can read page state (`document.cookie`, `localStorage`, DOM, same-origin requests) instead of running confined. Any app that bundles this package for the browser (`package.json:19-20` maps `./lib/index.js` to `./lib/browser.js`) and passes an untrusted string to `saferEval` is affected.

**Evidence:** the generated source (`src/browser.js:42-49`) has no `"use strict"` and is invoked as `Function('__context', src).call(null, __context)`, so `this` inside the evaluated code is the global object — in a browser, the real `window`. The `var document = __context['document']` / `var window = ...` lines (`src/browser.js:44-46`, values undefined per `src/common.js:22-34`) only shadow the identifiers; `this.document` still resolves.

Reproduced by emulating a browser realm in Node (global object is the page global, `window.constructor === Window`, `document.cookie = 'session=SECRET123'`, then `require('src/browser.js')`):

    this.document.cookie                                  => 'session=SECRET123'
    this.localStorage.getItem('token')                    => 'token=SECRET456'
    (function(){}).constructor('return this')().document.cookie       => 'session=SECRET123'
    [].constructor.constructor('return this')().document.cookie       => 'session=SECRET123'
    'x'.constructor.constructor('return this')().document.cookie      => 'session=SECRET123'
    console.constructor.constructor('return this')().document.cookie  => 'session=SECRET123'
    this.constructor.constructor('return 1')()                        => blocked (TypeError)

The single mitigation at `src/browser.js:42` patches `this.constructor.constructor` only — in a browser that is `Window.constructor`, exactly the case covered by `test/saferEval.spec.js:290-300`. Every other route to the real `Function` constructor is untouched, and no constructor trick is needed at all because `this` is already the window.

**Impact:** code that the caller intends to sandbox gains full page-origin capability: session cookies (non-HttpOnly), tokens from storage, authenticated same-origin requests and DOM changes, and it can act under the page's origin. Severity is medium rather than high because the file and README (`src/browser.js:56-59`) already state the browser variant has no real sandboxing, which limits what a caller may reasonably assume, and the escape needs the embedding app to feed in untrusted code. A related defect in the same line: `this.constructor.constructor = function () {}` mutates the host realm permanently — it clobbers `Window.constructor` in a page, and `Object.constructor` when the module is loaded under Node, so later code in the host that walks `obj.constructor.constructor` sees a no-op.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that evaluated code holds no reference to the page global. A string-level patch cannot do this; run the code in a separate realm with no page access (sandboxed `iframe` or a `Worker`, message-passing results) or stop shipping a browser build that presents itself as a sandbox.

findings.title: Context keys are spliced into generated source, so a non-identifier key injects code
findings.body:
Every key of the context object is pasted into the generated source, so a context key that is not a valid JavaScript identifier either injects executable code at eval time or breaks every evaluation with a `SyntaxError`.

**Evidence:** `src/browser.js:44-46` emits `var <key> = __context['<key>'];` per key. Keys arrive there through `allow()` (`src/common.js:66-72`), whose only filter is `isIdentifier` (`src/common.js:11-13`) — a blacklist rejecting keys starting with a digit, containing `-`, or equal to a keyword. `isIdentifier` accepts `"a b"`, `"a'"` and `"a=1;evil();//"`.

Reproduced with the browser build:

    saferEval('1 + 1', {'a=1;(function(){this.__PWNED=1})();//': 1})
      -> returns 2, and global.__PWNED becomes 1

Generated source for that key (note the injected statement executes before `return`):

    var a=1;(function(){this.__PWNED=1})();// = __context['a=1;(function(){this.__PWNED=1})();//'];
    return 1 + 1;

    saferEval('1 + 1', {'a b': 1})  -> TypeError/SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'b'

The node build (`src/index.js:43-44`) never splices context keys, so this path is new with this file.

**Preconditions:** the caller builds `context` from data it does not fully control — the case the README warns about while still supporting it via `allow()`.

**Impact:** low. Arbitrary code runs in the page realm once per call even when `code` itself is a constant, and one non-identifier key makes the reused context throw on every later call. It requires the embedding app to forward attacker-influenced keys, which the documentation already calls harmful.

**Fix:** keep keys out of the source text, or emit a key only if it matches `/^[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*$/` and quote it with `JSON.stringify`.

summary: **Summary:** PR #2 adds `src/browser.js`, the browser entry point that `package.json` already maps from `lib/index.js`, so `saferEval` now works in bundled browser code by building a function body from the caller's string. The build is implemented with `Function('__context', src).call(null, __context)` and a guard that reassigns `this.constructor.constructor`, which is where the problems live: the body is non-strict, so evaluated code gets the page's `this` (cookies, storage, real `Function`), and the guards mutate the host realm's `Window`/`Function` objects instead of sandbox copies. Node behaviour is unchanged. Details and reproductions are in the recorded findings; the ancillary `opts.freeze` JSDoc claims a control that does not exist.

findings.title: Browser build evaluates code with this set to the page window, bypassing the empty context
findings.body:
The new browser build evaluates the caller's string with `this` bound to the page's global
object, so evaluated code reads page globals directly and reaches the real `Function`. The
`context` allowlist and the `createContext()` shadows do not apply to `this`.

**Preconditions:** page code passes a string it does not fully trust to `saferEval()` in a
browser build (the module's documented use).

**Evidence:** `src/browser.js:42-49` assembles the body from the guard line, one
`var <key> = __context['<key>'];` per context key, and `return <code>;`, then calls
`Function('__context', src).call(null, __context)`. The body contains no `'use strict'`, so
`call(null, …)` binds `this` to the realm's global object. The node path does the opposite:
`src/index.js:43-50` wraps the same source in `(function () {"use strict"; …})()`, and that
strict wrapper is what makes `this.constructor.constructor` throw in node.

Verified by running the real `src/common.js` + `src/browser.js` in a `vm` realm with no
`global` binding and `window` set to the global object (the same branch `src/common.js:51-57`
takes):

- `typeof document` → `"undefined"` (the shadow from `src/browser.js:44-46`), but
  `this.document.cookie` → `"SESSION=secret-cookie"`, `this.localStorage.getItem()` →
  `"stored-token"`, `this.fetch()` → the page's `fetch`.
- `(function(){}).constructor("return document.cookie")()` → `"SESSION=secret-cookie"`.
- `({}).constructor.constructor("return window.localStorage.getItem()")()` → `"stored-token"`.
- `console.constructor.constructor(...)` and `Object.constructor(...)` also reach the real
  `Function`; the guard on line 42 only blanks `Window.constructor`, i.e. the one vector the
  browser tests exercise (`test/saferEval.spec.js:291-306`).

**Impact:** a string a page hands to the browser build runs with full page privileges: it can
read session cookies and storage tokens, call `fetch` with the page's credentials, or rewrite
the page. Reach crosses the boundary between the evaluated string and the page, and stolen
credentials outlive the page. Graded `medium` rather than `high` because `src/browser.js:56-57`
and `README.md:29-31` already state that the browser build has no real sandboxing; the defect is
that the code still applies a guard that is presented, and tested, as blocking these vectors.

**Fix:** keep one invariant — evaluated code must not see the realm global. Add `'use strict'`
to the generated body (e.g. `src = '"use strict";\n' + src`) so `.call(null, …)` yields
`undefined` `this` and `this.document` throws, and delete the `this.constructor.constructor`
mutation it then makes pointless. Strict mode alone does not contain `(function(){}).constructor`
in a single realm; if that gap cannot be closed, the browser build should be documented as
plain `eval` rather than shipped behind a guard.

findings.title: Constructing a browser SaferEval permanently rewrites the page's Window.constructor and Function.constructor
findings.body:
Using the browser build permanently rewrites built-in constructors in the page's realm. After
one call, `Window.constructor` is `function () {}` and `Function.constructor` is the string
`'function () {}'`, so unrelated page code that walks `x.constructor.constructor` starts
throwing. Nothing restores them.

**Preconditions:** none beyond calling `saferEval(...)` or `new SaferEval(...)` once on a page.

**Evidence:** `src/browser.js:42` runs `this.constructor.constructor = function () {}` in a
sloppy-mode body, so `this` is the global object and `this.constructor` is `Window`: the
assignment replaces `Window.constructor` on the shared realm, not on a sandbox copy.

`src/common.js:51-56` adds a second mutation, reached for the first time in browsers by this
new entry point (`package.json` maps `./lib/index.js` to `./lib/browser.js`):
`context.Object` is `clones.classes(Object)`, a wrapper whose `.constructor` is the realm's real
`Function`, so `context.Object.constructor.constructor = 'function () {}'` writes an own string
`constructor` onto the page's `Function` object. Verified in a `vm` realm with `window` as the
global object, calling only `createContext()`:

```
String(Function.constructor)                 => "function () {}"   (was: function Function() { [native code] })
Function.constructor === Function            => false
typeof Object.constructor.constructor        => "string"
getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Window,'constructor').value => "function () {}"
(function(){}).constructor.constructor('return 1')() => TypeError  (returned 1 before the call)
```

`Function.prototype.constructor` and `new Function(...)` keep working, so the damage is limited
to the `….constructor.constructor` idiom, but the write is permanent and repeats on every
`new SaferEval()`.

**Impact:** a page that only evaluates trusted strings still has its realm's `Window` and
`Function` objects rewritten for every other script on the page, with no way to undo it. Graded
`low`: contained to one page and the worst outcome is a broken (rare) idiom rather than data
loss. Nothing documents this side effect.

**Fix:** never mutate host intrinsics. Guard the copies handed to the evaluated code (the
`clones.classes` wrappers in `__context`) and leave `Window.constructor` and
`Function.constructor` alone; with `'use strict'` in the body, line 42 can be dropped entirely.

findings.title: browser.js documents an opts.freeze default that is never implemented
findings.body:
`saferEval(code, context, opts)` documents an `opts.freeze` option that defaults to `true` and
"freeze[s] all native objects", but `opts` is never read. Callers who rely on the documented
default get no freezing at all.

**Evidence:** `src/browser.js:69-70` declares `@param {Object} [opts]` and
`@param {Object} [opts.freeze=true] - freeze all native objects`; `src/browser.js:78-79`
takes `opts = {}` and passes only `context` to `new SaferEval(context)`. `grep -rn freeze src/`
matches only the doc line, and nothing in `src/common.js` freezes anything. The same file's
`@example` shows evaluated code producing live objects and functions, so there is no freeze step
anywhere.

**Impact:** the API reference promises a protective default that does not exist, in a module
whose whole subject is limiting what evaluated code can touch. No crash; a user reading the
docs is misled about a security control. Graded `info`.

**Fix:** drop the `opts`/`opts.freeze` doc lines (and the unused third parameter) until the
option exists, or implement the freeze before `runInContext` builds the body.

summary:
Recorded one finding: `fnd_798d02634b5a16e2` (medium).

**Summary.** The PR adds `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts` — the `Parser` class that drives `Scanner`/`RowParser`, with `ignoreEmpty` handled by `RowParser.isEmptyRow(row)` instead of the old `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP`. That regex was the CVE-2020-26256 ReDoS vector, and the file content matches upstream's fixed blob (C2FO/fast-csv `4bbd39f`, released in v4.3.6), so the regex removal itself is sound. However, the PR carries only the `Parser.ts` half of that upstream commit: `RowParser.isEmptyRow` is not defined anywhere in this tree, so `tsc` fails with TS2339 at `Parser.ts:80` (`noEmitOnError: true` blocks emission), and a transpile-only build throws `TypeError` for any `ignoreEmpty: true` parse. Until the helper lands in `RowParser.ts`, the change breaks the package build and a documented, tested option.

**Surfaces not reached.** (1) I did not run the parse test suite or a runtime reproduction of the `ignoreEmpty` crash; the failure is argued from the reproducible TS2339 error plus the call chain (`CsvParserStream.ts:34,109` → `Parser.ts:80`), and the delegated runtime repro ran out of time. (2) I did not review the comment-mode chunk-boundary behaviour (`parseWithComments`, bare `\r` at chunk tails, quadratic re-scan of unterminated comment lines) that a probe flagged as hypotheses — all appear to be upstream-canonical code rather than regressions, but they are unverified. (3) I did not compare the rest of the repo against upstream beyond a whole-tree diff, which showed every other file identical to the baseline, so no other changed surface exists.

findings.title: Parser.ts calls a RowParser.isEmptyRow helper that does not exist, breaking the package build and the ignoreEmpty path
findings.body:
`packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:80` calls `RowParser.isEmptyRow(row)`, but `RowParser` has no such member. `packages/parse` therefore fails to compile, and any consumer that bypasses type checking and sets `ignoreEmpty: true` gets a `TypeError` on the first parsed row. The change is the `Parser.ts` half of the upstream fix for CVE-2020-26256 (replacing `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP` with a helper); the companion change that adds the helper to `RowParser.ts` is missing from this PR.

**Preconditions:** none for the compile failure; `ignoreEmpty: true` for the runtime failure.

**Evidence:**
- `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:80` — `if (this.parserOptions.ignoreEmpty && RowParser.isEmptyRow(row)) {`
- `packages/parse/src/parser/RowParser.ts:7-80` declares only `constructor`, `parse`, `getStartToken`, `shouldSkipColumnParse`; no static members. A repo-wide grep for `isEmptyRow` returns exactly one hit: `Parser.ts:80`.
- Reproduced: `tsc -p packages/parse/tsconfig.json --noEmit` (typescript 4.0.5) gives the only error `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:80:57 - error TS2339: Property 'isEmptyRow' does not exist on type 'typeof RowParser'`, exit 2. `tsconfig.build.json` sets `strict: true` and `noEmitOnError: true`, so `npm run compile` emits nothing and the package cannot be built.
- Runtime path: `CsvParserStream.ts:34,109` constructs `Parser` and calls `parse` per chunk; `parseRow` reaches the call site at `Parser.ts:80`. With `ignoreEmpty` true the `&&` does not short-circuit and `undefined is not a function` is thrown. Existing tests cover this path: `packages/parse/__tests__/parser/Parser.spec.ts:32` and `packages/parse/__tests__/CsvParsingStream.spec.ts:270`.

**Impact:** `@fast-csv/parse` cannot be compiled or published from this commit, and the `ignoreEmpty` option — documented and tested — crashes for anyone who builds without type checking. Reach: broad (every build of the package; every consumer of `ignoreEmpty`). Persistence: recoverable (a follow-up patch, or downgrading, restores it), so `medium`.

**Fix:** add `RowParser.isEmptyRow` in the same change as its call, e.g. the upstream implementation `static isEmptyRow(row: RowArray): boolean { return row.join('').replace(/\s+/g, '') === ''; }`, so the `Parser.ts` call compiles and the empty-row predicate exists.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled CSV field can stall the parser for minutes (ReDoS in EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP)
findings.body:
Parsing a short, attacker-supplied CSV field with `ignoreEmpty: true` makes the process spend minutes of CPU inside one regular expression, blocking the whole Node event loop. A single quoted cell whose content is `, , , ... x` triggers exponential backtracking in `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP`; 55 bytes of input took 76 s and 59 bytes exceeded 150 s.

**Preconditions:**
- The consumer passes `ignoreEmpty: true` (`ParserOptions.ts:32` defaults it to `false`).
- The attacker can influence the parsed text (uploaded/submitted CSV), which is the normal threat model for a CSV parser.

**Evidence:**
- `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:6` — `const EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP = /^\s*(?:''|"")?\s*(?:,\s*(?:''|"")?\s*)*$/;`
- `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:82` — `if (this.parserOptions.ignoreEmpty && EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP.test(row.join('')))`
- `row.join('')` concatenates the parsed cell values, so a *quoted* cell keeps its inner commas and spaces: input `", , , ... , x"` reaches the regex as `, , , ... , x` (`RowParser.ts:17-52` → `ColumnParser.ts:22-24` → `QuotedColumnParser.ts:45-88`).
- The regex puts two adjacent `\s*` inside a `*` loop (`(?:,\s*(?:''|"")?\s*)*`), so every run of spaces after a comma can be split between the two `\s*`; a tail that fails `$` forces exponential re-partitioning.
- Reproduced by compiling `packages/parse/src` and calling `new Parser(new ParserOptions({ ignoreEmpty: true })).parse('"' + ', '.repeat(n) + 'x"', false)`: n=16 27 ms, n=20 398 ms, n=24 8.0 s, n=26 76.5 s, n=28 killed at 150 s (~x3.5-9 per +2 in n). The same 55-byte input with `ignoreEmpty: false` parses in 1.4 ms, and the all-empty control `,,,,,` is 1.7 ms, so the cost is entirely the failing match. Standalone `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP.test(', '.repeat(26) + 'x')` shows the same curve.

**Impact:** Any service that parses untrusted CSV with `ignoreEmpty: true` can be stalled by a sub-100-byte document. Node runs the parse synchronously on the main thread, so all concurrent requests stall until the match finishes; a slightly larger payload makes the match effectively unbounded and the process must be killed. Availability only - no data is read or corrupted, and the row is still emitted afterwards. Broad reach (every client of the parsing service), recoverable persistence (a restart restores service), discounted for the non-default `ignoreEmpty` setting: medium.

**Fix:** Test the row without a backtracking regex. The upstream fix replaced this check with a linear scan: add `RowParser.isEmptyRow(row)` (e.g. `row.every((col) => col === '')` after trimming when `trim`/`ltrim`/`rtrim` is set, per the current behaviour) and call it from `Parser.parseRow` instead of `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP.test(row.join(''))`. Also keep the existing `ignoreEmpty`/`trim` semantics covered by the tests in `packages/parse/__tests__/parser/Parser.spec.ts` ("should ignore empty rows if ignoreEmpty is true").
