findings.title: Unauthenticated POST with a ~16KB space-padded X-HTTP-Method-Override header blocks the event loop for ~0.7s
findings.body:
`createHeaderGetter` parses the attacker-controlled `X-HTTP-Method-Override` value with the
backtracking regex at `index.js:120`:

```js
return (req.headers[header] || '').split(/ *, */)
```

For a value made of one non-space character, a long run of spaces, and a trailing non-space
with no comma, the engine retries ` *` at every offset and then backtracks one character at a
time looking for `,`. Cost grows quadratically with the run length. A single header of about
16 KB — inside Node's default 16 KB header limit — keeps the process busy for roughly 0.7 s,
synchronously on the event loop, so every other request waits.

**Preconditions:** the app uses the built-in header getter (the default
`X-HTTP-Method-Override`) and the request method is listed in `options.methods` (default
`['POST']`). The spaces must be interior: Node's HTTP parser trims leading and trailing OWS
from header values, so `'x' + ' '.repeat(16000) + 'y'` is the shape that reaches line 120,
while `' '.repeat(16000) + 'x'` arrives as `'x'`.

**Evidence:** middleware mounted on a bare `http.createServer` (Node v24.22.2, deps installed
from package.json):

| header value | server CPU |
|---|---|
| `DELETE` | 0.03 ms |
| `x` + 2 000 spaces + `y` | ~9 ms |
| + 8 000 spaces | ~150 ms |
| + 16 000 spaces | ~650–750 ms |
| control server, same bytes, no middleware | ~2–4 ms |

Client latency tracked server CPU (715 ms vs 650 ms), and a benign request issued 50 ms after
the attack request waited 604 ms behind it (control: 5 ms), confirming the burn is synchronous
event-loop blocking rather than I/O. In isolation,
`('x' + ' '.repeat(16300) + 'y').split(/ *, */)` costs 742 ms of CPU, against 0.016 ms for the
`indexOf(',')` + `substr` + `trim` shape. The repo's 19-test suite passes; nothing covers long
header values.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated client spends one ~16 KB POST to buy ~0.7 s of the only event
loop thread — about a 20 000× amplification over a normal `DELETE` override request — and
stalls every other client of the process while it runs. Repeat requests, or a few concurrent
ones, degrade or deny service for all users. This is CVE-2017-16136; this file is byte-identical
to the 2.3.9 release, and upstream fixed it in 2.3.10 (HISTORY.md: "perf: skip unnecessary
parsing of entire header"). Graded high: unauthenticated actor crossing a trust boundary,
broad reach, recoverable persistence, reproduced end to end.

**Fix:** stop running a backtracking regex over the header. Restore the upstream 2.3.10 shape,
which also keeps the first-value semantics the existing tests assert:

```js
var header = req.headers[name]
if (!header) {
  return undefined
}
var index = header.indexOf(',')
return index !== -1
  ? header.substr(0, index).trim()
  : header.trim()
```

findings.title: Query-string getter throws an uncaught ERR_INVALID_URL on a malformed absolute request-target
findings.body:
The query-string getter reads the request URL through `parseurl` and then dereferences
`url.query` without any guard (`index.js:100-106`):

```js
var url = parseurl(req)
var query = querystring.parse(url.query || '')
```

`parseurl` only fast-paths targets starting with `/`; anything else falls through to the legacy
`url.parse`, which throws `ERR_INVALID_URL` when the host does not parse. Request line
`POST http://[::1 HTTP/1.1` (absolute-form targets are legal and reach the app) does it. The
throw happens inside the getter, called at `index.js:68`, and nothing in the middleware
catches it.

**Preconditions:** the app is configured with a query-string getter, for example the README's
`methodOverride('_method')`, and the request method is in `options.methods` (POST by default).
The default header getter never touches `parseurl` and is not affected.

**Evidence:** with the repo's dependencies installed,
`parseurl({ url: 'http://[::1' })` throws `ERR_INVALID_URL` (Node v24.22.2; `url.parse` throws
the same). A probe run of the middleware on a bare `http.createServer` with a query getter exited
with code 1 on that single request, stack `parseurl → index.js:102 → index.js:68`.

**Impact:** low. It needs a non-default getter configuration, and under Express/connect the
throw becomes a 500 for that one request rather than a crash; the process-wide crash applies to
apps mounting the middleware on a bare `http` server, and many deployments reject malformed
request targets at the proxy first. The failure is a missing input-validation guard rather than
a cross-tenant or data-loss issue. Node already warns that `url.parse` will throw for such URLs
by default in a future release, so the same path becomes easier to hit over time.

**Fix:** keep malformed request targets from escaping the middleware — treat an unparseable URL
as "no override" (call `next()` with no value), e.g. wrap the getter call at `index.js:68` in
try/catch or guard `parseurl`'s result before reading `.query`.

summary:
Review complete. Verification notes and recorded finding below.

**Delegation used:** one probe over the new file (ranked hypotheses on formatter coverage, env-var handling, init/require order); I independently reproduced the highest-ranked one and smoke-tested integration myself.

**Assessment:** PR #2 adds `src/node.js`, the Node.js backend of `debug()` that `src/index.js:9` already expected — the baseline tree was missing it, so nothing on the Node path could load. The file is byte-identical to upstream `debug` 3.0.0 (`diff` against the npm tarball is empty), and it wires up correctly: module-level `exports.enable(load())`, the `init()` hook that `src/debug.js:125-127` calls, `formatArgs`, `log`, ink colours and `%o`/`%O` all behave as `README.md` and the smoke tests expect (`%j` falls through to `util.format`, which handles JSON and `[Circular]`). The one real defect is the whitespace-collapsing regex in `formatters.o`, which is CVE-2017-16137 (quadratic backtracking: a 400 KB whitespace-heavy object blocked the loop for 38 s here, 20 ms with the 3.1.0 algorithm); the rest of the change is a faithful port with no behavioural regressions found.

findings.title: `%o` formatter blocks the event loop on whitespace-heavy input
findings.body:
The new Node backend collapses multi-line `util.inspect()` output with
`.replace(/\s*\n\s*/g, ' ')` (`src/node.js:86`). When the inspected text contains a
run of whitespace that is not followed by a newline — i.e. any user string of spaces,
tabs or NBSP — the regex restarts at every offset in the run and backtracks one
character at a time to look for `\n`. Cost grows with the square of the run length, so
`debug('%o', untrustedInput)` blocks the whole Node process for seconds to minutes.

**Preconditions:** the consuming application logs untrusted input with the `%o`
formatter from the documented formatter set (`README.md:168`, example at
`README.md:29`), and that namespace is enabled. `%O` and `%s`/`%d` are not affected,
and a string argument alone is capped by `util.inspect`'s default `maxStringLength`
of 10000, but a nested array or object of whitespace strings is not.

**Evidence:** `src/debug.js:95-107` dispatches `%o` to
`exports.formatters.o` (`src/node.js:83-87`), whose only transformation is that
regex. Measured with this checkout (`node_modules/ms` only, `debug.log` stubbed so
only formatting runs):

- `' '.repeat(10000)` → 596 ms
- 5 array elements of 10000 spaces → 6.6 s
- object with 10 keys of 10000 spaces → 15.3 s
- object with 40 keys of 10000 spaces (≈400 KB of input) → 38.1 s

Replacing the regex with `split('\n').map(str => str.trim()).join(' ')` — what
upstream debug 3.1.0 does — runs the same 10-key case in 20 ms. Repro:

```
node -e "var d=require('./src/node.js');d.enable('x');var o={};for(var i=0;i<40;i++)o['k'+i]=' '.repeat(10000);d('x')('%o',o)"
```

**Impact:** denial of service limited to availability: one crafted request (a JSON
body of whitespace-only strings, a long query value `%20%20%20…`) that reaches a
`%o` log call stalls every request the process is serving, and the attacker can
repeat it. Reach is broad for the affected service and persistence is recoverable
(re-triggerable at will), which the policy would put at medium; I drop one tier
because the damage needs the consuming app to pass untrusted data to `%o` and the
namespace to be enabled, so I file `low`. This is CVE-2017-16137; upstream fixed it
in debug 3.1.0.

**Fix:** restore the invariant "flatten `util.inspect` output in linear time" by
dropping the backtracking regex, e.g.
`util.inspect(v, this.inspectOpts).split('\n').map(function (s) { return s.trim(); }).join(' ')`.

summary:
Recorded. Final summary:

**What the change does:** PR #1 re-adds `src/decorators/Link/index.js` (79 lines), the DraftJS decorator that renders LINK entities and now routes the entity URL through `ensureSafeUrl` for both `href` (`src/decorators/Link/index.js:60`) and the hover "open link" action (`:36`) — the javascript:-URL XSS fix. The added content is byte-identical to upstream master's post-fix file.

**Assessment:** The decorator logic itself is unchanged, battle-tested upstream code and nothing downstream regresses, but the PR ships only the consumer of the sanitizer. `src/utils/url.js` is absent from the tree, and because `src/Editor/index.js:30` imports the decorator unconditionally, the whole package fails to build and to load — one medium finding filed. Adding the util (upstream's normalization plus scheme allowlist) restores everything.

findings.title: Link decorator imports missing src/utils/url, so the editor no longer builds or loads
findings.body:
The new Link decorator imports a helper that does not exist. `src/decorators/Link/index.js:3` does
`import { ensureSafeUrl } from '../../utils/url'`, but `src/utils/` holds only `BlockStyle.js`,
`common.js`, `handlePaste.js` and `toolbar.js`. Nothing in the tree defines `ensureSafeUrl`: the
committed `dist/react-draft-wysiwyg.js` (1.14.5) has no occurrence of it, and a grep for the name
outside the new file returns nothing. Once this file lands, the module graph cannot be resolved, so
the library neither builds nor imports.

**Evidence:**

- `src/decorators/Link/index.js:3` imports `../../utils/url`; `ls src/utils` shows no `url.js`,
  `url/index.js` or `url.json`.
- Resolution fails the way webpack and `@babel/register` do it:
  `require.resolve('./src/utils/url')` → `MODULE_NOT_FOUND: Cannot find module './src/utils/url'`.
  `config/webpack.config.js` sets only `resolve.extensions: ['.js', '.json']` and no alias or
  fallback, so `npm run build` stops with `Can't resolve '../../utils/url'`.
- The failure is global, not local to links: `src/Editor/index.js:30` imports
  `'../decorators/Link'` unconditionally, `src/Editor/index.js:209` always builds the decorator, and
  `src/index.js` exports `Editor`. Any import of the package source (or of `src/index.js`) dies at
  load.
- The test suite is red for the same reason: `src/decorators/Link/__test__/linkDecoratorTest.js:7`
  imports `'..'`, which now loads a module whose dependency is missing.
- Upstream master ships `src/utils/url.js` with `ensureSafeUrl` alongside this exact decorator file,
  so this PR adds only the consumer of the helper and omits the helper itself.

**Impact:** This commit is the javascript-URL XSS fix, and it cannot produce a working artifact:
every source build and every test run fails, and the published `dist` stays at the vulnerable
1.14.5 bundle. Reach is broad (all consumers of the source build and the whole test suite);
persistence is recoverable (adding the missing module restores it), so medium.

**Fix:** Add `src/utils/url.js` to this PR, exporting `ensureSafeUrl`, with upstream's behaviour:
normalize the value by stripping control and whitespace characters (`\u0000-\u0020`, NBSP and the
Unicode space range), then allow only `http`, `https`, `ftp`, `ftps`, `mailto`, or a value that is
relative/does not start with a scheme; return `'#'` otherwise. Keep the decorator unchanged. As a
guard against this class of break, importing `src/index.js` in a trivial smoke test would have
caught it.

summary:
Recorded findings. Closing summary:

**Summary.** The PR adds `src/node.js`, the Node.js backend for `debug` (colours, `%o`/`%O` inspect formatters, stderr logging, `DEBUG_*` env options, `DEBUG` persistence), which `src/index.js` already required — before this change `require('debug')` under Node threw. The added file is the upstream implementation with the CVE-2017-16137 quadratic regexp already replaced by a linear `split('\n').map(trim).join(' ')` (`src/node.js:83-89`; I diffed it against the npm 3.0.1 and 3.1.0 tarballs and against upstream commit `c38a016`, which is byte-identical), so the ReDoS is not reintroduced and no vulnerable `\s*\n\s*` regexp remains anywhere in `src/`. The Node test suite passes 4/4 and eslint is clean; the only defect I filed is cosmetic (unreachable 256-colour palette). Overall: the change is sound and the security-relevant formatter is correct.

**Not reached / next run should start here:**
- Browser/karma/PhantomJS suite and `make test-node` (istanbul + coveralls) were never run — `npm install` hangs on the phantomjs postinstall and needed `--ignore-scripts`.
- No real TTY was available, so true `tty.isatty` and the 256-colour path were exercised only via `DEBUG_COLORS=1`.
- The probe flagged but I did not verify: catastrophic backtracking via `*` wildcards in `debug.enable()`/`DEBUG` (`src/debug.js:164-168`) against a long namespace, and the `util.inspect` throw path when a `DEBUG_*` key names a function-typed option (e.g. `DEBUG_STYLIZE=1`). Both are inherited from unchanged `src/debug.js` / upstream behaviour rather than added by this PR, and need a pre-existing-issue judgement before filing.

summary:
Recorded three findings. Final assessment:

## Summary

The PR adds `src/renderer.js`, the Headless Chrome rendering core behind `/render/:url(*)` and `/screenshot/:url(*)`: it drives the page over CDP, applies a virtual-time budget with a 10 s hard limit, forwards server and `render:status_code` meta statuses, and either serialises the DOM or captures a JPEG. The implementation is recognisable upstream rendertron code (identical to the version at the fix commit apart from one cosmetic line), and the page-lifecycle logic reads correctly; the defects are in resource lifetime and input handling.

The costliest is that teardown (`CDP.Close`) exists only on the success path, so every failed render orphans a Chrome target and its CDP socket — an unauthenticated caller can repeat a request that returns 400 and exhaust the browser. Two contributions compound it: an async function used as a `Promise` executor means a CDP failure before the `try` leaves the request promise pending forever while feeding the restart counter in `src/main.js`, and the render URL is interpolated unquoted into the injected `<base>` expression.

Out of scope for this diff but worth a follow-up: `src/main.js` was not touched here and still serves `/node_modules` statically (absolute-path disclosure via package.json `_where` — the CVE-2017-18355 class) and passes any URL scheme, including `file://`, to the navigation sink without a protocol check.

findings.title: Failed renders leak a Chrome tab and CDP socket, letting callers exhaust the browser
findings.body:
Every render that ends in the error path leaves its Chrome tab open. An
unauthenticated caller can repeat that, so the browser accumulates targets and CDP
sockets until it runs out of memory and all rendering fails.

**Evidence:** both teardown calls sit on the success path only —
`CDP.Close({id: client.target.id, port: config.port})` at src/renderer.js:190
(serialize) and src/renderer.js:220 (captureScreenshot) — immediately before
`resolve`. The `catch` blocks at src/renderer.js:194-196 and 222-224 only call
`reject(error)`; the tab created at src/renderer.js:178 / 202 is never closed, and
the CDP client at src/renderer.js:179 / 203 is never closed either (no
`client.close()` anywhere in the repo). Nothing else frees a target: `CDP.Close`
appears in exactly those two places, and src/main.js:136 (`/_ah/stop`) kills the
whole browser.

The failure path is deterministic, not a race. `GET /render/http://unknown.blah.com`
makes `Network.loadingFailed` fire for the initial request, which rejects at
src/renderer.js:95-98; test/app-test.js:142-146 pins that request as returning 400,
so the path is exercised. The same leak happens for `Page.navigate` rejection
(src/renderer.js:74), for a failed `Runtime.evaluate` (186-189), for
`Page.captureScreenshot` failure (218), and for the rejected awaits before the try
block (see the companion finding). The 10 s timer at src/renderer.js:139-145 also
stays armed on those paths, holding the event loop for an abandoned tab.

**Impact:** reach is broad — the leaked tabs belong to the single browser process
that serves every user, and the trigger is an unauthenticated GET that returns 400
each time. Persistence is recoverable: restarting the process drops the leaked
targets. Broad + recoverable is medium; the kill-after-6-unhandled-rejections
restart in src/main.js:164-181 does not bound this leak, it just converts it into
outages.

**Fix:** release the target on every path. Move teardown into a `finally` that
awaits `CDP.Close` (and `client.close()`), so failures before the `try` are covered
too.

findings.title: A failing CDP call before the try block leaves the render promise pending, so the request never responds
findings.body:
If a CDP call made before the `try` block fails, the promise the caller awaits is
never settled: the HTTP response is never written and the socket stays open. The
same rejection is unhandled, so it also counts toward the restart counter in
src/main.js, which kills the process after six events.

**Evidence:** `serialize` returns `new Promise(async(resolve, reject) => {...})`
(src/renderer.js:177). The Promise constructor ignores the executor's return value,
so when the async executor rejects, only its own discarded promise is rejected —
`resolve`/`reject` are never called and the outer promise stays pending forever.
The `await`s before the `try` are exactly those cases: `CDP.New` and the CDP connect
at src/renderer.js:178-179, and likewise 202-203 plus
`Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`/`setVisibleSize` at 213-214. `_loadPage` has
the same shape at src/renderer.js:42 with its `Promise.all` at 45-51 outside any
`try`.

Reproduced the language semantics with node 24:

```
function f() { return new Promise(async (resolve, reject) => { await Promise.reject(new Error('boom')); resolve('never'); }); }
f(); // -> prints "unhandledRejection: boom"; the outer promise never settles
```

`CDP.New` rejects when the `/json/new` request fails (chrome-remote-interface
0.24.2, lib/devtools.js), e.g. after Chrome dies or during a restart. The consumer
awaits with no timeout: src/main.js:99 `await renderer.serialize(...)` — its
`catch` at 102-107 never runs, so no response is sent; the screenshot route's
`.catch` at src/main.js:118 cannot fire either. Then
src/main.js:180 `process.on('unhandledRejection', logUncaughtError)` increments
`exceptionCount` and, above 5, kills Chrome and calls `process.exit(1)`
(src/main.js:168-175).

I could not verify from this checkout whether Chrome rejects
`setDeviceMetricsOverride` for `?width=-1` (which reaches the call unvalidated:
`parseInt('-1') || 1000` is -1 and `Math.min(2000, -1)` is -1, src/renderer.js:211-213),
so the screenshot route may be an attacker-triggerable entry into this path; the
browser-failure path above is certain.

**Impact:** a request that should have produced a 400 instead holds a client socket
with no response, and each occurrence advances the process toward shutdown — the
leak in the companion finding makes browser-level failures likely, so the two
compound. Reach is broad, persistence transient (a restarted process clears it), and
the trigger is not proven attacker-controlled, so: low.

**Fix:** do not run an async function as a Promise executor. Make the awaits part of
the `try` (or wrap the body in `Promise.resolve().then(async () => ...)`), so every
failure reaches `reject` and the route's error handling and any future timeout apply.

findings.title: A quote in the render URL injects code into the page instead of setting the base tag
findings.body:
The render URL is pasted into a JavaScript expression without quoting, so a URL that
contains a single quote runs attacker-supplied code inside the rendered page instead
of setting the `<base>` tag. URLs that merely contain an apostrophe silently lose
their base tag.

**Preconditions:** the `<base>` injection only runs when the fetch succeeds, which is
the normal path.

**Evidence:** src/renderer.js:187 evaluates
`` `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})('${url}')` ``. `url` is
`request.params.url` (src/main.js:91, 99), which Express percent-decodes, so `%27`
arrives as `'`. Payload
`http://attacker.tld/');<code>;//` compiles to
`(function injectBaseHref(url){...})('http://attacker.tld/');<code>;//')` and runs
after `stripPage` (src/renderer.js:186) and before the page is serialised
(src/renderer.js:189). Checked with node:

```
function expr(url) { return `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})('${url}')`; }
new Function(expr("http://attacker.tld/');console.log('ran');//"))();   // runs
new Function(expr("http://example.com/it's-a-post"));                    // SyntaxError: missing ) after argument list
```

`Runtime.evaluate` resolves with `exceptionDetails` for a syntax error rather than
rejecting, and the result of that call is not inspected, so the benign case just
continues without a base tag.

**Impact:** the code runs in the page being rendered, and the resulting DOM is what
the caller receives, so a direct caller mainly harms their own response. The
meaningful cases are a deployment that sets `renderOnly` — `isRestricted` only
prefix-checks (src/main.js:66-73), so `https://allowed.example/');...` passes the
allow-list and gets script execution in an origin the operator meant to restrict —
and legitimate URLs with apostrophes (common in blog and wiki paths) losing their
base href. Contained and recoverable: low.

**Fix:** pass the URL as data, not source: `Runtime.callFunctionOn` with the URL in
`arguments`, or interpolate `JSON.stringify(url)`.

summary:
The PR adds a single file, `index.js`, restoring the upstream `decamelize` implementation (10 lines: a type check, a default separator, and two chained `replace` calls). I reproduced its behavior directly: all seven existing `test.js` assertions pass, and the string logic is correct for ordinary separators.

The defect is in `index.js:8`, where `sep` is concatenated into `new RegExp(...)` instead of being matched literally — the subject of CVE-2017-16023. I confirmed three distinct consequences (exponential backtracking, `SyntaxError` throws, silently wrong output) and recorded them as one medium finding, plus an informational finding for `$`-pattern expansion in the replacement strings at `index.js:7-8`. A fixed, metacharacter-free separator such as the default `_` is unaffected, so the change is fine for that common case but unsafe whenever the separator can come from outside the program.

findings.title: Caller-supplied separator is compiled as a regex, so crafted separators block the event loop or throw
findings.body:
The separator argument is concatenated into regular-expression source at index.js:8, so it is
compiled as a pattern instead of being matched literally. A caller that passes a separator
string through from outside the program hands regex syntax to the engine.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this commit.

1. Catastrophic backtracking. `sep = '(a*)*'` builds `/((a*)*[A-Z])([A-Z])/g`. Time grows
   exponentially with input length (`'a'.repeat(n)`):

   ```
   18 ->     19ms
   20 ->     80ms
   22 ->    388ms
   24 ->   1259ms
   26 ->   5308ms
   28 ->  19182ms
   ```

   Node runs the regex on the single main thread, so the whole process — every request it
   serves — is blocked while it runs.

2. Uncaught `SyntaxError` instead of a string. `sep = '('` builds `/(([A-Z])([A-Z])/g`:
   `SyntaxError: Unterminated group`. Same for `'*'` (`Nothing to repeat`), `'+'`, `'?'`.

3. Silent wrong output. `decamelize('thisIsATest', '|')` returns `'this||is||a|test'`; the
   expected result is `'this|is|a|test'`. `sep = '['` returns `'this[[is[[atest'`.

**Impact:** If a service forwards a user-chosen separator (for example a "format keys with
this separator" API option), an unprivileged remote caller can block or crash the process;
reach is broad (all traffic handled by that process) and the effect is recoverable by
restart, so medium. A fixed, metacharacter-free separator such as the default `_` is safe,
which is why this is not rated higher.

**Fix:** Do not build the pattern from `sep`. Either use a literal pattern, as upstream did
(`.replace(/([A-Z]+)([A-Z][a-z\d]+)/g, ...)`), or escape the separator first:
`const s = sep.replace(/[\\^$.*+?()[\]{}|]/g, '\\$&')` and interpolate `s`.

findings.title: $ patterns in the separator are expanded in the replacement string instead of being inserted literally
findings.body:
The separator is also concatenated into the replacement strings at index.js:7-8, where
`$&`, `$1`, `` $` `` and `$'` are replacement patterns rather than literal text.

**Evidence:** `require('./')('thisIsATest', '$&')` returns `'thissiissaatest'`; the expected
result is `'this$&is$&a$&test'`. The separator disappears and matched text is substituted for
it.

**Impact:** Silent wrong output, contained to the caller that chose the separator, and only
for separators containing `$`-patterns. Informational.

**Fix:** Insert a literal separator in the replacement too, for example by using a function
replacer (`(m, p1, p2) => p1 + sep + p2`) in both `replace` calls.

summary:
Coverage is complete for a 16-line, single-file change. Recording is done; here's the wrap-up.

**What the change does:** it adds `index.js` at the upstream commit that fixed CVE-2017-16023 — the separator is now passed through `escape-string-regexp` before being used as regex source, so a caller-supplied separator like `(` or `(A+)+` is treated literally instead of injecting into the pattern. I confirmed that fix works (`decamelize('aB','(')` returns `a(b`; the pre-fix form throws `SyntaxError`).

**Assessment:** the fix itself is correct, but the PR imports the new dependency without declaring it — a fresh `npm install` of the package leaves `require('decamelize')` throwing `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at `index.js:2`, so the package is unusable on a clean tree. I also confirmed two separator-literalness defects (raw `sep` in one replacement string, regex-escaped `reSep` in the other) that corrupt output for `$`-style and metacharacter separators. Both are recorded as findings; beyond those, the file matches upstream and the rest of the change is sound.

findings.title: Clean install cannot load the package: escape-string-regexp is required but not declared
findings.body:
The package cannot be loaded at all. `index.js:2` requires `escape-string-regexp` at
module load time, but `package.json` (untouched by this PR) still has no
`dependencies` block, so npm installs nothing for it. `require('decamelize')` throws
`MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, so every consumer fails before making a single call, and the
repo's own `npm test` (`xo && ava`, which imports `./`) fails too.

**Evidence:** A real install of the packed tarball installs only the package itself:

```
$ npm pack                                   # decamelize-1.1.1.tgz
$ mkdir /tmp/app && cd /tmp/app && npm install .../decamelize-1.1.1.tgz
added 1 package in 2s
$ ls node_modules
decamelize
$ node -e "require('decamelize')"
Error: Cannot find module 'escape-string-regexp'
    at Object.<anonymous> (/tmp/app/node_modules/decamelize/index.js:2:26)
```

The file is byte-identical to upstream commit 76d47d8, which added
`"dependencies": {"escape-string-regexp": "^1.0.4"}` to `package.json` in the same
commit. This PR brings only `index.js`, so the dependency half of that change is
missing.

**Impact:** Broad reach — every fresh install of the published package is unusable
and throws on load. Recoverable, which keeps it at medium: the module works as soon
as `escape-string-regexp` happens to be hoisted by another dependency or the
consumer installs it by hand. That also makes the failure erratic — it passes
locally where the hoisted copy exists and breaks in a clean tree.

**Fix:** Add the dependency the new `require` needs:
`"dependencies": {"escape-string-regexp": "^1.0.4"}` in `package.json` (or drop the
dependency by inlining the escape). Verify with a clean-room install, not the
existing `node_modules`.

findings.title: Separators with `$` patterns or regex metacharacters are not inserted literally
findings.body:
The separator is not inserted literally when it contains `$` replacement patterns or
regex metacharacters, so `decamelize(str, sep)` returns a corrupted string for such
separators.

Two lines build replacement strings by string concatenation:

- `index.js:13` — `'$1' + sep + '$2'` inserts the raw separator into a replacement
  string, where `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$n` are special. Separators such as
  `$` or `$&` are expanded or swallowed.
- `index.js:14` — `'$1' + reSep + '$2'` uses `reSep`, the regex-escaped form, in the
  replacement string. Escaping is only appropriate in the pattern, so a separator
  like `.` or `|` gains a stray backslash in the output.

**Evidence:** With `escape-string-regexp@1.0.5` present, running the added file:

```
decamelize('aB', '$')            => 'a$2'        expected 'a$b'
decamelize('unicornRainbow','$&')=> 'unicornnrrainbow'  expected 'unicorn$&rainbow'
decamelize('fooBarBaz','$1')     => 'fooobarrbaz'       expected 'foo$1bar$1baz'
decamelize('A.BCC', '.')         => 'a.b\\.cc'    expected 'a.b.cc'
decamelize('A|BCC', '|')         => 'a|b\\|cc'    expected 'a|b|cc'
```

The metacharacter case fires in the second `replace` (index.js:14), whenever the
input already contains `sep` followed by two capitals; the `$` case fires in the
first `replace` on any camelCase input.

**Impact:** Low. Output is silently wrong, but only for callers that pass such a
separator — the caller supplies `sep`, so no trust boundary is crossed and other
calls are unaffected. Upstream fixed the `$` half in v6 (commit d8f982a).

**Fix:** Keep the escaped form only in the pattern and build both replacements from
the literal separator, ideally with function replacers so no `$` expansion happens:

```js
.replace(/([a-z\d])([A-Z])/g, (m, a, b) => a + sep + b)
.replace(new RegExp('(' + reSep + '[A-Z])([A-Z])', 'g'), (m, a, b) => a + sep + b)
```

summary:
Recorded two findings. Summary:

This PR adds `index.js`, the published entry point of `apex-publish-static-files` 2.0.0: it validates six caller options and runs SQLcl through a single `execSync` command string. The file is the whole change, so its risk is entirely in how those options reach the shell.

The core problem is that none of the options are escaped — three are unquoted and three only wrapped in double quotes — so any value containing shell syntax executes as a command; I reproduced this with four distinct payloads (`connectString`, `appID`, `pluginName`, and the same shape applies to `sqlclPath`/`directory`). That is the vulnerability tracked as CVE-2018-16462 and it dominates the review. There is a smaller, separate disclosure path in the failure handler, which prints the full command including the database password: an independent probe of the rest of the file surfaced only design/robustness gaps (false success on per-file SQL errors, `maxBuffer`, `destination` typos) that I judged below the reporting bar. Overall: do not merge as is; switching to `execFileSync` with an argument array fixes the injection and is a small change.

findings.title: Unescaped publish() options are interpolated into a shell command, so any value can execute commands
findings.body:
`publish()` builds a single shell command out of `sqlclPath`, `connectString`, `appID`,
`destination`, `pluginName` and `directory`, then runs it with `execSync`
(`index.js:54-66`). `execSync` hands the string to `/bin/sh -c`, so any shell
metacharacter in any of those values runs as a command with the privileges of the
process calling `publish()`. Three of the six values (`sqlclPath`, `connectString`,
`appID`) are not quoted at all; the other three (`directory`, `destination`,
`pluginName`) are wrapped in double quotes, which a `"` in the value breaks out of.
The library validates that these options *exist* (`index.js:18-32`) but never
neutralises their content.

Values are not attacker-controlled by construction: `appID` may be an APEX
application alias taken from a URL (the sibling helper `lib/util.js:5-8` exists to
parse app IDs out of `f?p=` URLs), and `connectString`/`pluginName` commonly arrive
from config files, environment variables or CI parameters.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes a value for one of the six options that contains
shell syntax. No non-default setting is needed.

**Evidence:** all four payloads below were run against this tree and each one
executed a command before SQLcl was ever started.

```js
const p = require('./index.js');
// 1. connectString, unquoted
p.publish({connectString: 'dev/dev@h:1521/orcl; touch /tmp/pwned2 #',
           directory: './demo/demo-working', appID: 101});          // /tmp/pwned2 created
// 2. appID, unquoted (aliases are strings, so this is a normal shape)
p.publish({connectString: 'dev/dev@h/orcl', directory: './demo/demo-working',
           appID: '101 $(touch /tmp/pwned3)'});                     // /tmp/pwned3 created
// 3. pluginName, quote breakout from the "..." wrapper
p.publish({connectString: 'dev/dev@h/orcl', directory: './demo/demo-working',
           appID: 101, destination: 'plugin',
           pluginName: 'X"; touch /tmp/pwned4; echo "'});            // /tmp/pwned4 created
// 4. sqlclPath and directory behave the same way.
```

The same string is also what SQLcl never gets to run, because the injected command
runs first and the rest of the line is shell syntax.

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution in the publishing process — build server, CI
runner or desktop — whenever a value from outside the calling code reaches these
options. A publisher who builds an `appID` from a request URL hands command execution
to whoever controls the URL. Reach: crosses a trust boundary (an input the caller
believes is data becomes capability). Persistence: permanent (the attacker chooses
files to write or read; nothing in the library undoes it). That is `high` under the
default policy; no repository instruction defines `critical`.

**Fix:** restore the invariant "option values are data, never shell syntax" by
dropping the shell. `child_process.execFileSync(opts.sqlclPath, [...args], {encoding:
'utf8'})` with one array element per argument removes the parsing step entirely, so
no quoting is needed:

```js
execFileSync(opts.sqlclPath, [
  opts.connectString,
  '@' + path.resolve(__dirname, 'lib/script'),
  path.resolve(__dirname, 'lib/distUpload.js'),
  path.resolve(opts.directory),
  String(opts.appID),
  opts.destination,
  String(opts.pluginName)
], {encoding: 'utf8'});
```

If `execSync` must stay, escape every interpolated value with a single-quote shell
escaper (`'` → `'\''`) and wrap each in single quotes — including `connectString`,
which cannot be safely double-quoted.

findings.title: Failed publishes write the database password into the log
findings.body:
When the SQLcl command fails, `publish()` reports the failure with
`console.error(err)` (`index.js:74`). Node's `execSync` puts the entire command string
into `err.message` (`Command failed: <cmd>`), and that string embeds
`opts.connectString` verbatim (`index.js:56`), which by the README's own format is
`user/pass@server:port/sid`. Every failed publish therefore writes the database
password in clear text to stdout/stderr — CI logs, build artifacts, terminal scrollback.

**Evidence:** run against this tree with the default `sqlclPath` absent:

```
$ node -e "require('./index.js').publish({connectString:'dev/SuperSecret@localhost:1521/orcl',
                                          directory:'./demo/demo-working', appID:101})"
Error: Command failed: "sql" dev/SuperSecret@localhost:1521/orcl @".../lib/script" ...
```

Any failure path does this: wrong `sqlclPath`, SQLcl not installed, network error,
bad credentials, `maxBuffer` overflow on a large directory.

**Impact:** the credential the publisher was protecting is disclosed to anyone who can
read the build log, which is usually a wider audience than the database itself. The
library performs the disclosure itself, on a path a caller cannot intercept. Reach is
limited by who can read the log (a trust boundary, but one outside the library) and no
supported action un-leaks a log line once it is written, so this is `low`: it needs an
action outside the system (access to the log store) and the leaking process already
holds the secret.

**Fix:** log a redacted failure instead of the raw error — e.g.
`'SQLcl upload failed'` plus `err.status`/`err.stderr` only, or strip the substring
between the first `/` and `@` in the command text before printing. Do not pass `err`
itself to the logger.

summary:
Reviewed the change and reproduced the core issue. Summary:

The PR restores `index.js` for `mixin-deep` at the 2.0.0 tree, i.e. the deep-mixin implementation as it stood before the CVE-2019-10746 fix. It is a small, self-contained file whose only hardening is a literal `__proto__` key check in the merge loop, and the surrounding recursion still lets a source key walk into inherited prototype objects. I verified the consequence by running the module against a JSON payload, and recorded one high-severity finding; nothing else in the 34 added lines showed a concrete failure path.

findings.title: A crafted constructor.prototype key pollutes Object.prototype despite the __proto__ guard
findings.body:
`mixinDeep` only rejects the literal `__proto__` key. A merged object that carries a
`constructor` key still reaches `Object.prototype` through the recursion, so an
attacker-controlled object merged into any plain-object target adds arbitrary
properties to every object in the process.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes attacker-influenced data as one of the source
arguments, and the target has (or gains) a matching object property. This is the
normal use of the library: merging config, request bodies or defaults.

**Evidence:** `index.js:7` skips only `key !== '__proto__'`. For key `constructor`,
`index.js:17` reads the inherited `Object` function from the target, `isObject`
(`index.js:26`) accepts it as a function, and `index.js:19` recurses with `Object` as
the new target. The next key `prototype` resolves to `Object.prototype`, and
`index.js:21` writes onto it.

```
$ node -e "
const mixinDeep = require('./index.js');
const defaults = { db: { host: 'localhost' } };
const userConfig = JSON.parse('{\"db\":{\"constructor\":{\"prototype\":{\"isAdmin\":true}}}}');
mixinDeep(defaults, userConfig);
console.log(({}).isAdmin);"
true
```

`({}).isAdmin` is now `true` for all code in the process. `constructor.constructor`
reaches `Function.prototype` the same way.

**Impact:** a merge of untrusted input gives the attacker permanent, process-wide
control of object properties. Anything that reads a property without owning it —
authorization flags, `toString`/`valueOf` overrides, options objects — can be
influenced, which is a trust-boundary crossing for every consumer of the library. The
existing tests in `test.js` never exercise such keys.

**Fix:** reject the other keys that can walk to a prototype, not just `__proto__`:
treat `constructor` and `prototype` as invalid keys in the loop at `index.js:7`
(upstream 2.0.1 does this with a single `isValidKey` predicate). Restore the
invariant that no source key is ever used to reach a prototype object.

summary: Recorded. Summary of the review: **What the change does:** re-adds the DraftJS `Link` decorator (`src/decorators/Link/index.js`, 78 lines) — an entity strategy plus a component that renders `{children}` and a hover icon that calls `window.open(url, 'blank')`. **Assessment:** the wiring and lifecycle are sound for a draft-js decorator (the factory always receives a config from `getCompositeDecorator`, entity keys come from the content state, and the icon is a sibling of the anchor, so no double navigation). The defect is at the sink: the entity `url` is used verbatim with no scheme allowlist, and this is exactly the pre-fix code for CVE-2021-31712 — the published 1.14.6+ bundles wrap the same expression in a scheme-allowlist sanitizer, while this tree (and its committed `dist`) does not. One high finding recorded. I left two lower-value observations un-filed: `window.open(url, 'blank')` uses a non-reserved window name (so every link reuses one window), and links opened with `target="_blank"` carry no `rel="noopener noreferrer"`. The default target is `_self` (`src/config/defaultToolbar.js:180`) and modern browsers imply noopener for `_blank`, so both sit at info level and would be fixed by the same URL-sanitizing change, not separately.

findings.title: Link decorator puts an unvalidated entity URL into href, so javascript: links run script in the host page
findings.body: The new Link decorator writes a LINK entity's `url` straight into the anchor and into `window.open`, with no scheme check. A `javascript:` (or `data:`) URL therefore executes in the host page's origin when a viewer clicks the link or the hover "open link" icon. **Preconditions:** content reaches the editor from a source the viewer does not control, and the viewer clicks a link. Recorded: `fnd_34031706bb573e9e` [high].

**Summary:** PR #1 adds `lib/dialects/mssql/index.js`, the missing MSSQL client, which restores the MSSQL dialect (baseline could not even `require` it). The file is byte-identical to the upstream knex 0.19.4 client, so reviewing it means reviewing the dialect's own internals: connection/pool handling, binding positioning, `_query`/`_stream`, type inference, and response processing. I reproduced the one substantive defect in that code — identifier wrapping that never escapes `]`, which lets a `]` in a column, table or alias name break out into compiled SQL (`select [name] FROM [users] --]`), matching upstream CVE-2019-10757 fixed in 0.19.5. The remaining leads from probing that surface (stream-error hangs, inner `max: 1` pool, first-recordset-only responses) are upstream design limits that I could not confirm without a live SQL Server, so I left them unreported. Overall the change is the vendor implementation of a dialect and should not merge with the identifier-escaping defect unfixed; with that corrected it is otherwise routine.

findings.title: MSSQL identifier wrapping lets a ] in a column or table name break out into SQL
findings.body:
The MSSQL client wraps identifiers in `[...]` but never neutralises `]` inside them, so a
`]` in a column, table or alias name closes the quote and the rest of the string is compiled
as SQL. This is the defect that upstream fixed in knex 0.19.5 (CVE-2019-10757).

**Preconditions:** the application puts attacker-influenced text in an identifier position —
`select()`, `orderBy()`, `from()`/`table()`, a column alias, `groupBy()` — which is the usual
shape of sort/filter parameters (`orderBy(req.query.sort)`).

**Evidence:**

- `lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:210` — `value.replace(/\[/g, '[')` replaces `[` with itself
  (a no-op), and `]` is never escaped, so `` `[${value}]` `` terminates at the first `]` in
  the value. Every other dialect doubles its quote character: `lib/client.js:216`,
  `lib/dialects/mysql/index.js:57`, `lib/dialects/sqlite3/index.js:60`,
  `lib/dialects/postgres/index.js:101`.
- All identifier text reaches this function: `Formatter#wrapString`/`wrapAsIdentifier`
  (`lib/formatter.js:273-292`, `189-192`) → `Client#wrapIdentifier` (`lib/client.js:200-206`)
  → `wrapIdentifierImpl`. Values, by contrast, go to bindings
  (`lib/formatter.js:123-128`), so nothing else protects these strings.
- Reproduced against this checkout (mssql client, no server needed to see the compiled SQL):

  ```
  knex('users').select('name').orderBy("id] FROM [users] WHERE 1=1; SELECT password FROM [users] --")
  -> select [name] from [users] order by [id] FROM [users] WHERE 1=1; SELECT password FROM [users] --] asc

  knex('users').select('name] FROM [users] --')
  -> select [name] FROM [users] --] from [users]
  ```
  The same inputs on knex 0.19.5 stay inside one bracketed identifier.
- The compiled SQL is sent as a batch: `req.multiple = true` for both query and stream paths
  (`lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:272`, `:294`), so injected `;`-separated statements are not
  rejected by the driver.
- Upstream fix (verified by diffing the 0.19.4 and 0.19.5 npm tarballs) replaces this method
  with one that strips `[`, `]` and `'` from the identifier. NVD rates CVE-2019-10757
  CVSS 3.1 9.8 (`AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`).

**Impact:** an attacker who controls one identifier string runs arbitrary SQL with the
application's database credentials: read any table, modify or delete rows, and chain further
statements in the same batch. Reach crosses a trust boundary and the effect is permanent, so
severity is high (no repo-specific definition raises it to critical).

**Fix:** neutralise the bracket quote before wrapping, e.g.
`value.replace(/]/g, ']]')` (SQL Server's escape for `]` inside `[...]`), or adopt the
released form that removes `[`, `]` and `'`. Add a unit test asserting
`knex('t').select('a]b')` compiles to `select [a]]b] from [t]`; the existing escaping test
(`test/unit/query/builder.js:8033`) has no `[`/`]` input and cannot catch this.

summary: The change re-adds `index.js`, which drives the sqlcl upload: it validates arguments, pre-scans the directory, and replaces the old `execSync` shell string with `spawnSync(sqlclPath, argsArray)`. That removal of the shell is the security fix for the recorded command-injection CVE, and I confirmed it holds — `;`, `$()`, backtick and pipe payloads in `appID`, `connectString`, `pluginName` and `directory` reach sqlcl as literal argv elements and execute nothing. What the change gives up in the process is failure reporting: `spawnSync`'s `status`, `error` and `stderr` are ignored and the call always ends in a success message with an `undefined` return, so missing binaries, bad credentials, SQL errors and buffer-truncated uploads all look green (recorded). The rest of the file is straightforward and I found no other exploitable path; in particular the remaining SQL*Plus substitution surface in `lib/script.sql` could not be verified as command execution without a real SQLcl/Java runtime, so I left it unreported. Overall the fix is sound; only its error signalling should be restored before release.

findings.title: publish() reports a successful upload when sqlcl fails to start, exits with an error, or is killed by the output buffer
findings.body:
`publish()` prints `Files were uploaded successfully.` and returns `undefined` even when the
sqlcl child never ran, exited non-zero, or was killed because its output exceeded the
`spawnSync` buffer. A caller that trusts the call (a CI publish step, a build script) is told
the deploy worked when it did not happen or stopped partway.

**Preconditions:** none beyond normal use — any failing sqlcl invocation.

**Evidence:** `index.js:74-79` runs `spawnSync(...)`, then `index.js:81-82` logs `childProcess.stdout`
and the success line unconditionally. `status`, `error`, `signal` and `stderr` are never read, and
`publish()` has no `return`. `spawnSync` does not throw for these cases, so the `catch` at
`index.js:83-85` never fires.

Reproductions (Node v24, `directory: demo/demo-working`):

    # sqlcl missing -> spawnSync returns {error: ENOENT, status: null, stdout: undefined}
    publish({sqlclPath: '/nonexistent/sql', connectString: 'dev/dev@h:1/x', directory: ..., appID: 101})
    Uploading to 101 - Application Static Files...
    undefined
    Files were uploaded successfully.
    returned: undefined

    # sqlcl exiting non-zero (e.g. bad credentials) -> same output, still "success"
    publish({sqlclPath: '/bin/false', ...})   ->   "" then "Files were uploaded successfully."

Output is truncated at the per-stream `maxBuffer` default of 1 MiB (measured: 1048576 bytes
kept, over that `error.code === 'ENOBUFS'`, `status === null`, child `SIGTERM`ed). `lib/distUpload.js:110`
writes `Uploaded: <path>\n` per file, i.e. `11 + path.length` bytes, so roughly 4.6k files with
220-byte path lines overflow the buffer: sqlcl is killed mid-upload and the missing files are
reported as uploaded. Measured with 5200 files: truncation after 4614 files + the success line.

Contrary evidence checked: sqlcl's own stdout is echoed at `index.js:81`, so an ORA error that
sqlcl prints on stdout is visible to a human reading the log. That still gives a programmatic
caller (exit code, return value) no failure signal, and stderr is dropped entirely.

**Impact:** the failure is silent and the damage is a partial or absent static-file deploy that
the caller's pipeline records as green; re-running fixes it, so persistence is recoverable and
reach is one caller's upload job — `low`.

**Fix:** treat a non-zero `status`, a truthy `childProcess.error`, or a non-empty `stderr` as
failure: log `childProcess.stderr`, skip the success message, and return (or throw) a failure
value — restoring the `true`/`false` the previous implementation returned.

summary:
**Verdict: approve, no findings.**

The PR adds `index.js`, a 38-line dependency-free deep-merge helper, to a repo whose baseline has no implementation. The added file is byte-identical to the published `mixin-deep@2.0.1` release (`diff` clean), i.e. the official fix for CVE-2019-10746, and the repo's existing 15-test suite passes unchanged (`npx mocha`: 15 passing).

On the security question that matters here, I confirmed the fix is complete: `isValidKey` (index.js:7-9) rejects `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` at every recursion level, and arrays are excluded from recursion (index.js:4), so no attacker-reachable `target` in `mixin` (index.js:24-31) can ever be a builtin prototype object. An independent investigation enumerated ~18.6k key/depth/target combinations plus non-JSON sources (null-prototype objects, Proxies, getters, symbols, functions) and found no input that leaves a property on `Object.prototype`; the pre-fix ladder `constructor` → `prototype` that polluted `Object.prototype` in 2.0.0 is closed.

One non-blocking observation for follow-up, not filed as a finding because the behaviour is identical in upstream 2.0.0 and 2.0.1 and is unchanged by this fix: `mixin` reads `target[key]` without an own-property check (index.js:25), so a source key naming an inherited builtin member (`{"toString":{...}}`, `{"hasOwnProperty":{"call":...}}`) writes onto shared builtin function objects and can throw `TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'length'` — an own-property check on `target` would close that residual path.

The PR re-adds `src/renderer.js`, the headless-Chrome rendering backend that `src/main.js` already requires: it opens a tab per request, enables Page/Runtime/Network/Emulation, navigates to the caller's URL under a virtual-time budget with a 10 s hard limit, then serializes `outerHTML` or captures a JPEG. The file is functional, but it accepts whatever URL the `/render/:url(*)` route hands it and never releases the tab when a render fails.

I confirmed both of the top issues by running the app end to end against an era-appropriate Chromium: `file:///etc/passwd` and loopback-only services are returned in the response body, and six failed renders left six live Chrome targets plus six CDP sockets behind. I also reproduced the request that never answers when a CDP setup call rejects. The two lower findings (unescaped URL interpolation into `Runtime.evaluate`, and the async Promise executor swallowing setup errors) are grounded in the same code and verified mechanically. Not covered in depth: status-code forwarding from the page's meta tag and the page-spoofable `Rendering complete` signal.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read local files and internal services through /render
findings.body:
`_loadPage` hands the caller-supplied URL straight to `Page.navigate({url})` (src/renderer.js:75) with no scheme or host check. `/render/:url(*)` passes `request.params.url` through unchanged (src/main.js:91,99) and `isRestricted()` only restricts anything when `config['renderOnly']` is configured (src/main.js:65-74). The repo ships no `config.json`, so the default deployment restricts nothing: an unauthenticated caller can make the server read local files and reach loopback/internal services, and the serialized HTML with their content is returned. `/screenshot` goes through the same `_loadPage`. **Evidence:** app started from `src/main.js` (2017-era Chromium, no config.json), Chrome on 127.0.0.1:3000: ``` $ curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/render/file:///etc/passwd' | head -c 200 
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin

$ curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/render/file:///tmp/secretfile'

MARKER-9f3a2b local-file-secret

$ curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/render/http://127.0.0.1:8099/'
internal...
INTERNAL-ONLY-MARKER-4c1d


$ curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/render/http://127.0.0.1:37317/json/version'
{ "Browser": "HeadlessChrome/61.0.3162.0", ... }   # Chrome's own debug endpoint
```

The repository's own tests rely on `file://` renders working (test/app-test.js:117,124), so this is normal-operation behaviour, not an exotic configuration.

**Impact:** remote, unauthenticated read of every file the Chrome process can read (config, credentials, sources) and of services reachable from the host (loopback admin ports, Chrome's DevTools HTTP endpoints, internal network). This crosses a trust boundary and the leaked data cannot be un-leaked: high per the review severity table (reach: crosses a trust boundary; persistence: permanent).

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the renderer only navigates to remote http/https documents. Reject any other protocol before line 75, e.g. `if (!/^https?:/i.test(url)) throw new Error('Invalid URL');` (upstream applied this check in `isRestricted()` together with a `file url fails` test), and keep a host allow-list for internal addresses where the deployment needs it.

findings.title: Failed renders leak a Chrome tab and CDP socket per request
findings.body:
`serialize` and `captureScreenshot` close the Chrome tab only on the success path (`CDP.Close` at src/renderer.js:191 and src/renderer.js:221). The `catch` blocks (src/renderer.js:195-197, src/renderer.js:223-225) reject without closing the tab, and nothing in the file ever calls `client.close()`. The commonest rejection is a failed main-document request (`Network.loadingFailed`, src/renderer.js:96-101), i.e. every unresolvable or refused URL. Each such request permanently leaves a target, a CDP websocket and the renderer process behind.

**Evidence:** app running from `src/main.js`, repeated unauthenticated requests, target list read from the Chrome debug port:

```
targets BEFORE: 1
6 x GET /render/http://unknown.invalid.example/  -> 400 "... net::ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED", ~0.06 s each
targets AFTER:  7   (1 about:blank + 6 x "http://unknown.invalid.example/", still type=page)
established sockets to the Chrome debug port: 5 failed renders -> 6, 6 -> 7 (grows 1:1)
```

A successful render returns the count to 0, so the leak is specific to the error path. `captureScreenshot` has the same hole for a failing `_loadPage` or `Page.captureScreenshot`.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller leaks a tab, a socket and a Chrome child process per request and can exhaust the shared browser for every user of the service; recovery needs a restart. Reach broad, persistence recoverable: medium.

**Fix:** wrap the per-render work in `try/finally` in both methods and close the target (and `client`) in the `finally`, so a rejected render releases the same resources as a successful one.

findings.title: Request URL is pasted unescaped into Runtime.evaluate
findings.body:
src/renderer.js:188 builds a CDP expression by pasting the request URL into a JS string literal: `` `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})('${url}')` ``. `url` is the raw route parameter from `/render/:url(*)` (src/main.js:99). A URL path may legally contain `'`, so the caller controls the rest of the expression.

**Evidence:** with the same expression shape evaluated in Node, `url = "http://x/a');globalThis.PWNED=1;//"` produces

```
(function injectBaseHref(url) { ... })('http://x/a');globalThis.PWNED=1;//')
```

and `PWNED === 1`. A URL containing an apostrophe but no payload (e.g. `http://host/it's.html`) makes the expression a `SyntaxError`; `chrome-remote-interface` resolves `Runtime.evaluate` with `exceptionDetails` instead of rejecting, so the failure is invisible: no `<base href>` is injected, nothing is logged, and the response is still 200.

**Impact:** script the caller supplies runs inside the rendered document just before `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` is captured, so the HTML returned to callers can be rewritten, and URLs with quotes silently render without the base href that relative resources need. The attacker already chooses the page, so this stays contained: low.

**Fix:** stop building code from the URL — pass it as data, e.g. `Runtime.evaluate({expression: `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})(${JSON.stringify(url)})`})`, or use `Runtime.callFunctionOn` with an argument object.

findings.title: Setup errors inside the async Promise executor leave the request unanswered
findings.body:
`serialize` and `captureScreenshot` return `new Promise(async (resolve, reject) => {...})` (src/renderer.js:178, src/renderer.js:202), and `_loadPage` does the same (src/renderer.js:43). A rejection inside an `async` executor does not reach the outer promise's `reject`; it becomes an unhandled rejection. `reject` is only reachable from inside the `try` blocks, so every setup failure (`CDP.New`, `CDP`, `Animation.setPlaybackRate`, `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`/`setVisibleSize` at src/renderer.js:203-215, and in `_loadPage` the `Promise.all` at src/renderer.js:46-52, which runs before the 10 s timer at src/renderer.js:140 is even armed) leaves the returned promise pending forever.

**Evidence:** running `src/main.js` against a Chrome whose `/json/new` endpoint rejects GET (`Using unsafe HTTP verb GET to invoke /json/new`), `CDP.New` at src/renderer.js:179 rejects; the route never answers:

```
curl -m 60 'http://127.0.0.1:3001/render/http://127.0.0.1:8099/'  -> http=000 after 59.99 s (timeout)
server log: Uncaught exception ... Using unsafe HTTP verb GET to invoke /json/new
```

The connection is held past the documented 10 s budget because no timer was armed, and main.js counts the unhandled rejection toward its six-strike `process.exit` (src/main.js:164-181).

**Impact:** any CDP-level failure (browser version mismatch, crashed target, failed setup command) converts a per-request error into a connection that is never answered and resources that are never released; enough of them take the whole instance down. Requires a CDP failure to trigger, so reach is limited: low.

**Fix:** drop the `async` executor — do the work in an `async` method and return its promise (`serialize`/`captureScreenshot` can be `async` methods with a `try/catch`), or move every `await` inside the existing `try` and add `.catch(reject)` to the setup calls so each failure settles the outer promise.

summary:
**What the change does.** The PR adds `src/models/login.ts`, the dva login model. In the post-login redirect block (`src/models/login.ts:44-60`) it reads the `redirect` query param, rejects other-origin values, and on rejection does a full-page navigation to `'/'` instead of letting the raw value reach `window.location`.

**Assessment.** This is the upstream fix for CVE-2019-18350, byte-identical to the post-patch blob of ant-design/ant-design-pro commit `840034ca` (`index 740c8d6848..656902dfde`), where the removed line was `window.location.href = redirect;` — the reflected-XSS / open-redirect sink at `src/models/login.ts:56`. I confirmed the file in this PR carries `'/'` there, so the known sink is closed, and the same value survives in current upstream. No security regression introduced; no findings recorded.

Two non-blocking observations, neither of which I filed: a relative `redirect` value (`/user/login?redirect=%2Fdashboard`) makes `new URL(redirect)` at line 49 throw, so the effect dies after `changeLoginStatus` already ran — the user stays on the login form until a reload (this behaviour is identical in the pre-patch version). And the fragment strip at lines 52-53 can yield `//host` or `javascript:...` for `routerRedux.replace`, but the router stack in use (dva 2.4 / react-router-redux 5 / history 4.6.3) passes it straight to `history.replaceState`, which throws `SecurityError` for such URLs rather than navigating (verified in `history@4.6.3/lib/createBrowserHistory.js:196-220` — no `location` fallback in the replace path), so it is not reachable as a redirect or script execution.

## Summary

PR #1 re-adds `slug.js` (212 lines) to a tree whose baseline had it removed. The added file is byte-identical to the published `slug@0.9.2` (sha1 `fd676e5…`), i.e. the first release *outside* CVE-2017-16117's affected range — NVD pins `versionEndIncluding: 0.9.1` — and the entire 0.9.1→0.9.2 code delta is the two trim sites: `char.trim()` / `result.trim()` at `slug.js:57,64` replacing `/^\s+|\s+$/g`.

I confirmed the fix empirically rather than by reading alone: the vulnerable idiom is quadratic (`'x' + ' '*N + 'y'` ran 1.25 s at N=20k and 3.9 s at N=40k, matching NVD's "~50k characters blocks the event loop for 2 s"), while the added file stays linear (9.9 ms / 28 ms on the same inputs, and 357 ms at 500k). Every other regex that sees attacker data — `slug.js:60`, `:65`, the pretty-mode `remove` at `:180`, and the fixed-word `removelist` from `:8` — measured linear up to 1 MB inputs, and the only super-linear paths I found need caller-supplied configuration (an empty `multicharmap` key, or a `$'` replacement template), not untrusted input.

The repo's own suite passes 28/28 against the added file, and a 57k-case differential run against 0.9.1 found no output differences, so the change is behaviour-preserving apart from the timing fix. No findings filed; the change is the upstream security fix and is safe to merge.

One environment issue, unrelated to the change: `ozone knowledge save` reports success but never persists the concept (`list`/`tree`/`get` see nothing), so I filed a `needs_human`-style environment report with the reproduction.

Recorded. The change is a single new file, so I focused coverage there and on its downstream effects, and verified the one real defect end to end.

**Summary**

PR #2 adds `index.js` (155 lines) back to the `merge-options` fixture, restoring the deep-merge library — clone helpers, `mergeKeys`, `concatArrays`, and the exported `mergeOptions` with its `call`/`apply` config handling. The file is byte-identical to npm `merge-options@1.0.0`, the vulnerable release for CVE-2018-3752. All 26 existing tests pass, but `mergeKeys` merges into inherited properties (`key in merged` at `index.js:72`), so an option object carrying an own `__proto__` key — trivially produced by `JSON.parse` — is merged straight into `Object.prototype`; I reproduced process-wide pollution, including `opts.isAdmin === true` for a call that passed `admin: false`. The upstream 1.0.1 remedy (own-key check plus `Object.defineProperty` for all writes) blocks it and keeps the suite green. Lower-impact observations — quadratic `concatArrays` indexing, sparse-array compaction, receiver-as-config adoption, `Symbol` arguments producing the wrong error text, and `Object.propertyIsEnumerable` (which resolves fine via `Function.prototype`, contrary to first appearance) — did not meet the evidence bar for a second finding.

findings.title: Merging an option object with an own `__proto__` key pollutes Object.prototype
findings.body:
Merging an option object that carries an own enumerable `__proto__` key — what `JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {...}}')` produces — writes the attacker's properties onto `Object.prototype`, so every object in the host process inherits them. Any app that passes user-controlled data (JSON config, request body, CLI args) through `mergeOptions` is affected.

**Preconditions:** one merged argument has an own `__proto__` key. JSON parsers, query-string parsers and config loaders produce such keys; no special setting or privilege is needed.

**Evidence:** `index.js:72` tests `key in merged`, which is `true` for the inherited `__proto__` accessor, so `index.js:73` recurses with `merged.__proto__ === Object.prototype`. `isOptionObject(Object.prototype)` is true (its prototype is `null`), so `mergeKeys` then assigns the source's keys onto `Object.prototype` at `index.js:75`.

```
const mergeOptions = require('merge-options');
const userConfig = JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true, "polluted": "yes"}}');
const opts = mergeOptions({port: 80, admin: false}, userConfig);
Object.keys(opts)   //=> ['port', 'admin']   the `__proto__` key vanishes from the result
({}).polluted       //=> 'yes'
[].polluted         //=> 'yes'
(function () {}).isAdmin //=> true
opts.isAdmin        //=> true
```

The same recursion is reachable through:

- a nested plain-object key: `mergeOptions({a: {x: 1}}, {a: JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"p": 1}}')})` → `({}).p === 1`;
- the config receiver at `index.js:137`: `mergeOptions.call(JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"concatArrays": true}}'), {p: ['a']}, {p: ['b']})` → `Object.prototype.concatArrays === true`;
- cloning, where `index.js:60` does `result[key] = clone(obj[key])`, so `mergeOptions({}, JSON.parse('{"cfg": {"__proto__": {"evil": 1}}}'))` returns a `cfg` that inherits `evil` with no own key visible to `Object.keys`.

All reproductions run against this commit on Node 24.22.2.

**Impact:** prototype pollution of the host process, with a direct authorization consequence: `admin: false` was passed as an own property, yet `opts.isAdmin` reads `true` from the polluted prototype. Reach crosses a trust boundary — data supplied by an untrusted caller takes effect on objects it does not own. Persistence is recoverable: the pollution lasts the process lifetime, is re-triggerable at will, and nothing in the library removes it. Crosses trust boundary × recoverable = high.

**Fix:** restore two invariants: merge only keys the target owns, and store every key as an own data property. In `mergeKeys` replace `key in merged` with `hasOwnProperty.call(merged, key)` (with the `merged[key] !== Object.getPrototypeOf(merged)` guard) and use `Object.defineProperty` for the writes at `index.js:50`, `60`, `73`, `75`, `105` and `107`, so a `__proto__` key becomes an ordinary own key instead of invoking the prototype setter. Upstream 1.0.1 fixes CVE-2018-3752 exactly this way; that patch keeps all 26 existing tests passing and makes the reproduction return `opts.isAdmin === undefined` and `({}).polluted === undefined`.

summary:
## Summary

The PR re-adds `index.js`, which is byte-identical to the published `merge-options@1.0.1` — the upstream fix for CVE-2018-3752. The fix replaces assignment with a `defineProperty` helper (`index.js:6-11`) and adds the guard `merged[key] !== Object.getPrototypeOf(merged)` (`index.js:80`), so a JSON `__proto__` key becomes an own data property on the result instead of being merged into `Object.prototype`. I verified the guard holds against top-level, nested, multi-argument, `Object.create(null)`-target, `constructor.prototype` and `this`-config payloads, and confirmed the same payloads do pollute on `1.0.0`; the bundled 26-test ava suite passes (it also passes on `1.0.0`, so it is not a CVE regression test). No findings: the two remaining shared-object write paths (a symbol-keyed `Symbol.unscopables` input under `concatArrays`, and `slice(0,0)` destination hijacking via an own `constructor[Symbol.species]`) need the caller to supply functions or symbols, which JSON data cannot express and which grant no capability the caller lacks — hardening only.

Review complete. Findings and a knowledge note were recorded.

**Summary**

The pull request re-adds `slug.js`, the single module the package declares as `main` and that `bin/slug.js` loads; the file is byte-identical to the published `slug@0.9.1` tarball and to Trott/node-slug at `85ded30a`, with the rest of the tree unchanged. That release is the last affected version for CVE-2017-16117: the trim at `slug.js:64` is quadratic on an interior whitespace run, and I reproduced it (64k spaces ≈ 15 s for the regex alone, 100k ≈ 39 s end to end, event loop fully blocked while one request runs). The fix upstream shipped in 0.9.2 is to trim with `String.prototype.trim()`, so this should not land as-is. The remaining code is mostly charmap data; besides the ReDoS I recorded two small, separately reproducible correctness defects (non-BMP input dropped, and the trailing-separator cleanup being a no-op literal search).

findings.title: Non-BMP characters such as emoji are dropped, so emoji-only input yields an empty slug
findings.body:
Emoji and other non-BMP characters are deleted from slugs instead of being
transliterated, so an emoji-only title yields an empty slug and distinct titles can
map to the same slug.

**Evidence:** the character loop walks UTF-16 code units (`string[i]` at
`slug.js:37`) and looks the symbols table up with `string.charCodeAt(i)`
(`slug.js:50`), which returns a lone surrogate for a surrogate pair.
`require('unicode/category/So')[0x1F639].name` is `'CAT FACE WITH TEARS OF JOY'`,
yet `slug('😹')` returns `''` and `slug('foo 😹 bar')` returns `'foo-bar'`, because
`slug.js:60` strips the two lone surrogates. A BMP symbol works, which isolates the
cause: `slug('☀')` returns `'sun-with-rays'`. The repo's own smoke test shows the
same result: `test.js:1` prints a blank line.

**Impact:** content loss for any input outside the BMP: an emoji-only title becomes
an empty slug, and e.g. `slug('a😹')` and `slug('a😺')` both become `'a'`. Low: the
host still receives a string, but it is wrong and can collide.

**Fix:** iterate by code point: read `string.codePointAt(i)`, advance `i` one extra
unit when the value exceeds 0xFFFF, use `String.fromCodePoint` for the charmap
branch, and look the symbols table up by that code point.

findings.title: One long whitespace run in input blocks the event loop for minutes (CVE-2017-16117)
findings.body:
`slug()` pins the Node event loop for tens of seconds on one short input, so a
single request carrying a run of whitespace stalls every other request the host
process is serving. The added file is the last affected release of the package
(CVE-2017-16117, all versions up to 0.9.1); `package.json:4` still declares 0.9.1.

**Preconditions:** the host passes untrusted text to `slug()`, which is its
documented use, and that text contains a long whitespace run that is not at either
end of the string. Any `\s` character matches: space, tab, newline, NBSP.

**Evidence:** `slug.js:64` trims with `/^\s+|\s+$/g`. Inside an interior run the
anchored `^\s+` alternative cannot match, so `\s+$` consumes the rest of the run
and then backtracks one character at a time testing `$`, which only matches at end
of string; cost grows with the square of the run length. Measured on this checkout
(node v24.22.2):

- trim regex alone: `'a' + ' '.repeat(64_000) + 'b'` takes 15.2 s; the same 64k run
  at the start or the end of the string takes 0.3 ms.
- whole `slug()`: 16k interior spaces 0.96 s, 32k 3.9 s, 64k 13.3 s, 100k 39.3 s.
- in a two-route HTTP server that calls `slug()` on the request input, one request
  (32 KB body) held the loop for 3.8 s: a 10 ms `setInterval` heartbeat fired once
  instead of roughly 380 times.

Every other regex on the path is linear: `/[^\w\s\-\.\_~]/g` at `slug.js:60`,
`/[-\s]+/g` at `slug.js:65`, and the per-character trim at `slug.js:57`.

**Impact:** the event loop is single-threaded, so one unauthenticated request
denies service to every user of the process: about 40 s for a 100 KB body, on the
order of an hour for 1 MB, repeatable at will. One caller's input stops everyone
else's requests (reach crosses a trust boundary) and unprivileged replay is trivial
(recoverable, not transient). Upstream rates the CVE CVSS 3.0 7.5
(AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/A:H).

**Fix:** make the trim linear: `result = result.trim();` at `slug.js:64`, and the
same at `slug.js:57`. That is what upstream shipped in 0.9.2, so take that version
instead of re-adding the vulnerable one.

findings.title: Trailing separator is never removed because the pattern is a literal string
findings.body:
The trailing-separator cleanup never removes anything: `slug('Hello world -')`
returns `'Hello-world-'` instead of `'Hello-world'`.

**Evidence:** `slug.js:66` calls `result.replace(opts.replacement + "$", '')`. With
a string first argument `String.replace` searches for that literal substring, so
the code looks for the text `'-$'` in `result`. `'$'` can never be in `result` at
that point: `slug.js:159` maps it to `dollar`, and when the charmap is overridden
the allow-list filter at `slug.js:60` strips it (`slug('a$b', {charmap: {}})`
returns `'ab'`, a multicharmap or charmap value of `'$'` also yields `'ab'`). The
literal search therefore misses for every replacement value. Verified:
`slug('Hello world -') === 'Hello-world-'`, `slug('Hello world _', '_') ===
'Hello_world__'`, while the regex form does what the comment says:
`'hello-'.replace(new RegExp('-'+'$'),'') === 'hello'`.

**Impact:** slugs can end with the separator even though the code comment and the
library's URL-safe claim say otherwise. Low: one stray character in the output for
inputs that end with an allowed separator character.

**Fix:** strip a trailing literal separator directly, e.g.
`if (opts.replacement && result.slice(-opts.replacement.length) === opts.replacement) result = result.slice(0, -opts.replacement.length);`

summary: PR #2 re-adds `src/models/login.ts`, the dva model the login page and `connect.d.ts` already imported; its `login` effect parses the `redirect` query value and, on a successful login, compares its origin with the page origin — navigating to the raw value when they differ. I confirmed the redirect sink in real Chrome (headless, exact logic copied from `src/models/login.ts:44-60`): a `javascript:` value executes in the app origin and an absolute URL navigates off-site, and I filed that as a high-severity finding. I also filed, at info, the unguarded `new URL(redirect)` that throws for relative or repeated parameters after authority has already been stored. The rest of the model (reducer, `getCaptcha`, `logout`, typings) matches what its callers expect; a small note: `logout` only redirects and never clears the stored authority, which I treated as template design rather than a regression.

findings.title: Login redirect parameter runs attacker JavaScript in the app origin after login
findings.body:
After a successful login, an attacker-supplied `redirect` query value is assigned to
`window.location.href` whenever its origin differs from the page origin
(`src/models/login.ts:49-58`). On success `changeLoginStatus` first stores the new
authority (`src/models/login.ts:39-42`, `:85`), then the effect compares
`new URL(redirect).origin` with the page origin; any value that does not match falls to
the `else` branch, which navigates to the raw string.

A `javascript:` URL has origin `"null"`, so it always takes that branch and runs in the
app origin with the victim's fresh session:

    https://<app>/user/login?redirect=javascript:document.title="XSS";void 0

Any absolute URL is also followed, so the same parameter is an open redirect:

    https://<app>/user/login?redirect=https://evil.example/phish

**Preconditions:**
- The victim has to complete a login on the crafted link. In the shipped demo that is
  free: `mock/user.ts:82-97` returns `status: 'ok'` for `admin` / `ant.design` and
  `user` / `ant.design`, the credentials printed in the form placeholders
  (`src/pages/user/login/index.tsx:118`, `:128`). A real deployment needs those
  credentials; the link then rides on the ordinary login flow.
- The login page is directly reachable at `/user/login` (`config/config.ts:92-97`), so
  no prior navigation is needed.

**Evidence:**
- `src/utils/utils.ts:24` `getPageQuery()` returns the decoded query of
  `window.location.href` with no validation.
- `src/models/login.ts:49` `new URL('javascript:alert(1)')` yields `origin === 'null'`,
  never equal to the page origin, so line 56 runs `window.location.href = redirect`.
- Reproduced with headless Chrome 156 against a page running the verbatim logic of
  `src/models/login.ts:44-60`:
  - `?redirect=javascript:document.title="XSS-EXECUTED";void 0` -> document title
    changed from `SAFE` to `XSS-EXECUTED`.
  - `?redirect=javascript:alert(document.domain)` -> dialog fired showing the page
    origin `127.0.0.1`.
  - `?redirect=https://evil.example/phish` -> browser issued a navigation request to
    `https://evil.example/phish`.
- The repo's own producers emit absolute same-origin URLs
  (`src/layouts/SecurityLayout.tsx:41-43`, `src/models/login.ts:71-78`); nothing
  constrains incoming values.

**Impact:**
Attacker script runs in the app origin while the victim holds a valid session: it can
read `localStorage['antd-pro-authority']` (`src/utils/authority.ts:29`) and issue
authenticated requests (`credentials: 'include'`, `src/utils/request.ts:51-54`). The
open-redirect variant gives a post-login phishing hop from the real login page. Reach
crosses a trust boundary (the attacker acts inside the victim's session), and the
attacker can re-send the link at will, so severity is high, not critical — the victim
still has to log in.

**Fix:**
Treat `redirect` as untrusted and keep navigation inside the SPA: resolve it against
`window.location.origin`, and only route with `routerRedux.replace` when the result
stays same-origin and uses `http`/`https`. For any other value route to `/` instead of
assigning `window.location.href`.

findings.title: Relative or repeated redirect parameter throws in the login effect after authority is stored
findings.body:
A `redirect` value that is not an absolute URL makes the login effect throw, after the
login has already succeeded and authority has been stored. The user stays on the login
form with no error message.

`src/models/login.ts:49` calls `new URL(redirect)` with no base and no `try`. A value
such as `?redirect=/welcome` — the natural shape for a relative path, and the shape a
third-party integration or a hand-written link is likely to use — throws
`TypeError: Invalid URL`. `changeLoginStatus` has already run at that point
(`src/models/login.ts:39-42` -> `:85` writes `localStorage['antd-pro-authority']`), so
the session is authoritative but `routerRedux.replace` at `:60` never executes and the
page never leaves `/user/login`.

Repeated parameters hit the same line and a second failure: `querystring.parse` returns
an array for `?redirect=a&redirect=b`, `new URL(['a','b'])` throws the same
