`TypeError`, and the `redirect.substr(...)` call at `:51` would also break because the
cast at `:47` (`as { redirect: string }`) hides the `string | string[]` type.

**Evidence:**
Headless Chrome 156 running the verbatim logic of `src/models/login.ts:44-60`:
- `?redirect=/welcome` -> `TypeError: Invalid URL` raised, no navigation, page left on
  the login view.
- `?redirect=<same-origin absolute URL>` -> routes to the target as intended, so only
  the non-absolute form fails.

**Impact:**
A crafted link (or a same-origin link written as a path) breaks the login flow for that
visitor only; reloading recovers. The app's own producers always emit absolute URLs
(`src/layouts/SecurityLayout.tsx:41-43`, `src/models/login.ts:71-78`), so this needs an
externally supplied value, hence info.

**Fix:**
Resolve the value against the current origin instead of requiring an absolute URL:
`new URL(redirect, window.location.origin)` (plus a type guard, since the query parser
can return an array), and fall back to `/` when parsing fails.

summary:
The PR re-adds `lib/extract.js`, the public `Extract` API that pipes each parsed zip entry into `fstream.Writer` at `path.join(opts.path, entry.path)`. Benign archives extract correctly (`test/compressed.js` passes), but the entry name is taken verbatim from the zip header (`lib/parse.js:77-93`) with no containment check, so a member like `../../pwned.txt` writes outside the destination.

I reproduced the escape on this checkout (a file appeared at `/tmp/pwned.txt` while the destination stayed empty) and confirmed the Windows backslash variant, then recorded one high-severity finding with the containment fix. The remaining concerns I weighed — directory entries not drained, missing `opts` causing a silent stall, lost file modes/symlinks — are either misuse paths or gaps in an inherited design, not demonstrated failures, so I filed nothing else.

findings.title: Zip entries with ../ names are written outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
`Extract` writes zip entries to an attacker-controlled path. A member named
`../../pwned.txt` is joined straight onto the destination directory and the
concatenated path is written, so extracting an untrusted archive creates or
overwrites files anywhere the process user can write.

**Preconditions:** the application extracts an archive whose contents it does not
fully control (uploads, downloads, mail attachments, CI artifacts). Default
`Extract({ path: ... })` usage is enough; no option changes the behaviour.

**Evidence:** the entry name comes unmodified from the zip local file header
(`lib/parse.js:77-93` sets `entry.path = fileName`) and is used as the write
target with no containment check (`lib/extract.js:20-22`). `path.join` normalises
`..` instead of rejecting it, and `fstream` only resolves the result before
`mkdir`ing and creating the file (`node_modules/fstream/lib/writer.js:73,169`).

Reproduced on this checkout with an archive containing a single entry
`../../pwned.txt`:

```js
var unzipper = require('./unzip.js'), fs = require('fs');
fs.createReadStream('/tmp/zipslip/evil.zip')
  .pipe(unzipper.Extract({ path: '/tmp/zipslip/dest' }));
// after close: /tmp/pwned.txt exists with the payload; /tmp/zipslip/dest is empty
```

Same run confirmed the variants: POSIX absolute names such as `/etc/passwd` are
neutralised by `path.join` (`/tmp/zipslip/dest/etc/passwd`), but backslash names
escape on Windows (`path.win32.join('C:\\dest', '..\\..\\windest.txt')` is
`C:\windest.txt`), so the check must handle both separators.

**Impact:** high. Whoever supplies the archive chooses the write target — reach
crosses a trust boundary (untrusted input to local filesystem), and the write is
permanent: overwriting `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, a shell rc file, or a config read
by a privileged process gives code execution, and even plain overwrites destroy
data with nothing to undo them. No repo policy overrides the high cap.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the write target must stay inside `opts.path`.
Resolve both paths and skip (or error on) any entry that escapes, e.g.
`var root = path.resolve(opts.path); var target = path.resolve(root, entry.path);
if (target !== root && target.indexOf(root + path.sep) !== 0) { entry.autodrain();
self.emit('error', new Error('entry escapes extraction root: ' + entry.path)); return; }`
Treat `\` as a separator too, so the check holds on Windows.

summary:
Review complete.

The PR adds `lib/extract.js` (36 lines), the fstream-backed `Extract` implementation that `unzip.js:10` already required, including a guard intended to stop zip-slip. The parser side survives unchanged and the library's own extraction tests still pass (14/14), so nothing regressed in normal use. The guard, however, is a bare prefix comparison on joined paths rather than a containment test, and I reproduced files landing outside the destination from a crafted archive, including a script written into the destination's parent directory; the rejection path also leaves entries undrained, which wedges extraction for payloads above the stream buffer. Both findings are recorded.

findings.title: Zip-slip guard is a string prefix test, so hostile archives still write outside the destination
findings.body:
A hostile zip still writes files outside the extraction directory. `Extract` only checks that the joined target *string* starts with `opts.path`:

```js
var extractPath = path.join(opts.path, entry.path);   // lib/extract.js:24
if (extractPath.indexOf(opts.path) != 0) {            // lib/extract.js:25
  return;
}
```

`entry.path` is the raw filename from the archive header (`lib/parse.js:78,93`). `path.join` collapses `..`, and a plain `indexOf(...) != 0` test has no separator boundary, so any entry that resolves to a path beginning with the destination string passes and is written by fstream (`lib/extract.js:29-31`). That is the CVE-2018-1002203 path-traversal class this code claims to prevent ("to avoid zip slip").

**Evidence:** with `opts.path = '<base>/uploads'`, an archive containing `../uploads.php` produced `<base>/uploads.php`:

```
$ node -e "...Extract({path:'/tmp/repro/webroot/uploads'})..."   # zip entry: ../uploads.php
dest   : []
parent : [ 'uploads', 'uploads.php' ]
escaped: true "<?php system($_GET[0]); ?>"
```

Same with a sibling dir: `opts.path='/tmp/repro/slip2/dest'` + entry `../dest-evil/pwned.txt` wrote `/tmp/repro/slip2/dest-evil/pwned.txt` while a benign entry landed inside the destination. Also confirmed with `opts.path='.'`, where every entry passes the test (`'a.txt'.indexOf('.') === -1` for the safe case yet `'../evil'.indexOf('.') === 0` for the escaping one).

Contrary direction of the same bug: `opts.path` is never normalized, so a caller passing `'./out'` gets `'out/a.txt'.indexOf('./out') === -1` and *every* contained entry is silently dropped while `'close'` still fires — total data loss reported as success.

**Impact:** an archive author, not the application, chooses where bytes land: any path whose resolved name begins with the destination string — most usefully a sibling file in the destination's parent directory (`uploads` -> `uploads.php`), which in a web app is code placement. That crosses the trust boundary with permanent effect (a written config/script is not undone), and the change's whole purpose is to stop it. The residual limit — targets must share the destination string as a prefix, so `/etc/passwd` is out — narrows the target list but not the outcome, so it does not lower the severity. Rated high under the code-review rubric (crosses a trust boundary, permanent), no repo-specific critical definition.

**Fix:** restore one invariant: the resolved target is inside the resolved destination. Resolve both to absolute, normalized paths and require `target === dest || target.startsWith(dest + path.sep)` (or `path.relative(dest, target)` not starting with `..` and not absolute), then reject/`autodrain()` non-contained entries; use the resolved destination, not the raw `opts.path`, so `'./out'` and `'out/'` behave the same.

findings.title: Rejected archive entries are never drained, so a large traversal entry stalls extraction forever
findings.body:
Entries that the containment check rejects are `return`ed without draining, so the zip parser never resumes. If the rejected entry carries enough data to fill the stream buffer, the whole extraction stalls: no `'close'`, no `'error'`, later entries never extracted, and the source stream/file descriptor is never released.

```js
if (extractPath.indexOf(opts.path) != 0) {   // lib/extract.js:25
  return;                                     // lib/extract.js:26 — entry never consumed
}
```

`lib/parse.js:154-160` pipes the inflater into the entry `PassThrough` and only re-enters `_readRecord()` on its `'finish'`; an unconsumed entry blocks that callback (`README.md` documents `autodrain()` for exactly this case).

**Evidence:** archive `[../evil.txt (N bytes of 0x41), after.txt]`, `Extract({path: '<base>/dest'})`:

```
big.txt  65536  => CLOSE; dest: [ 'after.txt', 'big.txt' ]     # control: same size, contained name
../evil.txt 65536  => STALL (no close/error in 3s); dest: []
../evil.txt 200000 => STALL (no close/error in 3s); dest: []
../evil.txt 32768  => CLOSE; dest: [ 'after.txt' ]             # entry silently dropped
```

**Impact:** the archive author picks the entry size, so one traversal-named entry either wedges the extraction job indefinitely (until the process restarts) or is dropped without any signal while a later `'close'` reports success — partial extraction that the caller cannot detect. Contained to one extraction and cleared by restart or retry, hence low.

**Fix:** call `entry.autodrain()` before `return` on the rejected branch (and on the Directory branch, which relies only on such entries having no payload), and emit an `'error'` or at least a skip event so a dropped entry is observable.

summary:
The PR adds `index.js` (224 lines) to a baseline tree that had it removed: the whole `pdf-image` implementation, which shells out to `pdfinfo` and ImageMagick `convert` through `child_process.exec`, plus the page-caching and combine logic. I read the whole file, reproduced the main issues, and recorded three findings.

Assessment: the command-injection finding is blocking — I confirmed execution end-to-end with a crafted `pdfFilePath`, and the README's own Express snippet feeds URL parameters into that path, so the documented usage exposes remote command execution. The two low findings (silently pending `convertFile` promise; lexicographic page sort breaking 11+ page combined images) are reproducible correctness defects in the same new file. Outside those, the change is a faithful re-add of upstream: the caching, option-building and page-count handling behave as tested by `tests/test-main.js`, and I found no further evidence-backed issues.

findings.title: PDF path and conversion options are interpolated into shell commands, allowing command injection
findings.body:
A `"` or `$(...)` inside `pdfFilePath` or the conversion options closes the
double-quoted argument and the rest runs as shell commands under the process's
privileges. Every external tool invocation is a concatenated string passed to
`child_process.exec`, which runs it through `/bin/sh` with no `shell` option
(`index.js:8`, executed at `index.js:44`, `index.js:116`, `index.js:125`,
`index.js:170`). There is no escaping helper anywhere in the file.

**Preconditions:** the path or options are not fully trusted — the README's own
Express example builds them from URL parameters (`README.md:63-70`:
`new PDFImage(req.params[0])`).

**Evidence:** reproduced with a harmless payload:

```
new PDFImage('/tmp/repro/slide.pdf"; touch /tmp/repro/PWNED; echo "')
  .constructGetInfoCommand()
=> pdfinfo "/tmp/repro/slide.pdf"; touch /tmp/repro/PWNED; echo ""
```

Executing that command created `/tmp/repro/PWNED`. The same payload appears twice
in the convert command, once through `pdfFilePath` and once through the derived
output path (`index.js:88-93`, because `pdfFileBaseName` and `outputDirectory`
are derived from the same string at `index.js:21` and `index.js:79`).

Further sinks, same root cause:

- `index.js:96-101` — `imagePaths.join(' ')` is inserted into `convert -append`
  with no quoting at all.
- `index.js:125` — `exec("rm " + imagePaths.join(' '))` again unquoted, and the
  paths derive from the caller's base name, extension and page number.
- `index.js:103-111` — `convertOptions` keys and values are concatenated raw
  into the command (`index.js:106`), so `{"-resize": "1x1; id"}` injects.
- `index.js:66` — `pageNumber` is concatenated with `+` into the output path and
  reaches the shell through that path even though the `%d` slot coerces it.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated HTTP caller who can choose the PDF path (the
documented Express usage) reaches arbitrary command execution as the server
process, with its file system and network access. This crosses a trust boundary
and the damage can be permanent (data destroyed or secrets exfiltrated).
Severity: high.

**Fix:** build argument arrays and call `execFile`/`spawn` with `shell: false`
for `pdfinfo`, `convert` and the cleanup `fs.unlink`; validate that
`pdfFileBaseName`, `convertExtension` and `outputDirectory` cannot escape the
intended directory. Keep `convertOptions` out of the shell by passing its
tokens as separate argv entries.

findings.title: convertFile's promise never settles when pdfinfo fails or the page count is zero
findings.body:
`convertFile()` returns a promise that never settles when `pdfinfo` fails, when
the reported page count is zero or unparsable, or when `combineImages` fails.
The caller's `.catch` never runs and nothing is reported.

**Evidence:**

- `index.js:133` — `pdfImage.numberOfPages().then(...)` has no rejection
  handler, and the enclosing `new Promise` (`index.js:132`) is only settled from
  inside that handler. `getInfo` rejects on any `pdfinfo` error
  (`index.js:46-51`), so that rejection is dropped and the returned promise
  stays pending forever.
- `index.js:134-147` — the inner promise is resolved only from inside the
  `for (var i = 0; i < totalPages; i++)` loop (`index.js:139-142`). With
  `totalPages` of `0` or `NaN` the loop never runs and nothing settles.
- `index.js:151-153` — `combineImages(...).then(...)` has no `.catch`, so a
  failed `convert -append` (`index.js:118-123`) also leaves the outer promise
  pending. The sibling `.catch` at `index.js:157-159` only covers the per-page
  chain, which is why page conversion failures do reach the caller — the
  asymmetry shows this is an oversight.

Reproduced: `new PDFImage('/nonexistent.pdf').convertFile()` stayed pending
after several seconds (pdfinfo absent/failing), with no rejection and no
`unhandledRejection` warning under `es6-promise` 4.2.8. Rejections from
`convertPage` did propagate, confirming the difference.

**Impact:** a consumer that awaits `convertFile()` — for example an Express
route using the README's "convert full file" idiom — leaves the request open
until a proxy or client timeout, with no error logged. Reach is one request or
job, and a restart or retry clears it. Severity: low.

**Fix:** return the chain from `numberOfPages()` with a trailing `.catch(reject)`
(or `return pdfImage.numberOfPages().then(...)` from the executor), and reject
when `totalPages` is not a positive number. Add `.catch(reject)` to the
`combineImages` call.

findings.title: Combined image appends pages out of order for PDFs with 11 or more pages
findings.body:
With `combinedImage: true`, the pages of a PDF with 11 or more pages are appended
in the wrong order. `index.js:140` re-sorts the resolved image paths with the
default `Array.prototype.sort`, which compares them as strings, so page numbers
sort lexicographically instead of numerically:

```
slide-0.png, slide-1.png, slide-10.png, slide-11.png, slide-2.png, ...
```

`constructCombineCommandForFile` (`index.js:95-102`) then passes that list to
`convert -append` in exactly that order, and the combined file is written with
pages out of sequence.

**Evidence:** reproduced in node with the 12 paths `convertFile` would produce
for a 12-page document; `sort()` orders `slide-10.png` and `slide-11.png` before
`slide-2.png`. The string comparison is at `index.js:140`; the resulting order is
consumed at `index.js:99`.

**Impact:** silently wrong output for any document of 11+ pages converted with
`combinedImage`; it reproduces on every run. The outcome is a misordered preview
image, not lost data, so this discounts to low.

**Fix:** keep page numbers alongside the paths and sort by the numeric page
index (or collect results into an array indexed by page and avoid sorting
altogether).

summary:
Recorded one high-severity finding. Coverage summary:

**Verification performed**
- Traced the topic path end to end: `src/plugins/irc-events/topic.js:16,30-33` re-emits the raw IRC topic; `client/js/shout.js:317-318` writes it with `.html()`. Initial render (`client/views/chat.tpl:20`) and the topic-change message (`client/views/msg.tpl:21`) both escape via the `parse` helper, so the live header update is the only unescaped path.
- Corroborated against upstream: the added blob is the pre-fix revision (`5b02e23`); upstream commit `ef041d66` "Fix topic exploit" deletes these four lines and `4293336` replaces `.html()` with `.text()`.
- Ruled out other candidates: `setNick`'s `.html(nick + ":")` is only reachable with the victim's own nick (self-XSS); the unquoted selector `[data-target=#chan-N]` at `shout.js:568` does not throw — I reproduced it against the bundled jQuery 2.1.1 in jsdom (Sizzle's `identifier` class includes `#`), so badges/notifications still work; ids used in selector concatenation are integers, and all `render()` sinks depend on escaped templates.

**Summary**
The change re-adds `client/js/shout.js`, the whole browser client for the Shout IRC app (socket event wiring, DOM rendering, settings, keybindings), at the revision that predates the topic-injection fix. It is a straight file addition with no other files touched, so the risk sits entirely in how the client turns socket payloads into DOM. One security defect is filed: raw IRC topic text reaches `.html()` in the live topic handler, giving anyone who can set a channel topic script execution in other users' sessions. Aside from that, the client rendering consistently relies on the escaping `parse` helper and Handlebars-escaped templates; separately, and outside this diff, `client/views/toggle.tpl:12` has a similar unescaped `{{{head}}}` sink fed by remote page titles, which upstream fixed later in a different commit.

findings.title: Any channel member can run script in another user's browser by changing the IRC topic
findings.body: Any user who can set a channel topic runs JavaScript in the browser of every Shout user in that channel. The live topic update writes the raw IRC topic string into the channel header with jQuery `.html()`. **Preconditions:** the attacker shares a channel with the victim and can set its topic (channel operator, or any member when `+t` is not set), or the victim is connected to an attacker-controlled IRC server. The victim needs no interaction: `client/js/shout.js:317` is registered at page load with no option gate and no "active channel" check, so it fires for background channels too. **Evidence:** - Sink: `client/js/shout.js:317-318` — `socket.on("topic", function(data) { $("#chan-" + data.chan).find(".header .topic").html(data.topic); });` - Source: `src/plugins/irc-events/topic.js:16` takes `data.topic` straight from slate-irc and re-emits it unescaped at `topic.js:30-33`. Nothing in `src/` escapes it (`grep -rn "escape" src/` finds nothing); topics are free-form IRC strings, so `` is a valid topic. - The same field is escaped everywhere else, which shows the omission: initial render uses `{{{parse topic}}}` (`client/views/chat.tpl:20`) and `client/js/libs/handlebars/parse.js:26-35` replaces `<`, `>` and `'`; the topic-change message body goes through `{{{parse text}}}` too (`client/views/msg.tpl:21`). Only this handler bypasses the helper. - Upstream fixed exactly these four lines: commit `ef041d6612` "Fix topic exploit" deletes the handler, and commit `4293336f` replaces `.html()` with `.text()`. **Impact:** injected script runs in Shout's origin with the page's already authenticated socket.io session — it can read and send messages and `/raw` anything on the victim's networks. It can also read the `token` cookie (`client/js/shout.js:135-140`, set when the user ticks "remember"), which `src/server.js:147` accepts as the sole credential, giving the attacker control of all of the victim's networks until the Shout process restarts. A remote IRC peer reaches a victim browser session it otherwise cannot touch, and nothing in the product undoes it, so this scores high on the matrix. **Fix:** never feed the topic to `.html()`. Smallest change: use `.text(data.topic)` at `client/js/shout.js:318` (what upstream did in `4293336f`); alternatively drop the handler so the escaped topic-change message is the only update path (upstream `ef041d6612`). Escaping on the server side alone would double-escape in `chat.tpl`.

summary:
Review complete. Final state:

**What the change does:** adds `lib/unpack.js` (560 lines, the tar extractor). I verified it is byte-identical to the published `tar@4.4.1` file — in fact the whole `lib/` tree now matches upstream 4.4.1 exactly, so the change restores the extractor and nothing else.

**Assessment:** the extractor has two confirmed escapes from the extraction directory under default options, both reproduced first-hand (async and sync, as root and as an unprivileged user) and both permanently overwriting files outside `cwd`; one is CVE-2018-20834, whose upstream 4.4.2 fix (`b0c5843`, an `nlink <= 1` reuse check) is exactly the delta missing here. The two are independent: the `dirCache` symlink issue reproduces unchanged on the 4.4.2 code and is blocked only by invalidating the cache entry when `[CHECKFS]` removes a path. Rest of the file (path sanitising for `entry.path`, `keep`/`newer` handling, `PENDING` accounting) surfaced only lower-value robustness concerns that I did not confirm. The repo's `test/unpack.js` does not cover either behavior; its failures in this sandbox come from the old `tap@11` runner on Node 24 and root-only chown expectations, not from the added file.

findings.title: Archive hardlink plus file entry overwrites files outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
Extracting an untrusted archive with default options truncates and rewrites an existing file that lies **outside** `opt.cwd`. A `Link` (hardlink) entry whose `linkpath` points outside the extraction directory creates a hardlink inside `cwd`; the immediately following `File` entry with the same path is then written through that link.

**Evidence**

Archive with these two entries (built with python `tarfile`, typeflag `1` = LNKTYPE, then a regular file):

```
'pwn' b'1' '../victim.txt' 0      # hardlink to a file outside cwd
'pwn' b'0' '' 6                   # body "PWNED\n"
```

`new Unpack({cwd: '/tmp/ozrepro/xasync'}).end(buf)` and `new Unpack.Sync({cwd}).end(buf)` on the reviewed code, with `/tmp/ozrepro/victim.txt` = `ORIGINAL\n`:

```
=== async
/tmp/ozrepro/victim.txt "PWNED\n" nlink=2 ino=33632157
/tmp/ozrepro/xasync/pwn  "PWNED\n" nlink=2 ino=33632157
=== sync
/tmp/ozrepro/victim.txt "PWNED\n" nlink=3 ino=33632157
```

Same inode, truncated to 6 bytes, no warning or error emitted. Reproduced 20/20 async and 20/20 sync. The archive-level path sanitizer never looks at `linkpath`: `[CHECKPATH]` only tests `entry.path` (`lib/unpack.js:143-169`), while `[HARDLINK]` resolves `entry.linkpath` as `path.resolve(this.cwd, entry.linkpath)` (`lib/unpack.js:337`), so both `../victim.txt` and an absolute `/home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys` are accepted. `[CHECKFS]` then treats the existing file as reusable whenever it is a regular file (`lib/unpack.js:363` async, `lib/unpack.js:425` sync) without inspecting `st.nlink`, and `[FILE]` opens it with flag `w` — `fsm.WriteStream` at `lib/unpack.js:250`, `fs.openSync(..., 'w', mode)` at `lib/unpack.js:459` — which truncates the shared inode.

Also triggered when the extracting user merely re-extracts over a tree that already contains a hardlink: a lone `File` entry then overwrites the link target. As a non-root user the reach is bounded by `fs.protected_hardlinks`/permissions: files the user owns, or other-owned files writable by them (verified as `nobody` against a 0666 victim → overwritten; against a root-owned 0644 victim → `EPERM` warning, no write).

**Impact:** An archive author overwrites files outside the extraction directory — shell rc files, `authorized_keys`, git hooks — permanently, without needing any non-default option. That crosses the boundary between untrusted archive content and the extracting user's filesystem, so `high`.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant "never write through an existing file that has other links". Only reuse an existing regular file when `st.nlink <= 1` (and never on win32, where `nlink` is unusable), otherwise unlink and create a fresh file — i.e. the upstream 4.4.2 change (commit b0c5843) that adds an `ISREUSABLE(entry, st)` helper used by both `[CHECKFS]` implementations. That change alone prevents this reproduction, and it is the whole diff between 4.4.1 and 4.4.2.

findings.title: Symlink replacing a directory entry lets later files be written outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
A directory entry followed by a symlink entry of the same name leaves `this.dirCache` (`lib/unpack.js:62`) claiming that path is still a directory. Later entries whose parent is that path skip directory creation and are resolved through the symlink, so files are written **outside** `opt.cwd`.

**Evidence**

Three entries, default options (`{cwd}` only, `unlink`/`preservePaths` off):

```
Directory    'd'                     (mode 0755)
SymbolicLink 'd'  -> '../outside'
File         'd/victim.txt'  size 6  ("PWNED\n")
```

With `/tmp/vb2/outside/victim.txt` = `ORIGINAL\n` outside the extraction dir:

```
async victim: "PWNED\n"     d is symlink: true
sync  victim: "PWNED\n"     d is symlink: true
```

5/5 async and 3/3 sync runs, and also as an unprivileged user (`setpriv --reuid=65534`). Trace: `[DIRECTORY]` creates `cwd/d` via `[MKDIR]`, and `mkdir` caches it (`lib/mkdir.js:58`, cache hit at `lib/mkdir.js:68`). The symlink entry's `[CHECKFS]` finds a directory and removes it (`lib/unpack.js:372` async, `lib/unpack.js:434` sync) without removing `cwd/d` from `dirCache`, then `[SYMLINK]` creates the link (`lib/unpack.js:333`). The file entry calls `[MKDIR](path.dirname(entry.absolute), ...)` (`lib/unpack.js:357`), which returns immediately on the stale cache hit, so the `mkdir.js` `SymlinkError` guard never runs; `fs.lstat`/`WriteStream` on `cwd/d/victim.txt` follow the link and the write lands in the outside directory.

Controls that pin the cause: (a) the same archive without the leading `Directory` entry is blocked — `SymlinkError: Cannot extract through symbolic link` from `lib/mkdir.js:114`, victim intact, async and sync; (b) adding `this.dirCache.delete(entry.absolute)` after the `rmdir`/`rmdirSync` in both `[CHECKFS]` implementations restores the `SymlinkError` warning and leaves the victim intact in both modes. This is independent of the `nlink` issue: it reproduces unchanged on the 4.4.2 code. Later upstream versions removed the `dirCache` entirely (`src/mkdir.ts` in current node-tar takes no cache).

**Impact:** An archive author writes files anywhere the extracting user can write, one directory above or beside the extraction root, permanently (verified: a file outside `cwd` is replaced in place). That crosses the untrusted-archive/extracting-user boundary with no non-default option, so `high`.

**Fix:** Never trust `dirCache` for a path that extraction itself may have removed: drop the cache entry (`this.dirCache.delete(entry.absolute)`) whenever `[CHECKFS]` removes it, in both `[CHECKFS]` implementations, or re-`lstat` a cached directory before skipping creation.

summary:
Review complete. Six findings recorded.

**Summary:** PR #1 re-adds `index.js`, rewriting the library's process calls from `child_process.exec` shell strings to `spawn` with argv arrays — which does close the CVE's shell-injection vector on POSIX, and no shell-reaching call remains in the file. Two defects block it: the new `require("child-process-promise")` has no matching `package.json` entry, so a clean install cannot load the module at all, and `convertPage` drops the `resolve` on its cache-hit path, so re-converting an up-to-date page hangs forever (and stalls `convertFile`). The remaining findings cover promise-settlement gaps on error paths, `graphicsMagick` mode being unspawnable because the command string `"gm convert"` contains a space, an unhandled `rm` rejection that can kill the host process, and the three command-builder helpers whose changed return types leave the repo's own tests red.

findings.title: convertPage never settles when the cached page image is already up to date
findings.body:
`convertPage` resolves only when it had to run `convert`. When a page image already
exists and is not older than the PDF, neither `resolve` nor `reject` is called, so the
returned promise never settles. The common case of converting a page that was already
converted therefore hangs the caller forever instead of returning the cached path.
`convertFile` hangs with it, because it waits for `imagePaths.length === parseInt(totalPages)`
(`index.js:137`) that is never reached.

**Evidence:** `index.js:204-219` — inside the `fs.stat(pdfFilePath)` callback the
`if (imageFileStat.mtime < pdfFileStat.mtime)` branch converts, and there is no
`else` (and no code after the `if`) that settles the promise. The version this change
replaces ended the same callback with `return resolve(outputImagePath);`.

Reproduced with an up-to-date cached page image (`doc-0.png` with mtime newer than
`doc.pdf`) and no `convert` invocation needed:

```js
const img = new PDFImage('/tmp/hangtest/doc.pdf');
img.convertPage(0).then(() => console.log('RESOLVED'), () => console.log('REJECTED'));
// after 2s: neither callback ran
```

**Impact:** any caller that re-requests an already-converted page blocks forever —
the README's Express handler (`res.sendFile(await convertPage(page))`) is exactly this
pattern, so a second request for the same page never responds. Reach is contained to
the waiting call and persistence is permanent for that call, so medium; note that an
application-level timeout turns it into a failed request rather than a leaked process.

**Fix:** settle the cached path — after the timestamp comparison, resolve
`outputImagePath` when no conversion is needed (restore the trailing `resolve`).

findings.title: Library cannot load: child-process-promise is required but not declared as a dependency
findings.body:
`index.js` now requires `child-process-promise` at load time, but `package.json`
declares only `es6-promise`. Any consumer that installs the package from a tarball
or the registry gets no `child-process-promise`, so `require("pdf-image")` throws
`MODULE_NOT_FOUND` before any function runs. Every consumer of the package fails at
load, not just the code paths that spawn a process.

**Evidence:** `index.js:7` (`var spawn = require("child-process-promise").spawn`)
versus `package.json:13-15`, whose `dependencies` object contains only `es6-promise`.

Reproduced: `npm pack` the package contents, then in an empty project
`npm install file:pdf-image-2.0.0.tgz && node -e "require('pdf-image')"` gives

```
LOAD FAIL: MODULE_NOT_FOUND - Cannot find module 'child-process-promise'
```

The same happens with the repo's own `npm install && npm test`: the test file loads
the library through `require("../")`.

**Impact:** the published artifact is unusable. Reach is broad (every install of the
package) and persistence is permanent (the module never loads until a release adds
the dependency). This is the omission the change introduces: it swaps
`child_process.exec` for `child-process-promise` without adding the new module to
the manifest.

**Fix:** add `"child-process-promise": "^2.2.1"` to `dependencies` in `package.json`.

findings.title: convertFile hangs instead of rejecting when pdfinfo or the final combine fails
findings.body:
`convertFile` returns a promise that can never reject. `numberOfPages()` is chained
with `.then(...)` and no `.catch`, so when `pdfinfo` fails (missing binary, unreadable
or corrupt PDF, non-zero exit) the rejection is dropped and the outer promise stays
pending forever. The same happens when `combinedImage: true` and the final combine
fails: `combineImages(...)` (`index.js:149`) has no `.catch(reject)` either.

**Evidence:** `index.js:131` — `pdfImage.numberOfPages().then(function (totalPages) {...})`
is not followed by any error handler, and the enclosing `new Promise` only rejects
through the inner paths. `index.js:147-151` — the `combinedImage` branch resolves but
never rejects.

Reproduced by the repository's own suite: with `pdfinfo` absent, the "should convert
all PDF's pages to files" and "…to single image" tests time out
(`Timeout of 7000ms exceeded`) instead of failing with the `spawn pdfinfo ENOENT`
error that the "should return # of pages" test shows.

**Impact:** callers cannot tell a failure from a slow conversion and wait indefinitely;
`convertFile` is the documented whole-document API. Reach is contained to the calling
job and the hang is permanent for that call, so medium, discounted to low because the
trigger is an external command failing on the error path.

**Fix:** attach `.catch(reject)` to the `numberOfPages()` chain and to
`combineImages(...)`, so every path out of the outer executor settles it.

findings.title: graphicsMagick mode is broken: the command string "gm convert" cannot be spawned
findings.body:
With `graphicsMagick: true` the library builds `cmd: "gm convert"` — a command string
containing a space — and hands it to `spawn`. On POSIX `cross-spawn` passes the string
through unchanged (`node_modules/cross-spawn/lib/parse.js:99` only rewrites anything
under `isWin`), so `child_process.spawn("gm convert", …)` looks for an executable
literally named `gm convert` and fails with `ENOENT`. GraphicsMagick support, which
worked when the command went through a shell, is now dead on Linux and macOS.

**Evidence:** `index.js:85` and `index.js:94` (`cmd: this.useGM ? "gm convert" : "convert"`).
Reproduced:

```
command: {"cmd":"gm convert","args":["/tmp/x.pdf[1]","/tmp/x-1.png"]}
REJECTED: spawn gm convert ENOENT
```

On Windows the same string takes a different path: `resolveCommand("gm convert")`
fails, cross-spawn marks it `requiresShell` and wraps the call in
`cmd.exe /s /c` (`cross-spawn/lib/parse.js:114-128`), so a shell remains in that code
path — the shell-free guarantee this change aims for does not hold there.

**Impact:** every GraphicsMagick user of the package gets a hard error on Unix, and on
Windows a shell-wrapped invocation whose escaping this library does not control.
Reach is contained to users of a non-default option and the breakage is permanent until
fixed, so medium, discounted to low for the non-default setting.

**Fix:** pass the program and its subcommand as separate argv entries — `cmd: "gm"`,
`args: ["convert"].concat(convertOptions…)` — so both the POSIX and Windows paths run
without a shell.

findings.title: Command-builder helpers change return type and leave the repository's tests failing
findings.body:
The change makes `constructConvertCommandForPage`, `constructCombineCommandForFile` and
`constructConvertOptions` return objects and arrays instead of command strings. The
repository's test suite still asserts the string form, so `npm test` fails with five
assertion errors, and any consumer that used these helpers to build its own command
now passes an object where a string is expected.

**Evidence:** `index.js:84-87` returns `{ cmd, args }`, `index.js:93-96` returns
`{ cmd, args }`, `index.js:99-108` returns an array, while
`tests/test-main.js:49`, `:54`, `:60` and `:151` compare against strings.

```
4) should return correct convert command:
   AssertionError: expected { Object (cmd, args) } to equal 'convert "/tmp/test.pdf[1]" "/tmp/test-1.png"'
6) should use gm when you ask it to:
   AssertionError: expected { Object (cmd, args) } to equal 'gm convert "/tmp/test.pdf[1]" "/tmp/test-1.png"'
10) should construct convert options correctly:
   AssertionError: expected [ '-density', 300, '-trim' ] to equal '-density 300 -trim'
```

**Impact:** the change lands with a red test suite, and the three public helpers change
shape without a version bump or note, so callers break silently (a string-typed
argument becomes an object). Contained to code that uses the helpers — low.

**Fix:** update `tests/test-main.js` to assert on `{ cmd, args }` and the options
array in the same change that alters the helpers.

findings.title: Unhandled rm rejection can crash the host process during image cleanup
findings.body:
After a successful `combinedImage` conversion, `combineImages` deletes the per-page
images with `spawn("rm", imagePaths)` and throws the returned promise away. Any non-zero
exit from `rm` (read-only directory, file already removed by a concurrent run, a
relative name starting with `-` that `rm` parses as an option) becomes an unhandled
rejection, which terminates the Node process on Node 15 and later — after
`convertFile()` has already resolved successfully.

**Evidence:** `index.js:116` — `spawn("rm", imagePaths); //cleanUp`, no `.catch`.
Reproduced with the same call shape:

```
$ node -e "require('child-process-promise').spawn('rm', ['/tmp/absent-123'])"
ChildProcessError: `rm /tmp/absent-123` failed with code 1
process exit code 1        # Node.js v24.22.2
```

There is also no `--` separator, so an output file whose name starts with `-`
(`pdfFileBaseName: "-rf"`, `outputDirectory: "."`) is read as an option and survives.

**Impact:** a host application can be killed by a cleanup step that runs on a
successful conversion. Reach is broad when it fires (the whole process dies), but it
needs `rm` to fail on files the library has just written, so the likelihood is low.

**Fix:** pass `["--"].concat(imagePaths)` and handle the result —
`spawn("rm", args).catch(function () {})`, or use `fs.unlink` for each path.

summary:
**Review complete — no findings.**

**What the change does:** it re-adds `lib/unpack.js` (572 lines), which is byte-identical (sha256 `7cfc2852…`) to upstream npm/node-tar commit `b0c58433`, the released 4.4.2 fix for CVE-2018-20834. Its only behavioural delta against the pre-fix file is `[ISREUSABLE]` (`lib/unpack.js:358-364`), which refuses to reuse an existing regular file when `st.nlink > 1`; the async and sync `[CHECKFS]` paths (`lib/unpack.js:375`, `:437`) then unlink and create a fresh inode instead of writing through an archive-created hardlink.

**Assessment:** I reproduced the CVE against both versions with a hand-built ustar archive. Pre-fix, a hardlink entry to an out-of-tree file followed by a same-name `File` entry overwrites the victim (shared inode, `nlink=2`) in sync/async and absolute/relative `linkpath` forms; with this file, extraction succeeds, the victim keeps `nlink=1` and its content, and the extracted path gets a new inode. So the change is a faithful, effective fix. Two residual path-containment gaps in this code — `///tmp/x` escaping through `[CHECKPATH]`'s single-separator root strip, and a stale `dirCache` allowing extraction through an archive-created symlink — reproduce identically on the pre-fix file, so they are untouched by this change rather than introduced by it; upstream fixed that class in 4.4.18+.

Two side notes: the upstream regression test from the fix commit ("do not reuse hardlinks, only nlink=1 files") is not part of this PR, so nothing in `test/` covers the new guard; and `ozone knowledge save` reports success but persists nothing (recorded as an environment report, body left at `/tmp/knowledge.md`).

**Summary:** This PR restores `lib/validation.js` (removed in the fixture baseline) verbatim from upstream fastify at `854e150c`, the schema build/validate/serialize layer used by `lib/route.js`, `lib/handleRequest.js`, `lib/reply.js` and `lib/logger.js`. The restored file is byte-identical to upstream's pre-fix revision (blob `afb9b02`), so the PR ships the vulnerable state of the Ajv configuration that CVE-2020-8192 / HackerOne 903521 was filed about; I reproduced the consequence end-to-end over real HTTP. Everything else in the file matches the code the rest of the tree already calls, and `test/validation-error-handling.test.js` passes apart from two assertions that differ only in fast-json-stringify's quoted-property message format (version drift, unrelated to this change). Applying upstream's one-line fix also requires updating the multi-error expectations in that test file, which the finding notes.

findings.title: Default Ajv options collect every validation error, so one request stalls the server
findings.body:
`buildSchemaCompiler` enables Ajv's `allErrors: true` for every validator fastify
creates (`lib/validation.js:174`). Validation of request data then continues past the
first violation and records one error object per failing keyword. `wrapValidationError`
turns the whole array into one string through `schemaErrorsText`
(`lib/validation.js:120`, `:157-165`), and `lib/handleRequest.js:83-91` sends that string
as the 400 body. A client that submits a body failing many keywords forces the process to
materialize the full error set, spend quadratic time building the message, and answer with
a response far larger than its request. All of this happens during `preValidation`, before
any handler or authentication check, on the same event loop that serves every other
request.

**Preconditions:** Default Ajv configuration (no `customOptions: { allErrors: false }`) and
at least one route with a `body`, `querystring` or `params` schema whose failures can
repeat — a nested array of objects with several `required` properties is enough.
`bodyLimit` defaults to 1 MiB (`docs/Server.md:67-73`).

**Evidence:** Reproduced on this tree with `npm install` and node 24.

- Route schema: body `{ items: [ { a, b, c, d all required } ] }`. Payload
  `{"items":[{},{}...]}` × 300000 = 900,011 bytes, under the default 1 MiB limit.
- Real HTTP POST to a listening server: 400 response of 64,355,611 bytes, 37.5 s wall
  time, RSS 671 MB. A concurrent `GET /health` that answers in 18 ms when idle took
  1,765 ms, and no further ping completed before the POST finished — the event loop was
  blocked for the whole validation and error formatting.
- Isolated: Ajv produced 1,200,000 error objects in ~0.6-1 s, `schemaErrorsText`
  (`lib/validation.js:157-165`) took 104 s on the repeated `text +=`, and stringifying
  the 64 MB error payload took 4 s.
- The identical request with `customOptions: { allErrors: false }` returns a 100-byte
  response in a few milliseconds.

This file is byte-identical to upstream fastify's pre-fix `lib/validation.js` (blob
`afb9b02`, tree `854e150c`). Upstream fixed this in commit `74c3157c`, "Disable allErrors
in default Ajv config.", which changes exactly this line and cites
<https://hackerone.com/reports/903521> and Ajv's security notes: the mitigations for slow
validation (`maxLength`, `maxItems`, `patternProperties` limits) "would only work if you
do NOT use `allErrors: true` in production code". The post-fix blob is `c70b2e48`.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated caller can stall the whole instance and consume hundreds of
megabytes of heap with one request, and can repeat it at will. Reach is broad: the event
loop is shared, so every request and tenant on the process waits; reach is not limited to
the attacker's own request. Persistence is recoverable: the stall clears when the request
finishes, no restart is required unless the heap is exhausted. `bodyLimit` bounds a single
request to about 671 MB and 40 s here, which is already enough to trip health checks,
time out in-flight requests and OOM small instances; denser schemas (more required
properties per array item) raise the yield per byte. Severity medium under the review
policy for broad reach × recoverable persistence.

**Fix:** Default `allErrors` to `false` in `lib/validation.js:174` and leave the opt-in to
`options.customOptions`, which is upstream's fix and keeps the escape hatch for callers
that need every error. Test expectations that encode multi-error messages must change with
it: `test/validation-error-handling.test.js:63`, `:219-232`, `:258`, `:288`. Because
`customOptions: { allErrors: true }` is still reachable and recommended in
`docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md:341`, also cap how many errors `schemaErrorsText`
folds into the message so the 64 MB-body path cannot be reopened by configuration.

summary:
**Summary**

The PR re-adds `lib/validation.js` (194 lines) to a tree from which it had been stripped, and the content is byte-identical to upstream fastify commit `74c3157c` — the fix for CVE-2020-8192/GHSA-xw5p-hw6r-2j98, which turns the private Ajv's `allErrors` default from `true` to `false` so a crafted request cannot build an unbounded validation-error list (`lib/validation.js:174-176`). The mitigation itself is correct and cannot be silently inverted by normal route code; only an explicit `ajv.customOptions.allErrors: true` restores the old behaviour, which is the documented escape hatch.

The gap is that the change was carried over without its companion edits: five assertions in `test/validation-error-handling.test.js` still pin the two-error output and now fail (verified — flipping only that flag back to `true` makes them pass), and the docs still present `allErrors: true` as Fastify's baseline configuration, inviting readers back onto the DoS vector. I recorded those two items and left the file's other pre-existing behaviours out of scope.

findings.title: Existing validation tests still expect every Ajv error and now fail
findings.body:
The new `allErrors: false` default in the private Ajv instance changes how many
validation errors a request produces, but the repository's existing tests were
not updated. Five assertions in `test/validation-error-handling.test.js` still
expect every error, so the suite fails.

**Evidence:**
Run `node_modules/.bin/tap --no-esm test/validation-error-handling.test.js`:
27/34 assertions pass, and five failures are the truncated error list.

- `test/validation-error-handling.test.js:63` — wants `"body should have required
  property 'name', body should have required property 'work'"`, gets only the
  `'name'` clause.
- `test/validation-error-handling.test.js:219-232` — wants a two-element
  `validationError.validation` array (`missingProperty: 'name'` and `'work'`),
  gets one element.
- `test/validation-error-handling.test.js:258` — same two-clause message.
- `test/validation-error-handling.test.js:288` — `"Attached: Error: body should
  have required property 'name', body should have required property 'work'"`.
- `test/validation-error-handling.test.js:381` — same message inside the
  serialized 400 body.

Causality: copying the tree and flipping only `lib/validation.js:176` back to
`allErrors: true` takes the same file to 32/34; the five failures above pass
again. The two residual failures (`:323`, `:353`) come from
`fast-json-stringify` 1.21.0 quoting required-property names; they are unrelated
to this change.

**Impact:** `npm run unit` fails, and CONTRIBUTING.md requires all CI checks to be
green before merge. The runtime effect is intended — 400 responses and
`request.validationError.validation` now carry only the first error — but the
tests that pin the old output were left behind, so the change cannot merge and
the behaviour change is undocumented in the test suite.

**Fix:** Update the five assertions to the single-error expectation, as the
upstream fix did in the same commit. Keep the two tests at
`test/validation-error-handling.test.js:74` and `:132` as they are: they pass
`customOptions: { allErrors: true }`, which still overrides the default.

findings.title: Docs still advertise allErrors: true, the option this change disables as a DoS vector
findings.body:
The code now defaults its private Ajv to `allErrors: false` to close the
resource-exhaustion DoS, but the documentation still presents `allErrors: true`
as Fastify's own configuration. A reader who copies the documented baseline
re-enables the option the change exists to disable, with no warning.

**Evidence:**
- `docs/Server.md:385-393` — the `ajv` factory "Default" block lists
  `allErrors: true,` inside `customOptions`, i.e. as what Fastify uses.
- `docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md:334-342` — "Fastify's baseline ajv
  configuration is:" then `allErrors: true,   // check for all errors`.
- `docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md:353-358` — a custom-instance example
  commented as "the fastify defaults (if needed)", again with `allErrors: true`.
- `docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md:669` and `:718` — the `ajv-errors` and
  `ajv-i18n` examples set `customOptions: { allErrors: true }` without any note
  that this restores an unbounded error list.

`lib/validation.js:170-178` merges `options.customOptions` after the defaults,
so all of these snippets do override the new `allErrors: false`.

**Impact:** Documentation-only, but it points users back at the configuration the
change classifies as a DoS vector (`lib/validation.js:174-176`). Severity `info`:
no code path fails, and only a user who copies the snippet is affected.

**Fix:** Remove `allErrors: true` from the documented baseline and, where an
example needs multiple errors, state that `customOptions.allErrors: true` opts
back into the unbounded error list. The upstream fix commit updated
`docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md`; `docs/Server.md` was missed here.

summary:
The PR adds the jison-generated parser `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js` (934 lines), restoring the module that `src/parser.js:3` imports; its content is the CVE-2020-6836 fix, with the `ARRAY` production at line 225 replacing `eval("[" + yytext + "]")` with `yy.trimEdges(yytext).split(',')`. I confirmed the added artifact no longer executes formula text (the payload `SUM([require('fs')...])` runs against the pre-fix parser and is inert here), and that every `yy` function it calls is supplied by `src/parser.js:16-26`.

Two low-severity issues are recorded: the fix was applied only to the build artifact while `grammar-parser.jison:191` still holds the eval (running `npm run generate-parser` regenerates the vulnerable parser), and the new action passes bracket literals as strings, so `MAX`/`MIN`/`COUNT` over them silently return `0` and `AVERAGE` errors.

The eval removal itself is correct and matches upstream's fix; the security posture as merged is sound. Note the checked-in `dist/formula-parser.js:14123` (the `browser` entry) still carries the eval until the next build — untouched here and regenerated by the normal release path.

findings.title: Fix exists only in the generated parser; regenerating from grammar-parser.jison restores the eval RCE
findings.body:
The added parser is safe, but the grammar it is generated from is not. `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison:191` still evaluates the bracket-literal text with `eval("[" + yytext + "]")` on input captured by the lexer rule `'['(.*)?']'` (`grammar-parser.jison:18`). The repo's own `npm run generate-parser` (`package.json:20`, `jison grammar-parser.jison`) rebuilds `grammar-parser.js` from that grammar, and the result contains the eval again. Merging this file therefore leaves the source of truth on the vulnerable side, and the next regeneration reverts the fix.

**Preconditions:** a maintainer runs `npm run generate-parser` (documented script, needed for any grammar edit) and ships a release; a downstream application then passes user-controlled formula text to `parser.parse()`.

**Evidence:**
- Regenerating the checked-in grammar: `cp src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison /tmp/jg && npx jison grammar-parser.jison` (jison 0.4.18) emits `var arr = eval("[" + yytext + "]");` at generated line 226, plus a trailing `exports.main(...)` block, i.e. the output is not the file this PR adds.
- That regenerated parser executes formula text. With the pre-fix parser (same output) and the `yy` wiring of `src/parser.js:16-26`, `parser.parse("SUM([require('fs').writeFileSync('/tmp/pwned','yes')])")` creates `/tmp/pwned`; against the file added here (`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:225`, `yy.trimEdges(yytext).split(',')`) the same input yields the inert string `"require('fs').writeFileSync('/tmp/pwned'"`.
- The reverse direction holds too: this artifact cannot be produced from the grammar, so the two files will silently diverge on the next regeneration.

**Impact:** as merged, no runtime path is vulnerable — the added artifact has no `eval`/`Function`. The risk is self-inflicted rollback: one run of the project's documented generate step plus a release restores formula-driven arbitrary code execution in the host process (CVE-2020-6836), permanently, for every consumer of `hot-formula-parser`. It needs a developer action outside the runtime and nothing in `prepublish` triggers it, so I rate it low rather than high.

**Fix:** make the same one-line change in `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison:189-198` (`$$ = yy.trimEdges(yytext).split(',');`) and regenerate, so the grammar and the artifact carry the same non-eval action.

findings.title: Bracket-literal arguments become strings, so MAX/MIN/COUNT over them return 0 and AVERAGE errors
findings.body:
The new `ARRAY` action at `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:225` returns `yy.trimEdges(yytext).split(',')`, so every bracket literal now reaches formulas as an array of strings instead of numbers. Functions that do not coerce numeric strings then compute wrong values without raising an error.

**Evidence:** the repo's own dependency `@handsontable/formulajs@2.0.0` with the `yy` wiring of `src/parser.js:16-26`. Same input, added file (this PR) versus the pre-fix eval-based parser:

| formula | this PR | pre-fix |
|---|---|---|
| `MAX([1,2])` | `0` | `2` |
| `MIN([1,2])` | `0` | `1` |
| `COUNT([1,2])` | `0` | `2` |
| `AVERAGE([1,2])` | `#NUM!` | `1.5` |
| `SUM([1+1])` | `1` | `2` |
| `CONCATENATE(["a","b"])` | `"a""b"` | `ab` |
| `SUM([1,2],[3,4])` | `7` | `10` |

Items are neither trimmed nor typed, and quotes are kept: `SUM([1,2],[3,4])` passes `["1","2]","[3","4"]` to `callFunction` because the lexer rule `'['(.*)?']'` (`grammar-parser.jison:18`) matches across both bracket groups. No test under `test/` uses the bracket-literal syntax, so the suite does not catch any of this.

**Impact:** formulas that use bracket literals silently produce wrong numbers (or an error where a number was expected). The damage is bounded — the syntax is undocumented, untested and only reachable when a caller writes it explicitly — hence low severity, not a correctness break for the ranges, cell references and comma-separated arguments the tests cover.

**Fix:** keep the non-eval path but restore item types: split on `,`, trim each item, and convert items that are numeric literals with `Number(...)` before returning the array.

summary:
Review complete. Five findings recorded, all reproduced in the sandbox on Node 24.

The PR restores `lib/contextify.js`, the 699-line value bridge that vm2 loads into each sandbox context; `lib/main.js` already reads that file and `test/vm.js` exercises it. The file is upstream 3.6.10 code, i.e. the state just before the CVE-2019-10761 fix, so the escape is live: I reproduced host `process` access from `new VM()` with the issue-197 stack-exhaustion trigger, and confirmed that moving the two `WeakMap` lookups inside their `try` blocks stops it.

Two further problems survive that fix: the `Buffer` mock lookup calls a host builtin outside the trap's `try`, so a bare sandbox still escapes through `Buffer.foo`, and the mock itself is bypassable through `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, which hands back the real `allocUnsafe` and uninitialized host memory. The `freeze`/`protect` contracts have smaller, verified gaps. Overall the change cannot merge as-is: the first two findings are sandbox-to-host code execution, and the upstream patch alone does not close both.

findings.title: Stack-exhausted bridge call leaks a host RangeError, letting sandboxed code reach the host process
Sandbox escapes through the Buffer mock lookup when the stack is exhausted, even after the WeakMap fix
findings.body:
A stack-exhausted call into the host `hasOwnProperty` builtin at `lib/contextify.js:463`
throws a host-realm `RangeError` that is never converted, so sandboxed code receives it
and reaches the host `process` through `error.constructor.constructor`. The call sits
above the trap's own `try` (line 471), and it runs for every property read on `Buffer`
because `Buffer` is contextified with a `mock` (lines 686-693). A bare `new VM()` with no
embedder-supplied objects is enough, and the escape still works after both `WeakMap`
lookups (`:330-336`, `:624-630`) are moved inside their `try` blocks — i.e. the upstream
3.6.11 fix does not close this route.

**Evidence:** with a copy of this tree whose `Contextify.value`/`Decontextify.value`
lookups are inside their `try` blocks (upstream commit 4b22d70 shape), depth-scanning
against `Buffer.foo` still yields the host process:

```js
// sandbox code, default stack, no host objects supplied
function rec(k) { Buffer.foo; if (k > 1) rec(k - 1); }
function test(n) { try { rec(n); return 'ok'; } catch (e) { return e; } }
// binary-search the deepest non-throwing depth, then try depths just above it
const e = test(deepest + 1);
const p = e.constructor.constructor('return process')();   // host process
```

Output on that patched copy: `deepest non-throwing depth = 15628`,
`depth 15629 ESCAPED: "HOST process: pid=2614 argv=[...] typeof kill=function"`. An
unpatched run escapes the same way at `deepest + 1`. Suppressing the mock branch makes
the escape rate 0/20; scanning 20 depths above the boundary escaped 20/20.

**Impact:** same consequence as the recorded CVE-2019-10761 finding — untrusted
sandboxed code gets host-realm code execution in a default `new VM()` — and it survives
the fix that finding asks for, so it needs its own change. Reach crosses the sandbox
boundary, effect is permanent, so `high`.

**Fix:** keep the invariant that no host builtin runs outside a converting `try` inside
the `get` traps. Wrap the `mock` lookup (`:463`, `:491`, and the same shape at `:175`,
`:203`) so any thrown host exception is turned into a sandbox value, or replace
`host.Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(mock, key)` with a key list captured when the
mock is created, so no host code runs during trap dispatch.

findings.title: Buffer allocUnsafe mock can be bypassed through getOwnPropertyDescriptor, exposing uninitialized host memory
findings.body:
The `Buffer` mock that zeroes `allocUnsafe`/`allocUnsafeSlow`
(`lib/contextify.js:686-693`) is applied only in the proxy `get` traps (`:463`, `:491`).
`Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Buffer, 'allocUnsafe')` goes through the
`getOwnPropertyDescriptor` trap (`:517-547`), which never consults `mock`, so it returns
the real host `Buffer.allocUnsafe`. Sandboxed code calls it and reads uninitialized host
heap memory.

**Evidence:** node 24, this tree:

```
Buffer.allocUnsafe(16).toString('hex')                                        -> 00000000000000000000000000000000   (mock, zeroed)
Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Buffer,'allocUnsafe').value(16).toString('hex')-> 50b45e51ed7f000050b45e51ed7f0000   (raw host allocUnsafe)
Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Buffer,'allocUnsafe').value === Buffer.allocUnsafe -> false
```

`Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors(Buffer)` and `Reflect.getOwnPropertyDescriptor` reach
the same value. The mock's only purpose is to stop uninitialized allocation inside the
sandbox, so its descriptor path defeats the control.

**Impact:** sandboxed code reads bytes of host memory it is denied: Node's shared 8 KiB
Buffer pool and any larger host buffers still alive on the heap (which can hold request
bodies, tokens, keys). No code execution, but data leaves the sandbox boundary
permanently; `medium` reflects disclosure without a write primitive.

**Fix:** make the mock part of the descriptor path too — in `base.getOwnPropertyDescriptor`
(`:517`) and `base.defineProperty` (`:548`), return the mocked value when
`mock` owns the key (or hide `allocUnsafe`/`allocUnsafeSlow` from `ownKeys`), so every
route to a mocked property yields the same function.

findings.title: freeze() is silently ignored for objects already exposed to the sandbox
findings.body:
`VM.freeze(value, name)` / `NodeVM.freeze` do nothing when the object has already been
contextified once. `Contextify.value` returns the cached proxy before it looks at the
requested `traps` (`lib/contextify.js:627-629`), and `freeze` reaches the object through
that cache both in `Contextify.readonly` (`:679`) and in the follow-up `globalValue`
call (`lib/main.js:174-177`), so `FROZEN_TRAPS` is never installed on the proxy the
sandbox holds. Sandboxed code keeps write access to an object the embedder froze.

**Preconditions:** the object was exposed to the sandbox before `freeze` was called —
e.g. it was passed in `options.sandbox`, or read out of the sandbox earlier.

**Evidence:** node 24, this tree:

```js
const o = {a: 1};
const v = new VM({sandbox: {o}});   // proxy cached here without FROZEN_TRAPS
v.freeze(o, 'frozen');
v.run('frozen.a = 99');
// sandbox saw 99, host o.a === 99
```

Freezing a fresh object first (control) works: `v.freeze(p, 'fp'); v.run('fp.b = 42')`
leaves `p.b === 1`.

**Impact:** a documented read-only guarantee is silently unenforced, so the sandbox can
mutate host state the embedder believes is immovable. Needs the opt-in `freeze` call and
an earlier exposure, hence `low`.

**Fix:** make the protection level part of the proxy cache decision: when the requested
`traps`/`deepTraps` are stricter than the cached proxy's, build (and cache) the frozen
proxy for that object instead of returning the earlier unprotected one.

findings.title: protect() lets sandboxed code attach functions to protected host objects via function proxies and __proto__
findings.body:
`VM.protect(value, name)` promises that sandboxed code "cannot set functions as its
properties", but two paths in the new bridge let it do exactly that on the host object:

1. `Contextify.function` builds its proxy with `Contextify.object(fnc, assign(base, traps), deepTraps)`
   — `flags` is dropped (`lib/contextify.js:481`), so the `flags.protected` guards in
   `base.set` (`:506`) and `base.defineProperty` (`:552-553`) never fire for functions.
   `Contextify.instance` passes `flags` (`:427`); the function variant does not.
2. The `set` trap forwards the key verbatim (`object[key] = value`, `:511`), so
   `obj.__proto__ = {...}` reaches the host object's prototype setter even though
   `setPrototypeOf` is explicitly refused (`:578-580`). The replacement prototype is
   decontextified into a host proxy over the sandbox object, so host reads and calls on
   the protected object resolve to sandbox code.

**Evidence:** node 24, this tree:

```js
// 1: protected host function accepts a sandbox function
const fn = function hostFn() {};
const v = new VM(); v.protect(fn, 'pf');
v.run('pf.extra = function(){ return "sandbox"; }');
typeof fn.extra;                     // 'function' — sandbox function reached the host object

// 2: protected object's prototype replaced, sandbox method runs for host callers
const t = {safe: 1};
const w = new VM(); w.protect(t, 'pt');
w.run('pt.__proto__ = {greet: function(){ return "pwned"; }}');
t.greet();                           // 'pwned' — sandbox code, host receiver
```

**Impact:** the protection the embedder asked for is not enforced; host code that calls
methods or reads properties on a "protected" object can end up running sandbox code or
trusting sandbox-supplied values, which is how a `protect`ed config/options object turns
into an authorization bypass. Opt-in feature plus host code trusting the object, so
`low`.

**Fix:** forward `flags` in `Contextify.function` (`:481`) so callable proxies keep the
protected guard, and refuse the `__proto__` key in the `set`/`defineProperty` traps the
same way `setPrototypeOf` is refused, making the prototype immutable for wrapped objects.

summary:
Review complete. Both findings recorded.

**Summary:** PR #2 adds one file, `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js` — the jison 0.4.17 output for the existing `grammar-parser.jison`, which is the parser behind `Parser#parse()`. The file is byte-identical to the parser embedded in the shipped `dist/formula-parser.js`, so it is authentic generated code, not a hand edit; that also means it carries the package's known 3.0.0 behaviour rather than introducing anything new. I reviewed the generated actions, the parse loop and error-recovery machinery, and the lexer, and reproduced two issues by running the module directly and through the public API. The change does not follow the repository's own convention for generated artefacts: per CONTRIBUTING.md the `.jison` source should be the file under review, with the build output regenerated, so review comments and fixes belong there.

findings.title: Formula array literals are eval'd, giving arbitrary code execution (CVE-2020-6836)
findings.body:
`Parser#parse()` passes the matched text of an array literal to `eval()`, so any formula string that contains `NAME([...])` runs attacker JavaScript inside the host process. This is CVE-2020-6836 (CWE-94) in the file this PR adds.

The lexer rule `\[(.*)?\]` (`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:925`, rule index 13) takes everything from the first `[` to the last `]` of the input. The ARRAY action then evaluates it (`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:223-232`):

```js
var arr = eval("[" + yytext + "]");   // line 226
```

**Preconditions:** the host parses a formula it does not fully control that can reach a function-call argument list, which is ordinary use (`SUM([1,2])` is a valid formula).

**Evidence:** run against the shipped UMD build, which embeds the same generated parser (`dist/formula-parser.js:14123`):

```sh
node -e "const {Parser}=require('./dist/formula-parser.js');const p=new Parser();global.__HIT=null;
console.log(JSON.stringify(p.parse(\"SUM([1]];global.__HIT=require('child_process').execSync('id').toString()//])\")));
console.log(global.__HIT)"
# {"error":"#ERROR!","result":null}
# uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

`eval` receives `[[1]];global.__HIT=require('child_process').execSync('id').toString()//]]`. The injected statement runs, then `arr.forEach` throws a `TypeError` that `src/parser.js:52-60` converts to `#ERROR!`, so the caller sees an ordinary syntax error and the exploitation leaves no trace in the return value. `src/parser.js:42-50` performs no validation or length/character filtering before handing the string to the grammar parser.

**Impact:** arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the parsing process, driven by formula input. Reach crosses a trust boundary (a formula author gains code execution), persistence is permanent (commands run, data and secrets leave). NVD scores CVE-2020-6836 at 9.8. This repository defines no `critical` tier, so the finding is graded `high`.

**Fix:** remove the `eval` and parse the literal textually, as upstream 3.0.1 does: the `ARRAY` action in `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison` becomes `$$ = yy.trimEdges(yytext).split(',');`. Per CONTRIBUTING.md, edit the `.jison` source and regenerate with `npm run generate-parser` instead of editing `grammar-parser.js` by hand, and add a regression test under `test/integration/parsing/` that asserts an array-literal payload is not executed.

findings.title: Long letter-only formulas make the lexer backtrack quadratically and block the event loop
findings.body:
One formula of plain letters makes the lexer scan in quadratic time, blocking the JavaScript event loop for seconds. A 32 KB formula costs about 7 s of CPU; 100 KB would cost minutes.

Lexer rule 3 is `[A-Za-z]{1,}[A-Za-z_0-9\.]+(?=[(])` (`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:925`, rule index 3). Two overlapping quantifiers sit back to back in front of a lookahead that fails for every position when the input has no `(`. For a run of n letters the engine tries each split of the two quantifiers and backtracks the second one at each split, so the work is O(n²). The lexer retries every rule at every token start (`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:735-753`), and a long letter run matches only rule 10, so the scan is one quadratic attempt per parse.

**Evidence:** run through the public API (`dist/formula-parser.js` embeds the same generated parser):

```sh
node -e "const {Parser}=require('./dist/formula-parser.js');const p=new Parser();
for (const n of [8000,16000,32000]) {const t=Date.now(); p.parse('A'.repeat(n)); console.log(n, Date.now()-t, 'ms');}"
# 8000 393 ms
# 16000 1805 ms
# 32000 6793 ms
```

The growth factor is ~4 per doubling. Timing rule 3 in isolation reproduces it (8 000 → 416 ms, 16 000 → 1 741 ms, 32 000 → 6 382 ms), while the neighbouring single-quantifier rule `[A-Za-z\.]+(?=[(])` takes 0 ms on the same input, which pins the cost on the two-quantifier pattern.

**Impact:** in a service that evaluates user-supplied formulas, one ~32 KB cell value stalls every request sharing the process for several seconds; the input is otherwise unremarkable and `parse()` returns without error. Reach is broad for such a service and the effect is recoverable (re-triggerable at will), but I did not reproduce it in a deployment and the host must pass attacker-controlled strings, so it is graded `low`.

**Fix:** collapse rule 3 to a single quantifier, e.g. `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z_0-9.]*(?=[(])`, in `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison` and regenerate with `npm run generate-parser`. Alternatively bound the formula length in `src/parser.js` before parsing.

summary:
## Summary

PR #1 adds `library.js` (260 lines) to the plugin; relative to the pre-fix upstream version of that file, the substantive change is two lines in `Comments.init` that put `middleware.applyCSRF` in front of the two state-changing routes: `app.post('/comments/reply', …)` and `app.post('/comments/publish', …)` (library.js:251-252). I confirmed `middleware.applyCSRF` is csurf in NodeBB 1.12/1.13, that the GET route already mounts it and is the only source of the `_csrf` token (`library.js:105`) consumed by the hidden form fields in `public/templates/comments/comments.tpl:15,64,89`, and that both POSTs are the complete state-changing surface of the plugin — a live express+csurf harness reproduced `403 EBADCSRFTOKEN` for tokenless and forged-token POSTs while legitimate GET-minted tokens succeed. The fix therefore closes the reported CSRF hole (CVE-2020-15156) without introducing a new one, and I filed no findings. Two things worth knowing outside the scope of this diff: the file still contains older upstream weaknesses the fix does not touch (unvalidated `req.body.url` in `res.redirect` at `library.js:131,134`, raw HTML concatenation of the stored URL in `addLinkbackToArticle` at `library.js:219`, and errors from `async.parallel` never checked at `library.js:61,173`), and cross-origin posting from a blog on a genuinely different site may now be rejected when NodeBB 1.13+ serves HTTPS with its `SameSite=Strict` csurf cookie.

Review complete. Workspace is clean and all findings are recorded.

**Summary**

The PR adds `index.js`, the `serialize-javascript` implementation — byte-identical to upstream v3.1.0, which is the released fix for CVE-2020-7660 (a `randombytes`-derived per-process UID plus a backslash guard on the placeholder pass). I checked the vulnerability itself: upstream's own regression case, a string value mimicking `"@__R-<UID>-0__@"`, is no longer substituted, and the reported exploit class (placeholder injection through escaped quotes, `toJSON`, `String` objects, nested Map/Set, varying backslash parity) does not get through. The repository's 66 existing tests pass, so the import is functionally equivalent to the released library. The change is not shippable as it stands, however: the file's new runtime dependency is absent from the manifest, and a clean `npm ci` plus test run fails at `require` time — that, and the defects carried in from the upstream copy, are the findings above.

findings.title: Undeclared randombytes dependency makes the package fail to load
findings.body:
`index.js` requires `randombytes` at load time, but `package.json` still declares no
`dependencies` and `package-lock.json` contains no `randombytes` entry. Any clean
install — including this repository's own test run — fails at `require` time:
`Error: Cannot find module 'randombytes'`. The package's only export is unusable until
someone installs the missing module by hand.

**Evidence:**

- `index.js:9` — `var randomBytes = require('randombytes');`, called at module load by
  `var UID = generateUID();` (`index.js:13`, `index.js:37-44`), so the failure is at
  `require('serialize-javascript')`, not on first use.
- `package.json` has `devDependencies` only; `grep -c randombytes package-lock.json`
  returns `0`.
- Fresh checkout, `npm ci` (exit 0), then `npx mocha test/unit`:
  ```
  Error: Cannot find module 'randombytes'
  Require stack:
  - /tmp/clone/index.js
  - /tmp/clone/test/unit/serialize.js
  ```
  The suite's 66 tests pass only after `npm install randombytes` by hand.
- Consumer path: `npm pack` then `npm install ./serialize-javascript-3.0.0.tgz --omit=dev`
  installs exactly one package (itself), and `node -e 'require("serialize-javascript")'`
  throws the same `Cannot find module 'randombytes'`.

**Impact:** Broad reach (every consumer of the package and the repo's own CI run fails),
permanent (nothing in the package recovers it; only a release that declares the
dependency fixes it) — `high`.

**Fix:** declare the runtime dependency the file already uses, e.g.
`"dependencies": { "randombytes": "^2.1.0" }` in `package.json`, and regenerate
`package-lock.json`. Upstream 3.1.0 ships exactly that.

findings.title: ignoreFunction deletes function properties from the caller's live object
findings.body:
`serialize(obj, { ignoreFunction: true })` deletes every function-valued property from
the object the caller passed in, instead of skipping those properties on output. The
caller's object is left damaged, and frozen objects now throw.

**Preconditions:** the caller opts into `ignoreFunction: true` and keeps using the object
after serializing it (config/model objects, an express-state style render state).

**Evidence:**

The replacer calls `deleteFunctions(value)` for every visited value (`index.js:79-81`),
which runs `delete obj[key]` on that object (`index.js:46-56`, delete at `index.js:54`).
`'use strict'` (`index.js:7`) makes a failed delete throw.

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  var cfg={n:1,handler:function(){},nested:{id:7,m:function(){}}};
  console.log(s(cfg,{ignoreFunction:true}));
  console.log(Object.keys(cfg), Object.keys(cfg.nested), typeof cfg.handler)'
{"n":1,"nested":{"id":7}}
[ 'n', 'nested' ] [ 'id' ] undefined
```

Frozen input: `s(Object.freeze({a:1,f:function(){}}), {ignoreFunction:true})` throws
`TypeError: Cannot delete property 'f' of #<Object>`, while `JSON.stringify` on the same
object works. README:110-111 describes the option as "just treat function like
`JSON.stringify` do", and `JSON.stringify` never mutates its input; the repo's own test
(`test/unit/serialize.js:459-480`) only asserts the output string and never re-reads the
object, so it does not catch this. Returning `undefined` from the replacer for function
values produces the identical output without touching the input.

**Impact:** Contained reach (the caller's process), permanent (deleted properties cannot
be restored) — `medium` before discounts; the non-default opt-in setting and the fact
that only the caller's own object is affected bring it to `low`.

**Fix:** stop mutating. When `options.ignoreFunction` is set, return `undefined` from the
replacer for `typeof origValue === 'function'` and drop the `deleteFunctions` call
(`index.js:79-81`). Later upstream releases no longer delete functions.

findings.title: Shorthand methods whose bodies contain an arrow or nested function serialize to invalid JavaScript
findings.body:
A method defined in object-shorthand form is emitted verbatim when its body happens to
contain `=>` or `function(`, so `serialize()` returns text that is not a JavaScript
expression. The caller only finds out when the documented deserialization step
(`eval('(' + serialized + ')')`, README:122-124) throws `SyntaxError`.

**Evidence:**

`IS_PURE_FUNCTION = /function.*?\(/` (`index.js:17`) and `IS_ARROW_FUNCTION = /.*?=>.*?/`
(`index.js:18`) are unanchored, so they match anywhere in the source, including inside a
method body. The early returns at `index.js:132-139` then skip the method-to-function
rewrite at `index.js:151-156`.

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  var o={id:1}; o.sum={sum(){ return [1,2].reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0); }}.sum;
  var out=s(o); console.log(out); eval("("+out+")")'
{"id":1,"sum":sum(){ return [1,2].reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0); }}
SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{'
```

Same with a nested function in the body (`cb(){ return function(z){return z;} }` →
`{"id":1,"cb":cb(){ return function(z){ return z; }; }}` → `SyntaxError`). The control
case the test suite covers, `{ok(){ return true; }}` (`test/unit/serialize.js:121-127`),
is rewritten correctly to `function(){ return true; }`, which is why the tests pass.

**Impact:** Contained reach (the affected payload only), recoverable (a code change fixes
it) — `low`. The failure is silent at serialize time and surfaces as a thrown
`SyntaxError` in the browser, so the whole inline script of the page stops running.

**Fix:** anchor both patterns to the start of the source (a function expression starts
with `function`/`async function`/an arrow head), or move the method rewrite ahead of
these tests. Upstream later replaced them with
`/^(?:async…)?function\b/` and `/^(?:async…)?(?:\([\s\S]*?\)|[^\s()]+)\s*=>/`.

findings.title: Stateful native-function regex lets unparseable output through after one caught error
findings.body:
`IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP` is a module-level `/g` regex used with `.test()`, so a successful
match leaves `lastIndex` set and the next call starts scanning from the middle of the
string. After any caller catches one `TypeError`, the following native function slips
past the guard and is emitted as `function max() { [native code] }`, which is not valid
JavaScript, instead of being rejected.

**Evidence:**

`index.js:16` declares `/\{\s*\[native code\]\s*\}/g`; `index.js:127` uses `.test()` and
never resets `lastIndex`.

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  for (var i=1;i<=4;i++){ try { console.log("call",i,JSON.stringify(s(Math.max))); }
                          catch(e){ console.log("call",i,"THREW",e.message); } }'
call 1 THREW Serializing native function: max
call 2 Math.max -> "function max() { [native code] }"
call 3 THREW Serializing native function: max
call 4 Math.max -> "function max() { [native code] }"
```

`eval('(' + out + ')')` on the call-2 output throws `SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier
