'code'`. The trigger is a caller that survives the first error (a batch exporter, a
retry, a web handler that logs and continues); the state then alternates per call.

The same unanchored text match also rejects user functions that merely mention
`{ [native code] }` in a comment or string literal, and such a false-positive throw
poisons `lastIndex` in the same way. `test/unit/serialize.js:113-119` is single-shot, so
it passes.

**Impact:** Contained reach, transient state (it clears itself) — `info`. The guard that
exists to keep unparseable output out of the string silently stops working half the
time, and the bad output fails much later at parse time.

**Fix:** drop the `g` flag so `.test()` is stateless (current upstream main uses
`/\{\s*\[native code\]\s*\}/`), or reset `lastIndex` before testing.

findings.title: Function bodies bypass the HTML/line-terminator escaping, so they can close the embedding script element
findings.body:
The `<`, `>`, `/`, U+2028 and U+2029 escaping that makes the output safe to embed in an
HTML `<script>` element never applies to function bodies, because function sources are
inserted after the escaping pass. A serialized function containing `</script>` reaches
the output raw, while the same characters in a string value are escaped.

**Preconditions:** the application serializes a function whose source text contains
attacker-influenced characters — e.g. `new Function(userInput)`, a compiled template
handler, or a handler assembled by string concatenation. Objects made only of
application-written code are unaffected.

**Evidence:**

Escaping happens on the JSON text at `index.js:190-193`; `serializeFunc(fn)` runs
afterwards inside the placeholder replacement at `index.js:236`.

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  console.log(s(function(){ return "</script><script>alert(1)</script>"; }))'
function (){ return "</script><script>alert(1)</script>"; }

$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js"); console.log(s("</script>"))'
"\u003C\u002Fscript\u003E"
```

RegExp and Map/Set values are re-serialized through `serialize()` (`index.js:215`,
`index.js:219`, `index.js:223`) and are therefore escaped; function bodies are the one
path that bypasses it. Embedding the first output in a `<script>` element terminates the
element at the first `</script>`. README:62-76 states the escaping is what makes the
output safe to embed.

**Impact:** A reachable copy would cross a trust boundary (script injection in the page
that embeds the output), but it needs attacker-influenced function source, which is
outside this library; with that precondition the severity is `low`.

**Fix:** run the function source through the same escape map before it is inserted, e.g.
`serializedFn.replace(UNSAFE_CHARS_REGEXP, escapeUnsafeChars)` when
`options.unsafe !== true`. Upstream later added exactly this (`escapeFunctionBody`).

summary:
Verification complete. The added `server.js` is the genuine remediation for CVE-2017-16107 (upstream commit `7b3b4e5`, "Resolve directory traversal attack"), and I confirmed empirically that the guard holds.

What I checked:
- **Traversal guard** (`server.js:10`): `path.normalize(req.url)` then `.replace(/^(\.\.[\/\\])+/, '')`. I ran the real file under Node 24 with `ws` installed and sent raw request targets: `/../../../../etc/passwd`, `/./../../etc/passwd`, `//..//..//etc/passwd`, `..%2f..%2f…`, `..\..\`, duplicate-slash and semicolon variants, and absolute-form `http://x/../../etc/passwd`. Every request resolved inside `__dirname` (ENOENT for `<dir>/etc/passwd`, no read of `/etc/passwd`).
- **Why it holds**: Node's HTTP parser rejects relative request targets (400), so `req.url` is always root-anchored or absolute-form; `path.normalize` drops `..` at the root, and when a path is relative the leftover leading `..` sequences are exactly what the regex strips. A 4,352-payload fuzz of the normalize→strip→concat transform produced zero escapes, and `path.win32` semantics for the same payloads also stay inside the root (so the string concatenation at line 10 is not exploitable on Windows either).
- **Unchanged code that relies on this**: nothing else in the repo consumes the HTTP handler; `index.html`/`websocketworker.js` only use the WebSocket port, which is bound to `localhost` (`server.js:5`).

Not filed (too weak to meet the finding bar): error responses echo the absolute install path with status 200 (`server.js:17-19`), and the file server binds all interfaces (`server.js:34`) while serving the package directory. Both are minor hygiene observations on a demo server, not regressions this change introduces against its stated purpose.

**Summary:** The PR adds `server.js`, which starts a WebSocket relay and a static HTTP server, and it contains the CVE-2017-16107 directory-traversal fix (`path.normalize` plus stripping of leading `../`/`..\` sequences) rather than the vulnerable `__dirname + req.url` construct. I reproduced the handler and could not escape the served directory with any reachable request form on POSIX or Windows, so the fix is effective and the change looks safe to merge. No findings recorded.

## Summary

The change adds `library.js`, the server half of the NodeBB blog-comments plugin: three Express routes (`/comments/get`, `/comments/reply`, `/comments/publish`) plus hooks that render an admin link and a linkback to the source article. The file is byte-identical to the published 0.6.3 release, i.e. the pre-fix version of CVE-2020-15156.

Two findings are recorded. The significant one is that both POST routes are mounted without `middleware.applyCSRF` (library.js:251-252) although the plugin's own forms already send a `_csrf` token and the sibling GET route validates it; upstream 0.7.0 fixed exactly this, and NodeBB core loads plugin routes with no router-level CSRF. I also recorded a small unvalidated redirect in the reply handler.

Things I checked and chose not to report: the unescaped HTML sink in `addLinkbackToArticle` (library.js:219) is unreachable under the declared `^1.12.0` compatibility, because NodeBB ≥0.5 fires `filter:posts.custom_profile_info` with `{profile, uid}` and no `pid`, so `url` is always empty there; the remaining defects in the file (unguarded `JSON.parse(req.body.cid)` at library.js:145, ignored `err` in `getCommentData`, `Comments.template` populated after startup) only produce 500s or an empty widget, which is below reporting weight.

findings.title: Cross-site form posts can reply and publish as a logged-in user
findings.body:
`POST /comments/reply` and `POST /comments/publish` are mounted without
`middleware.applyCSRF` (library.js:251-252), while the sibling GET route uses it
(library.js:250). Any web page can therefore auto-submit a form to those routes with the
visitor's forum session and have the server act as that user: a reply authored in the
victim's name in an attacker-chosen topic (`Comments.replyToComment`, library.js:118-136,
takes `content`, `tid` and `url` from the body and `uid` from the session), or, when the
victim is an administrator or a member of the `publishers` group, a whole topic published
into an attacker-chosen category (`Comments.publishArticle`, library.js:138-201).

**Preconditions:** the victim is logged in and visits the attacker's page; for
`/comments/publish`, the victim must hold the admin or `publishers` role, which is the
only gate that handler applies (library.js:174).

**Evidence:** NodeBB applies CSRF per route — `middleware.applyCSRF = csrf()`
(NodeBB v1.12.0 `src/middleware/index.js:34`) is attached explicitly in core route
definitions, and plugin routes are mounted through `plugins.reloadRoutes` with no
router-level CSRF (NodeBB v1.12.0 `src/routes/index.js:113`). The plugin's own reply and
publish forms already send a token that the server never checks:
`<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="{token}" />`
(public/templates/comments/comments.tpl:15,64,89). Upstream fixed exactly this in 0.7.0 by
adding `middleware.applyCSRF` to both routes (commit cf43beedb05131937ef46f365ab0a0c6fa6ac618,
GHSA-43m5-c88r-cjvv / CVE-2020-15156).

**Impact:** medium. Reach crosses a trust boundary — content is created and attributed to
a victim who never acted. Persistence is recoverable: the post or topic can be deleted, so
nothing is lost permanently. Two limits reduce it: the publish path needs a privileged
victim, and browsers that now default to `SameSite=Lax` withhold cookies from cross-site
POSTs (NodeBB 1.12 sets no `SameSite` on its session cookie), leaving mainly the
Lax+POST grace window on recent cookies. The upstream advisory rates this MODERATE.

**Fix:** validate the CSRF token on both POST routes — `app.post('/comments/reply',
middleware.applyCSRF, Comments.replyToComment)` and the same for `/comments/publish`. The
client already posts `_csrf`, so no client change is needed.

findings.title: Reply endpoint redirects to an unvalidated URL from the request body
findings.body:
`Comments.replyToComment` redirects to a URL taken straight from the request body
(library.js:121, 131, 134):

	res.redirect(url + '#nodebb-comments');

so a form post carrying `url=https://attacker.example/` ends on the attacker's site while
the browser was on the forum. `err.message` is concatenated into the same Location value
on the error path (library.js:131). Nothing checks `url` against the configured blog hosts
(`blog-comments:url`, used for that purpose elsewhere at library.js:62-74 and 148-160).

**Evidence:** library.js:118-136; the value is never validated or allowlisted, and the
redirect is issued for both success and failure. The same pattern survives in later
releases (0.8.0 library.js:120-122), so it is not addressed by the CSRF fix.

**Impact:** info. The requester is redirected to a destination the attacker picks, which
aids phishing (`forum posted your comment, continue here`); no data or capability is
gained and the effect clears with the response. It is contained to the single request and
the victim must submit the post in the first place.

**Fix:** only redirect to a host allowlisted in `blog-comments:url` (or to
`req.headers.referer` when it matches), and fall back to `/` otherwise.

summary:
Review complete.

**What the change does:** PR #1 restores `lib/node-http-proxy.js`, the package entry point that the fixture baseline deleted, using the content of upstream commit `0e36912` ("Fixed large DoS vector in the middleware implementation") — the fix for CVE-2017-16014. Compared with the pre-fix content (`0c71119e`), the only difference is the `next(err)` branch of `exports.stack` (lib/node-http-proxy.js:223-239): instead of `throw err`, it answers 500 or destroys a response whose headers already went out. Everything else in the tree is byte-identical to upstream `0c71119e`.

**Assessment:** The change is correct for its stated purpose. I reproduced the pre-fix crash (middleware error → uncaught exception, process exit) and confirmed the post-fix behaviour returns a 500 and keeps the server alive; `res._headerSent`, `res.destroy()` and `setHeader` all exist in the declared engine range (Node 0.4.x/0.5.x), so the fix is valid there. One low finding remains: the error handler itself can throw when a middleware has rendered headers via `writeHead` without flushing, so the guard checks the wrong state. The many v0.6.3 API quirks in the restored file (e.g. `createServer({router: ...})` throwing in `_getAgent`) are pre-existing on both sides of the CVE fix and were repaired upstream during the v0.7.0 rewrite, so I did not report them as regressions.

findings.title: Middleware error path crashes the process when headers were written but not flushed
findings.body:
The new `next(err)` branch in `stack()` still lets a middleware error kill the
process when the response headers have been written but nothing has been flushed.
`res._headerSent` answers "have body bytes gone to the socket", not "are headers
committed". A middleware that calls `res.writeHead(...)` and then reports an error
leaves `_header` set and `_headerSent === false`, so the code takes the `else`
branch at lib/node-http-proxy.js:230 and calls `res.setHeader(...)`, which throws
"Can't set headers after they are sent". The exception unwinds out of the
middleware's own `next(err)` frame (lib/node-http-proxy.js:242) inside the HTTP
request listener; nothing catches it, so the process exits.

**Preconditions:** a stack layer calls `res.writeHead(...)` (or otherwise renders
headers) and then calls `next(err)` before any body byte is written - e.g. a layer
that stamps status/headers early and then fails on a template or upstream read.
Errors raised before `writeHead` (500 path) and after a body write (destroy path)
are handled.

**Evidence:**
- Node 0.4.12 `lib/http.js`: `writeHead` -> `_storeHeader` sets `this._header` and
  `this._headerSent = false` (lines 512-513); `setHeader` throws when `this._header`
  is set (lines 526-528); `_headerSent` turns true only in `_send`, on the first body
  write or `end`. Node 0.5.10 and 0.6.x are the same.
- lib/node-http-proxy.js:225 tests `res._headerSent`; lib/node-http-proxy.js:230
  then calls `res.setHeader`.
- Reproduction against the checked-out module (Node 24, no file edits): a stack
  middleware doing `res.writeHead(200, {'Content-Type':'text/html'}); next(new Error('boom'))`
  behind `http.createServer` exits the process with `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` thrown
  at lib/node-http-proxy.js:230; with an `uncaughtException` handler installed to
  observe it, the client gets no response. The same middleware without `writeHead`
  returns 500, and a middleware that writes a body first hits the `res.destroy()`
  branch. On Node >= 0.6 the guard is dead code (`headersSent` replaced
  `_headerSent`), which widens the same crash to every "headers already sent" error.

**Impact:** A middleware error after early header writing terminates the proxy
process - the availability failure this change is meant to remove. The process can
be restarted, and the trigger depends on the embedding application's middleware
shape, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Make the branch unable to throw: choose it from "headers committed"
(`res._header` on 0.4/0.5, `res.headersSent` later) and wrap the whole branch in
try/catch that falls back to destroying the socket.

summary:
Review complete.

The PR adds `lib/node-http-proxy.js` (307 lines), the module entry point of http-proxy 0.6.x: `createServer` argument parsing, the connect-style `stack` adapter, request `buffer`, and the `_getAgent`/`_getProtocol`/`_getBase` helpers that `lib/node-http-proxy/http-proxy.js` calls during construction. The file is byte-identical to upstream `0c71119e` (the commit recorded for the benchmark), i.e. the state just before the 0.7.0 fix, and I confirmed it reproduces CVE-2017-16014 rather than carrying the fix.

I traced the rest of the file outward to its consumers (`http-proxy.js`, `bin/node-http-proxy`, `examples/`, README) and found the remaining rough edges — `createServer` dropping all but the last function argument, `createServer(callback)` failing at construction, `options.https` truthiness choosing the listener type, `buffer` reuse semantics — are this upstream snapshot's own behaviour, with the repo's docs mid-refactor (README still shows `proxy.buffer(req)` and `proxyRequest(req, res, {host, port})` forms the unchanged sub-modules don't implement), so I did not file them. One confirmed finding is recorded: the uncaught throw on the middleware error path.

findings.title: Middleware error passed to next() throws inside the request handler and kills the proxy process
findings.body:
A middleware error passed to `next(err)` is thrown from inside the HTTP server's
`request` listener, so Node treats it as an uncaught exception and exits the whole
proxy process. One request that makes a middleware fail takes down every site the
proxy fronts, and the client that triggered it gets no response.

`exports.stack` (`lib/node-http-proxy.js:218-240`) is the adapter that turns a
connect-style middleware array into the handler passed to `http.createServer`. Its
`next` function does the only error handling the chain has:

```js
next = function (err) {          // :223
  if (err) {
    throw err;                   // :225
  }
  child(req, res);               // :231
}
```

The throw happens synchronously in the listener created at `:222` and dispatched at
`:235`. There is no `try`/`catch` anywhere in this file, and nothing in
`lib/node-http-proxy/http-proxy.js` catches on this path, so the exception reaches
Node's top level and the process terminates. This is CVE-2017-16014
(GHSA-9xw9-pvgv-6p76), fixed upstream in 0.7.0.

**Preconditions:** The application builds its handler with the exported
`httpProxy.stack(middlewares, proxy)` and at least one middleware passes a truthy
error to `next` (failed auth check, malformed body, failed upstream lookup). Note
that `createServer` in this snapshot (`lib/node-http-proxy.js:103-106`) does not
route through `stack`, so the vulnerable path is only reachable through the explicit
`stack` API.

**Evidence:** Reproduction against this checkout (copied to `/tmp/selfcheck`, only
`pkginfo` stubbed), Node v24:

```js
var handle = httpProxy.stack([
  function (req, res, next) { next(new Error('bad token')); }
], proxy);
http.createServer(handle).listen(18191);
```

```
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:18191/        -> no response (http_code=000)
$ cat server.log
/tmp/selfcheck/lib/node-http-proxy.js:225
          throw err;
          ^
Error: bad token
    at Server.handle (/tmp/selfcheck/lib/node-http-proxy.js:235:7)
    at Server.emit (node:events:514:28)
    at parserOnIncoming (node:_http_server:1293:12)
Node.js v24.22.2                       <- server exited, exit code 1
```

The same crash occurs when `next(err)` is called asynchronously from a middleware
callback. The only escape is a process-wide `uncaughtException` handler, which leaves
the request hanging because the library never ends the response.

**Impact:** Unauthenticated denial of service. Any single request that makes a
middleware error kills the process, so every client the proxy serves loses service
until it is restarted. Reach is broad (all traffic through the process); persistence
is recoverable (a restart restores it, nothing is lost), which is `medium` under the
repository's impact matrix. Upstream rates the availability impact high
(CVSS A:H); the discount here is only that reachability requires the application to
use the `stack` API, i.e. app-side setup rather than the default `createServer`
path.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant that a middleware error becomes a response and never
escapes the request handler. Replace the throw with: log `err.stack`; if the
response headers were already sent, destroy the response; otherwise reply `500
text/plain` and `end()`; then `return`. Guard the success path the same way — a final
middleware that calls `next()` without an error currently throws `TypeError:
child is not a function` at `:231` and crashes the process identically, so wrap
`child(req, res)` in `if (child)`. Upstream 0.7.0 fixes both in this function.

summary:
This PR adds `index.ts`, the implementation of `@actions/http-client` at version 1.0.8; the added blob is byte-identical to upstream `cde0b329`, the merge of the CVE-2020-11021 fix, so the change is that security patch applied verbatim and the redirect guard it adds works for the per-call `headers` path covered by `__tests__/basics.test.ts`.

I traced and reproduced the redirect logic against local servers: the guard closes the per-call-header leak but not the two other supported ways of supplying credentials, and it handles relative `Location` headers badly. Two low-severity findings are recorded, both reproduced against the compiled build rather than argued.

The rest of the file (proxy/agent selection, retry loop, response handling) also has rough edges, but each needs non-default options and matches long-standing upstream behavior rather than something this change altered, so I left them unreported.

findings.title: Cross-host redirect still forwards handler-injected and client-level Authorization headers
findings.body:
The cross-host redirect guard deletes `authorization` only from the per-call
`headers` object. Auth supplied the two other supported ways -- a credential
handler (`BasicCredentialHandler`, `BearerCredentialHandler`,
`PersonalAccessTokenCredentialHandler`) or `requestOptions.headers` on the
client -- is re-added on the redirected request and goes to the new host.

**Preconditions:** the client is built with a credential handler, or with
`requestOptions.headers` containing an authorization value. That is the
documented way to authenticate with this library (`__tests__/auth.test.ts`).
The first host then answers 3xx with a `Location` on another hostname.

**Evidence:** `index.ts:390-397` strips from `headers`, then `index.ts:400`
calls `_prepareRequest(verb, parsedRedirectUrl, headers)`, which builds a fresh
header map (`index.ts:553`) and runs `handler.prepareRequest(info.options)`
(`index.ts:561-566`) -- and each handler writes `options.headers['Authorization']`
(`auth.ts:13`, `auth.ts:42`, `auth.ts:70`). The strip therefore never sees the
header that is actually sent. Reproduced with the compiled `_out` and two local
servers (`127.0.0.1` redirector -> 302 -> `localhost` receiver):

```
per-call {authorization: 'shhh'}          -> receiver got: undefined      (guard works)
new HttpClient('t', [BearerCredentialHandler('SEKRET-TOKEN')])
                                          -> receiver got: Bearer SEKRET-TOKEN
new HttpClient('t', [], {headers: {authorization: 'client-level-secret'}})
                                          -> receiver got: client-level-secret
```

Secondary effect of the same lines: `delete headers[header]` (`index.ts:394`)
mutates the caller's object. Reusing one headers object across requests loses
auth permanently -- after the redirect above the caller's
`{authorization: 'reuse-secret'}` object was `{}`, and the next request to the
original host carried no authorization header.

**Impact:** a host that redirects off-origin receives the caller's token
(measured: the receiver logged the token), which is the leak class this change
is meant to close. Graded `low`: it needs a non-default client configuration
(handler / `requestOptions.headers`) and an origin that redirects to a host it
does not own, and the damage is a credential exposed to that host.

**Fix:** strip after the headers that will actually be sent are assembled, not
on the caller's input: in `_prepareRequest`, when the target hostname differs
from the original request's hostname, delete authorization from the merged
`info.options.headers` after the handler loop, and work on a copy so the
caller's object is never modified.

findings.title: Relative Location redirect sends the follow-up request to localhost:80
findings.body:
A relative `Location` header makes the client send the follow-up request to
`127.0.0.1:80` instead of the original host.

**Evidence:** `index.ts:374` parses the header with `url.parse(redirectUrl)`,
so `/login` yields `{protocol: null, hostname: null, pathname: '/login'}`.
`_prepareRequest` then takes the non-SSL branch and sets
`info.options.host = null` (`index.ts:547`) with the default port 80
(`index.ts:541-546`); Node treats a null host as `localhost`. Reproduced with
the compiled `_out` and a local server answering `302 Location: /rel-target`:
the client failed with `connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:80` and the original
server never saw the follow-up request. The same relative-location branch also
trips the cross-host guard (`null !== <host>`) and drops authorization.

**Impact:** any server that returns an RFC 7231 relative `Location` -- common
for `/login` and session redirects -- breaks the request when nothing listens
on port 80, and when a service does listen there the request method, path and
caller headers (cookies, custom tokens) reach an unrelated local service.
Graded `low`: contained to the redirected request, and normally surfaces as a
visible connection error.

**Fix:** resolve the redirect target against the current request URL before
parsing, e.g. `url.resolve(currentUrlHref, redirectUrl)` (or
`new URL(redirectUrl, currentUrlHref)`), and treat a null hostname as the
current host rather than letting it default to localhost.

summary:
The change adds one new file, `server.js`: a demo daemon that serves static files over HTTP on 8080, echoes WebSocket messages on loopback 8090, broadcasts its own stdin to connected clients, and installs a process-wide `uncaughtException` handler. It is small but it is a network-facing file server written without any path, origin or stream-lifecycle checks.

All three surfaced issues were reproduced against the actual code, not argued from inspection: arbitrary file read through unnormalized `req.url` on a listener bound to all interfaces (the CVE this fixture targets), an unbounded file-descriptor leak from aborted downloads that permanently wedges both listeners, and cross-site WebSocket hijacking of the stdin broadcast from any web origin. It needs rework before merge.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read any file on the server host via the static file handler
findings.body:
`GET /../../../../etc/passwd` is served verbatim: `req.url` is concatenated onto `__dirname` with no normalization and no root check (server.js:9). `hserver.listen(8080)` passes no host (server.js:33), so the listener binds `::` and accepts requests from any peer on the network, not just the machine's operator.

**Preconditions:** none beyond the process running.

**Evidence:** with `node server.js` running, `curl --path-as-is 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/../../../../../../etc/passwd'` returns `200`, 878 bytes, first line `root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash`. The same request against the host's non-loopback address also returns the file (listener verified on `::`, `172.17.0.12:8080/package.json` → 200). Any file the process can read is fetchable, including `/proc/self/environ` and the process's own sources.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated remote caller reads every file the process can read — secrets, credentials, environment, source. Reach crosses a trust boundary (a network peer obtains files its role denies) on a listener exposed on all interfaces; the disclosure is permanent, since served bytes cannot be recalled. No discount applies: no non-default setting and no precondition beyond reachability. Policy: crosses a trust boundary + permanent = high.

**Fix:** Confine every served path to the served directory. Take the pathname only (`url.parse(req.url).pathname`), resolve it with `path.resolve(__dirname, pathname)` so `..` collapses, and reject anything that does not start with `path.resolve(__dirname) + path.sep`. Answer 404 instead of streaming.

findings.title: A handful of aborted downloads leaks file descriptors until the service dies
findings.body:
`rs` is piped to `res` (server.js:14) but nothing destroys it when the response goes away. On a client abort, Node's pipe teardown only unpipes and pauses the source; `autoClose` (server.js:11) closes the descriptor only on `'end'` or `'error'`. The open file descriptor therefore stays for the life of the process. Repeated aborted downloads accumulate until `EMFILE`, after which every request gets `200` and an `EMFILE` error body (server.js:17) and both listeners stop serving.

**Preconditions:** the caller can reach the HTTP listener (it binds `::`, server.js:33) and can abort a response early.

**Evidence:** measured on Node 24.22.2 with this file, only the ports remapped. Baseline 20 fds; +1 per aborted request, linearly — 60 aborted `curl --max-time 0.2` requests → 80 fds, 260 → 292 open descriptors on the served file; 40 s idle and 8 forced `global.gc()` released none. Under `ulimit -n 64`, ~43 aborted requests left 63 fds and every later request, including a legitimate one, returned `200` with `Error: EMFILE: too many open files, open '.../small.bin'`.

**Impact:** Unauthenticated remote exhaustion of file descriptors that takes down the HTTP and WebSocket listeners for all users; only an operator restart restores service. Reach is broad (every user of the service), persistence recoverable, so medium. Nothing bounds it: the `uncaughtException` handler (server.js:40) keeps the wedged process alive instead of letting a supervisor restart it.

**Fix:** Tear the source down with the response: `res.on('close', function(){ rs.destroy(); })`, or use `stream.pipeline(rs, res, cb)`, which performs that teardown itself.

findings.title: Any web page can attach to the pooled WebSocket and read what is piped into stdin
findings.body:
The WebSocket listener (server.js:3-6) sets no `verifyClient`, no `origin` and no `path` option, and every `process.stdin` chunk is written to every entry in `clients[]` (server.js:34-39). A page on any origin can connect to the pooled socket and receive everything the operator pipes into the server.

**Preconditions:** the victim runs `node server.js` with meaningful data on stdin (a piped log, shell output, credentials) and loads an attacker page in a browser on that machine.

**Evidence:** the handshake with `Origin: http://attacker.example`, `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` and an arbitrary path was answered `101 Switching Protocols`; after the process wrote `TOPSECRET-FROM-STDIN\n` to stdin, the socket received it. Three clients with origins `http://attacker.example`, `https://evil.test` and `null` all received the broadcast.

**Impact:** Cross-site WebSocket hijacking: attacker-controlled web content reads local process output its origin should never see. Reach crosses a trust boundary and disclosure is permanent, but the listener is loopback-only (`host: 'localhost'`, resolved to `::1`) and recent Chrome gates public→loopback connections with Local Network Access, so this needs a browser without that gate (Firefox, Safari) or a user granting the prompt. Two discounts → medium.

**Fix:** Validate the handshake: pass a `verifyClient` that rejects any `Origin` not explicitly allowed, and gate on a shared token or an unguessable path. The loopback bind is not an access control.

summary:
Review complete. Summary:

The change adds `index.js`, a 219-line reimplementation of `serialize-javascript` v3.0.0 (byte-identical to the upstream tag), which serializes objects containing RegExps, Dates, Maps, Sets, functions, `undefined` and `Infinity` via string placeholders spliced back after `JSON.stringify`. The existing test suite passes (66 tests), and the core design works for trusted data. The problem is that this is the pre-3.1.0 code: the placeholder substitution is not confined to real JSON string tokens, so the library's documented escaping guarantee does not hold for attacker-controlled strings — the exact defect behind CVE-2020-7660, whose upstream fix (a preceding-backslash guard plus a CSPRNG-derived UID) is absent here. Two smaller defects in the newly added code — destructive `ignoreFunction` handling and a stateful `lastIndex` on the native-function guard — are recorded as well. I would not merge this version as-is.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled strings break out of their JSON string literal and land in code position
findings.body:
Attacker-controlled strings inside serialized data are not kept inside their JSON
string literal: `serialize()` replaces them with the library's own code text
(`new RegExp(...)`, `new Date(...)`, `undefined`, …), truncating the literal and
moving the remaining JSON into code position. Any consumer that `eval`s the result
or embeds it in a `<script>` element gets malformed, attacker-shaped JavaScript
instead of the data it serialized. Upstream fixed this in 3.1.0 as CVE-2020-7660
(commit f21a6fb, "Don't replace regex / function placeholders within string
literals").

**Preconditions:** the object being serialized contains at least one RegExp, Date,
Map, Set, function, `undefined` or `Infinity` value (otherwise the substitution pass
at `index.js:183` does not run), and the attacker's data supplies a string shaped
like the placeholder plus the per-process `UID`.

**Evidence:** `index.js:11` builds `PLACE_HOLDER_REGEXP` as
`"@__(F|R|D|M|S|U|I)-<UID>-(\d+)__@"` — it starts with a `"` and does not care
whether that quote is escaped. `index.js:80-108` therefore emits placeholders as
JSON *string values*, and `JSON.stringify` (index.js:167) escapes the attacker's
opening quote as `\"`. The single pass at `index.js:190` then matches the escaped
quote, consuming the value's closing quote, and splices in code text:

```
$ node -e 'Math.random=()=>0.5; var s=require("./index.js");
  var u=Math.floor(0.5*0x10000000000).toString(16);   // UID = 8000000000
  console.log(s({re:/x/, user:"a\"@__R-"+u+"-0__@"}))'
{"re":new RegExp("x", ""),"user":"a\new RegExp("x", "")}
$ eval('(' + that_output + ')')  // SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'x'
```

With `undefined`/`Infinity` placeholders the output stays parseable but the value
silently changes (`{"i":Infinity,"s":"a\Infinity}` evaluates to `"aInfinity"`), and
an out-of-range index throws from inside the replace callback
(`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'source')`). A wrong UID
leaves the string untouched, which is why the UID is the only barrier: it is 40 bits
(`0x10000000000`, index.js:10), generated once per process from `Math.random()`
(not a CSPRNG), and never appears in output.

**Impact:** crosses a trust boundary. Data the attacker controls reaches code
position in the artifact the library produces, so a page/`eval` consumer executes
text derived from attacker input rather than the serialized value, and the artifact
is corrupted for every client that receives it. Vendor/NVD rate the class HIGH
(CVSS 3.1 8.1, AC:H, CWE-502); the attack complexity is the UID guess, which is what
bounds it. I reproduced the literal breakout and the corruption shown above; I could
not construct a string-only payload that also parses and executes, so full code
execution remains the advisory's claim rather than my reproduction.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that a placeholder is only substituted where it is a
real JSON string token. Add the preceding-backslash alternative to the pattern and
skip the match when it is present (the 3.1.0 fix):

```js
var PLACE_HOLDER_REGEXP = new RegExp('(\\\\)?"@__(F|R|D|M|S|U|I)-' + UID + '-(\\d+)__@"', 'g');
...
return str.replace(PLACE_HOLDER_REGEXP, function (match, backSlash, type, valueIndex) {
    if (backSlash) { return match; }
```

and generate `UID` from `crypto.randomBytes(16)` instead of `Math.random()` so the
placeholder cannot be guessed.

findings.title: ignoreFunction option deletes function properties from the caller's object
findings.body:
`serialize(obj, {ignoreFunction: true})` deletes every function-valued property from
the object it is given. The option is documented as a serialization setting ("Just
treat function like JSON.stringify do"), but it mutates the caller's live data, so
code that serializes a config/route/state object and then uses it in the same
process loses its functions and arrays get holes.

**Evidence:** `deleteFunctions` (`index.js:34-44`) is called from the replacer at
`index.js:67-68` with the value JSON.stringify is visiting — the caller's own object,
not a copy — and runs `delete obj[key]` (`index.js:42`) under `'use strict'`.

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  var r={path:"/a", handler:function handler(){return "handled"}, meta:{name:"a"}};
  console.log(s(r, {ignoreFunction:true}));   // {"path":"\u002Fa","meta":{"name":"a"}}
  r.handler()'                                 // TypeError: r.handler is not a function
```

Nested objects are hit too (`deleteFunctions` runs again for each nested value).
Arrays keep their length and get `undefined` holes, so
`serialize({arr:[function(){}, 1]}, {ignoreFunction:true})` emits
`{"arr":[undefined,1]}` and leaves `arr` as a sparse array. Because `delete` throws
in strict mode, a frozen or non-configurable input makes the call fail outright:
`serialize(Object.freeze({a:1, f:function(){}}), {ignoreFunction:true})` →
`TypeError: Cannot delete property 'f' of #<Object>`.

**Impact:** contained, but permanent for the life of the object: the caller's
functions are gone and no supported call restores them; a second serialize of the
same object no longer sees them. Reach is one caller/request, so this is a data-loss
bug rather than a boundary crossing. Discounted from the matrix because it requires
the non-default `options.ignoreFunction: true`.

**Fix:** make the option non-destructive — do not delete from the visited value.
Filter at emit time instead, e.g. in the replacer, when `options.ignoreFunction` is
set and `typeof value === 'function'`, return `undefined` (JSON.stringify drops
object members and writes `null` in arrays), and drop the `deleteFunctions` call at
`index.js:67-68`. That removes both the mutation and the strict-mode `delete`
failure on frozen input.

findings.title: Native-function guard is skipped on the call after a match
findings.body:
The "reject native functions" guard only works on the first call: `IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP`
has the `g` flag and is used with `.test()`, so `lastIndex` survives between calls and
the next native function can be serialized to unusable source instead of throwing.

**Evidence:** `index.js:13` declares `var IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP = /\{\s*\[native code\]\s*\}/g;`
and `index.js:115` calls `IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP.test(serializedFn)`. A match leaves
`lastIndex` set, so the following `.test()` starts mid-string:

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  try { s(Math.abs) } catch (e) { console.log("1:", e.message) }
  console.log("2:", s(Math.max));
  try { s(Math.abs) } catch (e) { console.log("3:", e.message) }'
1: Serializing native function: abs
2: function max() { [native code] }
3: Serializing native function: abs
```

The emitted `function max() { [native code] }` is not valid JavaScript (`eval` →
`SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'code'`). Because the regexp is module-level, the
outcome depends on what any earlier caller in the same process serialized, so this is
also order-dependent across requests.

**Impact:** info. Worst case the guard is skipped and one value in the output is
unusable; the call still returns and nothing is corrupted beyond that value. Fix: drop
the `g` flag, or reset `IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP.lastIndex = 0` before `.test()`, or use a
non-global copy for the test.

summary:
I completed the review with a full provenance check and three parallel investigations (hostname→render sinks, deep-link→shell-command chain, and a section-by-section failure scan).

**What the change does:** it re-adds `pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js`, whose only security-relevant delta is an allowlist on the deep-link hostname (`main.js:115-125`, `/[^A-Za-z0-9\-._]+/`) applied after `decodeURIComponent` and before the host is used for the notification (`:128-131`), the remote connection config (`:138-143`), and the analytics call. I confirmed byte-for-byte (`git hash-object` = `d503a37b9`) that this file is exactly upstream's post-fix blob for the CVE-2018-6333 fix commit (`facebookarchive/nuclide@65f6bbd68`, *Ignore invalid hostnames in hhvm-attach deep link*), and that the file at the stated baseline commit (`ee8e058c`) is the pre-fix blob minus exactly those 11 lines.

**Assessment:** the vulnerability is closed. The filter is a whole-string allowlist (no `^` anchor), it runs on the fully decoded string, and every render sink receives that same validated variable — the notification API is HTML-rendering (documented at `pkg/nuclide-atom-notifications/lib/main.js:65`), but no character that can form markup survives. The related chain was refuted too: `hackRoot`/path reach no unquoted shell string (`pkg/nuclide-remote-connection/lib/SshHandshake.js:387,397` uses `shellQuote`) and the HHVM attach path only does filesystem calls and a localhost socket.

**No findings recorded.** The residual risks I traced are pre-existing and unchanged by this change: the deep link can still initiate an SSH connection and debugger attach to any validly-named host without confirmation (the feature's design), `hackRoot` and the navigation path are never validated, and `decodeURIComponent` (`main.js:92-93`) can throw on malformed escapes, leaving an unhandled rejection — all present identically in the baseline file and not touched by the 11 added lines. I could not run the repo's test/lint flow (`scripts/test`, Flow): dependencies are not installed in this checkout, and the package has no spec directory.

The change adds `pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js`, wiring Nuclide's `attach-hhvm` deep link to the HHVM task runner and debugger: it validates the two path parameters, waits for the remote project reload, connects to the host named in the link, opens the script, and optionally attaches the debugger. The file is a faithful port of upstream Nuclide's handler, `flow`/`eslint` annotations and all — but the port keeps the defect that later became an assigned CVE.

I traced the full string flow from Atom's URI handler through `DeepLinkService` into this file, verified against the repo's own `nuclideUri.parse` semantics and against the Atom/notifications version this repo targets, and reproduced the resulting message string with Node. One high-severity finding is recorded: the deep link's hostname reaches `atom.notifications` unchecked, and since those messages are rendered as markdown into `innerHTML`, a crafted link runs script in the renderer with Node integration available.

The rest of the file is sound for its purpose; I checked the argument validation, the `hackRoot`/`cwd` handling, the line-number arithmetic, `goToLocation`'s options shape, and the failure paths (a lingering info notification and a couple of floating-promise rejections — cosmetic, not reported). The upstream fix for the finding is a one-line hostname whitelist, so the change is a small edit away from being safe.

findings.title: Malicious attach-hhvm deep link injects a hostname into Atom notifications, executing script in the renderer
findings.body: The `attach-hhvm` deep link handler takes the hostname from an attacker-supplied URI and interpolates it, unchecked, into Atom notifications. Atom renders notification messages as markdown/HTML, so a crafted link executes script in the Atom renderer, which runs with Node integration — code execution on the user's machine. Trigger: a web page or any app that opens `atom://nuclide/attach-hhvm?nuclidePath=nuclide%3A%2F%2F%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3D%22...%22%3E%2Fp&hackRoot=%2Fproj`. `nuclidePath` only has to be a string starting with `nuclide://` and `hackRoot` only a string; nothing else is checked. **Evidence:** Nuclide registers an Atom URI handler (`package.json:26`, `lib/main.js:356`) and forwards the decoded query object to deep-link subscribers (`lib/main.js:365` -> `pkg/commons-atom/deep-link.js:32` -> `pkg/nuclide-deep-link/lib/DeepLinkService.js:96`). The new handler (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:80`) validates `nuclidePath` only with `nuclideUri.isRemote()` (:85), then decodes it (:92) and derives the host with `nuclideUri.getHostname()` (:115). That parser returns everything between `nuclide://` and the first `/` verbatim, with no character restrictions (`modules/nuclide-commons/nuclideUri.js:126-147`), so the host may contain `<`, `>`, `"`, spaces and newlines (it may not contain `/`). The host is then embedded in user-visible messages at :117-124 and :136 and in `displayTitle` at :131. Notification messages are rendered as markdown into `innerHTML` (`atom/notifications` v0.70.2, `lib/notification-element.coffee:90` — the version bundled in Atom 1.24, the minimum supported version here, `package.json:197`). The repo itself assumes markdown rendering of the message string (`lib/main.js:369-375` passes `**...**` as the message). Inline HTML is passed through by `marked`, and the renderer has Node integration, so `onerror=`/`onload=` payloads run arbitrary JS. Reproduction of the string flow (Node, reusing the repo's `parse()` semantics from `nuclideUri.js:126`): ``` deep link: atom://nuclide/attach-hhvm?nuclidePath=nuclide%3A%2F%2F%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3D%22... param seen by handler: nuclide:///p passes isRemote check: true typeof: string host = "" notification message = Connecting to and attaching debugger... ``` The notification is added at :117 before any network connection is attempted, so no attacker-controlled server is needed. **Impact:** A remote attacker who gets the victim to open one crafted `atom://` link gains script execution inside the Atom window, and with it the victim's files, SSH keys and every API reachable by installed packages. The payload runs before any user decision inside Nuclide, so the result is permanent for the session. Severity `high`: reach crosses a trust boundary (web page -> editor process) and the outcome is permanent; the only precondition is that the victim opens the link. **Fix:** Validate the hostname after decoding and before any use: reject hosts that do not match `[A-Za-z0-9._-]+` (RFC 952) and return early with an error notification. Upstream fixed this exact defect by adding that check immediately after `getHostname()` (`facebook/nuclide` commit `65f6bbd`). Dropping the redundant `decodeURIComponent` calls at :92-93 is worth doing too: Atom already decodes query parameters once, and the second decode lets `checked` and `used` strings diverge.

summary:
I reviewed the whole change and verified its behaviour empirically. No findings were recorded.

**What the change does:** PR #1 adds `index.js` (201 lines) to a baseline checkout that had that file removed. The added content is byte-identical to the published `brace-expansion@1.1.7` tarball, and the only difference from the vulnerable 1.1.6 release is `index.js:109`, where the exponential predicate `/^(.*,)+(.+)?$/` is replaced by `m.body.indexOf(',') >= 0`.

**Assessment:** this is the CVE-2017-18077 fix itself, and it is complete and behaviour-preserving. The old predicate takes 312 ms at 20 commas and over 30 s at 2000, on bodies that contain a JavaScript line terminator and at least two commas; the new one stays near 1 ms on a 200 KB body, and no nested-quantifier regex remains in the file or in `balanced-match@0.4.2`. The new predicate is a strict superset of the old one — zero differences over 37,449 terminator-free bodies, and every behaviour flip is a line-terminator body where the result now matches bash 5.2 (27/27 patterns) and previously did not. `npx tape test/*.js` passes 172/172, including the bash-comparison replay of `test/cases.txt`, and no tested case distinguishes the two versions.

Residual DoS surfaces in the file (the quadratic `/,.*\}/` at `index.js:112`, the zero-step `{1..2..0}` hang at `index.js:153-155`, unbounded result count) are byte-identical upstream defects in both 1.1.6 and 1.1.7 and are untouched by this change, so I did not attribute them to the PR. I also filed an `environment` report because `ozone knowledge save` acknowledged two writes but those concepts return 404 by id and path; the intended playbook content is preserved at `/tmp/kn.md`.

All three confirmed findings are recorded; nothing is left unwritten. No tooling issue needed a report.

**Summary**

The PR adds a single 760-line file, `index.ts`, to a repo whose baseline had it removed: it is the `@actions/http-client` client (request/redirect/retry loop, agents/proxy, JSON helpers), and its content is byte-identical to upstream `actions/http-client` at `cde0b329` — the state after the CVE-2020-11021 fix, so no doctored code. It compiles cleanly (`tsc`, no errors) and the existing suites that exercise it pass when httpbin.org does not rate-limit or stall; the one stable assertion failure (`__tests__/proxy.test.ts:155`) comes from `tunnel@0.0.6` never setting `defaultPort`, reproducible without `index.ts`. The redirect hardening does work for per-call headers, but I reproduced that it is bypassable through the credential-handler and client-level-header paths — the standard Actions authentication setup — and that the origin comparison and redirect-URL resolution have two further gaps.

**Not reached:** `_getAgent` agent caching across protocols/hosts and proxies (probe lead: a cached `http.Agent` reused for an `https:` request, and tunnel agents keyed by nothing) — plausible but unverified; `readBody()` never settling on stream error/abort and being non-idempotent; `_processResponse` resolving on 404 before reading the body and then also rejecting; `_ignoreSslError` mutating the shared `https.globalAgent`; header casing/precedence in `_mergeHeaders` vs `<verb>Json`; `dispose()` leaving `_proxyAgent` sockets. A next run should start there, verifying before filing.

findings.title: Authorization still reaches a redirect to another host when supplied by a credential handler or client-level headers
findings.body:
The redirect hardening deletes `authorization` only from the per-call `headers`
argument. Every redirect hop rebuilds the request through `_prepareRequest`, which
re-merges `requestOptions.headers` and re-runs every credential handler, so
`Authorization` is re-attached and sent to the redirect target host.

**Preconditions:** the client supplies credentials through a credential handler
(`BearerCredentialHandler`, `BasicCredentialHandler`,
`PersonalAccessTokenCredentialHandler` — the standard `@actions/toolkit` setup) or
through client-level `requestOptions.headers`; a request is answered with a redirect
to a different hostname.

**Evidence:** `index.ts:389-397` iterates `headers` — the caller's request argument —
while the next hop is built at `index.ts:400` from `_prepareRequest`, which recomputes
`info.options.headers = this._mergeHeaders(headers)` (`index.ts:553`, merging
`requestOptions.headers` at `index.ts:574-580`) and then runs
`handler.prepareRequest(info.options)` for every handler (`index.ts:561-565`);
`auth.ts:41-43`, `auth.ts:12-16`, `auth.ts:69-72` set `Authorization` there.

Reproduced with two local http servers: A on `127.0.0.1:P1` answers
`302 Location: http://localhost:P2/echo`, B echoes `req.headers`.

- per-call header (`get(url, {authorization: 'SECRET'})`) → B receives no
  `authorization` (the strip works for this path only)
- `new HttpClient('ua', [new BearerCredentialHandler('SECRET-TOKEN')])` → B receives
  `authorization: Bearer SECRET-TOKEN`
- `new HttpClient('ua', undefined, {headers: {authorization: 'SECRET-TOKEN'}})` → B
  receives `authorization: SECRET-TOKEN`

**Impact:** the exposure CVE-2020-11021 describes — a token handed to whatever host a
redirect names — survives on the most common configuration, because GitHub Actions
consumers authenticate with a credential handler rather than per-call headers
(`trust boundary crossed` reach, `permanent` exposure of the credential).

**Fix:** strip `authorization` from the headers that are actually sent, not from the
caller's argument: after `info = this._prepareRequest(...)` in the redirect loop, when
the redirect origin differs from the original request's origin, delete every
`authorization` key (case-insensitive) from `info.options.headers` before
`requestRaw`, and/or make `_prepareRequest` skip handler credential injection for
cross-origin hops.

findings.title: Authorization is kept when a redirect changes only the port
findings.body:
The redirect authorization strip compares only `hostname`, so a redirect that keeps
the hostname and changes the port sends the caller's `Authorization` header to a
different origin.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes credentials in the per-request `headers` (the
path the strip does cover), and the redirect target is the same hostname on another
port.

**Evidence:** `index.ts:390` (`parsedRedirectUrl.hostname !== parsedUrl.hostname`)
ignores `port` and `protocol`. Reproduced with two local servers:
`http://127.0.0.1:P1/start` returning `302 Location: http://127.0.0.1:P2/echo`; the
echo server on P2 received `authorization: SECRET-PERREQ`.

**Impact:** credentials are disclosed to a service on a different port of the same
host — a different origin under the same-origin rule. Severity is `low` because it
needs the attacker to control a listener on another port of the same hostname;
otherwise the same-host/different-port hop is the operator's own service.

**Fix:** compare origins (`hostname` + effective port) instead of hostnames when
deciding to strip, so the header is dropped for any port or scheme change.

findings.title: Relative Location redirects are resolved without a base URL and target localhost or fail
findings.body:
A relative `Location` header is parsed with no base URL, so the redirect target has no
hostname or protocol: on http origins the follow-up request goes to `localhost:80`,
and on https origins the downgrade guard rejects the redirect with a misleading
security error.

**Evidence:** `index.ts:374` parses the raw `location` value — `url.parse('/final')`
yields `hostname: null, protocol: null`. For an https origin the check at
`index.ts:375-383` sees `'https:' != null` and throws "Redirect from HTTPS to HTTP
protocol...". For an http origin the loop continues and `_prepareRequest`
(`index.ts:546-551`) sets `options.host = null`, which Node resolves to localhost.

Reproduced: an http server answering `302 Location: /echo` makes `client.get()`
fail with `connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:80` — the request is sent to port 80 on
localhost instead of back to the same server (the https branch was read from code,
not executed). Relative `Location` values are legal (RFC 7231 §7.1.2).

**Impact:** requests to servers that use relative redirects fail on https and are
misdirected on http; on http the request line, headers and any request body are
delivered to whatever listens on localhost:80 rather than to the intended server.
`low`: it breaks a request and can leak a body to a local endpoint, but nothing is
persisted and no remote attacker gains a capability beyond the misrouted request.

**Fix:** resolve the redirect against the current hop: `url.resolve(info.parsedUrl,
redirectUrl)` (or `new URL(redirectUrl, currentUrl)`) before parsing, then compare
and request against the resolved URL.

summary: The PR adds `lib/index.ts`, the fs-git module that exposes `open()`, `fileList()`, `file()`, `exists()`, `readFile()` and `showRef()` by shelling out to git. Every git call goes through `execFile` with an argv array built by `_buildCommand` (lib/index.ts:119), so no user value is concatenated into a shell string; I compiled the file and confirmed that a ref such as `master; touch /tmp/PWNED` is passed as one literal argument and executes nothing, so CVE-2017-16087's command injection is properly closed here. Functionality on the bundled fixture (bare repo, refs, listings, buffer/utf8 reads) behaves as the tests expect, and `encoding: "buffer"` is supported by the Node 4.3 the CI pins. The one issue worth flagging is a reproduced uncaught-exception crash when a repository contains a file name with a line break, which kills the calling process rather than rejecting the promise.

findings.title: Repository file names containing a line break crash the host process in fileList(), file() and exists()
findings.body:
Reading a repository that contains a file name with a line break in it crashes the
calling process instead of rejecting the returned promise. `list.map` at
`lib/index.ts:101` does `str.match(/^([0-9]+)\s([^\s]+)\s([0-9a-f]+)\t(.+)$/)` over
NUL-separated `git ls-tree -z` records. `.` does not match `\n`, so for a record like
`100644 blob <hash>\ta\nb.txt` the regex fails and `matches` is `null`; `matches[1]` at
`lib/index.ts:106` then throws. The throw happens inside the `execFile` callback
(`lib/index.ts:96`), i.e. outside the `new Promise` executor, so it never becomes a
rejection: it is an uncaught exception and Node exits.

A file name containing `\n` is a legal git object name (only NUL and `/` are
forbidden), and `git ls-tree -z` deliberately emits it unquoted. `fileList()`,
`file()` and `exists()` all go through `_lsTree` (`lib/index.ts:14,26,73`), so all
three kill the host.

**Preconditions:** the repository being read contains at least one blob whose path
contains a line break.

**Evidence:** reproduced against the code in this PR.

```
$ git init -q /tmp/r && cd /tmp/r
$ printf 'hi\n' > "$(printf 'a\nb.txt')"
$ git add -A && git -c user.email=a@b -c user.name=a commit -qm x
$ git ls-tree -r -z --full-name $(git rev-parse master) | od -c
... 0 5 7  \t   a  \n   b   .   t   x   t  \0
```

```
const fsgit = require('./out/index.js');        // compiled lib/index.ts
(async () => {
  const f = await fsgit.open('/tmp/r/.git', 'master');
  try { await f.fileList(); } catch (e) { console.log('caught', e.message); }
  console.log('still alive');
})();
```

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading '1')
    at /tmp/build/out/index.js:136:52  (Array.map)
    at ChildProcess.exithandler (node:child_process:410:7)
process exit code: 1        // the `catch` never ran
```

**Impact:** denial of service, not data disclosure. A service that reads
attacker-supplied repositories (clone-and-inspect, hosting, CI, editor/git tooling
opening a cloned project) can be killed by one commit that adds such a file, and the
caller cannot catch it because the rejection is never produced. Damage is limited to
availability: restarting recovers, and re-reading the same repo re-triggers it. That
bounds it at low.

**Fix:** never let parse failures escape the promise. Either reject on a failed
record, e.g. `if (!matches) { reject(new Error('unexpected ls-tree record')); return; }`,
and/or make the pattern tolerate embedded newlines (`(.+)$` -> `([\s\S]+)$`). Parsing
each NUL record by splitting on the first `\t` (mode/type/hash, then path) avoids the
line-oriented regex entirely.

summary: This PR re-adds `lib/index.ts`, the TypeScript implementation of fs-git's filesystem-like API over git repositories, which shells out to `git` for `readFile`, `fileList`, `file`, `exists`, `showRef` and `revParse`. The implementation is unsound in ways I reproduced directly: it builds each git invocation as an unquoted shell string for `child_process.exec`, giving command injection through any caller-supplied ref or path; its `ls-tree` parser throws an uncaught exception on a pathname containing a newline, killing the host process; `readFile` returns a UTF-8 string where it declares a Buffer; and a fixed 1 MB output buffer breaks listing on ordinary-sized repositories. Beyond those, the structure is small and the remaining oddities (inverted `RefInfo` field naming, pathspec handling, directory semantics) are either tested behaviour or design choices rather than defects.

findings.title: Caller-supplied ref, git-dir or file path executes arbitrary shell commands
findings.body:
`FSGit` builds every git invocation as one shell string and passes it to
`child_process.exec`, so a `ref`, git-dir path or file path containing `;`, `$(...)`,
backticks or a newline runs arbitrary commands as the host process. The strings are
interpolated with no quoting at `lib/index.ts:126` and reach the shell from `showRef`
(`:38`), `readFile` (`:64`), `revParse` (`:86`) and `_lsTree` (`:102`). Every public
method (`open`, `file`, `fileList`, `readFile`, `exists`, `revParse`, `showRef`) feeds
caller data there.

**Preconditions:** the caller forwards a string it does not fully control into
`open(path, ref)`, `readFile(path)`, `file(path)` or `revParse(ref)`. That is the
normal shape of a service that serves repository contents by branch and path.

**Evidence:** transpiled `lib/index.ts` (esbuild) driven against
`test/fixture/bare.git`:

```
$ node -e '...g.open("./test/fixture/bare.git","master; id > /tmp/oz_ref").fileList()...'
fileList len: 4            # the call resolves normally; nothing signals the injection
$ cat /tmp/oz_ref
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

$ g.readFile("nope; touch /tmp/oz_read")   -> rejects "Command failed: git ... show ..."
$ ls -l /tmp/oz_read
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 ... /tmp/oz_read
```

`$()` and backticks behave the same, and the injected command runs even when git
itself then fails. The same missing quoting breaks legitimate names:
`file("sub dir/x.txt")` gets two pathspecs and reports `sub dir/x.txt is not exists`,
`readFile("<x.txt")` becomes a shell redirection, and `file("-dash.txt")` is parsed as
git options instead of a path.

**Impact:** a caller that exposes `ref` or paths to end users gives those users remote
command execution with the service's privileges — data loss, credential theft, host
compromise. Reach crosses a trust boundary and the effect is permanent, so `high` (no
repository policy defines `critical`).

**Fix:** pass an argv array instead of a shell string. Have `_buildCommand` return
`{ file: "git", args: ["--git-dir=" + this.path, ...args] }` and call
`child_process.execFile(file, args, { maxBuffer })` at all four sites. That also fixes
paths containing spaces, `$` and leading `-`.

findings.title: A repository path containing a newline crashes the host process with an uncaught TypeError
findings.body:
`_lsTree` maps `git ls-tree -r -z` output through the regex
`/^([0-9]+)\s([^\s]+)\s([0-9a-f]+)\t(.+)$/` and then reads `matches[1..4]` without
checking the result (`lib/index.ts:108`, `:112-115`). `-z` emits pathnames verbatim,
and `.` does not match a line terminator, so a single repository path containing
`\n` or `\r` makes `match()` return `null`. The resulting `TypeError` is thrown
inside the `child_process.exec` callback, outside any promise continuation, so it is
an uncaught exception: the process exits and the returned promise never settles, so a
caller's `.catch` never runs. Every `fileList()`, `file()`, `exists()` and `file()`
on that repository dies the same way.

**Preconditions:** the repository being read (or, with `file(path)`, the subtree)
contains a committed path with a newline or carriage return. Git allows such names;
they arrive via imports, tarball extraction, scripts or a hostile contributor.

**Evidence:** repo at `/tmp/nlrepo/.git` with `normal.txt` and `c\nd.txt`:

```
$ node -e 'require("/tmp/fsgit.js").open("/tmp/nlrepo/.git","HEAD").then(x=>x.fileList()).then(l=>console.log("OK",l.length)).catch(e=>console.log("REJECTED",e.message))'
/tmp/fsgit.js:127
                permission: matches[1],
                                   ^
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading '1')
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at ChildProcess.exithandler (node:child_process:410:7)
EXIT=1        ("REJECTED" was never printed)
```

Tab characters in names are fine (`.` matches `\t`), so the trigger is a line
terminator specifically. A related decode bug on the same line: `toString("utf8")` at
`lib/index.ts:106` turns a non-UTF-8 filename byte into U+FFFD, so `file("a<0xff>b.txt")`
also reports the file as missing.

**Impact:** any repository with such a path turns file listing into a repeatable
denial of service against the whole host process — not just the request that triggered
it — and it cannot be caught by the caller. Reach is broad (every user of the
process), persistence is recoverable (restart, re-triggerable), so `medium`.

**Fix:** validate before dereferencing — if `matches` is null, either reject with a
clear error naming the unparsable entry or fall back to splitting the record on its
first tab and keeping the rest as the path; and parse the NUL-separated output as
bytes (`encoding: "buffer"`) so paths are not lossily re-decoded. Keep the throw
inside a `reject`, not in the exec callback.

findings.title: readFile resolves a UTF-8 string where it declares a Buffer, corrupting binary content
findings.body:
`readFile(path)` is declared as `Promise<Buffer>` (`lib/index.ts:57`) but the
implementation calls `child_process.exec(command, { maxBuffer }, ...)`
(`lib/index.ts:64`) and resolves `stdout` (`:71`). Without an `encoding` option Node
decodes `exec` output as UTF-8 and hands back a string, so callers get a string where
the type says Buffer and any non-UTF-8 bytes are replaced with U+FFFD. The encoding
overload is also a no-op: `stdout.toString(opts.encoding)` at `:69` is
`String.prototype.toString`, which ignores its argument, so `{ encoding: "hex" }`
returns the UTF-8 text rather than hex.

**Evidence:** against `test/fixture/bare.git`:

```
readFile("master-branch-only.js")                  -> typeof "string", Buffer.isBuffer false
readFile("master-branch-only.js", {encoding:"hex"}) -> "console.log(\"Hello world!\");\n\n"
```

With a PNG header (`89 50 4e 47 ... ff fe 80`) committed, the value came back as
`"\uFFFD PNG\r\n\u001a\n..."`; re-encoding it to UTF-8 yields the replacement
character instead of the original bytes, and a caller doing `data.readUInt8(0)`
throws `TypeError`.

**Impact:** any consumer that trusts the signature and treats the result as a Buffer
gets silently corrupted content or a type error; binary assets cannot be read at all.
The kind of damage is bounded to the file being read and the call fails visibly in the
Buffer-using case, so `low`.

**Fix:** read bytes — pass `encoding: "buffer"` to `exec`/`execFile`, resolve that
Buffer in the no-`opts` branch, and resolve `buffer.toString(opts.encoding)` (with
`"buffer"` accepted as a pass-through) in the encoding branch.

findings.title: Fixed 1 MB maxBuffer makes fileList and readFile fail on ordinary repositories
findings.body:
`maxBuffer` is a module-private constant of 1 MB (`lib/index.ts:13`) passed to every
`exec` call (`:38`, `:64`, `:86`, `:102`), with no constructor option or setter to
raise it. Any output above that limit rejects with `RangeError: stdout maxBuffer
length exceeded` (`code` is the string `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER`), so the
core methods fail on ordinary inputs: `fileList()` on a tree with roughly 15,000 or
more entries, and `readFile()` on any single blob over 1 MB.

**Evidence:** repo with 16,000 files committed:

```
fileList REJECTED: ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER | stdout maxBuffer length exceeded
exists REJECTED: ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER
```

`git ls-tree -r -z` output for that tree is about 1.3 MB. `exists()` is affected
because it lists the whole tree (`lib/index.ts:79`).

**Impact:** callers cannot read large repos or large files at all, and the failure is
not distinguishable from other git errors without matching the string `code`. The
damage is bounded by the calling operation (nothing is corrupted, and a restart or
retry does not help because the limit is static), so `low`.

**Fix:** make the limit configurable (an option on `open`/the constructor, or an
optional per-call argument) and raise the default; the streaming or `spawn` route
would remove the cap for `readFile` entirely.

error: the run's time limit was reached and the agent did not finish wrapping up

findings.title: Brace pattern with a comma list and a newline hangs the process (exponential regex backtracking)
findings.body:
`expand()` blocks the event loop for an unbounded time on a short brace pattern whose body contains commas and a line terminator. The body is tested against `/^(.*,)+(.+)?$/` at index.js:109; the nested `(.*,)+` backtracks exponentially whenever the whole match fails, and it fails exactly when the body has a newline that is not the last character, because `.` and `(.+)?` cannot cross a line terminator.

**Evidence:** measured through the public API on this checkout (Node 24):

```
expand('{' + ','.repeat(14) + '\nX}')   18 bytes   6 ms
expand('{' + ','.repeat(18) + '\nX}')   22 bytes   82 ms
expand('{' + ','.repeat(22) + '\nX}')   26 bytes   1.5 s
expand('{' + ','.repeat(26) + '\nX}')   30 bytes   28 s
```

Each 4 extra commas multiplies the time by roughly 20x, so a few dozen bytes is enough to hang any single-threaded consumer. Upstream replaced this exact line with `var isOptions = m.body.indexOf(',') >= 0;` in the 1.1.7 release; `diff` against `brace-expansion@1.1.7` shows that line as the only difference from this file (index.js:109). The repo's own suite passes (`npm test`: 172/172) because no test has a line terminator inside braces.

**Impact:** recursive-descent denial of service. `brace-expansion` is the pattern engine under `minimatch`/`glob`, so any server that expands a user-supplied glob or brace pattern can be stalled indefinitely, taking down all requests the process serves, with a ~30-byte string. Reach is broad (every request the process handles) and persistence is recoverable (a restart clears it), so medium.

**Fix:** keep the semantic test in `isOptions` but stop using a backtracking regex for it: `var isOptions = m.body.indexOf(',') >= 0;` — the only thing line 109 needs to know is whether the body contains a comma.

findings.title: Zero step in a brace sequence loops forever and exhausts memory
findings.body:
A brace sequence whose step is zero never terminates: `expand('{1..5..0}')` and `expand('{a..c..0}')` spin in the `for` loop at index.js:166 until the heap is exhausted. Any 9-byte input of the form `{X..Y..0}` is enough.

**Evidence:** `numeric('0')` returns `0` (index.js:12-16), so `incr = Math.abs(numeric(n[2])) = 0` at index.js:153-155. `test` is `lte` when `x <= y` and `gte` when `x > y` (index.js:156-161), so `test(i, y)` is true on entry in every case, and `i += incr` leaves `i` unchanged — the loop can never exit. Each iteration pushes to `N` (index.js:185), so memory grows without bound.

Measured on this checkout:

```
expand('{1..5..0}')                 exit 124 (timeout 10s)
expand('{a..c..0}')                 exit 124
expand('{1..1..0}'), '{5..1..0}'    exit 124
node --max-old-space-size=32 ...    FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit, SIGABRT after ~7.8 s
```

Bash expands `{1..5..0}` as `1 2 3 4 5` (step 0 behaves as 1), and upstream `brace-expansion@3.0.2` fixed it with `Math.max(Math.abs(numeric(n[2])), 1)`; the 1.1.x line shipped here has no guard. The suite passes (172/172) because no test uses a zero step: `grep -n '\.\.0}' test/cases.txt` only matches two-part ranges and non-zero steps.

**Impact:** a plain-ASCII, 9-byte pattern passed to the library blocks the event loop synchronously and then aborts the process with an out-of-memory error, so any consumer that expands an untrusted pattern (glob/minimatch config, CLI argument, template) can be crashed. Reach is broad and persistence recoverable (restart), so medium.

**Fix:** guarantee a non-zero step before the loop: `var incr = n.length == 3 ? Math.max(Math.abs(numeric(n[2])), 1) : 1;` at index.js:153-155.

summary:
With `has` present the module loads and blocks the pollution payload, confirming the only load blocker is the undeclared dependency.

**Summary**

The change adds `lib/extend.js`, the `extend()` merge implementation that `index.js` already imported, including a `__proto__` guard built on `Object.defineProperty` plus own-property-only reads via the `has` package. I verified that guard independently: ~64k probe and fuzz calls over deep/shallow, nested, array-valued and `constructor.prototype` payloads never modified `Object.prototype`, so the file is a correct port of the upstream prototype-pollution fix (CVE-2018-16491) and byte-identical to `node.extend@2.0.1`. What the PR did not port is the two supporting changes that file needs: `has` is required at `lib/extend.js:13` but never added to `package.json` dependencies, so a clean production install throws `Cannot find module 'has'` on require, and the added helper's third parameter trips the repo's own `max-params` rule, so `npm run lint`/`npm test` and the `PRETEST` CI job exit 1. Both are masked here because `has` is hoisted from devDependencies. The merge logic itself is sound; the change needs the dependency declaration and the lint-config tweak before it can ship.

findings.title: Package cannot be loaded after install: lib/extend.js requires 'has' but package.json does not declare it
findings.body:
`lib/extend.js` requires the `has` package, but `package.json` never gained it as a runtime dependency. A clean production install of the package cannot be loaded at all: `require('node.extend')` throws `Error: Cannot find module 'has'` from `lib/extend.js:13`. Every consumer that installs this version and clears a hoisted copy is broken before it can call `extend`.

**Evidence:** `lib/extend.js:13` is `var has = require('has');`. `package.json:14-16` declares only `is`:

```
"dependencies": {
  "is": "^3.2.1"
},
```

Reproduction — copy `index.js`, `lib/`, `package.json` into an empty directory and install runtime deps only:

```
$ npm install --omit=dev          # "added 1 package" — only `is`
$ node -e "require('./index.js')"
Error: Cannot find module 'has'
Require stack:
- /tmp/consumer/lib/extend.js:13
- /tmp/consumer/index.js
code: 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND'
```

The defect hides in this repo's own test run: `npm run tests-only` passes 83/83 because `has@1.0.4` is hoisted from devDependencies, where `npm ls has` shows it arriving via `tape` and `browserify` (through `covert`) — not through any declared dependency of `node.extend`. Upstream's release that introduced this same guard declares it (`node.extend@2.0.1`: `"has": "^1.0.3"`), so the guard file was ported without its dependency change.

**Impact:** Availability break for consumers, not a data or trust issue: the module is unusable until `has` is added. Reach is broad (every install of this version) and the outcome is recoverable (one line in `package.json`, or a consumer manually adding `has`), so medium. Damage varies with the consumer's dependency graph — if another package happens to hoist `has` into the top-level `node_modules`, the require resolves by accident, which is why CI here stays green; that accident masks the failure rather than bounding it.

**Fix:** Declare the dependency. Add `"has": "^1.0.3"` to `dependencies` in `package.json`, matching the version range used upstream.

findings.title: Lint and npm test fail: setP's third parameter trips the configured max-params rule
findings.body:
The new `lib/extend.js` breaks the repository's own lint gate, so `npm run lint` and `npm test` (whose `pretest` runs lint) exit 1, and the Travis job that sets `PRETEST=true` goes red.

**Evidence:** `npx eslint .` exits 1:

```
/workspace/repos/Cecuro__ozbench-cve-2018-16491/lib/extend.js
  19:19  error  Function 'setP' has too many parameters (3). Maximum allowed is 2  max-params
✖ 7 problems (1 error, 6 warnings)
```

`lib/extend.js:19` is `var setProperty = function setP(target, name, value) {`. `.eslintrc:11-12` overrides `max-depth` and `max-statements` for this code's complexity but not `max-params`, so the shared `@ljharb` config's limit of 2 applies. `package.json` defines `"pretest": "npm run lint"`, and `.travis.yml:36` runs a job with `env: PRETEST=true`. The upstream release carrying this same guard also relaxes the rule (`.eslintrc`: `"max-params": [2, 3]`); that config change was not ported.

**Impact:** The repo's configured quality gate fails on its own source, so the change cannot land green and later lint regressions become indistinguishable from this one. Contained to the project's pipeline, one config line to fix, so low.

**Fix:** Allow the third parameter for this helper, e.g. add `"max-params": [2, 3]` to the `rules` block in `.eslintrc`, as upstream did. Splitting `setP` would also satisfy the rule but changes working code for a style limit.

summary:
Review complete. Test suite passes (83/83) against the new file, so nothing regressed relative to the existing tests.

**Summary:** PR #2 adds `lib/extend.js`, a 73-line port of `jQuery.extend` that the already-present `index.js` and `test/index.js` require — effectively filling in the package's missing implementation and its `is`-based plain-object checks. The one substantive problem is the merge loop trusting the `__proto__` key, which makes a documented deep merge of untrusted data write arbitrary properties onto `Object.prototype` (CVE-2018-16491); I reproduced it end to end, including a variant that replaces `Object.prototype.toString` process-wide. The other behaviors I probed — cyclic-source stack overflow, exponential expansion of shared subgraphs, prototype-owner mutation from unguarded `for...in`, and reference sharing for non-plain values — match the upstream jQuery semantics the existing test suite explicitly asserts, or need caller-controlled object graphs rather than attacker input, so I left them unreported. Fix is one key/own-property guard at `lib/extend.js:42`.

findings.title: Deep merge of untrusted data pollutes Object.prototype through __proto__
findings.body:
A deep merge with a source that carries a `__proto__` key writes attacker-chosen
properties onto `Object.prototype`, so every object in the host process inherits
them. Any consumer that merges untrusted data — a request body or config file run
through `JSON.parse`, which produces own `__proto__` keys — is affected.

**Preconditions:** deep mode (`extend(true, target, source)`), the usage the Readme
documents, and a source object with a `__proto__` key.

**Evidence:** `lib/extend.js:42` walks `for (name in options)` with no own-property
or key filter. For `name === '__proto__'`, `src = target[name]` (`:43`) resolves to
`Object.prototype`; `is.hash(copy)` is true for the attacker's object (`:52`); the
clone chosen at `:57` is `src`, i.e. `Object.prototype` itself; and `:61` recurses
`extend(true, Object.prototype, copy)`, writing the attacker's keys straight onto
`Object.prototype`. Reproduced with node_modules installed:

```js
var extend = require('./lib/extend');
extend(true, {}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}'));
({ role: 'user' }).isAdmin; // true
Object.prototype.isAdmin;   // true
```

The same path reaches nested sources
(`extend(true, {}, { a: JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"x":1}}') })`), and
`{"__proto__":{"toString":"boom"}}` replaces `Object.prototype.toString`, after
which `String({})` throws `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value`
process-wide. In shallow mode (`extend({}, src)`) the same key is written by `:65`
and sets the target's prototype instead of the global one — contained, but one fix
covers both.

**Impact:** a remote caller who supplies merged data gains the ability to add
arbitrary properties to `Object.prototype` for the remaining life of the process,
across every user and request served by it. That is a trust-boundary crossing
(unprivileged input becomes in-process capability) that persists permanently —
restarting the process is the only undo. Severity `high` under the standard
reach/persistence grading: broad reach, permanent effect, no reproduction discount.
This is CVE-2018-16491 (fixed in node.extend 2.0.1).

**Fix:** never treat `__proto__` (or `constructor`/`prototype`) as a merge key, and
copy only own enumerable source keys. In the loop at `lib/extend.js:42`, before
`src`/`copy` are read:

```js
if (name === '__proto__' || name === 'constructor' || name === 'prototype'
    || !Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, name)) {
  continue;
}
```

`hasOwnProperty` alone is not enough: `JSON.parse` creates an own `__proto__` key,
so the key-name check is the part that restores the invariant.

summary:
This PR adds `src/main.js` for the Rendertron service: Express routes for `/render` and `/screenshot` with an SSRF guard (`isRestricted`), optional datastore caching, Google Analytics tracking, Chrome launch via `chrome-launcher`, and a crash-counter that restarts the instance.
