Compared with the copy that existed before the file was removed, this version is the hardened one — it rejects non-`http(s)` schemes (closing the `file://` local-file read that the CVE is about), stops serving `/node_modules`, drops the unauthenticated `/_ah/stop` endpoint, and no longer echoes the requested URL or upstream error text back to the caller, so the security direction is right and the protocol gate does block `file://`, `abc` and similar inputs (verified by running the exact check over Express-decoded paths).

The remaining concern is that the host allowlist is still a raw string prefix comparison rather than a host comparison, which an independent reproduction confirmed lets `http://allowed.example@10.0.0.5/` through to the backend host; the allowlist is also only evaluated once, before navigation, so redirects and subresources escape it. Two findings are recorded (one medium, one info about existing tests no longer matching the new 403 behavior); everything else I checked — the cache mount ordering, the progress-bar static mount, screenshot error handling, config loading — either behaves safely or is pre-existing code in unchanged files. I would merge this with the allowlist comparison corrected.

findings.title: renderOnly allowlist matches a URL prefix, so callers can render off-list internal hosts
findings.body:
When `renderOnly` is configured, an unauthenticated caller can render any host it likes by
putting an allowlisted string at the front of the URL. The rendered body of the
off-allowlist host is returned to the caller.

`isRestricted` compares the raw, Express-decoded request path against each allowlist entry
with `startsWith` (`src/main.js:76`) instead of comparing the URL's host. The same string is
then handed unmodified to `renderer.serialize` (`src/main.js:107`, `src/main.js:124`), which
navigates Chrome to it (`src/renderer.js:75`) and returns the serialized page
(`src/renderer.js:190-194`, `src/main.js:108`). `url.parse` at `src/main.js:70` already
computes the authoritative host and discards it.

**Preconditions:** `renderOnly` is set. Without it the endpoint is unrestricted by design
(`src/main.js:73`), so this is a bypass of the only host control the service offers.

**Evidence:** Reproduction with Express and the verbatim `isRestricted` body mounted on
`app.get('/render/:url(*)')` (no Chrome needed):

```
GET /render/http://allowed.example@127.0.0.1:32985/internal/admin
  param      = "http://allowed.example@127.0.0.1:32985/internal/admin"
  parsed host= "127.0.0.1:32985"
  restricted = false   -> renderer fetches 127.0.0.1 and returns
                          "[200] INTERNAL-SECRET: db_password=... path=/internal/admin"
GET /render/http://allowed.example.attacker.tld/x   -> restricted = false
GET /render/http://evil.example/x                   -> restricted = true  (403)
GET /render/file:///etc/passwd                      -> restricted = true  (403, correctly blocked)
```

The userinfo form (`user@host`) and the `.attacker.tld` suffix form both pass
`'http://allowed.example'.startsWith(...)`, and both make Chrome connect to the host that is
not allowlisted. The existing whitelist test (`test/app-test.js:155-164`) only tries
`http://anotherDomain.com`, which shares no prefix, so it never exercises this.

The allowlist is also only checked on the initial request: `src/renderer.js:44-52` enables no
request interception, so a redirect or subresource from an allowlisted page reaches any host
the same way.

**Impact:** The caller is the untrusted internet client that `renderOnly` exists to fence off,
and it receives content from loopback services, intranet hosts or cloud metadata endpoints
that its role denies. Nothing persists and it is re-triggerable at will, so this is high reach
x recoverable, discounted one tier to medium because it needs the non-default `renderOnly`
setting (README:197-199).

**Fix:** Compare parsed URLs, not strings. Parse each allowlist entry once and require the
request URL's protocol, hostname and port to match exactly (or match on a `.` label
boundary), then re-check the final URL after navigation so redirects and subresources obey
the same rule.

findings.title: Existing render tests expect 400/401 for blocked URLs that now return 403
findings.body:
Blocked and unparseable URLs now return 403, but three assertions in the existing suite still
expect the old 400/401 responses, so `npm test` fails on this tree.

`isRestricted` rejects a missing or non-http(s) protocol (`src/main.js:72`) and both handlers
answer 403 for that case (`src/main.js:101`, `src/main.js:118`). Before this file was added the
same requests fell through to the renderer and produced 400 (or the page's meta status code).

**Evidence:** comparing the handlers with
`test/app-test.js:117-118` (`/render/file://...` meta status, expects 400),
`test/app-test.js:124-125` (same, expects 401) and `test/app-test.js:138-139`
(`/render/abc`, expects 400). All three now take the 403 branch, e.g.
`url.parse('file:///...').protocol === 'file:'` fails `/^https?/` and `url.parse('abc').protocol`
is `null`. Only `test/app-test.js:163` (the renderOnly whitelist test) still matches.

**Impact:** CI is red for a behavior change the PR intends, with no runtime effect. `info`:
the fix is to update the expectations.

**Fix:** point the two meta-status-code tests at an `http://` fixture URL (they currently rely
on `file://`, which is exactly what the new check blocks) and expect 403 for `/render/abc`;
add a case for `/render/file:///dev/fd/0` to lock the protocol check in.

summary: The change adds `lib/print.js`, the console/debug-printing module that `seneca.js:30` requires, and it is byte-identical to upstream seneca 3.8.4 — the baseline tree simply could not load without it (`require('./lib/print')` was missing), so the file restores the library to a working state. I checked the whole file: argv handling (`--seneca.print.tree` in its number/string/boolean/object forms, `--seneca.print.options`), the tree builder, and every print/err/plugin-options helper, and exercised the tree printer against all four cmdspec shapes without error. The risk in this change sits in the printing sinks, which pass unredacted runtime data (process environment, argv, options) straight to stderr/stdout; two findings are recorded.

findings.title: Fatal crash reports written by Print.err leak the whole process environment in clear text
findings.body:
`Print.err` writes seneca's fatal-crash report verbatim to stderr, and that report
contains the whole process environment. Services using seneca pipe stderr into log
aggregators, CI logs, and issue trackers, so every secret in the environment (cloud
keys, database passwords, tokens) is copied in clear text into places with a wider
audience than the process itself.

**Preconditions:** `debug.print.fatal` set to `'full'` (non-default; settable through
options, `SENECA_OPTIONS='{debug:{print:{fatal:full}}}'`),
and the stderr text captured by a log aggregator or issue tracker. `Print.err` is the
only sink for the report text (`lib/common.js:413,416,437`); in this version the
built-in `die` path prints it under `so.test`. `argv` and `PWD` are included in every
mode, including the default `'summary'`.

**Evidence:** `lib/common.js:335-345` builds `procdesc` with
`', argv=' + Util.inspect(process.argv)` and, when `full`, `', env=' +
Util.inspect(process.env)`; `lib/common.js:386` appends `process.env.PWD`
unconditionally. That string is passed to `Print.err` (`lib/common.js:413-438`),
which is `console.error.apply(console.error, arguments)` at `lib/print.js:137-139`.
Reproduced on this tree with a fake AWS key in the environment:

```
process.env.MY_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = 'AKIAIMNOTREAL/verysecret'
Seneca({test:true, debug:{print:{fatal:'full'}}, legacy:{transport:false}})
  .die(new Error('boom'))
```

stderr then contains:
`PROCESS   :::  pid=733, ..., env={  HOSTNAME: ..., MY_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: 'AKIAIMNOTREAL/verysecret', ...}`

There is no option to turn the environment off; `seneca.js:75-81` only defines
`debug.print.options` and `debug.print.fatal`.

**Impact:** CWE-312/359 — sensitive data stored/logged in clear text. Once a crash
report lands in a log store or a public bug report the exposure is permanent: the
only remedy is rotating every credential that was in the environment at crash time.
That crosses the boundary between the process operator and everyone who can read the
collected logs. Graded `medium` rather than `high` because environment output needs
the non-default `'full'` mode and, in this version, the built-in stderr print path is
test-mode gated; `argv`/`PWD` leak with default options.

**Fix:** keep environment data out of crash output unless the operator explicitly asks
for it. Gate the `, env=` segment (and drop the `process.env.PWD` field) on a new
`debug.print.env` option that defaults to `false`, as upstream did for CVE-2019-5483;
`Print.err` should only ever receive text that has already been redacted.

findings.title: Instance creation throws when the debug option is falsy
findings.body:
`print_options` dereferences `options.debug.print.options` without a guard, so a
seneca instance whose `debug` option is a falsy non-object throws during creation
instead of starting. `seneca.js:288` calls `Print.print_options(seneca, options)` on
every instance, so the failure happens before any plugin or action runs.

**Preconditions:** `debug` set to a falsy non-object, e.g. `Seneca({debug:false})` or
`SENECA_OPTIONS='{debug:false}'` in a deployment environment.

**Evidence:** `lib/print.js:44-45`. Sibling code guards the same access —
`lib/plugins.js:173` checks `opts.$.debug.print && ...` and `lib/common.js:293-295`
checks `so.debug && so.debug.print && ...` — but `print.js` assumes both levels exist.

```
$ SENECA_OPTIONS='{debug:false}' node app.js
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'options')
    at module.exports.print_options (lib/print.js:45:27)
    at init (seneca.js:288:9)
```

**Impact:** the process aborts at startup with a TypeError rather than running with
debug printing disabled. Nothing crosses a trust boundary and the operator fixes it by
changing configuration, so this is `info`: it needs the non-default setting
`debug: false`, and only that deployment is affected.

**Fix:** guard the access the way the rest of the tree does —
`if (options.debug && options.debug.print && options.debug.print.options)` — so a
falsy `debug` simply turns the print off.

summary:
Review complete.

The PR adds `lib/print.js` (151 lines), the printing/logging helper module that `seneca.js:30` and `lib/common.js`/`lib/logging.js`/`lib/plugins.js` all `require`, so without it the package cannot even load. The module itself is byte-identical to the upstream seneca 3.8.4 file: CLI handling (`--seneca.print.options`/`--seneca.print.tree`), the initial options dump, the action-tree printer, and the log/err sinks that every log line and the fatal crash report flow through.

Functionally it is sound — I ran the option/tree paths (with a `util.isError` shim, since `norma` breaks on Node 24) and saw no failure in normal use; the remaining edge cases I found (numeric `print.tree` delays, hardcoded role filtering, a self-referential `priormeta`) are debug-flag quirks, not defects. What does need attention is what the module writes out: it is the unredacted sink for the fatal crash report, which appends the whole `process.env` (CVE-2019-5483, reproduced here), and it prints full configuration — including plaintext plugin credentials — whenever `debug.print.options` is enabled from any options source. Both are recorded as low-severity findings, with the fixes upstream later shipped (`debug.print.env`, printed-option redaction) named in each.

findings.title: Fatal crash report copies every environment variable to stderr
findings.body:
When a Seneca process dies, the fatal report written through this module's `err`
export copies the entire `process.env` to stderr, so deployment secrets (API keys,
database passwords, tokens) end up in whatever collects that output.

The report string is built in `lib/common.js:342-345`: the `PROCESS :::` line appends
`', env=' + Util.inspect(process.env)` whenever the `full` flag is set.
`lib/print.js:137-139` (`module.exports.err`) then writes it to `console.error`
unredacted. This PR supplies that writer, so this is the sink the review covers; the
`env=` composition itself is in unchanged code (`lib/common.js`).

**Preconditions:** `debug.print.fatal: 'full'` (default is `'summary'`, `seneca.js:76-82`)
and `test: true`, or `SENECA_TEST` set (`lib/optioner.js:91-93`) — `lib/common.js:411-421`
only writes the report when `so.test` is truthy.

**Evidence:** Reproduced on this checkout (Node 24 needs a `util.isError` shim for
`norma`; unrelated to the bug):

```
SECRET_TOKEN=supersecret123 AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=AKIAfoobar \
  node -r /tmp/shim.js /tmp/die2.js
# die2.js: Seneca({test:true, log:'silent', debug:{print:{fatal:'full'}}}).die(new Error('boom'))
```

stderr contains `PROCESS ::: pid=..., env={ ... SECRET_TOKEN: 'supersecret123', ...
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: 'AKIAfoobar', ... }`. Removing `test:true`, or leaving
`fatal` at its default, prints no env.

**Impact:** This is CVE-2019-5483. Every environment variable the process was given is
copied into the crash report and stays in log storage; anyone who can read those logs
(a log aggregator, CI job output, a support dump) gets the credentials. Graded `low`:
broad reach (whole deployment) x permanent (logs are kept), dropped two tiers because
it needs two non-default settings (`fatal: 'full'`, plus test mode). Upstream treated it
as a security fix and added a `debug.print.env` option defaulting to `false` in 3.9.0;
the code under review is 3.8.4, so the fix is not present.

**Fix:** keep environment data out of crash reports by default: add a `debug.print.env`
option (default `false`) and append `env=` in `lib/common.js:345` only when it is set.
Redacting secret-looking values inside `module.exports.err` before writing would be a
second line of defence.

findings.title: Options and plugin configs print with plaintext credentials
findings.body:
With `debug.print.options` enabled, every Seneca instance prints its fully resolved
options - and every plugin prints its resolved options - to stdout in clear text,
including plaintext credentials that applications pass to `seneca.use()` or keep in
`options.plugins`.

**Preconditions:** `debug.print.options` set through any options source:
`--seneca.print.options`, `--seneca.options='{"debug":{"print":{"options":true}}}'`,
the `SENECA_OPTIONS` environment variable, a `seneca.options.js` file, or code
(`lib/print.js:24-41`, `lib/optioner.js:83-142`). No CLI flag is required.

**Evidence:** `lib/print.js:44-52` prints `Util.inspect(options, {depth: null})` for the
whole options object, called unconditionally at `seneca.js:288`. `lib/plugins.js:175`
calls `Print.plugin_options` for each plugin on init, and `lib/print.js:141-151` prints
that plugin's resolved options. Nothing in `lib/` redacts. Reproduced:

```
SENECA_OPTIONS='{"debug":{"print":{"options":true}}}' node -r /tmp/shim.js /tmp/po.js
# po.js: Seneca().use(function myplug(opts){ this.add('a:1', ...) }, {password:'hunter2'})
```

output contains `{ password: 'hunter2' }` under `Seneca Options (...): plugin: myplug`.
The same line appears with `--seneca.print.options`. Plugin config supplied through
`Seneca({plugins: {...}})` also appears in the `before plugins` dump of the whole
options tree.

**Impact:** `low`. It is opt-in debug output, but options commonly come from the
environment in container and CI deployments, stdout goes to log aggregation, and the
flag is documented as the normal way to inspect options (`seneca.js:77`). Once set, DB
passwords and API keys land in logs readable by anyone with log access. Dropped two
tiers for the explicit non-default setting and for the operator being the one who
enables it.

**Fix:** redact before inspecting: run the object through a key-based redaction pass
(keys such as `password`, `secret`, `token`, `key`, `credential`, `apikey`) in
`print_options`, `plugin_options` and `print`. Upstream later added a dedicated
redaction module for exactly these printed options.

summary:
**Summary**

The PR adds `index.js`, the whole `dot-prop` implementation including a blocklist guard (`__proto__`, `prototype`, `constructor`) applied in `getPathSegments`. The file is byte-identical to upstream's CVE-2020-8116 fix commit (`3039c8c`, released as v5.1.1), and I reproduced that it blocks the attack: `set({}, '__proto__.polluted', …)`, `constructor.prototype.…`, nested and backslash-escaped variants all leave `Object.prototype` untouched (they pollute on the pre-fix v5.1.0 code). The unchanged test suite still passes against the added file, and `has()` correctly reports `false` for the disallowed paths.

I found one real defect the new guard introduces: `get()` returns bare `undefined` for rejected paths, discarding the caller's `defaultValue` and contradicting the `get<T>(…, defaultValue: T): T` contract in `index.d.ts:28-32`. Upstream later fixed exactly that line (`d400c8d`, #86). Everything else I probed — writes through inherited properties like `set({}, 'toString.x', 1)`, silent no-ops in `set`/`delete`, backslash-escaping quirks — behaves identically before and after this change, so it is pre-existing library design that the diff neither touches nor makes newly reachable. Verdict: the security fix is correct and the regression I found is minor, so one low finding.

findings.title: get() drops the caller's default value when the path is disallowed
findings.body:
`get(object, path, defaultValue)` returns `undefined` instead of the caller's
`defaultValue` whenever `path` contains a disallowed segment (`__proto__`,
`prototype`, `constructor`). Any caller that supplies a fallback for such a path
gets `undefined` and cannot distinguish it from a missing value.

**Evidence:** the new guard at index.js:41-43 returns before the loop that hands
back `value` (index.js:47, 59):

```js
const pathArray = getPathSegments(path);
if (pathArray.length === 0) {
    return;          // <- drops `value`
}
```

`getPathSegments` returns `[]` only via index.js:27-29, i.e. only for the three
disallowed segments, so this branch is reachable exactly where a caller is most
likely to be passing a fallback. Reproduced with `is-obj@2.0.0` on Node 24:

```
get({}, 'constructor', 'DEF')            => undefined
get({a: {}}, 'a.constructor', 'DEF')     => undefined
get({}, 'a.__proto__.b', 'DEF')          => undefined
get({}, 'constructor.prototype.x', 'DEF')=> undefined
get({a: 1}, 'foo', 'DEF')                => 'DEF'     (normal miss still works)
get({}, 'constructor', 0)                => undefined (falsy defaults too)
```

The behaviour contradicts the stated contract: index.d.ts:28-32 declares
`get<T>(object, path, defaultValue: T): T` (not `T | undefined`) and
readme.md:25-26 documents the default being returned. The repository's own
`test.js` has no disallowed-segment case (its default-value tests are test.js:18
and test.js:44), and the whole suite still passes against this file, so the
regression is invisible to CI. Upstream later fixed this same line — commit
d400c8d, "Return default value if path is invalid (#86)", `return;` -> `return value;`
with the test `get({}, 'constructor', '🦄') === '🦄'`.

**Impact:** low. A single call returns the wrong value (contained), deterministically
and without an error, so a consumer that assumes the declared `T` gets `undefined`
and can throw downstream (for example `get(config, p, 'x').length`). No trust
boundary is crossed and no data is lost; it is a silent API-contract break, not a
security hole. Blocking writes to those paths is the intended fix and remains correct.

**Fix:** restore the default value for rejected paths, as upstream did — replace
`return;` at index.js:42 with `return value;`, and add a regression assertion such
as `get({}, 'constructor', 'fallback') === 'fallback'`.

summary:
**Summary**

This PR adds `lib/index.js` (295 lines) — the full `mpath` get/set/has/unset implementation — and is byte-identical to upstream `mpath` 0.5.0, the first, incomplete fix for CVE-2018-16490. The `__proto__` guard it introduces in `set` (lib/index.js:186-192) covers only that one literal, so `set('constructor.prototype.<name>', value, {})` still reaches `Object.prototype` at the terminal write on lib/index.js:284; I reproduced it on Node 24 (including the array and array-of-parts forms, and an arbitrary function value). `unset` is not exploitable the same way only because its guard rejects non-object intermediates.

Everything else in the file checks out: the full test suite (76 tests) passes, and the remaining rough edges I surveyed — falsy intermediates aborting `set`, the `$` copy heuristic, `map`-arity overload detection, and `has`/`unset` lacking the Map support that `get`/`set` have — are long-standing upstream behaviours that persist in current `mpath`, not defects this change introduces. One finding recorded.

findings.title: Prototype pollution guard in set() only blocks __proto__, so constructor.prototype paths still write Object.prototype
findings.body:
`mpath.set()` blocks the path segment `__proto__` but not `constructor`/`prototype`, so a path of the form `constructor.prototype.<name>` still writes to `Object.prototype`. The guard added in this change (lib/index.js:186-192) is the only pollution check in the file, and it compares against a single literal.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes a path string or parts array that comes from untrusted input (the exact scenario the comment at lib/index.js:187-188 names). No options, `special`, `lookup`, or `$` copy mode are needed, and the target can be an empty plain object.

**Evidence:** with Node v24.22.2, requiring the repo as-is:

```
mpath.set('__proto__.polluted', 'yes', {})            // blocked -> ({}).polluted === undefined
mpath.set('constructor.prototype.polluted', 'yes', {})// -> ({}).polluted === 'yes'
mpath.set('a.constructor.prototype.nested', 'p', {a:{}}) // -> ({}).nested === 'p'
mpath.set(['constructor','prototype','x'], 'y', {})   // array form also pollutes
```

The walk loop reaches `Object` at part `constructor` (`{}['constructor']`), then `Object.prototype` at part `prototype` (lib/index.js:203-238), and the terminal write at lib/index.js:284 performs `Object.prototype[part] = map(val)`. Nothing rejects a function as an intermediate. Arbitrary value types work too: `set('constructor.prototype.toString', fn, {})` replaces `toString` for every object in the process. `exports.unset` is not exploitable through the same path only because its guard at lib/index.js:134 rejects non-object intermediates; `exports.set` has no such check.

**Impact:** any service that feeds user-supplied field paths into `mpath.set` (the mongoose-style `$set: {"constructor.prototype.isAdmin": true}` case) gets attacker-controlled writes into `Object.prototype` for the whole process, i.e. privilege checks, serialization, and template logic can all be flipped, and the write persists for the life of the process. Reach crosses a trust boundary and the effect is permanent, so this is high: the change leaves the very CVE it is fixing reachable by a one-word variation of the blocked path.

**Fix:** keep the invariant "no path segment may name a prototype-traversing property." Reject `constructor` and `prototype` in the same scan as `__proto__` (upstream later replaced the literal with `var ignoreProperties = ['__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype']` and used `ignoreProperties.indexOf(parts[i]) !== -1` in both `set` and `unset`), and add a test covering `set('constructor.prototype.x', v, {})` returning without mutating `Object.prototype`.

summary:
Review complete. Summary:

PR #2 adds `index.js` — the dot-prop 5.1.0 implementation (`get`/`set`/`delete`/`has` over dot paths with `\.` escaping) — which the baseline tree omitted, so the whole file is new surface.

The implementation has no guard against path segments that name prototype links, so `set` and `delete` walk into `Object.prototype` (`__proto__.x`, `constructor.prototype.x`, `__proto__.toString`); I reproduced process-wide pollution and a process-wide built-in deletion, and recorded it as one high finding with the upstream 5.1.1 fix shape (reject the three names once in `getPathSegments`). Beyond that I checked escaping edge cases, null/primitive intermediates, `get`'s own-enumerable gate, and `delete` crash paths against `test.js` and the upstream 5.1.1 tarball: the remaining behavior matches upstream 5.1.0 (whose suite passes here) and did not yield a separate reportable defect — notably `has`'s prototype-chain awareness and strict-mode `delete` throws are upstream-intended. I also recorded the durable fix shape as a knowledge concept under `security/prototype-pollution.md`.

findings.title: Dot paths with __proto__ or constructor.prototype pollute Object.prototype through set() and delete()
findings.body:
A dot path that names `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype` lets `set()` and
`delete()` walk into the prototype chain. `set({}, '__proto__.polluted', 'yes')` adds
`polluted` to `Object.prototype`, so every object in the process gains it; `set({},
'constructor.prototype.polluted', 'yes')` does the same. `delete({}, '__proto__.toString')`
removes `Object.prototype.toString` for the whole process. Applications that build the
path from request data (dot-prop's normal use) hand the attacker a process-wide write.

**Evidence:**
- `getPathSegments` (index.js:4-20) returns raw segments and rejects none of these names.
- `set` (index.js:54-77) does `if (!isObj(object[p]))` then `object = object[p]`. For
  `__proto__`, `object['__proto__']` is `Object.prototype`, which is an object, so the
  loop descends and the last-segment write at index.js:68-70 lands on `Object.prototype`.
  `constructor` works too: `object['constructor']` is a function, and is-obj 2.0.0
  (`node_modules/is-obj/index.js:5`) counts functions as objects, so
  `constructor.prototype.x` reaches `Object.prototype`.
- `delete` (index.js:79-100) has no guard either: it descends through `__proto__` and
  runs `delete object[p]` on the last segment against the prototype object.
- Reproduced on this checkout:
  ```
  $ node -e "const d=require('./index.js'); d.set({},'__proto__.p','yes'); console.log(({}).p)"
  yes
  $ node -e "const d=require('./index.js'); d.set({},'constructor.prototype.p','yes'); console.log(({}).p)"
  yes
  $ node -e "const d=require('./index.js'); d.delete({},'__proto__.toString'); console.log(typeof ({}).toString)"
  undefined
  ```

**Impact:** Untrusted path input modifies `Object.prototype` for the life of the process
(broad reach, permanent), which is the mechanism behind CVE-2020-8116 and a standard
step to auth bypass or RCE in consumers. Severity `high` on the reach × persistence table
(broad × permanent).

**Fix:** Reject these segments where paths are parsed, so every method inherits the guard.
In `getPathSegments`, after building `parts`, return an empty list when any segment is
`__proto__`, `prototype`, or `constructor`, and have `get`/`set`/`delete`/`has` bail out
(return the default / root / false) on an empty list. This is the shape of the upstream
5.1.1 fix and also covers `get` and `has`, which currently reach inherited members.
