**Summary:** PR #2 re-adds `lib/index.js` (283 lines) — the mpath 0.4.1 source with a `Map` shim — to a tree whose baseline had that file stripped. I compared it against the published npm tarballs: it is byte-identical to `mpath@0.4.1` apart from the shim, i.e. the pre-fix snapshot for CVE-2018-16490, lacking the `__proto__` guards that 0.5.0 and 0.6.0 add. I reproduced prototype writes (`__proto__`, `constructor.prototype`) and a prototype-member delete, and recorded one `high` finding. The other behaviours the probes surfaced (falsy intermediates short-circuiting, array fan-out on non-numeric segments, `instanceof Map`, `unset`/`set` asymmetries) are deliberate upstream semantics covered by the existing test suite, so I did not file them. The change is otherwise mechanically clean, but it must not ship without the traversal guard.

findings.title: Paths containing __proto__ or constructor.prototype let callers write to and delete from Object.prototype
findings.body:
Paths whose segments are `__proto__` reach `Object.prototype`. `set` and `unset` walk
segments with a bare property read and write, so nothing distinguishes an own key from
an inherited one. A path such as `__proto__.isAdmin` passed to `mpath.set` assigns the
value onto `Object.prototype`; `mpath.unset('__proto__.toString', ...)` deletes a member
of it. Every object in the process then sees the planted property, and a deleted built-in
breaks unrelated code.

**Preconditions:** the caller forwards an untrusted path (or `parts` array) into `set` or
`unset`. Any code that turns a user-supplied document key into an mpath call — the
mongoose `$set`-style update path this library is written for — meets it. No validation
exists in the library beyond `Array.isArray(parts)`
(lib/index.js:127-129, lib/index.js:176-178).

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e "var m=require('./');
  m.set('__proto__.isAdmin', true, {name:'victim'});
  console.log(({}).isAdmin, Object.prototype.isAdmin)"
true true

$ node -e "var m=require('./');
  m.set('constructor.prototype.pwned', 'y', {});
  console.log(({}).pwned)"
y

$ node -e "var m=require('./');
  console.log(m.unset('__proto__.toString', {a:1}), typeof ({}).toString)"
true undefined
```

Mechanism in `set`: the walk at lib/index.js:221-225 resolves `obj = obj['__proto__']`,
which is `Object.prototype` for any plain object, and lib/index.js:272 then assigns
`obj[part] = map(val)`. In `unset`, the guard at lib/index.js:134 uses `in`, which accepts
inherited names, lib/index.js:141 walks into `Object.prototype`, and lib/index.js:138
deletes there.

Upstream closed this in mpath 0.5.0 with an early `return` in `set` for `__proto__` and a
`return false` in `unset`, then widened it to `['__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype']`
in 0.6.0 (mpath@0.6.0 lib/index.js:3, :141-143, :192-194). The file under review has
neither guard.

**Impact:** Prototype pollution across a trust boundary: an actor who controls only a path
string gains a write into shared process state, and the effect is permanent for the life
of the process (nothing supported undoes it) and applies to every object and request.
Severity is `high` by reach (crosses a trust boundary) x persistence (permanent); it is
not `critical` because the application must pass the untrusted path through.

**Fix:** Reject `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype` segments before any traversal:
in `set`, scan `parts` after the `null == o` check and return; in `unset`, return `false`
when a segment matches. Then the invariant is that no write or delete can ever target a
prototype member, regardless of caller input.

summary:
Review complete. Summary:

PR #2 re-adds `src/main.js`, the Express front end for rendertron: `/render` and `/screenshot` routes that drive headless Chrome, a `/node_modules` static mount, an optional datastore cache and Google Analytics tracking, plus health/stop hooks and an uncaught-exception handler that exits after repeated failures. The code is the pre-release upstream version, and its only input validation is opt-in and prefix-based, so the service ships as an unauthenticated open renderer. I found the missing scheme/host validation on both render routes (reproduced end to end: `file:///etc/passwd` and loopback services are returned to the caller), the publicly reachable `/_ah/stop` that kills the shared Chrome instance, and two lower-impact error-handling defects. The change needs input validation and the stop route removed before it can be deployed publicly.

findings.title: Anyone can stop the shared Chrome instance with GET /_ah/stop, disabling rendering for all users
findings.body:
`GET /_ah/stop` (src/main.js:136-139) waits for `config.chrome.kill()` and answers `OK`. The route has no authentication and no restriction to internal callers, so one request from anyone who can reach the service kills the single Chrome instance that serves every render request for that instance. The Express server keeps listening afterwards, so the instance stays up and returns failures instead of being replaced.

**Evidence:**

- Route: `app.get('/_ah/stop', async(request, response) => { await config.chrome.kill(); response.send('OK'); })` — src/main.js:136-139. There is no auth middleware anywhere in the file; the other routes are `/render`, `/screenshot`, `/_ah/health` and `/`.
- After the kill, `renderer.serialize()` calls `CDP.New({port: config.port})` (src/renderer.js:179) and `CDP({tab, port})` (src/renderer.js:180) against a dead port, so every later render and screenshot fails.
- Nothing recovers it: `/_ah/health` is a constant `OK` (src/main.js:134), so a platform health check sees a healthy instance that cannot render. Only a manual restart or redeploy restores service.
- This is the issue recorded as CVE-2017-18353 (NVD: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N, availability only).

**Impact:** Broad (every user of the instance loses rendering) and recoverable (a restart restores it), so medium. Reach is the whole service; nothing bounds who can trigger it.

**Fix:** Remove the HTTP route. If an external shutdown hook is needed, keep an `app.stop()` function for `logUncaughtError` (as the internal handler at src/main.js:173 already does) and, for anything HTTP-facing, expose it only behind an internal-only check rather than a plain GET.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /render and /screenshot accept file:// and any host, exposing local files and internal services
findings.body:
`GET /render/<url>` and `GET /screenshot/<url>` pass the caller's string straight to headless Chrome. Neither route validates the scheme or the host, and neither route authenticates the caller. The only guard, `isRestricted()` (src/main.js:65-74), returns `false` immediately when the optional `renderOnly` config is absent (src/main.js:66-67), and this tree ships no `config.json`, so the endpoints are open by default.

**Evidence:**

- Untouched path to Chrome: src/main.js:92-99 and :111-118 forward `request.params.url` to the renderer; src/renderer.js:75 calls `Page.navigate({url: url})` with no parsing, and src/renderer.js:190 returns `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` as the response body, so whatever Chrome loaded comes back to the caller.
- Reproduced end to end, running the repo's own `src/renderer.js` against headless Chrome:
  - `GET /render/file:///etc/passwd` → 200, body contains `root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash` and the rest of the file.
  - `GET /render/http://127.0.0.1:4567/` (a service bound to loopback only) → 200, body contains that service's response.
- The repo already relies on `file://` working: test/app-test.js:113-127 renders `file://` + a local path and asserts on the status code the page sets via its own meta tag.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated network client can read files from the container (`/etc/passwd`, `config.json` with any credentials, application source) and can make the server fetch loopback, intranet and cloud-metadata addresses from the server's own network position. That is data the caller's role denies, and disclosed bytes cannot be recalled: high.

The `renderOnly` allow-list does not fix the host half either: it is a raw string prefix test (`url.startsWith(...)`, src/main.js:69), documented as a "strict prefix match" in README.md:197-200. With `renderOnly: ['https://good.example']`, `https://good.example.evil.net/` and `https://good.example@169.254.169.254/` both pass the check and are fetched by Chrome.

**Fix:** Parse the requested URL (`new URL(...)`), reject any protocol other than `http:`/`https:` with 403, and compare against `renderOnly` on `origin` (`protocol + '//' + host`) instead of a prefix of the raw string. Do it in one helper used by both routes, before the renderer is called.

findings.title: Error responses reflect the request URL into a text/html body and leak internal error text
findings.body:
Both failure paths build the response body from the caller's URL and the internal error text, then send it as a string. `res.send(string)` in Express sets `Content-Type: text/html`, so the URL is reflected into an HTML document unescaped.

**Evidence:**

- src/main.js:103-107 (`/render`) and :127-131 (`/screenshot`): `let message = \`Cannot render ${request.params.url}\`; if (err && err.message) message += \` - "${err.message}"\`; response.status(400).send(message);`
- `request.params.url` is URL-decoded by Express, so `%3Cscript%3E` arrives as `<script>`. A request such as `GET /render/%3Cscript%3Ealert(document.domain)%3C/script%3E` fails to render, reaches the catch block, and returns 400 with a `text/html` body containing a live `<script>` element.
- The same body also echoes `err.message`, e.g. Chrome/CDP errors and DNS failures that name internal hosts.

**Impact:** Script runs in the rendertron origin for anyone who opens the crafted link, and internal error details are leaked to unauthenticated callers. The service holds no session of its own, so the practical value of the script execution is limited: low. The information leak on its own would be info.

**Fix:** Answer with a fixed message (`Cannot render requested URL`) and log `err` server-side. If the URL must be echoed back, set `Content-Type: text/plain` so the browser cannot execute it.

findings.title: Analytics failures become uncaught exceptions, and six of them exit the instance
findings.body:
`track()` (src/main.js:77-88) creates an `https.request` and never attaches an `error` listener. A DNS or connection failure emits `'error'` on the request, which becomes an uncaught exception. The handler installed at src/main.js:176-179 counts those and calls `process.exit(1)` once the count passes 5, so a Google Analytics outage takes the whole render service down.

**Preconditions:** `analyticsTrackingId` set in `config.json` (off by default), and `www.google-analytics.com` unreachable from the host — blocked egress, DNS failure, or a proxy error.

**Evidence:**

- src/main.js:79-85 builds `https.request({host: 'www.google-analytics.com', ...})`, writes the event and calls `post.end()` with no `.on('error', ...)`.
- Repro of the mechanics with the same code shape: an unresolvable host produces `uncaughtException` with `code: 'ENOTFOUND'` and no `error` listener to absorb it.
- src/main.js:169-178: `exceptionCount++` and `if (exceptionCount > 5) { ... process.exit(1); }`.
- Every successful render and screenshot calls `track()` (src/main.js:101, :125), so any client that can make six rendering requests triggers the count while the analytics endpoint is failing.

**Impact:** The service exits for all users. It needs a non-default setting and a fault outside the system, so the medium reach/availability outcome is discounted to low.

**Fix:** Attach an `error` listener that logs and drops the event (`.on('error', () => {})` on the request, plus a response handler), so analytics failures never reach the fatal counter.

summary:
Both findings are recorded and every claim in them was verified by execution. Repo left clean (dependency install artifacts restored).

**Summary:** PR #1 re-adds `lib/processNested.js`, the parser that turns flattened multipart field names into nested objects when `parseNested` is enabled; upstream treats this file as the fix for CVE-2020-7699. The new prototype-pollution guard only denylists `__proto__`, so `constructor[prototype][...]` field names still reach `Object.prototype` process-wide — I reproduced that end to end through the public middleware, and the same missing own-property check also lets a request mutate shared built-ins such as `Object.prototype.toString`. Separately, a path that nests through a scalar value (`a=x` then `a[b][c]=y`) throws an uncaught `TypeError` from inside the busboy `finish` listener and takes the process down. Overall the guard is a partial fix that leaves the CVE's attack class exploitable whenever the option is on, plus one availability defect in the added code; everything else in the file is unchanged upstream behaviour.

findings.title: A field name containing constructor[prototype] still pollutes Object.prototype when parseNested is on
findings.body:
A multipart field name containing `constructor[prototype]` bypasses the new prototype-pollution guard and writes attacker-chosen properties onto the process-wide `Object.prototype`. Every object created later in the same Node process inherits them, including objects belonging to other requests and other users.

**Preconditions:** the app enables the non-default option `parseNested: true` (`lib/index.js:19`); field names come straight from the client (`lib/processMultipart.js:42`, `lib/utilities.js:84`).

**Evidence:** the denylist at `lib/processNested.js:1` lists only `__proto__`, so the guard at `lib/processNested.js:22` skips only that exact segment. For any other segment the traversal at `lib/processNested.js:29-30` uses `!current[k]`, which is false for inherited properties, so it follows the inherited value instead of creating an own property. `constructor` resolves to the `Object` constructor, `prototype` to `Object.prototype`, and `lib/processNested.js:27` then assigns the attacker value there.

Reproduced end to end against the public middleware (`express` app, `fileUpload({parseNested: true})`, `supertest`):

- `.field('constructor[prototype][polluted]', 'pwned')` → HTTP 200, `req.body` is `{}`, and `({}).polluted === 'pwned'` in the server process.
- `.field('f[constructor][prototype][z]', 'yes')` → `({}).z === 'yes'`, while the response body only shows a decoy `{f:{}}`.
- `.field('constructor[prototype][isAdmin]', 'true')` → `({}).isAdmin === 'true'` and the property is enumerable, so `for (const k in {}) { ... }` yields it.
- Direct call: `require('./lib/processNested')({'constructor[prototype][polluted]':'yes'})` returns `{}` and sets `Object.prototype.polluted`.
- The blocked form still works as intended: `__proto__[x]` leaves `({}).x` undefined, so the guard is effective only for the key it names.

The same gap lets a request mutate shared built-ins that are not in the denylist, e.g. `toString[p]=1` sets `Object.prototype.toString.p` and `valueOf[call][x]=1` sets `Object.prototype.valueOf.call.x` for the rest of the process lifetime. No error is raised and no field appears in `req.body` in any of these cases.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated client gains write access to state shared by every request in the process: it can define defaults that application code reads from plain `{}` literals (truthiness checks, options objects, `for..in` loops), which is capability its role denies, and it affects all users the service serves. Persistence is recoverable — a restart clears the polluted prototype and nothing is lost — so the grade is high before discounts; the required non-default `parseNested` setting drops it one tier to medium. This is the class of defect CVE-2020-7699 describes, so the fix in this PR does not close the issue.

**Fix:** stop trusting key lookups on a normal object. Before descending in `lib/processNested.js`, require that the segment is an own, safe property, e.g. `const has = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(current, k)` and skip (or abort the key) when `!has`; in the same check reject `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`. Adding `constructor` and `prototype` to `INVALID_KEYS` closes this exact bypass, but the own-property test is the invariant that also stops the `toString`/`valueOf` mutation. A unit test asserting `({}).polluted === undefined` after `processNested({'constructor[prototype][polluted]':'x'})` would catch a regression.

findings.title: Nesting a field name through a scalar value kills the Node process with an uncaught TypeError
findings.body:
Two multipart fields whose names nest through a scalar make `processNested` throw an uncaught `TypeError` from inside the busboy `'finish'` listener, which kills the Node process serving every user.

**Preconditions:** `parseNested: true` (`lib/index.js:19`). The client controls field order, so ordering is not an obstacle.

**Evidence:** with fields `a=x` and then `a[b][c]=y`, the segment `a` is already the string `'x'` when the second key is processed. `lib/processNested.js:29` sees `!current['a']` as false, so `current` becomes the string; assigning `current['b']` on a primitive is a sloppy-mode no-op and `current = current['b']` yields `undefined`; `lib/processNested.js:27` then throws. Reproduced against the public middleware:

```
TypeError: Cannot set properties of undefined (setting 'c')
    at module.exports (.../lib/processNested.js:27:20)
    at Busboy.<anonymous> (.../lib/processMultipart.js:132:18)
    at Busboy.emit (.../node_modules/busboy/lib/main.js:37:33)
    at process.processTicksAndRejections (node:internal/process/task_queues:85:11)
```

The stack shows the throw happens on a stream callback, not inside an express handler, so `next()` is never called and express cannot catch it; the process exits on the unhandled exception. The same shape occurs with `a[b]=1` + `a[b][c][d]=2` and `hobbies[0]=Cinema` + `hobbies[0][b][c]=y`.

**Impact:** one cheap unauthenticated request takes the whole server process down, so every user of the service loses it; the attacker can repeat the request at will, which makes the outage recoverable rather than transient. Reach is broad and persistence recoverable — medium before discounts — and the non-default `parseNested` requirement drops it to low. The outcome is genuine but the damage to data is nil, and apps that install an `uncaughtException` handler survive, though with a dangling request.

**Fix:** treat a path conflict as a rejected key instead of following a non-container value. In `lib/processNested.js:29`, only descend when `current[k]` is a plain object or array (`current[k] && typeof current[k] === 'object'`), and skip the key when an earlier segment holds a scalar; that removes the `undefined` write at line 27 without changing the happy path. Add a test with `{'a': 'x', 'a[b][c]': 'y'}`.

summary:
Review complete. Findings recorded against the diff.

**Change:** the PR adds `lib/processNested.js`, the flattened-field-name-to-nested-object converter that `lib/processMultipart.js:131-134` applies to `req.body` and `req.files` when `parseNested` is enabled. This is the file that carries CVE-2020-7699 in this fixture.

**Findings:**
- `medium` — `__proto__[...]` / `constructor[prototype][...]` field names reach and write into `Object.prototype` (reproduced end to end through express + a multipart POST; the response is a normal 200).
- `low` — `a[length]` after `a[0]` throws `RangeError: Invalid array length` inside the unguarded `busboy.on('finish')` handler, which I reproduced as an `uncaughtException` that ends the process.
- `info` — the same walk descends into `req.files`' File instances, so `f[mimetype]` replaces another upload's MIME string with a File object and breaks validators.

The existing `test/processNested.spec.js` and `test/options.spec.js` pass with the new file; the nested/flat behavior itself is correct for well-formed names. The defect is that the containment walk uses a truthiness test rather than own-property tracking, so it leaves the object it is building; a fix must restrict the walk to containers it created and reject `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype` segments.

findings.title: Multipart field name __proto__[...] pollutes Object.prototype when parseNested is enabled
findings.body:
`processNested` descends a bracketed field name by testing `if (!current[k])` (lib/processNested.js:21) and then writes the last segment with `current[k] = value` (lib/processNested.js:19). Nothing rejects `__proto__` or `constructor`, so the walk leaves the result object and lands on `Object.prototype`. A multipart field named `__proto__[polluted]` therefore writes `Object.prototype.polluted` into the whole process, and `constructor[prototype][polluted2]` does the same through the inherited `constructor`.

Field names reach the function untouched: busboy's `field` handler builds `req.body` at lib/processMultipart.js:44 and lib/processMultipart.js:131-134 passes it to `processNested`. The injected name itself never appears in the result, so the response is a normal `200` and nothing in `req.body` shows the attack.

**Preconditions:** the app creates the middleware with `parseNested: true` (default is `false`, lib/index.js:19) and accepts multipart/form-data requests.

**Evidence:** express app using `fileUpload({parseNested: true})`, one supertest POST with fields `__proto__[polluted]=yes` and `constructor[prototype][polluted2]=yes2`:

```
status 200 body {"body":{}}
Object.prototype.polluted = yes
Object.prototype.polluted2 = yes2
```

Unit level the same: `require('./lib/processNested')({'__proto__[polluted]':'yes'})` returns `{}` and leaves `({}).polluted === 'yes'`.

**Impact:** any unauthenticated client that can post a multipart form writes arbitrary properties into the prototype of every object in the Node process, for the life of the process. Every later `obj.polluted` read or `'polluted' in obj` check in the app or a dependency sees the injected value, which is the standard route to auth bypass and DoS through prototype-pollution gadgets. This is CVE-2020-7699. Base severity is high (a remote actor gains a capability their role denies, and the state survives until restart); the matrix drops one tier because it needs the non-default `parseNested` option, giving medium.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the walk may only use containers it created itself. Skip the prototype-shaping segments and require own properties:

```js
if (k === '__proto__' || k === 'constructor' || k === 'prototype') continue;
if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(current, k)) {
  current[k] = !isNaN(keyParts[index + 1]) ? [] : {};
}
```

findings.title: A multipart field named a[length] throws RangeError inside the busboy finish handler and kills the process
findings.body:
Two multipart fields make `processNested` throw a `RangeError` from inside busboy's `finish` handler: `a[0]=x` first creates an array at `d.a` (lib/processNested.js:21), then `a[length]=abc` writes `current['length'] = 'abc'` at lib/processNested.js:19, and V8 rejects a non-numeric array length. The throw is unguarded at lib/processMultipart.js:131-134 (no `try`/`catch` anywhere in that handler), so it escapes the `busboy.on('finish')` emit and becomes an `uncaughtException`, which ends the process.

The same input works through `req.files`: two file fields named `f[0]` and `f[length]`.

**Preconditions:** `parseNested: true` (default `false`, lib/index.js:19) and a multipart/form-data request.

**Evidence:** express app with `fileUpload({parseNested: true})`, POST with `.field('a[0]','x').field('a[length]','abc')`. The request receives no response and the process reports:

```
UNCAUGHT EXCEPTION (would crash the server): RangeError: Invalid array length
    at processNested (lib/processNested.js:19)
```

Unit level: `require('./lib/processNested')({'a[0]':'x','a[length]':'abc'})` throws the same error, and so does `{'f[0]':f1,'f[length]':f2}`.

**Impact:** one small unauthenticated request stops the server for every user while `parseNested` is on. A supervisor restarts the process, so the outage is short and repeatable rather than permanent. Base severity medium (broad reach, recoverable); the matrix drops one tier because it needs the non-default `parseNested` option, giving low.

**Fix:** never treat `length` as a child key of an array. Restore "array indices only": skip the segment when `Array.isArray(current) && k === 'length'`, or only descend into containers this function created and reject keys that are not integer indices on arrays.

findings.title: Bracketed file field names overwrite another uploaded file's metadata
findings.body:
`processMultipart` runs `processNested` over `req.files` (lib/processMultipart.js:133), whose values are File instances, not containers. The walk at lib/processNested.js:21 sees the existing File as truthy and descends into it, then lib/processNested.js:19 assigns into it. So a file field named `f[mimetype]` rewrites the `mimetype` of the file stored under `f`:

```
filesKeys: ["f"]
fMimetype: "[object File]"   // was "image/png"
```

(`f[name]`, `f[size]`, `f[data]`, `f[hash]` behave the same.) Any app code that treats these as strings then fails: `file.mimetype.startsWith('image/')` throws `TypeError: file.mimetype.startsWith is not a function`, which typically becomes a `500` or an uncaught rejection.

**Preconditions:** `parseNested: true` (default `false`, lib/index.js:19); the request uploads one file as `f` and another as `f[mimetype]`.

**Evidence:** express app with `fileUpload({parseNested: true})`, supertest `.attach('f', buf, 'orig.png').attach('f[mimetype]', buf, 'evil.html')`; the handler reports `req.files.f.mimetype` as a File object rather than a MIME string.

**Impact:** the caller corrupts the metadata of its own upload, so no other user's data is exposed and the usual validation fails closed; the practical effect is a broken request and an avoidable `500`/crash in code that validates `mimetype` or builds a path from `name`. Contained and per-request, and it needs the non-default `parseNested` option, so this is info.

**Fix:** the same invariant as for the prototype-pollution finding, but stated for values: only descend into (and write leaves into) containers this function created. Track created nodes, or check `current[k] !== null && typeof current[k] === 'object' && Object.getPrototypeOf(current[k]) === Object.prototype || Array.isArray(current[k])` with an own-property test; otherwise replace the value with a fresh container instead of mutating the existing object.

summary:
**Summary** The PR re-adds `src/ajax.js` (844 lines) to a tree that had it removed; the file is byte-identical to upstream jquery/jquery commit `a938d7b1` ("compress ajax", the child of the baseline `c27dc018`), and it is the state that shipped in jQuery 1.9.0. That matters here because the baseline version's `jQuery.fn.load` stripped response scripts with the `rscript` regex, which the CVE-2020-7656 advisory describes as failing on ``; the added file instead uses `jQuery("
").append( jQuery.parseHTML( responseText ) )` (`src/ajax.js:177`), and `parseHTML` deletes the collected script nodes in `src/core.js:495-498`, so a whitespace-bearing closing tag no longer survives into the DOM. I confirmed this empirically (jsdom: payload `
` executes through the selector path in the baseline version and does not in the added version), and checked that the partial application — only `ajax.js` updated while `src/ajax/{script,jsonp,xhr}.js` stay at the parent version — is contract-compatible (their abort arguments, prefilter/transport signatures and module-scope identifiers all match), and that the grunt concatenation still parses. No findings recorded: no security regression and no demonstrable defect introduced by the change.

The change adds `utils/find-opencv.js`, the OpenCV discovery helper that `binding.gyp` shells out to during a source build. The file is verbatim upstream except for one line: `flag` is pinned to `"--exists"` instead of read from `process.argv`, so the `--cflags` and `--libs` calls made from `binding.gyp` (lines 29, 34, 109, 114, …) all run `pkg-config … --exists`, which prints nothing. I reproduced that with a real `pkg-config` and a discoverable OpenCV: the script emits a single newline where the upstream version emits the include and link flags, so a source build gets empty `include_dirs` and `libraries`; on Windows the fallback reaches `printPaths` with `--exists` and throws "unknown argument", leaving no working path at all. Alongside that I recorded a `low` entry for the Windows fallback's unquoted `%OPENCV_DIR%`, which `cmd.exe` expands into a shell string. I checked the other Windows path arithmetic against the README's `OPENCV_DIR` convention and found it consistent, so nothing else qualified.

findings.title: find-opencv.js ignores --cflags/--libs, so builds get empty include dirs and link flags
findings.body:
`utils/find-opencv.js` never reads `process.argv`, so `--cflags` and `--libs` are ignored and every invocation runs `pkg-config <opencv> --exists`. That option prints nothing, so the script prints one blank line and exits 0. `binding.gyp` uses this output for both `include_dirs` and `libraries` (`binding.gyp:29`, `binding.gyp:34`, and the same substitutions in the `test_nativemat` target), so both lists come back empty and a source build fails later with `opencv2/core/core.hpp: No such file or directory`. Every platform and every flag path is affected.

**Evidence:**
`utils/find-opencv.js:5` is the only assignment to `flag`: `var flag = "--exists";`. Nothing in the file mentions `argv`.

Reproduced with a real `pkg-config` 1.8.1 and a discoverable OpenCV:

```
$ pkg-config "opencv >= 2.3.1" --exists; echo $?
0
$ pkg-config "opencv >= 2.3.1" --cflags
-I/usr/local/include -I/usr/local/include/opencv
$ node utils/find-opencv.js --cflags | od -c
0000000  \n
$ node utils/find-opencv.js --libs | od -c
0000000  \n
```

The same script with `var flag = process.argv[2] || "--exists";` prints `-I/usr/local/include ...`. Upstream `cfc96ba0` has exactly that line.

On `win32` the break is louder: `pkg-config` normally fails, so `fallback()` runs and `printPaths()` is reached with `flag === "--exists"`, which falls through both branches and throws `Error: unknown argument '--exists'` (`utils/find-opencv.js:70`). Windows builds have no working path at all.

**Impact:** Broad, recoverable. No attacker is involved; anyone building node-opencv from source cannot compile because OpenCV headers and libs are never discovered. Severity `medium` (broad reach, a one-line fix restores it).

**Fix:** Restore the flag from the command line, and keep the value constrained to the two flags the build passes, e.g. `var flags = {"--cflags": "--cflags", "--libs": "--libs"}; var flag = flags[process.argv[2]] || "--exists";` — the whitelist also keeps the value safe for the shell string at `utils/find-opencv.js:15`.

findings.title: Unquoted OPENCV_DIR reaches cmd.exe in the Windows fallback, allowing command injection
findings.body:
On Windows, the `pkg-config` fallback runs `exec("echo %OPENCV_DIR%")`, and `exec` uses `cmd.exe`. `%OPENCV_DIR%` is expanded by the shell before `echo` sees it, so a value containing `cmd` metacharacters (`&`, `|`, `&&`) executes extra commands with the privileges of whoever ran `npm install` / `node-gyp configure`.

**Preconditions:** `process.platform === "win32"`, `pkg-config` missing or failing (the normal case on Windows), and `OPENCV_DIR` set to a value the build user did not choose — for example a value inherited from a shared CI image, a container, or a setup snippet copied from an untrusted repository. `README.md:34` instructs users to set this variable.

**Evidence:** `utils/find-opencv.js:33` interpolates the environment value straight into a shell command string:

```js
exec("echo %OPENCV_DIR%", function(error, stdout, stderr){
```

`exec` runs the command through the platform shell, and on `cmd.exe` `%VAR%` substitution happens before command parsing, so `OPENCV_DIR=C:\OpenCV&calc` becomes `echo C:\OpenCV&calc`. The rest of that function (`utils/find-opencv.js:33-42`) only post-processes the output; nothing validates the value.

**Impact:** Command execution as the developer on a Windows build host. Contained to one machine and one build, but permanent in effect (the executed command can do anything the user can). Discounted for requiring the attacker to already control an environment variable outside this system, and for being Windows-only, so `low`.

**Fix:** Do not build a shell string from the environment variable. Read it from `process.env` directly instead of shelling out, or at minimum use `execFile` with an argument array and no shell.

summary:
## Summary

PR #2 adds the missing `util/utils.js` (202 lines, byte-identical to upstream `cthackers/adm-zip` at the pre-fix commit `e116bc1`), which is the filesystem layer the rest of the library already requires: directory creation, the async and sync write helpers, CRC32, and the local-directory walker. The rest of the tree is untouched, so the library goes from unloadable to fully functional with this PR — and the extraction path it enables has no confinement between archive entry names and the paths it writes. I reproduced the zip-slip write end to end (outside-file creation with the default `overwrite=false`, overwrite of an existing outside file with `overwrite=true`) and two smaller defects in the new helpers; the existing test suite still passes silently, so nothing in the repo pins these behaviours. Assessment: the new file is a faithful copy of upstream code, but it lands in a tree with no containment check, so the change re-introduces a known arbitrary-file-write vulnerability and needs path confinement before merge.

I also recorded a security-model concept (`security/extraction-boundary.md`) noting where entry names become writes and that the CVE-2018-1002204 fix belongs in `adm-zip.js`, not in this file.

findings.title: Extracting an untrusted archive writes files outside the target directory (zip slip)
findings.body:
Extracting an archive from an untrusted source writes files anywhere the process can write, not only under the target directory.

`extractAllTo`, `extractAllToAsync` and `extractEntryTo` resolve each archive entry name against the target (`adm-zip.js:432`, `adm-zip.js:470`, `adm-zip.js:356`) and pass the result to the `writeFileTo`/`makeDir` helpers added by this change (`util/utils.js:92-119`, `util/utils.js:52-54`). Those helpers create and truncate whatever path they are given; nothing checks the result stays inside the target. The `escapeFileName` filter (`adm-zip.js:30-32`) only rewrites Windows-reserved characters and only runs on Windows, so it does not touch `..`, and `pth.resolve` discards the target entirely for absolute entry names.

**Preconditions:** the caller extracts an archive it did not create (user upload, downloaded zip, shared bundle). Creating new files outside the target works with the default `overwrite === false`; clobbering an existing file needs `overwrite === true`.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this tree:
- zip containing `../../pwned.txt`, extracted with `extractAllTo('/tmp/zipslip/target/sub', true)`: `/tmp/zipslip/pwned.txt` is created and the call returns normally instead of erroring.
- python-built STORED entry `../../escaped_by_archive.txt` with `overwrite=false`: `/tmp/v7/escaped_by_archive.txt` is created outside the target.
- same entry with `overwrite=true`: an existing `/tmp/v7/victim.txt` changed from `"ORIGINAL"` to `"OVERWRITTEN"`.
- `escaped_by_archive.txt`-style names also work through `extractAllToAsync` (`adm-zip.js:488`), and an absolute entry name such as `/etc/cron.d/x` resolves to that absolute path.

**Impact:** an archive author controls file creation and overwriting with the privileges of the extracting process: shell rc files, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, cron entries, application config, and other users' files on the same host. This is CVE-2018-1002204. Reach crosses a trust boundary (the archive author is not the extracting user) and the writes are permanent until something outside the library removes them, so this is `high`.

**Fix:** restore one invariant: an extracted write must land inside the extraction root. Resolve the root once, then reject any entry whose `pth.resolve(root, entryName)` leaves it, comparing with `pth.relative(root, target)` (reject when it is `..` or starts with `..` + separator) rather than a string-prefix test. Apply it in the `extract*` methods before calling `writeFileTo`/`makeDir`, and reject paths whose components are symlinks (`lstat`) so a link inside the target cannot redirect the write outside it.

findings.title: mkdirSync duplicates the first path segment, so writeZip to a missing relative directory fails
findings.body:
`mkdirSync` rebuilds a relative path with its first component duplicated, so writing a file into a relative directory that does not exist yet fails with `ENOENT` (or creates stray `x/x/...` directories).

`resolvedPath` is seeded with `path.split(PATH_SEPARATOR)[0]` and the loop then re-appends that same first component (`util/utils.js:16-19`): `build/out.zip` is walked as `build/build`. Absolute POSIX paths escape the bug because segment 0 is `""` and skipped at `util/utils.js:18`, which is why normal extraction (always `pth.resolve`d by the caller) is unaffected.

**Evidence:** reproduced on this tree:
- `Utils.writeFileTo('build/out.zip', buf, true)` with `build` absent throws `ENOENT: no such file or directory, mkdir 'build/build'`.
- `AdmZip#writeZip` passes the caller's string straight through (`adm-zip.js:526`), so `new AdmZip(...).writeZip('build/out.zip')` fails the same way.
- With `build` present and `build/sub` absent, `Utils.writeFileTo('build/sub/out.zip', ...)` creates `build/build/sub` and then fails with `ENOENT ... chmod 'build/sub/out.zip'`, leaving the stray tree behind.

**Impact:** `writeZip` to a relative path such as `dist/out.zip` throws when `dist` is missing, when it should simply be created. Contained to the caller making that call and recoverable by creating the directory first, so `low`.

**Fix:** build each prefix with `pth.join`/`pth.resolve` from an empty seed (or just call `fs.mkdirSync(folder, {recursive: true})` in `writeFileTo`), so the first segment is appended once.

findings.title: A failed fs.open retry in writeFileToAsync throws uncaught and kills the extracting process
findings.body:
When both `fs.open` attempts in `writeFileToAsync` fail, the error from the retry is ignored, `fd` stays `undefined`, and `fs.write(undefined, ...)` throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` inside an fs callback. Nothing catches it and the caller's callback never runs, so the extraction process dies on the exception.

The retry path (`util/utils.js:143-146`) checks `err` from the first `open` but not from the `chmod` or the second `open`, and unlike the success branch (`util/utils.js:156`) it has no `if (fd)` guard. The same block also discards every `fs.write`, `fs.close` and `fs.chmod` error (`util/utils.js:146-167`), so a failed write still reports `callback(true)`.

**Preconditions:** the application extracts with `extractAllToAsync` (`adm-zip.js:488`); a crafted entry name long enough to exceed the filesystem name limit makes both opens fail.

**Evidence:** reproduced end to end:
- STORED zip entry named 300 `a`s + `.txt`, extracted with `new AdmZip('/tmp/v5/long.zip').extractAllToAsync('/tmp/v5/out', true, cb)`: `UNCAUGHT TypeError: The "fd" argument must be of type number. Received undefined`; `cb` is never called.
- `Utils.writeFileToAsync('/dev/full', buf, true, cb)` calls back `true` although every write fails with `ENOSPC`, so extraction of a truncated file reports success.

**Impact:** an archive the application does not control can crash the extracting process (the same archive crashes it again on retry), and a disk-full or I/O error is reported as a successful extraction, leaving the caller using truncated files. Contained to the extracting job and recoverable by restarting/re-extracting, so `low`.

**Fix:** propagate errors instead of ignoring them: check the `err` from the retry `open` and the `fs.write`/`fs.close`/`fs.chmod` callbacks and call back `false` on failure (only writing when `typeof fd === 'number'`), so the caller sees the write did not happen.

summary:
Recorded two findings. Summary:

**What the change does:** adds `utils/find-opencv.js` (81 lines, the only changed file), the build helper that `binding.gyp` already calls at eight sites to obtain OpenCV compiler and linker flags via `pkg-config`, with a Windows fallback that reads `OPENCV_DIR`.

**Assessment:** the script works on the normal Linux path — `pkg-config` flags flow through gyp's `shlex` splitting correctly, and `PKG_CONFIG_OPENCV3` is safely gated by an exact `=== "1"` compare. The real defect is that the pkg-config flag comes from `process.argv[2]` and is concatenated into a `child_process.exec` shell string (`utils/find-opencv.js:5,15`); I reproduced arbitrary command execution with `node utils/find-opencv.js '--version; id'`, though every in-tree caller passes a literal, which is why I graded it `low` rather than the CVE's 9.8. Secondary issues I left unfiled because they need Windows or non-default layouts to trigger and I could not reproduce them: the fallback's `OPENCV_DIR\..\..\include` arithmetic disagrees with the `...\vc12\bin` value this repo's own `appveyor.yml:50,76` sets, `--libs` can emit an empty list with exit 0 when no `.lib` is found, and `cleanupEchoOutput` slices two characters unconditionally at `:34` before the error check at `:35`.

findings.title: Failed pkg-config lookup reports no cause, leaving install errors unactionable
findings.body:
When pkg-config cannot find OpenCV, the script reports the failure without its
cause, so the most common install failure cannot be diagnosed from the build log.

**Evidence:** `utils/find-opencv.js:21` passes `opencv` and `flag` as second and
third arguments to `Error`, which ignores them — checked on node v24.22.2:
`new Error("msg","opencv","--libs").message === "msg"`, `cause` undefined. The
`stderr` argument of the exec callback at :15 is never read, and the fallback at
:36 throws away its error object. A missing `opencv.pc` (OpenCV 4 installs
`opencv4.pc`; pip and conda builds ship none) therefore produces only:

```
Error: ERROR: failed to run: pkg-config
    at ...
```

The package spec (`opencv >= 2.3.1` or `opencv3`), the flag, and pkg-config's own
"Package opencv was not found in the pkg-config search path" are all lost, and
node-gyp only adds "Call to ... returned exit status 1 while in binding.gyp".

**Impact:** info. Nothing is corrupted and no data is exposed; the cost is that a
failed `npm install` gives the user nothing to act on.

**Fix:** interpolate the values into the message instead of passing extra
constructor arguments, and append pkg-config's stderr:
`"ERROR: failed to run: pkg-config " + opencv + " " + flag + (stderr ? ": " + stderr : "")`.

findings.title: Unvalidated pkg-config flag is concatenated into a shell command, allowing command injection
findings.body:
`utils/find-opencv.js` pastes the pkg-config flag straight from the command line
into a shell string, so an argument carrying shell metacharacters runs arbitrary
commands as the user doing the build.

**Preconditions:** the caller controls the flag argument. Every in-tree call site
passes a literal (`binding.gyp:29,34,44,69,109,114,125,150` all run
`node utils/find-opencv.js --libs` or `--cflags`), so nothing in this repo's own
build can be attacked through it. A wrapper, CI step, or downstream build script
that forwards a variable flag can.

**Evidence:**

```
utils/find-opencv.js:5   var flag = process.argv[2] || "--exists";
utils/find-opencv.js:15  exec("pkg-config " + opencv + " " + flag, function(error, stdout, stderr){
```

Reproduced in the checkout with `pkg-config` installed (node v24.22.2):

```
$ node utils/find-opencv.js '--version; id'
1.8.1
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

`;`, `&&`, `$(...)` and backticks all execute. A trailing injected command that
exits 0 also clears `error`, so the throw at :21 is skipped and the injected
output is printed at :25. The only check on `flag` lives in `printPaths`
(:48, :52, :69); it runs after the shell command and only on the Windows fallback
path. `opencv` (:11) is not injectable: `PKG_CONFIG_OPENCV3` is compared with
`=== "1"` and both branches are literals.

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution with the build user's privileges (source
tree, npm token, CI secrets) during one build invocation — contained reach,
permanent persistence. Discounted one tier because the trigger needs a caller
that forwards an untrusted flag, which no in-tree caller does, so this is `low`
rather than the 9.8 NVD assigns: that score assumes a remote unauthenticated
actor this code does not have. Same defect as CVE-2019-10061 (CWE-78, npm
advisory 789); upstream fixed it in 81a4b862 by allowlisting the flags.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the flag never reaches a shell unvalidated. Map
it through `{"--cflags":1,"--libs":1}` with a fallback to `--exists`, and call
`execFile("pkg-config", [opencv, flag], ...)` so no shell parses the value.

summary:
The change re-adds `crud-file-server.js` (269 lines, a new file in this tree): a dependency-free HTTP file server with GET/HEAD/PUT/POST/DELETE over a served directory. I reviewed the whole file and reproduced the main paths against the shipped CLI.

Three findings are recorded. The central defect is that the only path guard is dead code — `while(url.indexOf('..').length > 0)` at crud-file-server.js:6 is always false, because a Number has no `.length` — so `relativePath = path + url` (:53-55) reaches `fs` calls unsanitised. I confirmed live traversal reads (`/../secret.txt`, `/%2e%2e%2f…`, `/etc/passwd`) plus writes, deletes, renames and directory creation outside the root, with and without `-v`, and with `-r` still allowing reads. Two further issues are independent of that: a malformed percent-encoded URL (`GET /%`) throws `URIError` from `decodeURIComponent` (:5 via :38, before the `try` at :57) and there is no guard in `bin/crud-file-server`, so one request kills the process; and directory listings insert raw filenames into `text/html` (:143), giving stored XSS in the server's origin.

Lower-impact defects I verified but did not file, because the traversal already dominates them: an aborted `PUT` truncates the target before any bytes arrive and leaks one file descriptor per dropped upload; the undefined `method` at :258 makes unsupported verbs return 500 with internal text instead of 405; and error bodies serialise raw `fs` errors, leaking absolute paths. Nothing to approve here — the traversal fix (resolve the path and compare it against the root, including the rename target) is required before this can be merged.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read, overwrite, and delete files outside the served root
findings.body:
Any unauthenticated client can read, overwrite, move, or delete files outside the
directory the server was told to serve. The traversal scrubber never runs, so `..`
segments reach the filesystem unchanged.

**Evidence:** `cleanUrl` (crud-file-server.js:4-8) guards its loop with
`while(url.indexOf('..').length > 0)`. `indexOf` returns a Number, `.length` of a
Number is `undefined`, and `undefined > 0` is false — so the body never executes and
`..` survives (the only real work the function does is `decodeURIComponent` at
crud-file-server.js:5). `relativePath` is then built by plain concatenation,
`path + url` (crud-file-server.js:53-55), with no `path.resolve`/prefix check, and is
passed to `fs.readFile` (:170), `fs.createWriteStream` (:185),
`fs.rename(relativePath, path + query.rename)` (:212, after `cleanUrl` at :202 which
has the same defect), `fs.mkdir` (:221), `fs.unlink` (:246) and `fs.rmdir` (:238).

Reproduced against the shipped CLI (`node bin/crud-file-server -f /tmp/ct2/served -p 8973 -q`,
served dir `/tmp/ct2/served`, secret at `/tmp/ct2/secret.txt`):

```
GET  /../secret.txt                       -> 200 "SECRET-OUTSIDE"
GET  /%2e%2e%2fsecret.txt                 -> 200 "SECRET-OUTSIDE"   (no --path-as-is needed)
GET  /../../../../../etc/passwd           -> 200 root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash ...
PUT  /../pwn.txt                          -> 200, created /tmp/ct2/pwn.txt (outside root)
DELETE /../secret.txt                     -> 200, /tmp/ct2/secret.txt removed
POST /a.txt?rename=../outside/moved.txt   -> 200, file moved out of the root
POST /../outside/newdir?create=directory  -> 200, directory created outside the root
```

Reading works with `-r` too (read-only only gates non-GET methods, :58). `-v filez`
does not help: :45 checks only a string prefix, so `/filez/../secret.txt` is accepted.

**Impact:** This is the CVE-2018-3726 class: an unauthenticated network caller crosses
the served-root boundary in both directions. Reads expose any file the process can read
(keys, config, `/etc/passwd`); writes and deletes are permanent — a file removed by
`DELETE` cannot be recovered through any supported path. Reach crosses the trust
boundary, persistence is permanent, so `high`.

**Fix:** Enforce containment on the resolved path instead of string-stripping dots. In
`handleRequest`, resolve once (`var root = require('path').resolve(path); var
relativePath = require('path').resolve(root, url);`) and reject the request with a 403
when `relativePath !== root && !relativePath.startsWith(root + require('path').sep)`.
Apply the same check to the rename target (`path + query.rename`, :212). Do not rely on
the `..` loop — also delete or fix it (:6 should test `indexOf('..') !== -1`, but a
resolve-and-compare check is what actually holds).

findings.title: A malformed percent-encoded URL crashes the whole server process
findings.body:
One unauthenticated request kills the server process. `cleanUrl` calls
`decodeURIComponent` (crud-file-server.js:5) from :38, before the request-wide `try`
block that starts at :57. A URL with malformed percent-encoding makes that call throw
`URIError`, which escapes `handleRequest`, and `bin/crud-file-server` installs no
try/catch or `uncaughtException` handler, so Node exits.

**Evidence:** served dir `/tmp/x/served`, started as
`node bin/crud-file-server -f /tmp/x/served -p 8971 -q`:

```
GET /a.txt   -> 200
GET /%       -> connection dropped (000)
next request -> 000, no listener; process gone
```

Server stderr:

```
crud-file-server.js:5
	url = decodeURIComponent(url);
	      ^
URIError: URI malformed
    at cleanUrl (crud-file-server.js:5:8)
    at exports.handleRequest (crud-file-server.js:38:15)
    at Server.<anonymous> (bin/crud-file-server:32)
```

The same shape exists at crud-file-server.js:47 (`throw 'url [...] does not begin with
vpath [...]'`), which is also before the try: with `-v filez`, `GET /` (or any URL not
prefixed with `filez`) ends the process. That variant needs the non-default `-v` flag;
the `%` variant needs nothing but the default configuration.

**Impact:** The service is single-process and has no supervisor in this repo, so the
listener stays down until someone restarts it. Any network client can repeat the
request at will and keep it down, while no one is served. Reach is broad (all users of
the server), persistence is recoverable (restart, but re-triggerable by an unprivileged
actor), so `medium`. The `-v` variant is one tier lower (`low`) because it needs a
non-default flag.

**Fix:** Make request parsing non-throwing: wrap the URL/vpath prelude (:36-55) in the
existing try, or catch the `URIError` locally and answer 400. Also replace the `throw`
at :47 with a 404/403 response, and add a `process.on('uncaughtException')` guard in
`bin/crud-file-server` so no single request can take the listener down.

findings.title: Stored XSS: directory listings insert unescaped filenames into HTML
findings.body:
Directory listings render filenames into HTML without escaping, so a file with a crafted name executes script in the server's origin for anyone who browses that directory. **Evidence:** crud-file-server.js:143 writes `'\r\n

' + name + '

'` into a `text/html` response (:137). `name` comes straight from `fs.readdir` (:107, :121); `normalized` (:141) is not URL-encoded either. Reproduced on port 8951 with served dir `/tmp/xss/served`: ``` PUT /%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3Dalert(1)%3E.txt -> 200 ls -> .txt GET / responds:

.txt

``` Parsing that body yields real elements with the attacker's handler: `STARTTAG a [('href','/.txt')]`, `STARTTAG img [('src','x'),('onerror','alert(1)')]`. A name containing `"` breaks out of the `href` attribute the same way. No CSP and no `X-Content-Type-Options` header are set. The upload is unauthenticated: `readOnly` is `argv.r` (bin/crud-file-server:30), undefined by default, so `PUT` (`:185`) accepts the filename from the URL. **Impact:** Stored script execution against the file server's own origin. The discount is large: this server has no authentication or session state, so script running in its origin grants nothing a caller could not already do directly, and an attacker who can create the file can also delete or overwrite it. Severity `low` — it matters when a trusted user browses an attacker-writable directory (the shipped `example/example.html` does exactly that), not as a route to the server itself. **Fix:** Escape filenames on output: HTML-escape `name` for the text node and `encodeURIComponent` each path segment for the `href`. Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; a `Content-Security-Policy` that forbids inline script would also neutralise leftover injection points.

findings.title: jQuery.fn.load keeps script tags whose end tag contains whitespace and runs them
findings.body:
`jQuery.fn.load()` with a selector strips ``. HTML also closes a script element with ``, ``, ``, or ``. Those forms survive the strip, reach the page, and their contents execute in the calling page's origin. A page that trusts `load()` to remove scripts from attacker-influenceable HTML therefore gets XSS. **Preconditions:** the app calls `$( ... ).load( url + " selector" )` and the HTML at `url` is attacker-influenceable (stored/reflected user content, third-party or CORS-permissive endpoint). Without a selector, scripts in the response execute by design, so only the selector form is affected. **Evidence:** - `src/ajax.js:15` — `rscript = /)<[^<]*)*<\/script>/gi`. The end pattern `<\/script>` requires `>` immediately after `script`, and `[^<]*` cannot consume the `<` of a malformed end tag, so no match, so `responseText.replace( rscript, "" )` at `src/ajax.js:190` leaves the tag intact. - `src/ajax.js:190` strips, `src/ajax.js:193` extracts the matched elements from the detached dummy div, `src/ajax.js:183` injects them with `.html()`. - Execution path: `domManip` collects scripts and evaluates them once the node is in the document (`src/manipulation.js:358-374`, `jQuery.globalEval` at `src/manipulation.js:374`; `node.src` scripts are fetched with a synchronous `dataType:"script"` request at `src/manipulation.js:363-372`). The first append into the detached div does not run them because `jQuery.contains( doc, node )` is false; the second insertion through `.html()` does. - Reproduction with this tree's sources (concatenated with the sizzle source the gitlink points at, run under jsdom against a local HTTP server): - response `
hi
`, called as `$("#target").load("/space.html #victim")` → `window.pwned === "space"` and the inserted markup still contains the ``) → script removed, `window.pwned` stays undefined. **Impact:** arbitrary JavaScript runs in the origin of the page that called `load()`, so an attacker who controls the fetched HTML can read cookies/DOM, act as the user, or exfiltrate data. Reach crosses a trust boundary (remote content becomes same-origin code); persistence is recoverable (the attacker can re-trigger it on every load). The script strip is the only protection `load()` offers, and this bypasses it for exactly the tags it is meant to remove. **Fix:** stop matching tags with a regex. Parse the HTML and let the fragment builder drop the scripts, as later jQuery does: `jQuery("
").append( jQuery.parseHTML( responseText ) ).find( selector )` (`jQuery.parseHTML` collects script elements during `buildFragment` and removes them, `src/core.js:477-500`). If the regex must stay, at least accept attributes and whitespace in the end tag, e.g. `<\/script\s*[^>]*>`.

summary:
Recorded and deduplicated. Final state: one high, one medium finding open.

**Summary**

The change adds `crud-file-server.js`, a small Node http file server exporting `handleRequest` with GET/HEAD/PUT/POST/DELETE over a directory, plus a CLI in `bin/`. I reproduced both reported issues end-to-end against the checked-out tree: `cleanUrl` (`crud-file-server.js:6`) tests `url.indexOf('..').length > 0`, which is always false, so `..` survives and any unauthenticated client can read `/etc/passwd`, write and delete files outside the served root; separately, three throw sites reachable from request data (`:5`, `:47`, `:143`) bypass the `try` at `:57` and terminate the process with one request. The remaining findings from the probe (broken 405 path, vpath rename, cache headers, CSRF on POST, duplicate-keyed query params, symlink escape) are functional and were left out or folded into the two findings' fix notes. Overall assessment: the file must not ship as-is — the traversal is the whole point of the CVE, and the crash paths make it worse. Test-only `mime`/`optimist` stubs live in the gitignored `node_modules`; the working tree is clean.

findings.title: Unauthenticated clients can read, overwrite and delete files outside the served directory
findings.body:
`cleanUrl` never removes `..`, so every request path is concatenated onto the
served directory unchanged. Any unauthenticated client can read, overwrite,
rename and delete files anywhere the server process has permission.

Trigger: `GET /../outside/secret.txt` on a server started with `-f /tmp/srv`.
`relativePath` becomes `/tmp/srv/../outside/secret.txt` (`crud-file-server.js:53-55`)
and the file is served. The same construction feeds `fs.createWriteStream` (PUT,
`:187`), `fs.rename` (POST `?rename=`, `:214`), `fs.rmdir`/`fs.unlink` (DELETE,
`:240`/`:248`) and `fs.mkdir` (`:223`).

**Evidence:** the guard at `crud-file-server.js:6` is
`while(url.indexOf('..').length > 0)`. `url.indexOf('..')` is a number, whose
`.length` is `undefined`, so `undefined > 0` is false and the loop body never runs.
`decodeURIComponent` at `:5` does not help: `%2e%2e` decodes to `..` and survives.
Reproduced against the checked-out tree:

```
$ crud-file-server -f /tmp/srv -p 3111;  ls /tmp/srv        # only ok.txt
GET /ok.txt                              -> hello-inside
GET /../outside/secret.txt               -> TOP-SECRET-OUTSIDE-SERVED-ROOT
GET /%2e%2e/outside/secret.txt           -> TOP-SECRET-OUTSIDE-SERVED-ROOT
GET /../../../../../../etc/passwd        -> root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
PUT /../outside/planted.txt  "PWNED"     -> 200, file created outside root
DELETE /../outside/secret.txt            -> 200, file removed from /tmp/outside
```

The directory-listing and JSON branches inherit the same hole (e.g.
`GET /../outside?type=json` lists a directory outside the root), and there is no
`realpath`/prefix containment check anywhere, so a symlink inside the served tree
also escapes — fixing the `..` filter alone does not contain the tree.

**Impact:** unauthenticated read of arbitrary files (credentials, keys, source),
plus arbitrary file write and deletion as the server user. Reach crosses a trust
boundary and the damage is permanent, hence high. Verified in-run; no precondition
beyond the server running.

**Fix:** make the containment check explicit instead of a string filter. Resolve the
request path against the root (`path.resolve(root, url)`) and reject unless the
result is `root` itself or starts with `root + path.sep` (after `fs.realpath` so
symlinks cannot escape), answering 400. As a stopgap, `while (url.indexOf('..') !== -1)`
closes the reported requests but not the symlink escape.

findings.title: A single unauthenticated request crashes the file server process
findings.body:
Request-derived input throws outside the `try` block, so a single request ends the
server process. Browsers and scanners send the triggering requests unprompted.

Three verified triggers, all unauthenticated:

1. `crud-file-server.js:5` — `decodeURIComponent(url)` raises `URIError: URI
   malformed` for a path with an invalid escape. `GET /%` (raw, not `%25`) reaches
   `cleanUrl` at `:38`, before the `try` at `:57`.
2. `crud-file-server.js:47` — `throw 'url [...] does not begin with vpath [...]'`
   when `vpath` is configured and the URL does not start with it. With the
   documented `-v filez` option, every browser's automatic `GET /favicon.ico`
   kills the server.
3. `crud-file-server.js:143` — `throw new Error('unsupported file name')` inside
   the `fs.stat` callback, so it cannot be caught by the enclosing `try`. A file
   name containing `"` triggers it, and `PUT` can create such a name.

**Evidence:** reproduced on the checked-out tree:

```
# 1, default config
GET /%                     -> empty reply (curl exit 52); stderr:
                              URIError: URI malformed
                                  at cleanUrl (crud-file-server.js:5:8)
                              Node.js v24.22.2      # process exited
# 2, crud-file-server -f dir -v filez
GET /filez/x.txt           -> 500/200 as normal
GET /favicon.ico           -> empty reply; stderr:
                              throw 'url [favicon.ico] does not begin with vpath [filez]'
                              Node.js v24.22.2      # process exited
# 3
PUT /evil%22name.txt       -> 200
GET /                      -> empty reply; stderr:
                              Error: unsupported file name
                                  at search.stats (crud-file-server.js:143:55)
                              Node.js v24.22.2      # process exited
```

`bin/crud-file-server` installs no `uncaughtException` handler and no supervisor,
so the process stays down until someone restarts it.

**Impact:** any unauthenticated client can take the file service offline for every
user with one request; recovery needs an operator restart. Reach is broad and the
outage is recoverable, so medium. Note that the throw at `:210` inside the POST
branch is *not* affected — the `try` covers it and it yields a 500.

**Fix:** validate URL input and answer with a 4xx instead of throwing: move the
`vpath` check and `decodeURIComponent` into the `try` (or a wrapper that catches and
calls `writeError(..., 400)`), and replace the throw in the listing callback at
`:143` with a `writeError`/skip for that entry.
