summary:
Recorded four findings on the new `src/renderer.js`.

**Summary:** The PR re-adds `src/renderer.js`, which drives headless Chrome over CDP to render or screenshot a caller-supplied URL. The change makes the whole `/render` and `/screenshot` surface functional, and with it the CVE-2017-18354 issue: the URL goes to `Page.navigate` unvalidated, so callers reach local files and internal services and get the content back. I also confirmed three further defects in the new file — a negative `width`/`height` hangs the screenshot request and feeds the instance-kill counter, failed renders leak tabs and CDP clients, and the URL is spliced unescaped into a `Runtime.evaluate` expression. The rendering logic is otherwise the upstream design; the risk is concentrated in the untrusted-URL path.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can make the renderer fetch internal URLs and local files
findings.body:
`/render/<url>` and `/screenshot/<url>` hand the caller's URL straight to Chrome, so an
unauthenticated caller chooses what the server fetches. The fetched document comes back in
the HTTP response. That covers loopback and intranet HTTP services, cloud metadata
endpoints, and `file://` paths on the container.

**Evidence:**
- Path: `src/main.js:99` / `src/main.js:118` → `src/renderer.js:184` / `:217` →
  `src/renderer.js:74` `Page.navigate({url: url})`. Nothing between the Express route and
  `Page.navigate` parses the URL.
- The only check is `isRestricted` (`src/main.js:65-74`): it returns `false` when
  `renderOnly` is unset (the default), and otherwise does a raw `startsWith` prefix match
  on the submitted string. No scheme check, no host or resolved-IP check, no re-check
  after redirects.
- The response body is returned: `src/renderer.js:189` + `:191-193` → `src/main.js:100`
  (serialized DOM); `src/renderer.js:218` + `:221` → `src/main.js:119-124` (JPEG).
- The test suite treats local-file rendering as supported: `test/app-test.js:117` and
  `test/app-test.js:124` request `/render/file://` + an absolute path.
- Reproduced with a CDP-driven headless Chrome: navigating to `file:///tmp/secret.txt`
  put the file contents into `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` (exactly what
  `src/renderer.js:189` returns) and navigating to `http://127.0.0.1:18080/admin.html`
  reached a loopback-only server, whose response body came back in the DOM.

**Impact:** Crosses a trust boundary: an unauthenticated caller reads files on the render
host and responses from loopback/intranet/cloud-metadata services, with the data returned
to them. The documented deployment (README, `app.yaml`) has no authentication, and the
default config has no `renderOnly` allowlist. Severity `high`.

**Fix:** refuse any URL that is not `http:`/`https:` before navigating — this is the
upstream CVE-2017-18354 fix (`url.parse(urlReq).protocol` must match `/^https?/` in
`isRestricted`). To also close host-level SSRF, resolve the hostname and reject
loopback/private/link-local addresses, compare the parsed origin against `renderOnly`
instead of a prefix match, and re-check on navigation requests so redirects cannot escape.

findings.title: A negative width or height makes /screenshot hang forever and counts toward instance shutdown
findings.body:
`GET /screenshot/<url>?width=-1` never gets a response. The rejected Chrome call happens
outside the `try` block inside an `async` promise executor, so nothing settles the returned
promise: the request hangs, the tab created for it is never closed, and an
`unhandledRejection` is counted toward instance shutdown.

**Preconditions:** the caller appends `?width=-1` (or a negative `height`) to a
`/screenshot/...` request. `?width=0` is remapped to 1000 by the `|| 1000` fallback, so
only negative values trigger it.

**Evidence:**
- `src/renderer.js:211-212`: `Math.min(2000, parseInt(options['width']) || 1000)` — no
  lower clamp, `-1` passes through.
- `src/renderer.js:213-214` `await Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride(...)`. Verified
  against headless Chrome 156 over CDP: `{width:-5,height:-5}` is rejected with
  `Screen width and height values must be positive, not greater than 10000000`;
  `setVisibleSize` rejects with `Width and height must be non-negative`.
- Those awaits sit before the `try` at `src/renderer.js:216`, inside
  `new Promise(async (resolve, reject) => {...})` opened at `src/renderer.js:201`. The
  async executor's own promise is discarded, so the rejection reaches neither `reject` nor
  a caller. Reproduced with the same code shape: the outer promise never settles and one
  `unhandledRejection` fires.
- Consequence: `src/main.js:118` awaits forever, so the HTTP response is never sent and the
  socket stays open. `src/main.js:180` counts the rejection and
  `src/main.js:169-175` kills Chrome and exits the process after more than five.
- The tab created at `src/renderer.js:202` is leaked on this path (`CDP.Close` only runs at
  `:220` after success).

**Impact:** One unauthenticated request permanently occupies a request slot, and a handful
of them stop the instance for every user. Reach is broad, persistence recoverable by
restart, so `medium`.

**Fix:** make the promise executor non-`async` and cover every await with one `try`/`catch`
that rejects (and a `finally` that closes the tab and client); clamp or reject non-positive
`width`/`height` before calling `setDeviceMetricsOverride`.

findings.title: Failed renders never close their Chrome tab or CDP client
findings.body:
Every render that fails leaves its Chrome tab, its CDP websocket, and all of its listeners
open. Only the success paths close the target, so a caller who sends URLs that fail grows
the browser's tab count without limit.

**Evidence:**
- `src/renderer.js:190` and `src/renderer.js:220` are the only `CDP.Close` calls; both
  follow a resolved render. `client.close()` is never called.
- The catch blocks (`src/renderer.js:194-196`, `:222-224`) only `reject`; there is no
  `finally` in the file.
- Failure paths that reach those catches: navigation error
  (`src/renderer.js:74`, `:96-98`), and the 10-second hard limit
  (`src/renderer.js:139-145`, which resolves but leaves listeners attached). The
  repo's own test expects a 400 for an unreachable URL (`test/app-test.js:135-139`) —
  that response is produced by this catch, so the leak is on a routinely reachable path.
- No concurrency limit exists anywhere in `src/`, so N bad URLs mean N tabs and N
  renderer processes; the exception counter at `src/main.js:164-181` never trips because
  a leak raises nothing.

**Impact:** Unauthenticated callers degrade the shared browser for all users until Chrome
refuses new targets or the instance is OOM-killed. Broad reach, recoverable by restart, so
`medium`.

**Fix:** close the target and the CDP client in a single `finally` that runs on every exit
path.

findings.title: Request URL is spliced unescaped into a JavaScript expression in Runtime.evaluate
findings.body:
The requested URL is interpolated into a JavaScript expression with single quotes and no
escaping, so a `'` in the path breaks the base-href injection and a crafted path runs
arbitrary statements in the rendered document before it is serialized.

**Evidence:**
- `src/renderer.js:187`:
  `Runtime.evaluate({expression: `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})('${url}')`})`.
- Verified against headless Chrome over CDP with that exact expression:
  - URL containing `'` → `Runtime.evaluate` resolves with
    `exceptionDetails: SyntaxError: missing ) after argument list`. It is not a protocol
    error, so `src/renderer.js:187` succeeds silently: no `<base>` is injected and the
    request still returns 200.
  - URL `http://x/');document.body.textContent='PWNED-BY-URL'//` executes; the DOM read at
    `src/renderer.js:189` then returns the rewritten body, so the caller controls the
    response body independently of the page's own markup.

**Impact:** `low`. In the common case the caller already controls the requested page, so
script in that document adds little; it matters when the URL redirects to a document the
caller does not control, where `Runtime.evaluate` runs with the final document's origin and
is not subject to its CSP, and it silently breaks base-href injection for any URL
containing an apostrophe.

**Fix:** pass the URL as data rather than source — `JSON.stringify(url)` inside the
expression, or a `Runtime.callFunctionOn` call with `arguments: [{value: url}]`.

summary:
Review complete. The finding is recorded and the repo is left clean.

**Summary:** PR #2 adds the entire merge implementation as a new file, `lib/deep-extend.js` (144 lines), wired up by the pre-existing `index.js` and `package.json` `main`. The implementation is a faithful copy of upstream deep-extend 0.5.0: `Object.keys` + recursive `deepExtend(src, val)`, with special-case cloning for Buffer/Date/RegExp and arrays. I reproduced the CVE-2018-3750 prototype-pollution path end to end and recorded it as `high`; the fix upstream shipped in 0.5.1 (`safeGetProperty`) is described there. The existing 15-test suite passes unmodified against the new file, so no documented behaviour regressed. Beyond that, the remaining candidate issues (cyclic-input stack overflow, non-plain objects losing type, `new Buffer` deprecation, `null` target throwing instead of returning `false`) are either documented upstream limitations or contained, low-value defects, so I did not file them.

findings.title: Untrusted JSON keys named __proto__ pollute Object.prototype process-wide
findings.body:
Merging a source object with its own `__proto__` key — which is what any
`JSON.parse`d document with a `"__proto__"` member looks like — writes the
attacker's properties onto the real `Object.prototype`. This change adds the
whole merge implementation as new code (`lib/deep-extend.js`), and nothing in it
filters the key, so every consumer that merges parsed JSON is exposed.

**Preconditions:** the caller merges attacker-influenced JSON, e.g.
`deepExtend({}, JSON.parse(body))`, or passes it as any source argument, or as
an element of an array-valued source. Default usage; no special setting.

**Evidence:**
- `lib/deep-extend.js:104` — `Object.keys(obj)` yields `"__proto__"` because
  `JSON.parse` creates it as an own enumerable data property.
- `lib/deep-extend.js:105` — `src = target[key]` resolves to `Object.prototype`
  on a fresh target.
- `lib/deep-extend.js:131` — the guard `typeof src !== 'object' || src === null ||
  Array.isArray(src)` is false, since `Object.prototype` is an object.
- `lib/deep-extend.js:137` — `target[key] = deepExtend(src, val)` therefore
  recurses with `Object.prototype` as the merge target, and the inner call writes
  the payload keys as own properties of `Object.prototype`
  (`lib/deep-extend.js:117`).

Reproduction (also works with the key nested in an object, or inside an array
element via `deepCloneArray`, `lib/deep-extend.js:64`):

    node -e "require('./lib/deep-extend.js')({}, JSON.parse('{\"__proto__\":{\"isAdmin\":true}}'));
             console.log(({}).isAdmin, Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('isAdmin'), 'isAdmin' in {})"
    # -> true true true

The added property is writable, enumerable and configurable, so it also shows up
in `for...in` over unrelated objects.

**Impact:** attacker-supplied data becomes a capability in the host process: an
authorization check that reads `user.isAdmin`, a default that reads
`opts.role`, or a `for...in` loop over any object now sees values the attacker
chose, for the lifetime of the process and with no supported way to undo it.
Reach crosses a trust boundary (untrusted input changes code behaviour for
every consumer) and the effect is permanent for the process, which puts this at
the top of the matrix. This is CVE-2018-3750; `package.json` still declares
`"version": "0.5.0"`, the last version before the upstream `safeGetProperty`
fix in 0.5.1.

**Fix:** never read or write the `__proto__` key. Upstream 0.5.1 wraps both
reads, `src = safeGetProperty(target, key)` and `val = safeGetProperty(obj, key)`,
with `safeGetProperty(object, property) { return property === '__proto__' ?
undefined : object[property]; }`. An early `if (key === '__proto__') return;` in
the loop at `lib/deep-extend.js:104` also closes all four entry paths. Add a
regression test to `test/index.spec.js` asserting `({}).polluted` stays undefined
after merging a `JSON.parse`d payload.

summary:
Review complete. Summary:

The PR adds `lib/deep-extend.js`, the library that `index.js` (and `package.json`'s `main`) load, so the whole 148-line merge implementation is new code. It contains the `safeGetProperty` `__proto__` guard that is the upstream fix for CVE-2018-3750, and I confirmed by running node that the classic payloads — direct, nested, inside array items, via `constructor`/`prototype`, multi-argument, and against class-instance and `Object.create(null)` targets — no longer reach `Object.prototype`, `Array.prototype`, or `Function.prototype`; the file also matches the published patched 0.5.x/0.6.0 text apart from cosmetic differences, and still satisfies the expectations encoded in `test/index.spec.js`. The CVE fix itself is therefore sound, and the residual problems I recorded are the vendored version's merge semantics that the `__proto__` guard does not cover.

findings.title: Merging into a target that inherits an object-valued property writes attacker keys into shared prototype state
findings.body:
Merging untrusted data into a target that inherits an object-valued property writes the attacker's keys into that shared prototype object, so every instance sees them.

**Evidence:** With `Config.prototype.defaults = {isAdmin: false}` and `extend(new Config(), JSON.parse('{"defaults":{"isAdmin":true}}'))`, lib/deep-extend.js:105 reads `src = target['defaults']`, which resolves through the prototype chain to the shared object. Because `src` is a non-null object, the merge recurses with it as the mutation target at lib/deep-extend.js:137 and writes the attacker's keys there at lib/deep-extend.js:116-117. Result on Node 24: `Config.prototype.defaults` becomes `{"isAdmin":true}` (same object identity) and `new Config().defaults.isAdmin === true`. The same path works for `Object.create(sharedProto)` targets and for inherited properties further up the chain.

**Impact:** attacker-controlled values reach other requests or instances that read the same prototype object — for example a default like `isAdmin` flips for every instance in the process, and the injected values persist until a restart. Global `Object.prototype` pollution stays blocked: `safeGetProperty` (lib/deep-extend.js:146-148) drops `__proto__` on both reads. So this needs the caller to merge into an object that inherits object-valued properties (class with prototype defaults, `Object.create(shared)`); that non-default usage is what limits severity.

**Fix:** keep the recursion target own-property-only, e.g. `src = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, key) ? safeGetProperty(target, key) : undefined;` so an inherited object is never passed to `deepExtend` as the target.

findings.title: deepExtend(null, ...) throws a TypeError instead of returning false as documented
findings.body:
`deepExtend(null, src)` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null` instead of returning `false` as the file documents.

**Evidence:** The guard at lib/deep-extend.js:83 uses `typeof arguments[0] !== 'object'`, which is false for `null`, so a null target passes validation; the first key then evaluates `safeGetProperty(null, key)` at lib/deep-extend.js:105 and throws. Reproduced on Node 24: `extend(null, {a:1})` throws, and `extend(null)` returns `null`. The docstring at lib/deep-extend.js:76 promises "Returns extended object or false if have no target object or incorrect type".

**Impact:** a caller that relies on the documented contract (`var out = deepExtend(opts, defaults)` with a possibly absent target) crashes instead of receiving `false`, for example when forwarding optional config. The failure is contained and the caller can catch it, so severity is info.

**Fix:** reject null in the same guard: `if (arguments.length < 1 || arguments[0] === null || typeof arguments[0] !== 'object') { return false; }`.

summary:
Coverage check before closing: the diff is one new 31-line file plus its two call paths (`index.js`, `scripts/dns-lookup-script.js`), all of which I read; the only attacker-influenced value is `hostname`, and I reproduced its path to the shell.

**Summary:** The PR re-adds `lib/dns-sync.js`, the synchronous DNS helper that spawns a child Node process per lookup. That file interpolates the caller's `hostname` into a shell command line and runs it through `shell.exec`, which I reproduced executing an injected command; it is CVE-2017-16100 and is recorded as a high-severity finding with a shell-free fix. The surrounding files (`index.js`, `scripts/dns-lookup-script.js`, tests) introduce no further attacker-controlled paths, and nothing else in the change warrants a finding.

findings.title: Hostname reaches the shell unquoted, giving command injection in dnsSync.resolve()
findings.body:
`resolve()` builds a shell command line with the caller-supplied `hostname` unquoted and
passes it to `shell.exec`, so any shell metacharacter in `hostname` runs an extra
command in the host process. Anyone who can influence the hostname a consumer passes in
(HTTP parameter, config value, CLI arg) gets arbitrary command execution with the
Node.js process's privileges.

**Preconditions:** the application passes an untrusted value to `dnsSync.resolve()`;
no other access is needed.

**Evidence:** `lib/dns-sync.js:21` formats the command as
`util.format('"%s" "%s" %s', nodeBinary, scriptPath, hostname)`. The two fixed paths are
quoted; `hostname` is not. `lib/dns-sync.js:23` then runs it through
`shell.exec(cmd, {silent: true})`, which uses `/bin/sh`, so `;`, backticks, `$()` and
`|` are interpreted. Reproduced with this repository's file and
`shelljs@0.2.6`:

```
$ node -e "require('./lib/dns-sync').resolve('127.0.0.1; touch /tmp/pwned')"
$ ls -l /tmp/pwned
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 ... /tmp/pwned
```

`net.isIP(output)` at `lib/dns-sync.js:26` does not help: it only validates the return
value after the command has already run. `scripts/dns-lookup-script.js` never sees the
payload as data, because the shell splits it first.

**Impact:** the library turns a hostname string into shell input, which is a
trust-boundary crossing — a value the caller only meant to be a domain name becomes
code execution in the host process, with whatever file system, network and credentials
that process holds, and nothing in the API reports it. The damage is permanent
(commands run for real, output discarded by the `net.isIP` check but side effects are
not). This is CVE-2017-16100. Per review policy severity is capped at `high`.

**Fix:** stop going through a shell. Keep the child-process call but pass arguments as
an array, e.g. `require('child_process').execFileSync(nodeBinary, [scriptPath, hostname], {encoding: 'utf8'})`,
so `hostname` is a single argv entry. As defense in depth, reject input that is not a
valid DNS name before calling out.

findings.title: Package fails to load after install: math-random is required but never declared
findings.body:
`index.js:12` requires `math-random`, but `package.json:31-33` declares only `is-number` and `kind-of`. A normal install therefore resolves no `math-random`, and the first `require('randomatic')` throws `Error: Cannot find module 'math-random'`. The whole library is unusable for anyone who installs it; only this repo's own dev tree loads, by accident.

**Evidence:** packed the repo (`npm pack`; the tarball ships `index.js` and the unchanged `package.json`), installed the tarball into an empty project, then ran `node -e "require('randomatic')"`:

```
Error: Cannot find module 'math-random'
Require stack:
- /tmp/ozc/consumer/node_modules/randomatic/index.js
    at Object.<anonymous> (.../randomatic/index.js:12:18)
```

`npm install --omit=dev` inside the repo produces `node_modules` with `is-number` and `kind-of` only, and `require('./index.js')` fails the same way. `npm test` appears green only because a devDependency chain (`benchmarked → micromatch → braces → expand-range → fill-range → randomatic@3.1.1`) hoists `math-random@1.0.4` into `node_modules`; remove that copy and all 34 tests fail to load at `index.js:12`. `randomatic@3.0.0` upstream, whose `index.js` is byte-identical to this one (md5 `1b8a03f70e3e81572683246d5f7d7916`), declares `"math-random": "^1.0.1"`.

**Impact:** The change is meant to fix CVE-2017-16028 by replacing `Math.random()` with `math-random`, which uses `crypto.randomBytes` in Node. As written the fix cannot ship: every published or production install of the package throws at load, so the library serves no caller at all. Reach is broad (all consumers) but the failure is loud and immediately reproducible, so severity is medium rather than high; nothing is silently weakened, the module just dies.

**Fix:** declare the dependency — add `"math-random": "^1.0.1"` to `dependencies` in `package.json` (line 33) and to `bower.json:15` — so the package resolves the generator `index.js:12` requires.

findings.title: Generated passwords come from Math.random and are predictable from the process PRNG state
findings.body:
Every character of a generated string comes from `Math.random()`, a non-cryptographic PRNG whose 128-bit state is shared by every `Math.random()` consumer in the process. This package is documented as a password generator — README.md:3 calls it "The original generate-password", `package.json` keywords include `password` and `generate-password`, and the README examples are credential-shaped (`randomize('A0', 16)`, `randomize('0', 12)`). The strings it produces are therefore predictable to anyone who learns the process PRNG state, and it offers no CSPRNG option.

**Preconditions:** The attacker must observe a few `Math.random()` outputs from the target process (a co-resident library that logs or exposes them, or observations of the package's own generated values). Node seeds `Math.random` from OS entropy at startup, so a remote attacker with no such leak cannot predict output.

**Evidence:** index.js:81 is the only entropy source: `res += mask.charAt(parseInt(Math.random() * mask.length, 10));`. There is no `crypto` use anywhere in index.js, and README.md:23-29 / README.md:77-88 document no strength or crypto option.

I reproduced the predictability primitive against this Node build (v24.22.2, V8 xorshift128+ with a 64-entry reversed cache):

- A reimplementation of V8's generator (`RefillCache` + `ToDouble = (x >> 11) / 2**53`) reproduces 64 consecutive `Math.random()` values of `node --random-seed=42` with 0 mismatches (`compared 64 mismatches 0`).
- A z3 solve over 6 consecutive observed doubles recovers the internal 128-bit state and replays the observed window (`replay of the observed window matches: true`), including recovering the exact seeded state for `--random-seed=42`.

So 6 observed doubles in a process are enough to compute every later value `Math.random()` will return in that process, and therefore every later string this package emits. Full end-to-end string prediction was wired up but not executed before the run's budget ran out; the state-recovery step itself is verified.

**Impact:** Crosses a trust boundary: predicting another tenant's generated password or one-time token takes over that account. Permanent if the credential is used. Discounted one tier because exploitation needs an out-of-band PRNG-output leak from the same process, giving `medium`. This matches upstream's own rating (GHSA-6g33-f262-xjp4 / CVE-2017-16028, CWE-330/CWE-338, CVSS 3.0 5.3 moderate).

**Fix:** Draw the index from a CSPRNG instead of `Math.random`, e.g. `crypto.randomInt(mask.length)`. Upstream did exactly this in 3.0.0 by taking its random function from the `math-random` package, which uses `crypto.randomBytes` when available (randomatic 3.1.1 index.js:12, index.js:19 `module.exports.isCrypto = !!mathRandom.cryptographic`).

findings.title: Negative, fractional or infinite length makes the generation loop run forever
findings.body:
`while (length--)` only stops when `length` reaches exactly 0. A negative, fractional, or infinite `length` moves away from 0 and never hits it, so the loop appends characters forever, blocking the event loop and growing `res` until the process is killed.

**Evidence:** index.js:80-81. Reproduced from the repo root with dependencies installed:

```
$ timeout 5 node -e "require('./')('A',-5)"; echo $?      # 124 (never returns)
$ timeout 5 node -e "require('./')('A',5.7)"; echo $?     # 124
$ timeout 5 node -e "require('./')('A',Infinity)"; echo $?  # 124
```

The argument shuffling (index.js:46-65) validates neither `pattern` nor `length`; a numeric pattern also reaches the loop, so `require('./')(-5)` hangs the same way. Coercible values pass: `require('./')('A','5')` returns 5 characters.

**Impact:** A caller that computes or forwards the length (for example from a request parameter) hands any unprivileged user a way to wedge the whole process, since the loop is synchronous. The outage clears on restart and the caller must pass a bad length, so `low`.

**Fix:** Normalise the loop bound once and reject non-positive or non-integer lengths, e.g. `var n = Math.floor(Number(length)); if (!(n > 0) || !isFinite(n)) throw new Error('randomatic expects a positive integer length');` then loop `for (var i = 0; i < n; i++)`.

findings.title: Unusable pattern or length silently returns an empty string instead of an error
findings.body:
When the assembled mask is empty — a pattern containing none of `? a A 0 ! *`, an empty pattern, an empty `chars`, or a `length` that does not coerce to a number — the function returns `''` instead of throwing. A caller that treats the return value as a generated credential gets an empty password and no signal that generation failed.

**Evidence:** index.js:72-78 leaves `mask` as `''`; index.js:81 then does `''.charAt(parseInt(Math.random() * 0, 10))` → `''`, and the `while` loop appends nothing. Reproduced:

```
$ node -e "console.log(JSON.stringify(require('./')('xyz',5)))"   # ""
$ node -e "console.log(JSON.stringify(require('./')('A','abc')))" # ""
$ node -e "console.log(JSON.stringify(require('./')('?',5,{chars:''})))" # ""
```

Related silent path in the same lines: `mask += opts.chars` (index.js:72) is unguarded, so `require('./')('?',10)` draws from the literal string `"undefined"` (`"eeenndndni"`) and `require('./')('?',8,{chars:null})` draws from `"null"`.

**Impact:** Contained to a single call and only when the caller passes a pattern or length the mask builder cannot use, so `info`.

**Fix:** Throw when `mask.length === 0`, and skip/validate the `opts.chars` concatenation when the pattern asks for `?` but `chars` is not a non-empty string — e.g. `if (pattern.indexOf('?') !== -1) mask += typeof opts.chars === 'string' ? opts.chars : '';` followed by `if (!mask) throw new Error('randomatic could not derive any characters from the pattern');`.

summary:
The change adds `src/renderer.js`, the Chrome DevTools-driven renderer behind `/render/:url(*)` and `/screenshot/:url(*)`: it opens a tab, navigates, waits on a virtual-time budget, then returns the serialized DOM or a JPEG.

The renderer accepts whatever URL the caller supplies and does not constrain the protocol, so `file://` renders return local file contents (confirmed live against Chromium); it also pastes that URL into a `Runtime.evaluate` expression, allowing JavaScript breakout; and it closes the tab only on success, leaking a target and socket per failed render. The status-code path (page-controlled `render:status_code`) was investigated and refuted as a DoS — Express/Node throws inside the route's own try/catch, producing a clean 400.

findings.title: /render accepts file:// URLs, letting an unauthenticated caller read server-side files
findings.body:
An unauthenticated caller can read any file the Chrome process can read by asking
Rendertron to render a `file://` URL. `/render/:url(*)` (src/main.js:91-99) passes
the URL straight to `Page.navigate({url: url})` (src/renderer.js:75), and nothing
restricts the scheme: `isRestricted()` (src/main.js:65-74) only checks an optional
`renderOnly` prefix list and returns `false` when it is unset. The serialized
document is returned to the caller (src/renderer.js:190 then src/main.js:100), so
the file's text comes back in the HTTP response. `/screenshot/file://...` reads
files the same way through `captureScreenshot`.

**Evidence:** `GET /render/file:///etc/passwd`. Reproduced against Chromium 156
driven by the same DevTools calls the renderer makes: `Page.navigate` to
`file:///etc/passwd` returns a frameId (no error), and the exact expression this
file evaluates at src/renderer.js:190,
`document.firstElementChild.outerHTML`, returns
`<html>...<pre>root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\n...`. The repo's own tests already
navigate to `file://` URLs and assert on the returned content
(test/app-test.js:122-134), so the path needs no special Chrome flag - the launch
flags at src/main.js:142 are only `--headless --disable-gpu
--remote-debugging-address`. `data:` URLs reach the same navigation call.

**Impact:** a trust-boundary crossing with permanent consequences: an anonymous
HTTP client obtains server-side files - `/etc/passwd`, `config.json` (read from the
working directory, src/main.js:34-39), SSH keys or service-account JSON in the
container, `/proc/<pid>/environ`. Disclosure cannot be undone, so this is `high`.
Policy: CVE-2017-18354 was assigned for exactly this and is fixed by rejecting
non-HTTP protocols.

**Fix:** restore an invariant that only network schemes are rendered. In the route
(or in `Renderer`), parse the URL and reject anything whose protocol is not
`http:`/`https:` before calling `serialize`/`captureScreenshot`, e.g. add
`if (!/^https?/.test(require('url').parse(u).protocol || '')) return true;` to
`isRestricted()` at src/main.js:65.

findings.title: Requested URL is pasted into a Runtime.evaluate expression, allowing JavaScript injection
findings.body:
The requested URL is interpolated unescaped into a JavaScript expression that the
renderer executes in the browser tab through the DevTools protocol:

`await Runtime.evaluate({expression: `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})('${url}')`});`
src/renderer.js:188

A URL containing an apostrophe closes the string literal, and a trailing `//`
comments out the leftover `')`, turning the single helper call into an arbitrary
program. Nothing between the HTTP route and this line escapes or validates the
value: `request.params.url` is decoded by Express (so `%27` becomes `'`, and a raw
`'` is a legal path character anyway) and handed verbatim to `serialize`
(src/main.js:99).

**Preconditions:** none. `isRestricted()` (src/main.js:65-74) is a `startsWith`
test on the same poisoned string, so a payload appended after an allowlisted
prefix passes even when `renderOnly` is configured.

**Evidence:** `GET /render/http://attacker.example/x');globalThis.PWNED=1;//`
produces the expression
`(function injectBaseHref(url) { ... })('http://attacker.example/x');globalThis.PWNED=1;//')`.
Parsing it as `new Function(expr)` runs the injected statement (verified against a
stubbed `document`/`fetch`); parsing it as a single call expression
(`new Function('return (' + expr + ')')`) throws a syntax error, proving the
breakout. With `fetch('http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/')` as the payload
the injected code runs from the renderer's network position. Navigation still
succeeds because `'`, `)`, `;` and `/` are valid in a URL path (src/renderer.js:75).

**Impact:** an anonymous caller runs JavaScript that Rendertron - not the rendered
site - placed in the tab, in the origin of whatever URL was rendered. With
`renderOnly` set, that is code execution inside an origin the operator believed was
the only one reachable, and it executes between `stripPage` and serialization
(src/renderer.js:187-190), so it can also rewrite the HTML returned to the caller
and re-insert the `script`/`link[rel=import]` tags that were just stripped. Fresh
tab per request, so the effect is `medium`.

**Fix:** never build code from strings. Pass the URL as a CDP argument instead of
interpolating it: `Runtime.evaluate({expression: `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})`,
arguments: [...]})` is not available in this API version, so evaluate
`(${injectBaseHref.toString()})(window.__renderUrl)` after setting the value with a
`JSON.stringify(url)`-escaped literal, or at minimum interpolate
`JSON.stringify(url)` instead of `'${url}'` at src/renderer.js:188.

findings.title: Failed renders leak their Chrome tab and DevTools socket
findings.body:
Every render that fails leaves its Chrome tab and DevTools WebSocket open.
`serialize()` and `captureScreenshot()` create a tab and a client (src/renderer.js:179-180,
203-204) but call `CDP.Close` only on the success path (src/renderer.js:191, 221).
Both `catch` blocks just `reject(error)` (src/renderer.js:195-197, 223-225), and the
awaits before the `try` blocks are not covered at all.

**Preconditions:** none - the routes have no auth or rate limit (src/main.js:91,
110), and `renderOnly` is unset by default.

**Evidence:** the cheapest trigger is `GET /render/abc` (Page.navigate rejects,
src/renderer.js:75) or `GET /render/http://127.0.0.1:1/` (`Network.loadingFailed`
rejects the initial request, src/renderer.js:96-101); both are already used as
expected-failure tests (test/app-test.js:128-140). Reading chrome-remote-interface
0.24.2: `CDP.New` issues `GET /json/new` (lib/devtools.js:73-85), `CDP.Close` issues
`GET /json/close/<id>` (lib/devtools.js:98-107) - the only thing that destroys the
target - and `client.close()` would only close the WebSocket (lib/chrome.js:99-117).
There is no finalizer or cleanup in the package, and src/renderer.js never calls
`client.close()`, so per failed request one Chrome target, one WebSocket/file
descriptor and the closed-over `outstandingRequests` map stay alive. The unclosed
tab is still driven afterwards: the 10 s timer (src/renderer.js:140-146) later runs
`Runtime.evaluate` against it. Nothing bounds the accumulation - Chrome is launched
once per process (src/main.js:141-147), and the cache only stores 200 responses
(src/cache.js:94-99).

**Impact:** an anonymous client can loop failing requests until the browser runs out
of memory and the instance dies for everyone it serves. Capacity is restored by a
restart, so `medium`.

**Fix:** release the tab on every path. Wrap the body in `try { ... } finally {
await CDP.Close({id: client.target.id, port: config.port}); await client.close(); }`
in both methods, and move `CDP.New`/`CDP` inside the guarded block so a failed
client handshake is cleaned up too.

summary:
This PR re-adds `lib/dns-sync.js`, the single implementation behind the package's `resolve(hostname)` export: it spawns `process.execPath` on a helper script through `shell.exec`, with the caller's hostname pasted unquoted into the command line, and it now tries to guard that with a hostname allowlist.

The allowlist does not close the hole. The `\.` in the regex source is written inside a JS string literal, so it collapses to `.` and the separator matches any character — `resolve("a;touch$IFS/tmp/pwned")` passed the check and created the file in my run against the declared `shelljs@0.2.6`, so the shell injection (CVE-2017-16100, whose upstream fix added exactly this allowlist) is still exploitable. The right fix is to pass the hostname as an argument to `execFileSync`/`spawnSync` rather than shell text, which also removes two reliability defects in the same code path: stderr is merged into the result field, so `DEBUG=dns-sync` makes successful lookups return `null`, and a spaced temp-directory path leaves `resolve()` spinning forever. Lint is clean; the only noise is pre-existing (`index.js` lacks `"use strict"`).

findings.title: Hostname is interpolated into a shell command, so any resolve() caller input runs arbitrary commands
findings.body:
`resolve(hostname)` pastes the caller's hostname, unquoted, into a command line (`lib/dns-sync.js:31`) and hands that string to `/bin/sh` through `shell.exec` (`lib/dns-sync.js:33`). The hostname allowlist added at `lib/dns-sync.js:10` does not stop shell metacharacters, so any hostname that reaches `resolve()` can run arbitrary commands as the process user.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes a hostname that is not fully trusted (URL/`Host` header, tenant config, CLI argument, upstream API response). Nothing else is needed — the hostname is never escaped or quoted.

**Evidence:** the allowlist's label separator is an unescaped dot. `lib/dns-sync.js:10` writes `"\.)*"` inside a JS string literal, so `\.` collapses to `.` and the compiled pattern is

    ^(([a-zA-Z0-9]|[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9-]*[a-zA-Z0-9]).)*([A-Za-z0-9]|...)$

whose separator matches *any* single character. One arbitrary character between two label-shaped tokens is therefore enough (`;`, `|`, `"`, `$`), so `a;id` and `a1;b2;c3` pass. Reproduced in this checkout with the declared dependency `shelljs@0.2.6`:

    $ node -e 'console.log(require("./index").resolve("a;touch$IFS/tmp/pwned_dns_sync"))'
    null
    $ ls -l /tmp/pwned_dns_sync
    -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 ... /tmp/pwned_dns_sync

The line that runs is `"<node>" "<repo>/scripts/dns-lookup-script" a;touch$IFS/tmp/pwned_dns_sync`. `resolve("a;id")` likewise passes the allowlist (return value stays `null`; the injected command's side effects are the point).

Non-string input bypasses the allowlist too, because `RegExp.test` and `util.format` both coerce: `resolve(2130706433)` shells out with `2130706433`, and `null`/`undefined` stringify to `null`/`undefined` and pass.

**Impact:** a hostname that should be resolved as a name becomes OS commands in the host process — remote code execution, secret/credential theft, permanent filesystem or network changes. High: this crosses a trust boundary (a caller-supplied value becomes shell access) and the result is not undoable. Published as CVE-2017-16100 / GHSA-jcw8-r9xm-32c6; the upstream fix for it added exactly the allowlist above, so that mitigation is not effective as written.

**Fix:** make the hostname an argument rather than shell text — `require('child_process').execFileSync(nodeBinary, [scriptPath, hostname], {encoding: 'utf8'})` (or `spawnSync`), and drop the `shelljs` shell-out. Then repair the allowlist as defence in depth: escape the separator (`\\.`), and reject non-string hostnames instead of letting `RegExp.test` coerce them.

findings.title: Successful lookups return null when the lookup process writes to stderr (for example DEBUG=dns-sync)
findings.body:
`resolve()` returns `null` for hostnames that do resolve whenever the lookup child process writes anything to stderr. The result check at `lib/dns-sync.js:35-36` reads `response.output`, and shelljs 0.2.6 merges stderr into that field (`node_modules/shelljs/src/exec.js:43` appends `2>&1` to the command), so `net.isIP(output)` sees the diagnostics instead of the address.

**Preconditions:** stderr output from the child. The module's own debug channel triggers it: `scripts/dns-lookup-script.js:5,12` writes `debug` lines to stderr, so setting `DEBUG=dns-sync` — the package's documented way to inspect it — breaks every lookup. Node warnings or `NODE_OPTIONS` diagnostics have the same effect.

**Evidence:**

    $ node -e 'console.log(require("./index").resolve("www.google.com"))'
    192.0.0.88
    $ DEBUG=dns-sync node -e 'console.log(require("./index").resolve("www.google.com"))'
    null
    (stderr) dns-sync hostname fail to resolve hostname www.google.com

**Impact:** a valid resolution is reported as a failure, so callers that gate startup or upstream selection on the result take the error path. Contained to the calling process and it clears when `DEBUG` is unset, so this is informational: a documented contract (`README.md`: returns the IP or `null`) breaks silently under a non-default setting.

**Fix:** separate the streams. Run the lookup without a shell (`execFileSync(nodeBinary, [scriptPath, hostname], {encoding: 'utf8'})`) and trim/parse its stdout only; keep the child's diagnostics on stderr where they belong.

findings.title: resolve() hangs forever when the temp directory path contains a space
findings.body:
`resolve()` never returns when the OS temp directory path contains a space: the process spins at 100% CPU until it is killed. `shell.exec` builds a shell command that redirects output to a temp file whose path it does not quote (`node_modules/shelljs/src/exec.js:43`, `cmd += ' > '+stdoutFile+' 2>&1'`), so the redirect lands on a truncated path; shelljs then waits in `while (!fs.existsSync(stdoutFile))` (`exec.js:67-68`) for a file that is never created.

**Preconditions:** `TMPDIR`/`TMP`/`TEMP` (or the platform default) contains a space. On POSIX this needs a deliberate setting; on Windows the default temp path is `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp`, which contains a space for any user name with one.

**Evidence:** with `shelljs@0.2.6` as declared by `package.json` (`"shelljs": "~0.2"`):

    $ mkdir -p "/tmp/has space"
    $ TMPDIR="/tmp/has space" timeout 6 node -e 'console.log(require("./index").resolve("www.google.com"))'
    exit=124          # still inside resolve() after 6s
    $ ls "/tmp/has space"
    shelljs_07b6f5ca5a44a7196c0d  shelljs_2d85c4f0bf08d5a4c14a  ...

**Impact:** a DNS call that must complete before the server starts (the use case in `README.md`) blocks forever and burns a CPU core instead of failing. Low: the trigger is an environment property, not attacker input, and a restart on a different temp path clears it. Verified on Linux; the Windows default path is inferred from the same unquoted-redirect mechanism.

**Fix:** stop routing a fixed, known-good command through a shell — `execFileSync(nodeBinary, [scriptPath, hostname], {encoding: 'utf8'})` in `lib/dns-sync.js:33` removes both the shell parsing and shelljs's temp-file handshake.

summary:
Findings recorded. Final summary:

**What the change does:** the single new file `index.js` is `serialize-javascript` 2.1.0 with one line changed — regexps are now emitted as `new RegExp("source", "flags")` instead of `/source/flags` (`index.js:191`). That is the shape of the upstream CVE-2019-16769 fix, but it drops the step that fixed it: the source is concatenated raw into a double-quoted string, while the package's HTML/line-terminator escaping runs on the JSON text *before* placeholders are substituted (`index.js:174-176` vs `index.js:185-209`).

**Assessment:** I reproduced both halves of the consequence — a route regexp `^\/(\d+)$` round-trips to `^(d+)$` and stops matching (the package's own advertised use, `README.md:14`), and a crafted pattern `"+(globalThis.__pwned=1)+"` is emitted as executable code that runs when the output is embedded in a `<script>` element. I also ran the existing suite (after `npm install`, then restored the lockfile): 54 passing, 7 failing, six of them the un-updated RegExp expectations. The function branch at `index.js:208` bypasses the same escaping pass and needs the same treatment; the probe hypotheses I could not turn into demonstrated, change-related failures (placeholder collisions needing a predicted UID, getter double-reads, `ignoreFunction` mutating caller data — still present in upstream v6) were left unreported.

findings.title: Unescaped RegExp source breaks out of the generated string literal: crafted patterns execute code, ordinary patterns silently change meaning
findings.body:
`serialize()` emits `new RegExp("…", "flags")` by concatenating `RegExp.prototype.source` into a
double-quoted JavaScript string (`index.js:191`). Nothing quotes or escapes that text: the
HTML/line-terminator pass runs on the JSON string at `index.js:174-176`, and placeholders are
replaced afterwards at `index.js:185-209`. So a `"` in a pattern closes the emitted string
literal, and every `\` in a pattern is decoded by the JS parser instead of reaching the RegExp.
The result is broken or silently different regexps for ordinary data, and arbitrary script when
the pattern is attacker-influenced.

**Preconditions:** For code execution, the serialized RegExp must come from an untrusted pattern
and the output must be embedded in a `<script>` element — the package's documented use
(`README.md:62-76`). The corruption and syntax-error paths need no attacker: any pattern
containing `\` or `"` triggers them.

**Evidence:**
- Escaping ordering: `index.js:171-176` (escape) vs `index.js:185-209` (substitution);
  `index.js:191` concatenates `regexps[valueIndex].source` with no quoting.
- Silent corruption of a common pattern — `serialize({route: new RegExp('^\\/users\\/(\\d+)$')})`
  yields `{"route":new RegExp("^\/users\/(\d+)$", "")}`. `eval` of that gives `/^\/users\/(d+)$/`:
  `\d` became `d`, and `/users/42` matches `true` before and `false` after the round trip. The
  package advertises exactly this use — regexp route tables shipped to the browser
  (`README.md:14`). The repo's own test at `test/unit/serialize.js:292-295` fails the same way:
  `/\..*/` round-trips to `/..*/`.
- Invalid output — `serialize({re: new RegExp('\\')})` -> `new RegExp("\\", "")`, which throws
  `SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression: /\/: \ at end of pattern`; `new RegExp('"')` ->
  `new RegExp(""", "")`, `SyntaxError: missing ) after argument list`.
- Code injection — `serialize({re: new RegExp('"+(globalThis.__pwned=1)+"')})` ->
  `{"re":new RegExp(""+(globalThis.__pwned=1)+"", "")}`; evaluating that output sets
  `globalThis.__pwned` to 1. The payload is a valid regexp, so it survives `new RegExp()`.
- HTML characters — `serialize({re: new RegExp('<script>')})` keeps raw `<`/`>`, while
  `serialize('<script>')` gives `"\u003Cscript\u003E"`. Published 2.1.1, which serializes the
  source the same way as any other string, returns `new RegExp("\u003Cscript\u003E", "")`.

**Impact:** Every regexp containing a backslash (`\d`, `\.`, `\/` — the norm for route tables)
is silently altered, so server-serialized route matching and filtering behave differently in the
browser with no error. With an attacker-influenced pattern, the string-literal breakout runs
attacker JavaScript from the generated script, in the embedding origin (reach: crosses a trust
boundary; persistence: recoverable) -> `high`. GitHub's advisory for this code path
(CVE-2019-16769) scores the XSS half medium (CVSS 4.2, AC:H); the corruption half is
unconditional.

**Fix:** Quote the source with the same escaping path as any other serialized string, i.e.
`return 'new RegExp(' + serialize(regexps[valueIndex].source) + ', "' + regexps[valueIndex].flags + '")';`
This JSON-escapes `"` and `\` and routes `<`, `>`, `/`, U+2028/U+2029 through
`escapeUnsafeChars`. Function bodies at `index.js:208` bypass the escaping pass for the same
ordering reason and need equivalent treatment.

findings.title: RegExp output format changes without updated tests: 7 of 61 existing unit tests fail
findings.body:
The change alters the serialized form of every RegExp from the literal `/source/flags` to
`new RegExp("source", "flags")` (`index.js:191`) but leaves the repository's expectations
untouched, so the package's own suite fails after the change: 54 passing, 7 failing.

**Evidence:** `npm install` then `./node_modules/.bin/mocha test/unit` (or `npm test`) on the
reviewed commit:

- `test/unit/serialize.js:254` expected `/asdf/`, got `new RegExp("asdf", "")`
- `test/unit/serialize.js:265` expected `/asdf/`, got `new RegExp("asdf", "")`
- `test/unit/serialize.js:276` expected `/^asdf$/gi`, got `new RegExp("^asdf$", "gi")`
- `test/unit/serialize.js:288` expected `/\\..*/`, got `new RegExp("\\..*", "")`
- `test/unit/serialize.js:295` expects `/\..*/` to round-trip; it comes back as `/..*/`
  (the corruption reported separately in the finding on `index.js:191`)
- `test/unit/serialize.js:335` (maps with a RegExp key) and `:357` (sets) fail on the same
  representation change.

**Impact:** The suite is red, so the change cannot land through CI, and the serialized
representation of regexps — a public output that consumers persist and compare — changes with
no test or doc update to record it (reach: contained, persistence: recoverable) -> `low`.

**Fix:** Update the seven expectations to the new `new RegExp(...)` form, add a case for a
pattern containing `\` and `"` (which the current suite never covers), and re-run `npm test`.

summary: Recorded all four findings; the existing suite (61 tests) still passes, so none of these break tested behaviour — they are uncovered failure paths. **Summary** The PR adds `index.js`, the single source file of `serialize-javascript` v2.1.0, which serializes dates, regexps, maps, sets, `undefined` and functions to literal JavaScript. The code is a faithful copy of the pre-fix 2.1.0 release, so it carries CVE-2019-16769: the unsafe-character pass at `index.js:174-176` runs before placeholders are substituted, and `regexps[i].toString()` at `index.js:190-191` is inserted raw — I confirmed an attacker-supplied pattern (`[]`, raw `/` inside a character class) survives V8 escaping and ends the HTML script element, which I filed as high. Three further reproducible defects were filed at lower severity: unanchored `IS_PURE_FUNCTION`/`IS_ARROW_FUNCTION` emit method-shorthand at a value position (`index.js:14-15`, 115-122), the stateful `/g` native guard silently emits `[native code]` on every second built-in (`index.js:13`, 110), and `ignoreFunction` deletes the caller's own properties and crashes on frozen input (`index.js:34-44`, 66-68). The fix for the security issue is the upstream 2.1.1 patch (escape the regexp source rather than inserting `toString()` output); none of the four are covered by the existing tests.

findings.title: Regexps built from untrusted input keep raw </script> and break out of the HTML script element
findings.body: `serialize()` promises to escape `<`, `>`, `/`, U+2028 and U+2029 so the result can be embedded in an HTML `]")}))' {"re":/[]/} ``` The ``, so the HTML tokenizer ends the script element there and parses the injected `` as markup. The identical text as a plain value is escaped correctly — `serialize({s:""})` gives `{"s":"\u003C\u002Fscript\u003E"}` — so the bypass is the ordering, not the input. Function sources are spliced in at the same post-escape point (`serializeFunc`, index.js:206-208) and keep raw `` as well: `serialize({f: function(){ return ""; }})`. Upstream fixed the regexp path in 2.1.1 (GHSA-h9rv-jmmf-4pgx / CVE-2019-16769, commit 16a68ab) by emitting `new RegExp(, "")`; this file is the pre-fix 2.1.0 code. **Impact:** an attacker who controls one pattern string gets script execution in the browser of every user who loads the page, with that user's session. Reach crosses a trust boundary; a reload clears the injected code, so recoverable — high. **Fix:** restore one invariant — no raw `<`, `>`, `/`, U+2028 or U+2029 may appear in the output unless `options.unsafe === true`. Escaping must cover every substituted segment: serialize the regexp as `new RegExp(` + `serialize(source)` + `, "")` (the 2.1.1 patch), and pass `serializeFunc`'s result through the same escape before insertion.

findings.title: Shorthand methods whose body contains => or function( serialize to unparseable JavaScript
findings.body:
Serializing a shorthand method (`{ m() {...} }`, a class prototype method, getter, setter) normally emits `function() {...}`, an expression that fits where the JSON holds a value. Two unanchored tests in `serializeFunc` skip that rewrite and return the method source unchanged — `m() {...}`, a `MethodDefinition`, not an expression — so the documented `eval('(' + out + ')')` deserialization throws `SyntaxError`. The whole client script fails, not just that value.

**Preconditions:** the serialized function is in method form and its source contains `=>`, or `function` followed by `(` on one line, anywhere in it — body, default parameter, string literal, or comment.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  var m = ({ list(req, res) { res.json([1].filter(i => i)); } }).list;
  console.log(s({list: m}));'
{"list":list(req, res) { res.json([1].filter(i => i)); }}
$ node -e '... eval("(" + s({list: m}) + ")")'
SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{'
```

`IS_PURE_FUNCTION = /function.*?\(/` (index.js:14, tested at index.js:115) and `IS_ARROW_FUNCTION = /.*?=>.*?/` (index.js:15, tested at index.js:120) match anywhere, so the early `return serializedFn` fires for the method form. When they do not fire, the rewrite at index.js:124-139 produces valid output for the same function (`function() { var a = 1; return a; }`), which shows the expressions are used at a value position. Bodies with `function(x) {...}`, `"is not a function (x)"`, `/* uses function( */`, `m(cb = () => 1) {}`, class methods, async and generator methods fail the same way.

**Impact:** any page or bundle carrying such a value is a syntax error for every client that loads it; recoverable by a code fix. Broad reach, recoverable — medium.

**Fix:** anchor the two detection regexes so they can only match a definition head, e.g. `IS_PURE_FUNCTION = /^\s*(?:async\s+)?function\b/` with an equally anchored arrow test, and let every method form fall through to the rewrite at index.js:124-139. Anchoring rather than banning `=>` outright is required by test/unit/serialize.js:239-249 (an arrow inside an arrow body must stay verbatim).

findings.title: Native-function guard skips every other built-in and emits [native code] as output
findings.body:
`IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP` is a module-level `/g` regexp used with `.test()` (index.js:13, 110) without resetting `lastIndex`. After one native function is rejected, `lastIndex` points past the marker in the next native function's source, so its `.test()` fails and the guard passes it through. The library then emits `function String() { [native code] }` — a `SyntaxError` for the consumer — instead of the `TypeError` it documents.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  try { s(Number) } catch (e) { console.log("1st:", e.message) }
  console.log("2nd:", s(String));
  try { s(Boolean) } catch (e) { console.log("3rd:", e.message) }'
1st: Serializing native function: Number
2nd: function String() { [native code] }
3rd: Serializing native function: Boolean
```

The calls alternate throw / silent pass. A failed `.test()` resets `lastIndex` to 0 and a match leaves it at the end of the match (`Number`'s source matches at index 18, ending at 35; `String`'s is the same length, so the search starts past its marker). `eval('(' + s(String) + ')')` gives `SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'code'`. The same state makes the guard over-eager in the other direction: a genuine function whose source merely contains `{ [native code] }` throws `TypeError: Serializing native function: <name>`. The neighbouring tests at index.js:14-15 have no `g` flag, which points at the flag as the defect.

**Impact:** any process that serializes a built-in once (codegen, doc dumps, a caught-and-logged error path) silently produces invalid JavaScript on the next native value; the payload is only traceable at eval time. Contained and clears between calls — low.

**Fix:** make the guard stateless: drop the `g` flag from `IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP` (or reset `.lastIndex = 0` before each `.test()`).

findings.title: ignoreFunction deletes the caller's own properties and throws on frozen objects

summary:
The change re-adds `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js` at the exact upstream commit `d85f8cf` ("Dont return paths outside webroot"), the fix for CVE-2018-16478: it adds a `..` segment check and a `path.relative(webroot, …)` containment check to the catch-all `GET *` handler that generates directory listings, alongside the earlier listing HTML-escaping. I ran the server against the declared dependencies and confirmed the traversal fix holds for every payload I tried (`../../`, `..%2f`, `%2e%2e`, `%c0%ae`, `....//`, `..;/`, backslash and null-byte variants all 404, nothing outside the webroot read or listed).

The fix's own logic is sound, but the newly added file ships three unhandled-exception paths that terminate the process, and I reproduced all three live: an asterisk-form `GET *` request (no precondition, one unauthenticated request kills the server), a directory listing containing an entry `fs.stat` cannot resolve, and the `send(res, indexpath)` call that passes the response where `send` expects the request. All are availability issues with server restart as the only recovery; I filed them at medium/low with their preconditions and smallest fixes.

I also recorded a short knowledge concept on where webroot containment is enforced, so the undecoded-path assumption and the symlink limitation are not re-litigated in later reviews.

findings.title: A single unauthenticated `GET *` request kills the server
findings.body:
A single unauthenticated request with the asterisk-form request target (`GET * HTTP/1.1`) kills the
process. Express does not install its response helpers for that target, so the catch-all handler at
simplehttpserver.js:57 receives a bare `http.ServerResponse`: the path checks pass (`*` has no `..`),
`fs.stat` fails with ENOENT, and `res.sendStatus(404)` at simplehttpserver.js:82 is not a function.
The throw happens inside the `fs.stat` callback, so nothing catches it and the process exits.

**Preconditions:** none. Any client that can open a TCP connection to the listen port can do it.

**Evidence:** run `node simplehttpserver.js -p 8123 -b 127.0.0.1 <webroot>`, then send
`printf 'GET * HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n'` to port 8123. Server output:

    TypeError: res.sendStatus is not a function
        at /…/simplehttpserver.js:82:56
        at FSReqCallback.oncomplete (node:fs:197:21)

The connection closes with no response and the process is gone; further requests are refused until
it is restarted. `OPTIONS *` does not reach the handler (Express answers 500), so `GET` is the
trigger.

**Impact:** the entire server and every page it serves go down after one request, and the attacker
can repeat it after each restart. Availability only: reach is broad, the effect clears only with a
restart, so medium.

**Fix:** do not assume the Express response object in this handler — for example `res.statusCode =
404; res.end()` on the not-found paths, or reject request targets that are not origin-form.

findings.title: Directory listing crashes the server when an entry cannot be stat'ed
findings.body:
`directoryHTML()` starts its `fs.stat` callback with `if ( !stat ) cb();` (simplehttpserver.js:144)
and falls through without returning. When stat fails — a dangling symlink in the listed directory, or
an entry removed between `fs.readdir` and `fs.stat` — `stat` is undefined and the next statement,
`stat.isDirectory()` (simplehttpserver.js:147), throws. The throw is inside a filesystem callback, so
Express cannot catch it and the process exits. The client gets a truncated 200 page.

**Preconditions:** the listed directory holds an entry `fs.stat` cannot resolve (dangling symlink,
or a file deleted while the listing is built).

**Evidence:** in the webroot, `mkdir links && ln -s /nonexistent/target links/dangling`, then
`curl http://127.0.0.1:8123/links/` returns 200 with a partial page and the server prints

    TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'isDirectory')
        at /…/simplehttpserver.js:147:23
        at FSReqCallback.oncomplete

after which the process is dead. The same callback reaches `cb()` a second time at
simplehttpserver.js:152 when the throw is fixed, which would corrupt async 0.7 queue accounting.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated `GET` of any directory listing containing such an entry stops the
whole server and needs a restart. It requires a dangling symlink (or a concurrent deletion) in the
webroot, so low.

**Fix:** `if ( err || !stat ) return cb();` and only build a link after stat succeeded.

findings.title: Index.html branch passes the response to send() and kills the server
findings.body:
The index.html branch calls `send(res, indexpath)` (simplehttpserver.js:89), but `send`'s signature
is `send(req, path, options)`; the Express response is passed where the request is expected.
`SendStream.send()` reads `req.headers.range` (send/index.js:520) and a bare `ServerResponse` has no
`headers`, so the call throws inside send's own `fs.stat` callback: uncaught, no response, process
exits.

The branch is reachable where `express.static` refuses a path and leaves it to the catch-all. send
ignores dot-prefixed paths, so `GET /.hidden` without a trailing slash reaches simplehttpserver.js:89
when the webroot has `.hidden/index.html`. With the trailing slash, `express.static` serves the index
itself, and it does the same for ordinary directories, so this branch is dead code everywhere it is
not broken.

**Preconditions:** the webroot contains a dot-directory with an index.html file, requested without a
trailing slash.

**Evidence:** `curl --path-as-is http://127.0.0.1:8123/.hidden` closes the connection with an empty
reply and the server prints

    TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'range')
        at SendStream.send (/…/send/index.js:520:28)
        at onstat (/…/send/index.js:624:10)

then exits.

**Impact:** unauthenticated process kill (availability), but it needs an unusual webroot layout, so
low.

**Fix:** pass the request object: `send(req, indexpath).pipe(res)`.

summary: The PR re-adds `lib/main.js`, the deploy CLI for the `aws-lambda` npm package, at a revision that predates the 1.0.5 fix (version 1.0.4 in `package.json`, no `FunctionName` validation). I reproduced the reported issues locally with a stubbed `aws-sdk` and the real parser, and confirmed the upstream fix diff plus the OSV advisory match the code under review. The file is a faithful re-add of the vulnerable release, so it ships CVE-2019-10777 along with a second shell-injection source, a credential leak in docker mode, and a broken error path. Beyond that, the rest of the file's defects (unset `!Ref` falling back to ambient AWS credentials, missing region validation, `invoke` ignoring `FunctionError`, `~` never expanded) are robustness issues that need argument rather than a demonstrated failure, so I left them out; the watchpack string-`ignored` suspicion I checked and refuted.

findings.title: Hostile package.json files entries run shell commands during deploy
findings.body:
Before zipping, `deploy` reads the target project's `package.json` and joins its `files`
array with spaces into the same `exec` string. Entries are never quoted, so a shell
metacharacter in any entry runs a command on the machine doing the deploy.

**Preconditions:** the user deploys a project tree whose `package.json` they did not
author (cloned repository, template, generated project).

**Evidence:** `lib/main.js:174-181` reads `JSON.parse(packageJson).files` and does
`zipfileList = packageJsonFiles.join( ' ' )`; `lib/main.js:185` concatenates the result
into `"zip -r -9  " + tmpfile + ' ' + zipfileList` and `lib/main.js:187` runs it with
`exec`. Reproduction with `package.json` containing
`{"files":["index.js ; touch /tmp/pwned_files"]}` and `FunctionName: safe-name`:
`/tmp/pwned_files` was created by the `/bin/sh` that `exec` spawned. Separately, an empty
`files` array yields an empty operand list rather than the `.` default, so the zip gets
no input files.

**Impact:** local code execution triggered by nothing more than deploying a third-party
Lambda project — no code from that project runs locally otherwise. Permanent (commands
cannot be undone). Medium: the attacker must get the user to deploy their tree, and the
same actor can usually reach the path in the FunctionName finding instead.

**Fix:** the invariant is that no project data is ever shell-parsed. Pass the file list
as separate `execFile`/`spawn` arguments; validating `FunctionName` (the fix for the
other injection) does not cover this input.

findings.title: Crafted FunctionName runs shell commands during deploy
findings.body:
`deploy` builds the `zip` command with string concatenation and runs it through
`child_process.exec`, which passes the string to `/bin/sh`. `FunctionName` reaches that
string unsanitised, so a `.lambda` config whose function name contains shell
metacharacters runs arbitrary commands as whoever invokes `lambda deploy`.

**Evidence:** `lib/main.js:150` puts `$config.FunctionName` into the temp zip path, and
`lib/main.js:185-187` concatenates that path into `"zip -r -9  " + tmpfile + ' ' +
zipfileList` and calls `exec`. `FunctionName` comes straight from the config file
(`lib/main.js:136-137`; when absent it defaults to the basename of the config path, so
the file name alone is enough).

Reproduction (stubbed `aws-sdk`, real `js-yaml`, `lib/main.js` unchanged):

```
FunctionName: "x; touch /tmp/pwned_cve ; echo"
```

`node bin/lambda deploy cfg.lambda` executed
`/bin/sh -c "zip -r -9  /tmp/x; touch /tmp/pwned_cve ; echo-<ts>.zip"` and
`/tmp/pwned_cve` was created. Upstream fixed exactly this in 1.0.5 by validating the
name against `/^([a-zA-Z0-9-_\.]+)(:(\$LATEST|[a-zA-Z0-9-_]+))?$/` (GHSA-934x-72xh-5hrg,
CVE-2019-10777); the added file has no such check.

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution under the developer's account, with the AWS
credentials the tool is about to use available in that process. The config is often
checked in or handed over with the project, so this crosses a trust boundary, and
executed commands leave permanent effects. High.

**Fix:** stop using a shell for the zip invocation — build an argument array
(`['-r', '-9', tmpfile, ...files]`) and pass it to `execFile`/`spawn` — and reject a
`FunctionName` that does not match the Lambda function-name pattern before it is used
in a path or request.

findings.title: Malformed .lambda file crashes deploy with TypeError instead of the config error
findings.body:
`deploy`'s YAML error handler reads `_this.settings`, but `_this` is only assigned later
in the function. `var` hoisting leaves it `undefined`, so a malformed `.lambda` file
throws a `TypeError` inside the `catch` block instead of reporting the config error.

**Evidence:** `lib/main.js:121` (`if ( _this.settings.exitOnError !== false )`) executes
before `lib/main.js:148` (`var _this = this`). Reproduced with a bad YAML file:
`node bin/lambda deploy bad.lambda` printed the js-yaml exception and then
`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'settings')` at
`lib/main.js:121`, aborting the stack instead of the intended clean exit.

**Impact:** info. The command still fails, but the real cause is buried in an unrelated
stack trace and the `exitOnError` handling for the YAML failure never runs. The same
`exitOnError !== false` guard in the sibling `_parse_config_file` path works, so the
failure mode is also inconsistent.

**Fix:** initialise `var _this = this` before the `try` block (or use an arrow-function
`this`), so the error path can run as written.

findings.title: Docker mode exposes AWS credentials on the command line
findings.body:
`start_docker` forwards env-referenced secrets to `docker run` as `-e NAME=VALUE`
arguments. Command lines are readable by every local user (`ps`, `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`)
and `docker` also records them in the container configuration that any user with docker
access can read back.

**Preconditions:** `--docker` mode and a `!Ref env.X` reference for a secret (the pattern
the README documents), on a host with other local users or a shared docker daemon.

**Evidence:** `_resolve_refs` copies env values into `this.envs`
(`lib/main.js:22,27,33`); `start_docker` turns each into a pair at
`lib/main.js:532-536` (`envs.push('-e'); envs.push(env_k + '=' + l.envs[env_k])`) and
passes them in the `spawn('docker', [...])` argv (`lib/main.js:542-558`).
Reproduction with a stub `docker` on `PATH` and `AWS_KEY: !Ref env.MYTEST_SECRET`
showed `MYTEST_SECRET=AKIA_SUPERSECRET` in the received argv.

**Impact:** AWS access keys and session credentials leak to local users and to the
container record; the leak persists until the keys are rotated. Medium: needs the
non-default `--docker` mode and a shared host.

**Fix:** keep values off the command line — push only `'-e', env_k` into argv and pass
the values through `spawn`'s `env` option (docker copies a value-less `-e NAME` from its
own environment), or use a mode-0600 `--env-file`.

summary:
Coverage is complete. One probe hypothesis I checked and dropped: the `tagResource`/`data` shadowing lead (lib/main.js:299-301) is a false alarm — `data` there is the `updateFunctionConfiguration` response, which does carry `FunctionArn`. Two findings recorded, both reproduced against the committed file.

**Summary**

This PR adds `lib/main.js`, the whole implementation of the `lambda` CLI: config parsing with `!Ref` env lookups, `deploy` (zip the function folder, then create/update the Lambda and tag it), `delete`, `invoke`, a watchpack-based `start`, and a `start_docker` mode. It includes a function-name sanity check at lib/main.js:139, which does close the one injection path into the temp-zip filename, so that part of the change is sound.

The remaining problem is in the same command: the zip invocation at lib/main.js:190-192 is still a concatenated shell string, and the project's `package.json` `files` array is pasted into it unquoted — deploying an untrusted project therefore executes attacker commands on the developer's machine, which I reproduced end to end. I also confirmed a smaller error-path defect where `_this` is dereferenced before assignment, turning a bad config into an uncaught `TypeError`. The rest of the file (SDK parameter plumbing, docker spawn, watch wiring) is plausible CLI code with the usual rough edges around malformed configs, and nothing there warranted a further finding.

findings.title: Untrusted package.json files entries run as shell commands during deploy
findings.body:
`lambda deploy` runs a shell command built from the deployed project's `package.json`
`files` array. A project whose `files` entry contains shell metacharacters executes
arbitrary commands on the machine doing the deploy, before any AWS API call.

**Preconditions:** The developer runs `lambda deploy <file>.lambda` (or `lambda start`,
which re-runs deploy on every watched change, lib/main.js:525) on a project whose
`.lambda` `PATH` resolves to a directory whose `package.json` was written by someone
else — a cloned repo, a vendored module, or a tarball. Both files ship in the same
tree, so the victim only has to deploy the project.

**Evidence:** after `process.chdir($fullFunctionPath)` (lib/main.js:174),
`fs.readFileSync('package.json')` reads that directory's manifest (lib/main.js:179);
when `files` is an array it is joined with spaces with no quoting or escaping
(lib/main.js:182-186) and concatenated into `"zip -r -9  " + tmpfile + ' ' +
zipfileList` (lib/main.js:190), which is executed by `child_process.exec`, i.e.
`/bin/sh -c` (lib/main.js:3, 192).

Reproduced with the file as committed (`zip` absent, aws-sdk/watchpack stubbed, no
AWS call made):

    .lambda:      {"PATH": "/tmp/injcheck/proj", "FunctionName": "repro", ...}
    package.json: {"name":"p","files":["index.js; touch /tmp/inj_marker"]}
    $ node -e "require('/tmp/injcheck/main.js').deploy('/tmp/injcheck/proj/f.lambda')"
    ...
    $ ls -l /tmp/inj_marker          # created
    -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 ... /tmp/inj_marker

The command handed to the shell was
`zip -r -9  /tmp/repro-<ts>.zip index.js; touch /tmp/inj_marker`; `$(...)`, backticks,
`&&` and `|` execute the same way. The payload runs even when `zip` is missing,
because the shell still evaluates the `;`-separated segment (the deploy then dies at
lib/main.js:198 reading the zip that was never written). The `FunctionName` check at
lib/main.js:139 closes only the `tmpfile` part of the command; nothing validates
`zipfileList`.

**Impact:** Arbitrary command execution as the deploying user, with the AWS access
key/secret that `aws.config.update` just loaded from the config (lib/main.js:144-148)
plus the process environment, and with the watcher re-executing it on every file
change. Nothing undoes it and credentials can be exfiltrated silently; a normal run
still prints "Deployed!". The same unquoted join also breaks benign input: a `files`
entry such as `"my file.js"` is word-split and produces a broken or empty package.

**Fix:** stop treating the file list as shell text. Use `execFile('zip', ['-r', '-9',
tmpfile].concat(files))` (the file already does this for docker at
lib/main.js:547-563), default to `['.']`, and reject a `files` value that is not an
array of strings. The `tmpfile` argument should be passed the same way, since
`os.tmpdir()` can itself contain spaces.

findings.title: Malformed .lambda config throws TypeError instead of the intended clean exit
findings.body:
A `.lambda` config that fails to parse makes `lambda deploy` throw
`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'settings')` from
lib/main.js:121 instead of printing the error and exiting.

**Preconditions:** any malformed config file — bad indentation, a tab character, an
unknown YAML tag.

**Evidence:** the parse error handler at lib/main.js:119-124 reads
`_this.settings.exitOnError`, but `var _this = this` is only assigned later, at
lib/main.js:153. `var` is hoisted, so at line 121 `_this` is `undefined`. Reproduced
with the committed file:

    $ node -e "require('/tmp/injcheck/main.js').deploy('/tmp/injcheck/proj/bad.lambda')"
    Invalid config file (/tmp/injcheck/proj/bad.lambda) YAMLException: ...
    THREW: TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'settings')

The intended `process.exit(-1)` at lib/main.js:122 and the `return` at line 123 are
never reached.

**Impact:** a user error in the config file surfaces as an uncaught exception and a
stack trace from a command-line tool, with exit code 1 rather than the tool's exit
code 255. Callers that construct `new Lambda({exitOnError:false})` — which `start()`
does at lib/main.js:469 — get an exception thrown out of `deploy()` instead of a
return, defeating the setting this branch is trying to honour.

**Fix:** move `var _this = this` above the `try` at lib/main.js:110, or read
`this.settings.exitOnError` here, as `_parse_config_file` already does at
lib/main.js:62.

summary:
The repo is clean and all findings are recorded.

The PR adds the entire `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js` module (158 lines): a static file server on express 4.13 with a catch-all GET handler that renders directory listings and serves `index.html`. The catch-all re-implements path handling that `express.static` already refused, and does it without confinement — the changed lines are the whole surface, so I covered each branch with runtime reproduction on the pinned dependency versions (express 4.13.4, send 0.13.2). Three defects reproduce on one unauthenticated request: filesystem-wide directory listing outside the web root (CVE-2018-16478), and two distinct process-killing crashes. HTML/URL escaping of filenames and the request URI is sound, and one suspected status-code bug (`res.send(404)`) was refuted against express 4.13.4's source.

findings.title: A single unauthenticated request crashes the server when a directory with index.html is reached through the catch-all
findings.body:
One unauthenticated GET that resolves to a directory containing `index.html` terminates the server process. `send()` is called with the HTTP response object in the request position, and send dereferences `req.headers` inside an fs callback, so the resulting `TypeError` is uncaught and node exits.

**Preconditions:** the requested path must reach the catch-all (anything serve-static declines) and resolve to a directory that contains `index.html`. A traversed path is the easy route: with web root `/srv/www` containing `index.html`, `GET /../www/ HTTP/1.1` (raw, e.g. `curl --path-as-is`) hits it. A dot-prefixed directory with an `index.html` also reaches it without traversal, because serve-static ignores dotfiles and calls `next()`.

**Evidence:**
- `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:66-72`: after `fs.stat(indexpath)` proves the file exists, it runs `send(res, indexpath).pipe(res)`. The `send` module's signature is `send(req, path, options)` (send 0.13.2 `index.js:70-88`), so `res` becomes `this.req`.
- The throw is unconditional: `SendStream.prototype.send` executes `var req = this.req; var ranges = req.headers.range;` at `send/index.js:519-520`, reached from `pipe()` → `sendFile()` → the internal `fs.stat` callback → `onstat` → `send()` (`index.js:431, 503, 614, 624`), before any guard. `http.ServerResponse` has no `headers` property in any node version (only `IncomingMessage` sets it), and express 4.13.4's `lib/router/layer.js:94-99` catches only synchronous throws.
- Reproduced on the pinned deps: `GET /../webroot/` → curl `000` / "Empty reply from server"; stderr `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'range') at SendStream.send (/node_modules/send/index.js:520:28) at onstat (...:624:10) at FSReqCallback.oncomplete`, process gone; port refused afterwards. Restarting and repeating gives the same result, also with `HEAD`.

**Impact:** Reach is broad — the single-process server has no supervisor, so one request takes the service down for every client at once. Persistence is recoverable (a restart restores it) and trivially re-triggerable, which puts this at medium: unauthenticated remote denial of service on a tool whose README advertises default binding to `0.0.0.0`. It also silently breaks the intended feature: serving `index.html` for a directory reached through the catch-all never succeeds on any supported dependency version.

**Fix:** pass the request, not the response — `send(req, indexpath).pipe(res)` — and add an error handler on the stream (`on('error', ...)`) so a stream failure becomes a 500 instead of an uncaught throw from an fs callback.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can list directories anywhere on the host outside the web root
findings.body:
An unauthenticated HTTP request containing `..` segments makes the catch-all handler resolve a path outside the configured web root, so the server returns a directory listing of any readable directory on the host (`/etc`, `/root`, `/home`, sibling projects).

**Preconditions:** none. The traversal must arrive un-normalized on the wire (`curl --path-as-is`, a raw socket, or any HTTP client that does not collapse `..`); browsers and plain `curl` normalize it client-side, so it is trivially attacker-controllable but not one-click.

**Evidence:**
- `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:58-59` takes the raw request path and joins it: `var pathname = url.parse(req.url).pathname; pathname = path.join(dir, pathname);`. `path.join` collapses `..`, and nothing checks that the result is still inside `dir`.
- `express.static(dir)` at `simplehttpserver.js:44` does reject traversal: send 0.13.2 raises a 403 for paths matching its `..` regex. serve-static 1.10.3 then discards that 403 by calling `next()` (`serve-static/index.js:114-121`, `fallthrough: true`), so the request falls into the catch-all at `:57` with `req.url` untouched and the escape happens.
