- Reproduced with the pinned dependencies (express 4.13.4, send 0.13.2) on node v24: `GET /../../../../etc/ HTTP/1.1` → `200`, 4520-byte listing of `/etc`; `GET /../ HTTP/1.1` → listing of the web root's parent; `GET /../secretdir/noindex2/` → listing of a directory that is not under the web root. Encoded forms (`/%2e%2e/`) return 404 because `:58` does not decode, which does not mitigate anything — the raw form works.

**Impact:** Reach crosses a trust boundary: an actor with no role on the host obtains filesystem structure it was never meant to see, anywhere the server process can read, on every deployment since the bind default is all interfaces (`simplehttpserver.js:25`). Persistence is permanent — a listing cannot be recalled. Graded down one tier because the code bounds the leak to listings: non-directory targets 404 at `:63` and the only file-sending branch (`:66-72`) always crashes, so file contents outside the root are not obtainable. That leaves metadata disclosure at arbitrary depth — medium, matching NVD's CVSS 3.0 5.3 (`C:L/AV:N/PR:N`) for CVE-2018-16478.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the resolved path must stay inside `dir`. In the catch-all, resolve and compare:

```js
var pathname = path.resolve(dir, url.parse(req.url).pathname);
if (pathname !== dir && pathname.indexOf(dir + path.sep) !== 0) return res.sendStatus(404);
```

Resolve `dir` once at startup (`path.resolve`), and keep the check on the resolved form so it also covers `url.parse` not decoding.

findings.title: Directory listing of a dangling symlink crashes the server: missing return after the stat error check
findings.body:
When `fs.stat` fails for one entry of a directory being listed, the worker falls through to `stat.isDirectory()` on `undefined`, throwing a `TypeError` inside an fs callback and exiting the process.

**Preconditions:** a directory being listed contains an entry whose `stat` fails — a dangling symlink, a symlink loop, or an entry deleted between `readdir` and `stat`. The client cannot create such an entry through this server (it exposes one catch-all GET plus `express.static`; body-parser is commented out at `simplehttpserver.js:10,15`), so the trigger is tree state or a local race. Dangling symlinks are common in served trees (`node_modules/.bin`).

**Evidence:**
- `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:123-135`: `fs.stat(path.join(pathname, item), function(err, stat) { if ( !stat ) cb(); ... if ( stat.isDirectory() ) {`. The `cb()` at `:125` has no `return`, so execution continues into `:128` with `stat === undefined`. async 0.7 does not guard worker callbacks, and `:125` also calls `cb()` a second time at `:133` if the throw were ever caught, which would let `q.drain` fire twice.
- Reproduced with the pinned deps: web root containing a directory with `ln -s /nonexistent broken-link` plus one regular file, `GET /dirA/` → process exits on the first request, 3 of 3 fresh restarts, with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'isDirectory') at /simplehttpserver.js:128:22 at FSReqCallback.oncomplete`. With the broken entry sorting first the client gets an empty reply; otherwise a truncated listing is flushed before the crash. A directory of only regular files, and a symlink to an existing file, do not crash. Combined with the traversal at `:59`, the crashing directory does not have to be inside the web root.

**Impact:** Reach is broad in effect (the whole process dies) but the trigger needs a pre-existing dangling entry, so it is one tier below the request-driven crash: low. `chmod 000` on files is not a trigger, since `stat` needs only search permission on the directory.

**Fix:** return after the error callback and answer 500 (or skip the entry): `if (!stat) return cb();` in the worker, and give the worker a way to report the error so `q.drain` is not reached on a failed listing.

findings.title: Directory listing links 404 for directory names that need percent-encoding
findings.body:
Directory listings emit links that 404 for any subdirectory whose name must be percent-encoded (space, non-ASCII, `#`, `?`, `%`, `+`), and such a directory cannot be listed directly either, because the catch-all joins the still-encoded path onto the web root. **Evidence:** - `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:126` writes the href with `escape(item)` (`querystring.escape`), producing `parent%20dir/`. The follow-up request is handled at `:58-59`, which never decodes: `url.parse('/parent%20dir/').pathname` stays encoded, so `path.join(dir, '/parent%20dir')` names a literal `parent%20dir` entry that does not exist. `fs.stat` fails and `:63` answers 404. - Reproduced on the pinned deps: web root containing `plain/nested/n.txt` and `parent dir/nested/n.txt`. `GET /` → `
  • parent dir/
    • `; following it, `GET /parent%20dir/` → `404`, while `/plain/` and `/plain/nested/` → `200`. A subdirectory that contains `index.html` recovers only because `express.static` decodes the path first (`GET /parent%20dir/sub-with-index/` → `200`). **Impact:** Correctness only, contained to the browsing feature of a development tool: a listed subdirectory is unreachable from the listing, so the listing gives no way to descend into it. Severity is `info` — names are still disclosed and no attacker gains anything. **Fix:** decode before resolving, in the same place that fixes the containment check: `path.resolve(dir, decodeURIComponent(url.parse(req.url).pathname))`, then apply the prefix check, returning 400 on a malformed escape.

summary:
Review complete. Two findings recorded; no knowledge concepts existed to update.

**Summary**

This PR adds `index.js`, the package entry point that was missing from the baseline, and its one functional difference from the shipped 6.0.2 source is in `ctorName` (index.js:68-70): `val.constructor.name` is now used only when `val.constructor` is a function, which is the CVE-2019-20149 fix. I checked it against the real upstream 6.0.3 file (identical apart from a redundant truthiness test) and against the 6.0.2 source, and reproduced the spoof: `{constructor:{name:'Map'}}` now returns `object` instead of `map`, including when built by `JSON.parse`. A 184-value differential run (primitives, boxed forms, all built-ins, subclasses, cross-realm `vm` values, Proxies, iterators, `Object.create(null)`) found no legitimate type change and no new throw, and both test files pass (36 assertions), so the patch is correct and safe to merge. What it does not do is close the wider class the CVE describes or update the tracked browser bundle; those two limits are recorded as findings.

findings.title: kindOf still returns 'regexp' or 'error' for plain objects built from JSON
findings.body:
`kindOf` still reports a plain object as `regexp` or `error` when the object is built from parsed JSON. The
change hardens `ctorName` (index.js:68-70) so the constructor-name switch can no longer be spoofed, but the
duck-typed checks that run before it still accept attacker-chosen property types. A consumer that uses
`kindOf` to decide how to handle untrusted input can be steered to the wrong branch, which is the failure
CVE-2019-20149 describes.

**Evidence:** with the patched file in this tree:

```
$ node -e "var k=require('./index.js');
  console.log(k(JSON.parse('{\"flags\":\"g\",\"ignoreCase\":false,\"multiline\":false,\"global\":false}')));
  console.log(k(JSON.parse('{\"message\":\"x\",\"constructor\":{\"stackTraceLimit\":1}}')));"
regexp
error
```

Both inputs are ordinary objects: `x instanceof RegExp` and `x instanceof Error` are false and
`Object.prototype.toString.call(x)` is `'[object Object]'`. `isRegexp` (index.js:88-94) and `isError`
(index.js:78) compare property types only, and they run at index.js:20-21, before the `[object Object]`
branch at index.js:56.

**Impact:** any downstream gate of the form `if (kindOf(body) === 'object')` treats a four-property JSON
body as a RegExp (or as an Error) and takes the other path. Severity is low because this behaviour is
byte-identical in the released 6.0.2 (verified against the 6.0.2 source): the change narrows the attack
surface rather than widening it, and the damage needs a consumer that turns the returned string into a
security decision.

**Fix:** brand-check before trusting shape. Either move the `[object Object]` test ahead of the
isDate/isError/isRegexp heuristics, or require the brand inside each fallback, e.g.
`typeof val.flags === 'string' && toString.call(val) === '[object RegExp]'`.

findings.title: Checked-in browser.js still carries the pre-fix ctorName, so browser users keep the CVE-2019-20149 spoof
findings.body:
`browser.js` in the repository still contains the pre-fix `ctorName`, so anyone who loads the checked-in
browser bundle gets the CVE-2019-20149 spoof that this change closes in index.js.

**Preconditions:** the consumer copies `browser.js` out of the repo (bower, git, a CDN path) instead of
using the npm tarball or index.js.

**Evidence:** browser.js:69-71 still reads
`return val.constructor ? val.constructor.name : null;`. Running that bundle,
`kindOf({constructor:{name:'Map'}})` returns `'map'`; the patched index.js returns `'object'`.

The blast radius is limited: `package.json:22-24` ships only `index.js`, and the released 6.0.3 tarball
contains no `browser.js`; `package.json:31` rebuilds the bundle from index.js with
`browserify -o browser.js -e index.js -s index --bare`.

**Impact:** info. npm consumers never see this file, and the build step regenerates it, but the tracked
artifact contradicts the source it is generated from, so the fix appears absent to browser users who read
the repo.

**Fix:** regenerate the bundle in this commit with the existing prepublish command so `browser.js` matches
index.js.

summary:
Recorded the finding. Final coverage check on the one remaining surface — bundle consistency and test status — was already confirmed (browser.js is byte-identical to the new index.js, and the 53 documented assertions in test/test.js and test/es6/index.js pass against it).

## Summary

The PR adds the missing `index.js` for kind-of 6.0.2: a single 129-line type-detection module whose implementation is byte-identical to the published 6.0.2 source and consistent with the pre-built `browser.js` bundle and the existing test suite. The change restores a package that was unusable (`package.json` points `main` at the absent file), so approving it is close to neutral on intent — but it also reintroduces the exact code for CVE-2019-20149, where an attacker-supplied `constructor` name controls the returned type string. I filed that as one medium finding; I did not file the module's many other duck-typed detections (`isBuffer`, `isDate`, `isRegexp`, `isError`) separately, since upstream 6.0.3 leaves them intact and they need code-level values rather than parsed data.

findings.title: Crafted `constructor` property makes `kindOf()` report the wrong type
findings.body:
`kindOf()` reports the type an attacker chooses instead of the value's real type. Any
object whose `constructor` property is a truthy non-function with a `name` field is
classified as that name.

**Preconditions:** a consumer passes an attacker-controlled value to `kindOf()` and
uses the returned string for validation or dispatch. The value can be plain parsed
data — no functions or getters needed.

**Evidence:** `ctorName()` returns `val.constructor.name` whenever `val.constructor`
is truthy (index.js:68-70), and that unvalidated string is the switch discriminant at
index.js:23-47, which runs before the `[object Object]` → `object` fallback at
index.js:54-56. Against the file added by this PR:

```
$ node -e "var k=require('./index.js');
  console.log(k(JSON.parse('{\"constructor\":{\"name\":\"Map\"}}')));
  console.log(k(JSON.parse('{\"constructor\":{\"name\":\"Symbol\"}}')));
  console.log(k(JSON.parse('{\"a\":1}')));"
map          # not a Map: no get/set
symbol       # not a symbol
object
```

`{constructor: {name: 'Set'}}`, `'Promise'`, `'Uint8Array'`, `'WeakMap'` and the other
names in that switch spoof the same way. No input I tried makes this file throw
(`Object.create(null)` and `{message: 'x'}` are handled), so the impact is a wrong
classification, not a DoS. This is the defect fixed in kind-of 6.0.3; the only source
difference from 6.0.3 is this one line.

**Impact:** the library's whole contract is "Get the native type of a value"
(README.md:3), so a consumer's `kindOf(x) === 'object'` allow-list or `'map'`/`'set'`
dispatch branch is decided by attacker data. A nested object that claims `'map'` skips
`object`-only recursive copying or sanitizing and can then crash the consumer
(`x.get is not a function`) or alias data across the boundary. Reach is broad: every
consumer that trusts the string. I drop one tier because the exploit needs an action
outside this repo — a consumer that treats the string as a security decision — and
because the worst outcome I can demonstrate here is a wrong return value, not a crash
or data loss.

**Fix:** gate the read on it being a function, as shipped in 6.0.3:

```js
function ctorName(val) {
  return typeof val.constructor === 'function' ? val.constructor.name : null;
}
```

Then `{constructor: {name: 'Map'}}` falls through to `object`. A constructed
`constructor` function can still spoof a name, but parsed data cannot carry one.
test/test.js has no case for this; add one asserting
`kindOf({constructor: {name: 'Map'}}) === 'object'` (it currently has only the
`Object.create(null)` case at test/test.js:56).

summary:
**Summary**

This change adds `src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx`, the checkbox renderer for `additionalSignUpFields` — and it is the core of the fix for CVE-2019-20174: the field's `placeholder` was previously injected with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and it is now rendered as text, with raw HTML only on an explicit `placeholderHTML` prop. That security change is correct and closes the sink: `placeholder` reaches the component only from `custom_input.jsx` via `additionalSignUpFields` (`src/connection/database/index.js:98,116,198`), so untrusted placeholder content is now escaped.

The port is incomplete, though. The upstream fix also touched `src/field/custom_input.jsx` and `src/connection/database/index.js`; without those halves the new `placeholderHTML` branch can never fire, and the existing checkbox snapshot still records the old raw-HTML output, so the test suite stays red. Both are recorded; neither undermines the security intent, so I would approve once the snapshot is regenerated and the `placeholderHTML` plumbing is either finished or removed.

findings.title: Checkbox input change leaves the CustomInput checkbox snapshot stale, so the test suite fails
findings.body: The checkbox sign-up field test fails after this change. The stored snapshot still records the old output, so `yarn test:jest` reports a snapshot mismatch for `CustomInput when type == checkbox renders correctly as a CheckBoxInput`. **Evidence:** `src/__tests__/field/custom_input.test.jsx:99-103` renders ``, which reaches `src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx:17-21`. `placeholderHTML` is undefined on that path, so the branch at `checkbox_input.jsx:20` renders `placeholder` — a text child and no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` prop. The snapshot at `src/__tests__/field/__snapshots__/custom_input.test.jsx.snap:16-22` expects ``. `expectComponent` (`src/__tests__/testUtils.js:4-7`) serialises with react-test-renderer and compares exactly, so the two cannot match. Only this case is affected; the file's other six cases are unaffected now that the module resolves. **Impact:** CI's test job (`yarn run test:jest`, `.circleci/config.yml`) is red, so the security fix cannot land as-is. It is a one-command repair and affects only the test suite, hence `low`. **Fix:** regenerate the snapshot (`yarn test:jest -u`) or hand-edit it to `placeholder`. While there, add the case upstream added for the HTML branch: render with `placeholderHTML={'Placeholder'}` and snapshot it, so the dangerous branch has coverage.

findings.title: New placeholderHTML prop is never supplied, so HTML labels for checkbox fields silently stop rendering
findings.body:
The new `placeholderHTML` opt-in cannot be reached, so it is dead code and the format
option it exists for is gone. Any app that put markup in a checkbox sign-up field's
`placeholder` — bold text, a link to terms — previously saw it rendered; after this
change it sees the escaped literal tag, with no way to opt back in.

**Evidence:** `src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx:5,17-18` reads `placeholderHTML`, but no
caller supplies it. `src/field/custom_input.jsx:9-16` rebuilds its props from a fixed
whitelist and `:30-35` renders `<CheckboxInput>` without the key. Behind that,
`src/connection/database/index.js:98` destructures only known keys from each
`additionalSignUpFields` entry and `:198` rebuilds the whitelist, so a developer-supplied
`placeholderHTML` is dropped silently. `:116` also still requires a non-empty
`placeholder`, so an entry that offers only `placeholderHTML` is discarded with
"Ignoring an element ... does not contain a valid `placeholder` property" and the field
disappears from the form. Repo-wide, `placeholderHTML` appears only in the new file.

**Impact:** a documented escape hatch that does nothing, plus a silent label-formatting
regression for existing configurations. No security consequence: the branch being
unreachable is what keeps the raw-HTML sink dormant, and rendering `placeholder` as text
is the intended fix for the placeholder XSS. `info` because the worst outcome is a
label losing formatting or a field vanishing, and only for a non-default configuration.

**Fix:** finish the port — pass `placeholderHTML` through
`src/field/custom_input.jsx` (destructure and forward it, as `placeholder` is), and in
`src/connection/database/index.js` accept it, validate it as a non-empty string,
warn when both are given, and require only one of `placeholder` / `placeholderHTML`.
Otherwise drop the prop and the `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` branch from
`checkbox_input.jsx` and keep the plain-text render only.

summary: The PR adds one file, `src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx`, which renders a checkbox custom sign-up field for Auth0 Lock: a labelled `<input type="checkbox">` whose label text is the configured field placeholder. I traced it through its only consumer chain (`connection/database/index.js` → `engine/classic/sign_up_pane.jsx` → `field/custom_input.jsx`), checked the option validation there, and confirmed the repository's existing snapshots match this exact output. One issue is recorded: the label text is inserted as raw HTML. Otherwise the component's structure (controlled checked state, forwarded `onChange`, aria-label) matches the sibling inputs, and the unused `InputWrap` import is cosmetic.

findings.title: Custom checkbox placeholder is inserted as raw HTML, allowing XSS in the Lock widget
findings.body: The new `CheckboxInput` renders the configured label text with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, so any HTML in a custom sign-up field's `additionalSignUpFields[].placeholder` is executed in the Lock widget's origin. The value is only checked for being a non-empty string, so the widget turns a documented plain-text option into an HTML injection sink. **Preconditions:** the host app passes `additionalSignUpFields` with `type: "checkbox"` and a `placeholder` that carries text it did not author (a query/hash parameter, stored profile data, CMS or tenant copy, or a wrapper that forwards user-editable config). The sign-up screen must be reachable and `onlyEmail` false. **Evidence:** `src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx:18` — ``. The value arrives unmodified: `src/engine/classic/sign_up_pane.jsx:48` passes `x.get('placeholder')`, `src/field/custom_input.jsx:28-36` routes `type === 'checkbox'` to this component, and the only validation is `typeof placeholder != 'string' || !placeholder` at `src/connection/database/index.js:116`. Rendering the same sink with `` under React 15.6.2 (the pinned version) produces ``; the sibling `text_input.jsx:44` renders the same config value as an escaped `placeholder` attribute, and `README.md:499-505` documents it as plain text. The upstream fix for CVE-2019-20174 (v11.21.0) made this text-only and added a separate opt-in `placeholderHTML` prop. **Impact:** HTML event handlers run on the widget page, so an injected payload can read the email/password being typed, and any tokens or codes the widget holds, for every user who reaches the sign-up screen. Severity is medium: the XSS crosses the user/attacker boundary and persists in the app's options, but exploitation needs the embedding app to forward untrusted text into the placeholder and a non-default checkbox custom field, so the library alone does not expose it. **Fix:** restore the invariant that `placeholder` is text. Render it as a child (`{placeholder}`); if raw markup is wanted, take it from a new, explicitly named prop such as `placeholderHTML` and keep `placeholder` escaped.

summary:
Recorded both findings. Final summary:

**What the change does:** PR #2 re-adds `src/index.ts` (devalue v1.1.0-era, 268 lines) at the upstream commit whose parent is the CVE-2019-13506 fix — it introduces `unsafeChars`/`escapeUnsafeChars` and routes `safeKey`/`safeProp` through them so object property names are escaped. I confirmed the fix is effective: the pre-fix file emits an attacker-supplied key verbatim (`{"</script><script>alert(1)</script>":1}`), while this version escapes `<`/`>` and never lets a raw `<` reach the output; string values were already safe. The file passes the repo's suite (45/45, run without installing deps by stubbing `describe`/`it`).

**Assessment:** the security change is correct and I found no remaining XSS path reachable from attacker-influenced data (the RegExp, symbol, and spoofed-`toStringTag` sinks all need server-side objects, not attacker input). Two `low` defects live in the key helpers this PR rewrites: the escape/`JSON.stringify` order is inverted, so keys with unsafe characters (including ordinary legal keys containing the resulting text) are silently corrupted or merged — the regression upstream fixes in the immediate follow-up commit `14cae90`; and a `__proto__` key name, reachable from plain parsed JSON, is emitted as a bare identifier and turns into the reconstructed object's prototype instead of a key.

findings.title: Keys with unsafe characters are double-escaped and no longer round-trip
findings.body:
`safeKey`/`safeProp` escape a key *before* JSON-stringifying it, so the backslash they
insert is escaped again. Any object key containing a character in `unsafeChars`
(`< > \b \f \n \r \t \0 U+2028 U+2029`) is emitted with two backslashes, and the
documented deserialization path (`(0,eval)('(' + str + ')')`, README) yields a
*different* key: the literal escape text instead of the original character.

**Evidence:** src/index.ts:228-230 turns `<` into the six characters `\u003C`;
src/index.ts:233 and :237 then pass that text through `JSON.stringify`, which
escapes the backslash to `\\`. Both call sites are affected: object-literal keys
(src/index.ts:119) and the assignment statements used for repeated/cyclic objects
(src/index.ts:183).

Reproduced with Node 24 running the file directly:

```
devalue({'<svg onload=alert("xss_works")>': 'bar'})
  -> {"\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\"xss_works\")\\u003E":"bar"}
  case of eval -> key "\u003Csvg onload=alert(\"xss_works\")\u003E"   (not the input key)

devalue({'a\nb': 1})       -> {"a\\nb":1}    case of eval -> key "a\nb"  (backslash + n)
devalue({['<x>']: (<cyclic>)})
  -> (function(a){a["\\u003Cx\\u003E"]=a;return a}({}))    key is corrupted the same way
```

Distinct keys also collapse: `{'a\nb': 1, 'a\\nb': 2}` serializes to
`{"a\\nb":1,"a\\nb":2}`, which evaluates to a single key `a\nb` with value `2` — one
entry is silently lost, and the surviving key collides with a key that contains no
unsafe character at all. Keys without unsafe characters (`x-y`, `a"b`, `a\b`, `a/b`),
and all string *values* (src/index.ts:240-268, which never re-stringifies), still
round-trip. The XSS mitigation itself is sound: no reproduction emitted a raw `<` or
`>`.

The repo's test encodes the corrupt output (`test/test.ts:92-95` expects
`{"\\u003Csvg ...}` with two backslashes), so the suite passes (45/45) and does not
observe the round-trip break. Upstream corrects the argument order to
`escapeUnsafeChars(JSON.stringify(key))` in the next commit, `14cae90` "prevent
double escaping".

**Impact:** devalue's core contract — output that deserializes back to an equal value
— fails for keys holding these characters, and the corruption can merge or overwrite
unrelated keys with no error. Reach is contained (a single object's key) and the
source value is unharmed, so `low`: silent data corruption for unusual key names, no
XSS, no trust-boundary crossing.

**Fix:** escape the *serialized* key instead of serializing the escaped one:
`escapeUnsafeChars(JSON.stringify(key))` at both src/index.ts:233 and :237, and update
the expected string in test/test.ts:94 to the single-backslash form.

findings.title: A __proto__ property name sets the deserialized object's prototype instead of a key
findings.body:
A `__proto__` property name is emitted as a bare identifier, so the serialized object
literal sets the reconstructed object's prototype instead of creating a key. The key
disappears and the prototype's contents become inherited properties of the value the
client receives.

**Preconditions:** the server serializes an object graph that has an own `__proto__`
key. That is ordinary JSON — `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}')` creates an
own enumerable `__proto__` key — so any app that stores parsed user JSON (preference
maps, per-key settings keyed by user input) and passes it to devalue reaches this.

**Evidence:** `safeKey` (src/index.ts:232) returns `__proto__` unquoted because it
matches `^[_$a-zA-Z][_$a-zA-Z0-9]*$`; `safeProp` (src/index.ts:236) likewise emits
`.__proto__`. Those feed src/index.ts:119 (`{${safeKey(key)}:...}`) and
src/index.ts:183 (`${name}${safeProp(key)}=...`). Reproduced:

```
devalue(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}'))
  -> {__proto__:{isAdmin:true}}
  case of eval -> Object.keys(v) = [], v.isAdmin === true, own "__proto__" = false

devalue(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":null}'))
  -> {__proto__:null}
  case of eval -> Object.getPrototypeOf(v) === null, v.hasOwnProperty === undefined

// null-prototype branch, src/index.ts:121-124:
devalue(Object.assign(Object.create(null), {['__proto__']: {isAdmin: true}}))
  -> Object.assign(Object.create(null),{__proto__:{isAdmin:true}})
  case of eval -> keys [], isAdmin undefined        // key dropped entirely
```

**Impact:** attacker-chosen properties appear on the deserialized state object as
inherited properties, so app code that reads `state.user.isAdmin` or uses `in` sees a
value the attacker supplied under a key name that was supposed to be data, and the
renamed key is missing from `Object.keys`; with `{"__proto__":null}` the object loses
even `hasOwnProperty`. The pollution stays on that one object — `Object.prototype` is
untouched — so the reach is contained and the effect is recoverable, hence `low`.

**Fix:** treat `__proto__` as unsafe in `safeKey`/`safeProp` so it is emitted in
bracket form and assigned rather than as a literal prototype slot — e.g. emit
`{...}` built via `Object.assign`/computed key, or reject the key outright. Upstream
devalue later resolved this by throwing on `__proto__` keys.

summary:
Both findings are recorded with full bodies.

## Summary

The PR re-adds `lib/index.js`, a memoizing wrapper around `path.relative`; it is byte-identical to upstream release 1.0.2, the version that only *partially* fixed CVE-2018-16472 by moving the initial cache to `Object.create(null)` while leaving both `{}` sites inside the function. I confirmed the residual bug by reproduction: one `process.chdir()` after load reverts the cache to a plain object, after which `relative('__proto__', key)` writes to the global `Object.prototype` permanently, and `relative('constructor', 'prototype')` returns `Object.prototype` instead of a path. Upstream 1.1.0 closes it by making lines 30 and 38 null-prototype as well — that is the smallest correction here. I also recorded a lower-severity drop-in-compatibility break: the unconditional `process.cwd()` at line 28 makes the shim throw `ENOENT` on arguments the native function handles, whenever the process's directory has been deleted.

findings.title: Prototype pollution resumes after a working-directory change, letting callers write to Object.prototype
findings.body:
A caller can write attacker-chosen keys onto the global `Object.prototype` after the
process changes its working directory once. The cache is created with a null prototype
(`lib/index.js:13`), which blocks the attack, but the cwd-change branch replaces it with
a plain object (`lib/index.js:30`), so every later lookup and write goes through the
prototype chain.

**Preconditions:**
- `cached-path-relative` or its shim is loaded.
- One `process.chdir()` happens afterwards. `lib/index.js:26-32` exists precisely to
  support this, so it is a normal path, not an exotic setting.
- A call whose `from` is exactly `'__proto__'`. This is the point where a host that
  forwards an attacker-influenced relative path into `path.relative` becomes exposed.

**Evidence:**

After the chdir, `cache['__proto__']` resolves to `Object.prototype`; the truthiness
test at `lib/index.js:34` accepts it, `lib/index.js:38` keeps it, and
`lib/index.js:39` (`cache[from][to] = result`) assigns onto `Object.prototype`.

```
$ node /tmp/repro1.js            # no chdir, then chdir
before chdir, own prop: "../evil"
Object.prototype.evil after no-chdir call: undefined
after chdir, result: "../evil"
Object.prototype.evil: ../evil
inherited by unrelated object: "../evil"
```

Same call, same arguments, before and after the chdir: only the `{}` at line 30
distinguishes them. Through the shim, an ordinary downstream read sees the injected
value:

```
$ node /tmp/repro3.js           # requires shim.js, then process.chdir('/tmp')
before: undefined | own props: [ 'name' ]
after : ../isAdmin | hasOwn: false
any object now carries it: ../isAdmin
```

The property is enumerable, writable and configurable, and it survives for the life of
the process; further chdirs only rebuild the cache container, never `Object.prototype`.

The same broken invariant has a second, non-`__proto__` symptom, fixed by the same
change, so it is reported here rather than separately: after a chdir a prototype name as
`from` short-circuits at line 34 and returns an inherited value instead of a path.
`relative('constructor', 'prototype')` returns `Object.prototype` itself, `relative('toString',
'constructor')` returns `Function`, and a caller doing `.replace()` on the result throws
`TypeError: r.replace is not a function`. The leak also runs the other way: once keys are
on `Object.prototype`, later cache misses read them (`relative('someName', 'length')` →
`11`), so innocent callers get silently wrong paths.

**Impact:** Permanent, process-wide pollution of every object in the process. Any
authorization or option flag read off an object without a `hasOwnProperty` guard is
settable by whoever controls the path string. Severity follows the repo's
reach × persistence rule: the write is permanent and broad (every object in the process),
discounted one tier because the trigger needs a host that passes an untrusted relative
path as the first argument — the documented browserify use passes absolute paths, so that
use is not exposed. Bounded in that polluted values are always relative-path strings.

**Fix:** Keep a null-prototype object on every path into the cache. Change
`lib/index.js:30` to `cache = Object.create(null)` and `lib/index.js:38` to
`cache[from] = cache[from] || Object.create(null)`. Upstream 1.1.0 fixed it this way;
this file is byte-identical to 1.0.2, which only fixed line 13 and left both `{}` sites.

findings.title: Memoized path.relative throws ENOENT when the working directory has been deleted
findings.body:
`cachedPathRelative` calls `process.cwd()` on every invocation (`lib/index.js:28`), a
syscall the native `path.relative` never makes. When the process's working directory has
been deleted, `process.cwd()` throws `ENOENT`, so the function fails on arguments that do
not depend on the cwd at all.

**Preconditions:** the directory the process is sitting in is removed while it runs
(temp-dir cleanup in builds, CI harnesses, container image updates).

**Evidence:**

```
$ node /tmp/repro2.js
B native path.relative with deleted cwd: "../c"
B cached THROWS: ENOENT
```

The native call returns `"../c"`; the memoized wrapper throws before it can compute
anything.

**Impact:** Contained to the affected calls and recoverable by chdir-ing to a valid
directory, so low. It matters because `shim.js:12` replaces `path.relative` for the whole
process, so any third-party call that previously worked with absolute arguments starts
throwing. The Readme advertises the wrapper as a drop-in for `path.relative`.

**Fix:** Only reach for `process.cwd()` when it can be read without changing behaviour,
or wrap the check so a `getcwd` failure falls through to the uncached computation instead
of propagating.

summary:
Recorded six findings. Summary of the review:

The PR adds `src/index.ts`, the TypeScript implementation of `devalue` (value → JavaScript source, evaluated inside a `<script>` tag), including the fix that escapes unsafe characters in object keys. The key-escaping fix itself is right: keys now round-trip correctly (`{'<svg onload=alert("xss_works")>': 'bar'}` → `{"\u003Csvg onload=alert(\"xss_works\")\u003E":"bar"}`), so the CVE-2019-13506 defect is closed for keys. However, the same escaping invariant fails elsewhere: `RegExp` values are emitted as raw `thing.toString()`, and V8 does not escape `/` inside a character class, so a pattern built from untrusted input can put a literal `</script>` into the page and execute attacker code — I confirmed with a spec-compliant HTML parse that the output splits into two script elements. I also recorded the stale `Dangerous key` test that now fails (the expectation still encodes the old double-escaped output), plus three narrower emit defects found while probing the new file: an own `__proto__` key becoming the revived object's prototype, a repeated empty `Set`/`Map` emitting an empty statement, and NUL-before-digit / `Symbol` values producing corrupted or invalid output.

findings.title: RegExp values are emitted as raw source, so a character class can close the script element
findings.body:
`devalue` emits RegExp values as raw `thing.toString()` text, skipping the escaping used for every
other string. V8 escapes `/` only outside a character class, so a pattern can carry a literal
`</script>` into the output, close the surrounding script element, and run whatever follows it.

**Preconditions:** the serialized value contains a RegExp derived from untrusted input (a stored
search or validation pattern, an SSR payload field), and the output is inlined in a `<script>`
element — the usage documented in README.md:74.

**Evidence:**
- src/index.ts:104 (`return thing.toString();`) and src/index.ts:156
  (`values.push(thing.toString());`) are the only RegExp emit paths and neither escapes the source.
- `new RegExp('[</script><script>alert(1)</script>]').source` is `[</script><script>alert(1)</script>]`,
  because `/` is escaped only outside a class (`new RegExp('</script>').source` is `<\/script>`).
  So `devalue({q: new RegExp('[</script><script>alert(1)</script>]')})` returns
  `{q:/[</script><script>alert(1)</script>]/}`. The same text is emitted when the RegExp sits in a
  `Set`, a `Map`, an array, or the repeated-reference values list
  (`(function(a){return [a,a]}(/[</script>]/))`).
- Parsing `<script>var preloaded = {q:/[</script><script>alert(1)</script>]/};</script>` with a
  spec-compliant parser (parse5) yields two script elements: `var preloaded = {q:/[` and `alert(1)`.

**Impact:** attacker-controlled script execution in the page that hydrates the state — the bug class
the escaping exists to prevent, and the README's "XSS mitigation" claim ("Strings generated by
`devalue` can be safely deserialized") is false for this value type. The untrusted actor gains script
execution in another user's browser rather than data it is allowed to hold, and nothing supported
undoes it: high.

**Fix:** emit from the escaped source instead of the raw literal, e.g.
`new RegExp(${stringifyString(thing.source)}, ${stringifyString(thing.flags)})` (drop the flags
argument when empty), so the pattern passes through the same escaper as strings.

findings.title: Key-escaping change leaves the XSS 'Dangerous key' test asserting the old double-escaped output
findings.body:
The PR's key escaping escapes *after* `JSON.stringify`, which changes the emitted form of unsafe
object keys, but test/test.ts still asserts the old double-escaped form, so `npm test` fails.

**Evidence:** `npx mocha --opts mocha.opts` reports 44 passing, 1 failing:
`AssertionError: '{"\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\\"xss_works\\")\\u003E":"bar"}' == '{"\\\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\\"xss_works\\")\\\\u003E":"bar"}'`
at test/test.ts:9. The actual output (src/index.ts:233) is
`{"\u003Csvg onload=alert(\"xss_works\")\u003E":"bar"}`; the expectation at test/test.ts:94 encodes
`\\u003C`, the form that revives the key as the literal text `\u003Csvg ...`.

**Impact:** the repository's only regression test for key escaping no longer matches the shipped code,
so CI is red and the fixed behaviour is unverified. Contained to the test suite and recoverable: low.

**Fix:** change the expectation at test/test.ts:94 to
`'{"\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\\"xss_works\\")\\u003E":"bar"}'` and assert the round-trip key
(`<svg onload=alert("xss_works")>`) held by evaluating the output, so double escaping cannot return.

findings.title: An own __proto__ key becomes the revived object's prototype instead of a property
findings.body:
An own `__proto__` key is emitted as an identifier (`{__proto__:...}` or `a.__proto__=...`), which the
language treats as a prototype assignment, not a property assignment. The key disappears and its
value becomes the prototype of the revived object.

**Preconditions:** the serialized object carries an *own* `__proto__` key, which `JSON.parse` (or
`Object.defineProperty`) creates from untrusted JSON. Object literals cannot create it, so it arrives
via parsed data.

**Evidence:**
- src/index.ts:233 and src/index.ts:237 match `__proto__` with `/^[_$a-zA-Z][_$a-zA-Z0-9]*$/` and
  return it verbatim; it is used at src/index.ts:119 (object literal) and src/index.ts:183
  (`name + safeProp(key) + '='`).
- `devalue(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}'))` → `{__proto__:{isAdmin:true}}`. Evaluated:
  `Object.keys` is `[]`, `hasOwnProperty('__proto__')` is false, `result.isAdmin === true`, and
  `for..in` yields `isAdmin`.
- Repeated form: `devalue([o, o])` → `(function(a){a.__proto__={isAdmin:true};return [a,a]}({}))`,
  same result.
- Scalar value: `devalue(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":1}'))` → `{__proto__:1}`; the key is dropped and
  the value discarded.
- Global `Object.prototype` is not polluted (checked after every case); only the revived object's
  prototype chain changes.

**Impact:** the round-trip is not faithful, and attacker-supplied JSON can hand the revived object
inherited properties that consumers read with `in`, `for..in` or plain property access, which makes
it a prototype-injection gadget in state hydration. Contained to the values revived from that payload
and recoverable: low.

**Fix:** reject own `__proto__` keys in `walk`, like functions and non-POJOs
(`Cannot stringify an object with a __proto__ key`), or emit them with `Object.defineProperty`.

findings.title: A repeated empty Set or Map emits an empty statement and produces unparseable output
findings.body:
An empty `Set` or `Map` that is referenced more than once emits `<name>.` with nothing after the dot,
so the generated source does not parse.

**Evidence:**
- src/index.ts:172 and src/index.ts:177 push
  `${name}.${Array.from(thing).map(...).join('.')}`; with no entries the join is `''`.
- `const s = new Set(); devalue([s, s])` → `(function(a){a.;return [a,a]}(new Set))`;
  `vm.runInNewContext` throws `SyntaxError: Unexpected token ';'`. Same for `new Map()`.
  A single (non-repeated) empty collection is fine (`new Set([])`).

**Impact:** a supported value type revives as unparseable code, so hydration of the whole payload
fails. Contained to that payload and recoverable: low.

**Fix:** emit `${name};` (or skip the statement) when the collection has no entries.

findings.title: NUL followed by a digit forms an octal escape, corrupting strings and breaking strict-mode parse
findings.body:
NUL is escaped as `\0`, which fuses with a following digit into a legacy octal escape: the string is
silently corrupted, and strict-mode consumers cannot parse the payload at all.

**Evidence:**
- src/index.ts:14 maps `'\0'` to `'\\0'`, applied at src/index.ts:249 with no lookahead for a digit.
- `devalue({k:'\u00001'})` → `{k:"\01"}`; reviving it gives `"\u0001"` (U+0001, not NUL + `1`).
  `devalue({k:'\u000011'})` → `{k:"\011"}`, which revives as `"\t"`.
- `vm.runInNewContext('"use strict";(' + devalue({k:'\u00001'}) + ')')` →
  `SyntaxError: Octal escape sequences are not allowed in strict mode`.

**Impact:** state containing NUL before a digit comes back with a different character, and payloads
revived in strict mode fail to parse. Contained and recoverable: low.

**Fix:** escape NUL as `\\u0000` (valid in both modes), or add a lookahead so a digit after `\0` is
escaped as well.

findings.title: Symbol values are emitted unquoted as String(symbol), producing invalid JavaScript
findings.body:
Symbol values pass the walker and are emitted as unquoted `String(symbol)`, which is never valid
JavaScript and which copies the symbol description into the page as raw text.

**Evidence:**
- src/index.ts:24 rejects only functions, and `walk` skips primitives at src/index.ts:35, so symbols
  are accepted and counted.
- src/index.ts:215 returns bare `String(thing)` for them: `devalue([Symbol('x')])` → `[Symbol(x)]`
  (`ReferenceError: x is not defined` on revive); `devalue(new Set([Symbol('a b')]))` →
  `new Set([Symbol(a b)])` (`SyntaxError`).
- `devalue({s: Symbol('</script><script>alert(1)</script>')})` →
  `{s:Symbol(</script><script>alert(1)</script>)}`: the element text does not parse as JS, but the raw
  `</script>` still ends the surrounding script element in HTML before any JS runs.

**Impact:** state containing a symbol revives as unparseable code, and the raw-description path is a
`</script>` breakout when an attacker influences the symbol description (an unusual precondition, so
this is graded on the unparseable output). Contained and recoverable: low.

**Fix:** throw for symbols in `walk` alongside functions ("Cannot stringify a symbol").

summary:
Review complete. Findings are recorded on PR #2.

**Summary:** PR #2 adds `_read.js`, the GET implementation that `index.js:5` exports as `tiny.get`; the baseline tree had the file deleted, so this restores the read path. The added file is byte-identical to the upstream revision at `41468a2` and is an older, buggier sibling of the `_write.js` already in the tree — it reintroduces CVE-2018-1000096 and carries several request-handling defects that `_write.js` has since fixed or guarded. I reproduced each reported issue against local HTTP/HTTPS servers (Node v24.22.2) rather than reasoning from the diff alone.

findings.title: HTTPS GETs accept any TLS certificate, letting a network attacker read and rewrite responses
findings.body:
Every `tiny.get({url: 'https://…'})` accepts any TLS certificate. An attacker on the
network path can read request headers and bodies (auth tokens, cookies) and rewrite
responses that callers then treat as trusted JSON. All consumers of `tiny.get` are
affected, since `index.js:5` wires `get` straight to this function.

**Evidence:** `_read.js:35` sets `opts.rejectUnauthorized = false`, which turns off
Node's certificate verification for `https.get`. Reproduced with a self-signed HTTPS
server on `127.0.0.1`:

```
PR code:     request to untrusted cert SUCCEEDED -> {"secret":"intercepted",...}
fixed code:  rejected -> DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT
```

The "fixed" run is the same file with only that one line deleted — exactly upstream
commit `1460a81` ("Don't disable SSL certificate validation", PR #15, merged as
`3c1e36d`). The file added by this PR is byte-identical to upstream blob `f10f808`
at `41468a2`, the revision CVE-2018-1000096 (CWE-295) records.

**Impact:** A network attacker gains data their role denies: request payloads and
header secrets, plus the ability to substitute response bodies (integrity). The leak
is permanent — captured credentials cannot be recalled — and the attacker can repeat
it at will, so this is high under the reach/persistence table and matches the CVE's
CVSS 3.0 score of 8.1. Note `_write.js:38` carries the same line for POST/PUT/DELETE;
fixing both closes the whole surface.

**Fix:** Delete the hardcoded line so Node's default verification applies. If
self-signed endpoints must be supported, honour an explicit per-call
`options.rejectUnauthorized` opt-in instead of defaulting to off.

findings.title: A 2xx GET response without a Content-Type header rejects with an internal TypeError
findings.body:
A 2xx GET response that carries no `Content-Type` header — including the common
`204 No Content` — is reported as an error. The caller gets
`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')` instead of a
successful, empty or plain-text body.

**Evidence:** `_read.js:60` calls `res.headers['content-type'].startsWith(...)`
without checking that the header exists. The surrounding `try` at line 59 converts
the TypeError into `err`, so the request rejects. Reproduced against a local server:

```
/no-type => ERR TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')
/204     => ERR TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')
/plain   => ok "ok"
```

`_write.js:46-50` already defines an `is(headers, type)` helper that guards for a
missing header (used at `_write.js:100`), so the write path handles this correctly
and the read path silently diverges.

**Impact:** Contained to the single request and reproducible on every retry, so
`low`: any endpoint returning 204 or an untyped body is unusable through `tiny.get`,
and the error message points at library internals rather than the response. A
secondary effect is that on the error path `body` is the raw `Buffer` from line 61
even when `options.buffer` is unset, so the shape differs from the documented one.

**Fix:** Default the header before matching, e.g.
`var ctype = res.headers['content-type'] || ''` and test `ctype.startsWith(...)`, or
reuse the `is()` guard from `_write.js`.

findings.title: A truncated response never calls back, leaving the returned promise pending forever
findings.body:
A response whose body is cut short — server closes or resets the socket before the
declared `Content-Length` is reached — never invokes the callback. In promise mode
`await tiny.get(...)` stays pending forever: no error, no result, no timeout.

**Evidence:** `_read.js:52-56` listens only to the response's `'data'` and `'end'`
events, and `_read.js:75` attaches `req.on('error', ...)` to the *request*, not the
response. A truncated response emits `'aborted'`/`'error'` on `res`, which nothing
handles, and `'end'` never fires. Reproduced against a local server that writes a
partial body with `Content-Length: 100` and then destroys the socket:

```
after 1500ms callbacks fired = 0 (0 means the promise never settles)
```

On Node v24.22.2 no uncaught exception surfaced, so the failure is silent. `_write.js:88-118` has
the same gap; the read path is where it is first reachable here.

**Impact:** Contained to one request but permanent for it: the awaiting caller never
continues, and nothing in the library bounds the wait (there is no timeout and no
abort handle — `opts` at line 24 only carries `url.parse` output plus headers). A
broken server, a proxy cutting the connection, or a truncated TLS-off connection
stalls the calling handler or Lambda until its own outer timeout fires.
**Fix:** Attach `res.on('error', callback)` (and treat `'aborted'`/premature close
the same way) so a truncated body rejects instead of hanging.

findings.title: Lowercase caller headers are overwritten by the library defaults
findings.body:
Callers who supply headers in lowercase — the convention for HTTP/2 and most client
libraries — have `user-agent` and `content-type` silently replaced by the library
defaults. The server receives a different request than the caller asked for.

**Evidence:** `_read.js:37-38` looks up `opts.headers['User-Agent']` and
`opts.headers['Content-Type']` with one exact casing, while Node's header handling is
case-insensitive. Reproduced with a server echoing request headers:

```
caller sent : {'user-agent':'my-app/1.0','content-type':'application/vnd.api+json',
               'authorization':'Bearer t'}
server saw  : {"ua":"tiny-http","ct":"application/json","auth":"Bearer t"}
```

The caller's object is also mutated: it comes back with both lowercase keys and the
added `User-Agent`/`Content-Type` defaults. `_write.js:46-50` shows the repository
already knows about case-insensitive header matching (its `is()` helper checks both
casings) but applies it only to the response side.

**Impact:** Contained and recoverable (`low`): content negotiation that depends on
`content-type` on a GET, or a service that filters on the user agent, gets a request
it did not expect, with no error to signal it. A caller who happens to use the same
casing that the library checks is unaffected, which makes the failure depend on
client convention rather than on anything visible in the call.
**Fix:** Match headers case-insensitively when applying defaults (reuse the `is()`
helper from `_write.js`), and set the default under a single canonical casing.

summary:
Recorded three findings and corrected one line reference. Summary:

**What the change does:** adds `_read.js`, the `tiny.get` implementation, exporting GET via `index.js`. The added code is the post-fix version of the CVE-2018-1000096 file: it no longer sets `rejectUnauthorized = false`, and I verified GET now rejects a self-signed HTTPS host (`DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT`) where the same request through `tiny.post` succeeds. The certificate-validation defect the CVE describes therefore remains reachable in this tree, because `_write.js:38` (untouched by the diff, identical to the pre-fix upstream file) still disables validation for POST/PUT/DELETE.

**Assessment:** the new file's security posture is right, but it carries two smaller defects I reproduced — a `TypeError` on any 2xx response that omits `Content-Type` (`_read.js:59`), and in-place mutation of `options.url` that duplicates or silently drops `data` (`_read.js:29`). Broader issues raised during probing (no settle on truncated responses, thin non-2xx error metadata, case-sensitive `+json` detection) match pre-existing patterns in `_write.js` or are feature gaps, so I left them unreported.

findings.title: HTTPS POST, PUT and DELETE accept any TLS certificate because _write.js disables validation
findings.body:
`tiny.post`, `tiny.put` and `tiny.del` send `rejectUnauthorized: false` on every HTTPS request (`_write.js:38`), so Node accepts self-signed, expired and wrong-host certificates. An attacker on the network path can impersonate the target server and read or rewrite the POST/PUT/DELETE bodies, which is where a client like this carries API tokens and credentials. This PR re-adds `_read.js` without that line, so GET now validates certificates; the write path keeps the CVE-2018-1000096 defect.

**Preconditions:** an `https://` URL passed to `tiny.post`/`put`/`del`; attacker able to intercept the connection.

**Evidence:** `_write.js:38` sets `opts.rejectUnauthorized = false` on the options object later handed to `https.request` (`_write.js:84`). Reproduced against this tree's `_write.js` with a self-signed HTTPS server: `write('POST', {url:'https://localhost:3443/x', data:{secret:'hunter2'}})` returned SUCCESS and the server received the body, while the same request through the new `_read.js` failed with `DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT`. Upstream removed the line from both files in the CVE fix (brianleroux/tiny-json-http 1460a81, "Don't disable SSL certificate validation"); this tree carries only the `_read.js` half.

**Impact:** A network attacker defeats TLS server authentication and permanently harvests credentials and payloads, so normally high. Discounted to medium because the line predates this diff and the change does not touch `_write.js`; it is however the same defect this change exists to fix, so the fix is incomplete until the line goes.

**Fix:** delete `opts.rejectUnauthorized = false` from `_write.js:38` (let callers opt out explicitly if they must), matching what `_read.js` now does.

findings.title: GET of a response without a Content-Type header fails with a TypeError
findings.body:
`_read.js:59` dereferences `res.headers['content-type']` without checking it exists. A response that legally has no Content-Type header (a bare `200`, a `204`, many health and static endpoints) throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')`; the catch at `_read.js:66` turns that into the callback error, so the caller gets a spurious failure and never sees the body it received.

**Evidence:** Local server answering `res.writeHead(200); res.end('hello')` for `/noct`: `tiny.get({url:'http://localhost:3111/noct'})` called back with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')` instead of `{body:'hello'}`. Same on a 204. A `text/plain` response returns normally. `_write.js:47-48` already guards for a missing header; the new file does not.

**Impact:** Contained to the single request and recoverable by the caller using another client or HTTP method, so low. It breaks every endpoint that omits Content-Type.

**Fix:** guard the header before use (`var ct = res.headers['content-type'] || ''`; treat a non-JSON type as text), and read the header outside the `try` so a header mistake cannot masquerade as a JSON parse error.

findings.title: Reusing options for a GET duplicates query params, and URL fragments silently swallow data
findings.body:
`_read.js:29` appends the serialized `data` to `options.url` in place and re-parses the result. Two failure paths follow:

- the caller's object is mutated, so a retry or a second `tiny.get(opts)` with the same options sends the params twice (`/x?q=1&q=1`);
- when the URL has a fragment, the params are appended after the `#`, so they never reach the server (`/y#frag` plus `{q:1}` requests `/y`).

**Evidence:** Against a local echo server: first call requested `/x?q=1`, the second call with the same object requested `/x?q=1&q=1` (`options.url` had become `http://localhost:3222/x?q=1&q=1`); `{url:'http://localhost:3222/y#frag', data:{q:1}}` requested `/y`. `_write.js` has the same string-append pattern for DELETE only; the new file applies it to every GET with `data`.

**Impact:** Contained to the affected request, and the caller can work around it by building a fresh URL each call, so low. The fragment case silently drops `data` and returns a normal-looking result, so the caller cannot tell the query was lost.

**Fix:** build the URL locally instead of mutating `options.url`, stripping any fragment first, e.g. `opts = url.parse(options.url.split('#')[0] + (opts.search ? '&' : '?') + qs.stringify(options.data))`.

summary:
The change adds `lib/index.js`, a memoizing wrapper around `path.relative` (the upstream 1.0.1 code) on top of an otherwise complete package, so the review surface is that one file plus its shim and test.

I read all 43 lines, the module's `shim.js`, `test/index.js` and `Readme.md`, and reproduced the module's behaviour under Node 24. One high-severity finding is recorded: the plain-object cache trusts caller-supplied `from`/`to` as property keys, so `relative('__proto__', key)` writes a truthy string onto `Object.prototype` for the whole process, and inherited-key hits return wrong paths (`relative('constructor','name')` gives `"Object"`). I verified that prototype-less maps at lines 13, 30 and 38 fix both, and that upstream 1.0.2 left line 30 exploitable after a `chdir` while 1.1.0 applies it at all three sites.

A broader probe of the same file turned up only second-order leads — unbounded cache retention, over-invalidation on every cwd change, non-string arguments bypassing `path.relative`'s validation, and a load-time `process.cwd()` throw when the cwd has been deleted. None crosses into reportable impact on its own, and the first two are the memoization design rather than defects this change introduces.

Overall: correct memoization semantics, but the file reintroduces CVE-2018-16472 and should not merge without the prototype-less cache maps.

findings.title: Path arguments named __proto__ pollute Object.prototype, and inherited keys return wrong cached paths
findings.body:
`cachedPathRelative(from, to)` stores results in plain-object maps keyed by the
two path arguments, with no own-property check. When `from` names an inherited
property, `cache[from]` resolves to the prototype's property instead of a cache
miss. With `from = "__proto__"`, line 38 keeps `Object.prototype` and line 39
writes `Object.prototype[to] = <relative path>`, so every object in the process
gains that property.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e 'var r=require("./lib"); r("__proto__","admin"); console.log(({}).admin)'
../admin
$ node -e 'var r=require("./lib"); console.log(r("constructor","name"))'
Object          # path.relative("constructor","name") is "../name"
```

The first call creates `Object.prototype.admin` as a truthy string and returns
normally. The second shows the read side of the same missing check: line 34 hits
the inherited `Function.name` and returns `"Object"` instead of the real path.

Two write sites are vulnerable — the initial `cache = {}` (line 13) and the
cwd-change reset (line 30) — and neither protects the nested map created at
line 38. `shim.js:12` assigns this function to `path.relative` process-wide, so
with the shim installed every `path.relative` call routes caller strings here.

The pollution outlives the module's own cache reset (line 30), so nothing inside
the library undoes it. The attacker controls the key fully and the value only
loosely (a `path.relative` result), but a truthy string is enough for the usual
`if (obj[key])` gadget.

**Impact:** A caller that forwards a user-influenced path triggers a permanent
write to `Object.prototype` that reaches every object in the process — broad
reach, permanent persistence, `high` under the reach × persistence policy. The
preconditions are a consumer passing an untrusted `from`, and the polluted value
being a relative path rather than an arbitrary object; this module takes no
untrusted input on its own. This is the prototype-pollution flaw recorded as
CVE-2018-16472.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant that cache keys are only ever own properties, by
using prototype-less maps — this fixes the pollution and the wrong-path return:

- line 13: `var cache = Object.create(null)`
- line 30: `cache = Object.create(null)`
- line 38: `cache[from] = cache[from] || Object.create(null)`

(Equivalently, guard lines 34 and 38 with `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`.)
Verified: with these three changes `r("__proto__","polluted")` leaves
`Object.prototype.polluted` undefined and `r("constructor","name")` returns
`"../name"`. Upstream 1.0.2 fixed only lines 13 and 38, which leaves line 30
exploitable after a `chdir`; 1.1.0 applies `Object.create(null)` at all three
sites.

summary:
All preconditions are verified with my own reading of the code, and the XSS is reproduced end-to-end. I also probed the rest of the added file for independent defects.

**Summary of coverage:**
- **§mapTextNodes** — primary risk; reproduced in headless Chromium via the `.caps` behavior. Filed.
- **§modal/toggle/hover/sticky/groupChildren/observe** — probed against MooTools 1.6 and every real caller (`Wiki.js`, `Wiki.Edit.js`, `Prefs.js`, `Columns.js`, `Flip.js`, `Tabs.js`). Found only minor long-standing quirks (`event.preventDefault;` without a call at `Element.Extend.js:155`, a stray `div` from `groupChildren` before its guard, a radio dirty-check miss in `getDefaultValue`). None has a demonstrated failure path with real impact in this tree, and all match upstream's long-standing behaviour, so I left them unreported rather than pad the review.
- **§load order / callers** — confirmed the file is wired into `wro-haddock.xml` after `String/Array.Extend`, and that existing callers pass only the arguments this revision supports.

**Summary:** The PR re-adds `jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/moo-extend/Element.Extend.js`, the MooTools element extensions (ifClass, hover/modal/sticky/toggle helpers, getDefaultValue, groupChildren, mapTextNodes, observe, getBackdrop) that the rest of the haddock frontend already calls. The file is broadly correct, but its `mapTextNodes` helper re-parses text-node content through `innerHTML`, and the `.caps` behavior feeds it page-derived text, so a wiki page can turn escaped markup into a live DOM node — this is the unpatched side of the CVE-2019-10090 change and I recorded it as a high-severity stored XSS. Apart from that one sink, the change looks safe to merge.

findings.title: Stored XSS: mapTextNodes re-parses escaped page text as HTML
findings.body: `Element.mapTextNodes()` re-parses unchanged text-node content as HTML, so a page containing escaped HTML turns into live DOM: stored DOM XSS. Any wiki page can carry `%%caps /%`; on page load the `.caps` behavior lowercases the text node, `mapTextNodes` sees a `<` in the result and assigns it to `dummy.innerHTML` (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/moo-extend/Element.Extend.js:527-537`), splicing a live `` into the document. The payload runs in the wiki origin for every visitor, including admins. **Preconditions:** none beyond being able to edit a page. The shipped policy grants `modify` to `Anonymous` (`jspwiki-war/src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/jspwiki.policy:68-72`), so an unauthenticated visitor can author the payload. **Evidence:** - Sink: `s = fn( n.nodeValue )` (`Element.Extend.js:525`), then `if( hasHTML.test(s) ){ dummy.innerHTML = s; ... parent.replaceChild( frag, n ); }` (`:527-537`). There is no guard for "the callback returned the text unchanged". - Caller: `.add(".caps", function(element){ element.mapTextNodes( function(s){ return s.toLowerCase(); }); })` (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/wiki/Wiki.Behaviors.js:214-217`), run by `Behavior.update()` at DOM ready (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/moo-extend/Behavior.js:98`, `wiki/Wiki.js:252`). - Source of the `<`: JSPWiki escapes raw HTML by default (`jspwiki.translatorReader.allowHTML = false`, `jspwiki-main/src/main/resources/ini/jspwiki.properties:252`, escaping at `JSPWikiMarkupParser.java:531-538`), so `` inside a `%%caps` block reaches the browser as `<img ...>`, i.e. a text node whose `nodeValue` contains a literal `<`. Passing an already-entity-encoded `<img ...>` also works, because `escapeHTMLEntities` leaves existing entities alone (`JSPWikiMarkupParser.java:687-716`). - Reproduced in headless Chromium with the repo's own `mootools-core-1.6.0.js` + `Element.Extend.js` and `<img src="x" onerror="alert('xss-marker'+(window.__pwned=1))">`: before the call there are 0 `img` elements and the node is `#text`; after the `.caps` callback there is 1 live `img[onerror]` and the handler fires (`alert` fired, `window.__pwned === 1`). No user interaction is needed beyond opening the page. **Impact:** Stored XSS in the wiki origin with a cross-trust-boundary reach: an unprivileged or anonymous editor executes script in every viewer's session and can act with their privileges (session/cookie theft, actions as an admin). No CSP with `script-src` is shipped (`commonheader.jsp:48` sets only `upgrade-insecure-requests`), and no client-side sanitizer runs on page content. Severity high: cross-trust-boundary reach with a stored, self-retriggering payload. **Fix:** Restore the invariant "text that came from a text node is never re-parsed as HTML." The smallest change is to skip the `innerHTML` branch when the callback returned the original string, e.g. `if( s === n.nodeValue ){ /* leave the node alone */ } else if( hasHTML.test(s) ){ ... }`. That guard is only partial for the `.caps` caller, because `toLowerCase()` makes `s` differ from `n.nodeValue` whenever the payload contains an uppercase letter (verified: `` still fires behind that guard). The durable fix is to stop routing callback output through `innerHTML`: parse only caller-supplied template markup (e.g. the `` in `HighlightQuery.js:61`) and insert the replaced text as text nodes.

summary:
Review complete. Findings recorded: 1 (high).

**Summary:** PR #2 adds `src/get-static-value.js`, the 417-line `getStaticValue()` evaluator that `src/index.js` already imports, so the change is what makes the package build again. The implementation matches the pre-fix upstream code at 587cca2f and performs host-realm side effects while evaluating: any statically reachable function, constructor, or template tag is invoked, which turns linting attacker-controlled source into code execution in the linter process (reproduced end-to-end with espree/eslint 5, including through `ReferenceTracker`'s `require()` argument at src/reference-tracker.js:100). Minor semantic divergences I checked (computed `__proto__` keys, hole-plus-spread array length, `typeof` of undeclared names) match current upstream and are wrong-value only, so I did not report them.

findings.title: getStaticValue executes attacker-supplied source code in the linter process
findings.body:
`getStaticValue()` treats any statically reachable property as callable, so analysed source code can run arbitrary JavaScript inside the process that is linting it. Source text alone is enough: `[].filter.constructor("globalThis.__rce = 1")()` makes the evaluator compile and then invoke that string, because `MemberExpression` hands back the host realm's `Function` and `CallExpression` calls whatever it was given.

**Preconditions:** a rule reaches `getStaticValue()` for a node of the file being linted. No `initialScope`, globals, or explicit call is needed: `getStringIfConstant(node.arguments[0])` at src/reference-tracker.js:100 evaluates the first argument of every `require()` call in the linted file with no scope, so any plugin built on `ReferenceTracker` is exposed too. The documented direct usage is docs/api/ast-utils.md:311-328.

**Evidence:**
- src/get-static-value.js:179 `receiver[methodName](...args)` and :185 `func(...args)` invoke any value that resolution produced; `NewExpression` :283 and `TaggedTemplateExpression` :342 do the same for constructors and template tags.
- src/get-static-value.js:265-275 `MemberExpression` returns any property, including the inherited `constructor`, so `"".constructor.constructor` / `[].filter.constructor` resolve to the host `Function` (`Function` is also allowlisted at :22).
- Reproduced with espree@5 + eslint@5, rule calling `getStaticValue(node, context.getScope())` as documented:

```js
// linted file — attacker-controlled
[].filter.constructor("globalThis.__rce = 1")()   // rule received a non-null value; globalThis.__rce === 1
Object.freeze(Array.prototype)                    // after this, Object.isFrozen(Array.prototype) === true in the linter
```

The same payloads evaluate with `initialScope = null`, including as `require()`'s argument through src/reference-tracker.js:100 (`require([].filter.constructor("globalThis.__rce3 = 1")())` sets `globalThis.__rce3`). The second payload matters on its own: the evaluator froze the linter's real `Array.prototype`, breaking the "built-in global objects have not been modified" assumption that docs/api/ast-utils.md:282 relies on for every later rule in the process.

**Impact:** statically evaluating untrusted code turns a lint run into remote code execution: linting a third-party pull request in CI, an editor language server, or any tool that scans untrusted repositories writes files, reads credentials, or runs shell commands with the linter's privileges. Reach crosses a trust boundary (author of the linted source → host process) and the effect is permanent, so `high`; the only precondition is the usage this new module exists for.

**Fix:** keep the invariant that static evaluation never invokes a function chosen by the analysed source. Gate the callee, receiver method, `new` callee and template tag on a fixed set of pure built-ins (the upstream 1.4.2 fix adds `callAllowed`/`callPassThrough` sets and limits tagged templates to `String.raw`), and skip member reads that would trigger an accessor (`isGetter` over `getPropertyDescriptor`), so `Object.freeze(Array.prototype)`-style calls and getter side effects stop reaching the host realm.

summary:
Review complete.

The PR re-adds `js/src/tooltip.js` — the Bootstrap 4.3.1 Tooltip plugin, byte-identical to upstream v4.3.1 apart from its version string, and the source of the CVE-2019-8331 fix (`sanitize` of `title`/`content` and of `config.template`). That code itself is sound and matches the surrounding tree (`util.js`, `popover.js` are also 4.3.1 content), so nothing in the added logic is a defect.

The one real problem is completeness: the file imports `./tools/sanitizer`, which is absent from the repo, so the bundle cannot resolve and the sanitize calls never run. I reproduced this with rollup (`Could not resolve './tools/sanitizer' from js/src/tooltip.js`) and traced the consequences through `js/src/index.js:12`, the build scripts, karma, and the committed `dist/js`/`js/dist` bundles, which still carry the pre-fix, unsanitized tooltip. One medium finding is recorded; the surrounding surfaces (`popover.js`, tests, build config) turned up only upstream-intended behaviour or pre-existing issues.

findings.title: Tooltip plugin imports a sanitizer module missing from the tree, so the CVE-2019-8331 fix never executes
findings.body: The re-added Tooltip plugin imports `./tools/sanitizer`, a module that does not exist anywhere in this tree, so nothing that includes the plugin can be built and the sanitization that is the point of the file never executes. **Evidence:** - `js/src/tooltip.js:8-11` — `import { DefaultWhitelist, sanitizeHtml } from './tools/sanitizer'`. - `ls js/src/tools` fails and `git ls-files js/src | grep tools` is empty: the directory is absent and not ignored, so the relative import cannot resolve. - Reproduced against the bundle entry point: `npx rollup@1.1.2 --format umd --file /tmp/out.js js/src/index.js` → `[!] Error: Could not resolve './tools/sanitizer' from js/src/tooltip.js` (`jquery`/`popper.js` are only reported as external, so this is the fatal error). - The same import is pulled in by `js/src/index.js:12`, `build/rollup.config.js` and `build/build-plugins.js:38-39` (Tooltip and Popover), so `npm run js-compile`, `js-compile-plugins` and `js-test` all stop here. - The file is upstream v4.3.1's `js/src/tooltip.js` verbatim apart from the version string (`js/src/tooltip.js:3`, `:23`); upstream added `js/src/tools/sanitizer.js` in the same change, so the dependency is not optional. **Impact:** The CVE-2019-8331 fix arrives without the module that implements it. The two calls that sanitize attacker-reachable strings (`js/src/tooltip.js:448` for `title`/`content`, `:696` for the `template` that closed the `data-template` XSS) can never run, so the plugin cannot be compiled or tested. The artifacts that actually ship are still the pre-fix 4.3.0 code: `package.json` `"main": "dist/js/bootstrap"`, and `dist/js/bootstrap.js:2989` / `js/dist/tooltip.js:441` insert `content` with `$element[html ? 'html' : 'text'](content)` and `dist/js/bootstrap.js:2964` / `js/dist/tooltip.js:418` insert `config.template` raw — i.e. the `data-template=""` path that CVE-2019-8331 describes is unchanged for anyone loading the committed bundles. Reach is broad (every build and every consumer of the bundles) and the condition is recoverable by restoring the missing module, hence medium. Note the baseline could not build either — `js/src/index.js:12` imported the then-absent `./tooltip` — so this PR does not regress buildability, it moves the unresolved import one level deeper and leaves the security fix inert. **Fix:** Restore `js/src/tools/sanitizer.js` (exporting `DefaultWhitelist` and `sanitizeHtml(unsafeHtml, whiteList, sanitizeFn)`) in this same change, keep it inside the published `files` glob (`package.json` currently matches `js/{src,dist}/*.{js,map}`, not nested `js/src/tools/*`), then rebuild `dist/js` and `js/dist` so the shipped bundles contain the sanitizer instead of the 4.3.0 tooltip.

summary: The change re-adds the `Text Encoding Brute Force` operation (a 92-line, single-file addition) — a presenter-style operation that runs the input through every code page in `IO_FORMAT` and renders the results as an HTML table. The operation is otherwise wired correctly: it is already listed in `Categories.json`, uses the standard `json`/`html` type pair, and its argument handling matches sibling operations. The single blocking issue is that the presented table interpolates operation output straight into HTML, which the web UI assigns to `innerHTML` and `eval`s for `

findings.title: Unescaped output in Text Encoding Brute Force executes attacker script in the CyberChef origin
findings.body:
The new `Text Encoding Brute Force` operation puts its input into the output HTML without escaping it, so attacker-supplied text runs as script in the CyberChef origin. A link to the hosted app is enough: recipe and base64 input in the URL hash are loaded and baked automatically, and the presented HTML is assigned to `innerHTML` with every `")` yields plain ASCII bytes `60 115 99 ...` that UTF-8-decode back to the payload, and `decode(65001, ...)` returns it unchanged. - Render path: `presentType "html"` (`:39`), `Recipe.present` (`src/core/Recipe.mjs:263-271`), `src/core/Chef.mjs:96,102-112`, then `src/web/OutputWaiter.mjs:73` `outputHtml.innerHTML = data` and `:76-79` `eval(scriptElements[i].innerHTML)`. An `` payload fires without the eval path at all. - Auto-load: `src/web/App.mjs:398-441` reads `recipe=` and `input=` from the URL, then dispatches `statechange`, which auto-bakes (`src/web/App.mjs:143-155`). URL: `https://gchq.github.io/CyberChef/#recipe=Text%20Encoding%20Brute%20Force('Encode')&input=PHNjcmlwdD5hbGVydCgxKTwvc2NyaXB0Pg` **Impact:** script runs in the victim's CyberChef origin, so a link can read the DOM and localStorage (saved recipes and inputs, which commonly hold secrets), drive the app, or redirect the page. This crosses a trust boundary with a single click and needs no privilege on the app, so it is high. Persistence is recoverable (a reload clears it), which does not lower the tier for a cross-boundary compromise. **Fix:** escape the value before interpolating: `const value = Utils.escapeHtml(Utils.printable(encodings[enc], true));`. Charset names come from `IO_FORMAT` and need no escaping. While there, the closing tag at `:86` is written `""` and should be `"
"`.

summary: ## Summary The only reviewable file, `src/core/operations/TextEncodingBruteForce.mjs`, is byte-identical (blob `169e6ad7b6…`) to upstream's post-fix version of that operation (gchq/CyberChef commit `01f0625`, "Fixed XSS in 'Text Encoding Brute Force'", shipped in v8.31.2). The security-relevant line is `Utils.escapeHtml(Utils.printable(encodings[enc], true))` at `src/core/operations/TextEncodingBruteForce.mjs:82`, which neutralises the input before it reaches the one scriptable HTML sink, `outputHtml.innerHTML` plus the `eval` of embedded `

The change adds `index.js` (343 lines) to npm/ssri: the SRI parsing, serialization, hashing and stream-verification implementation. Compared with the packaged `ssri@5.2.1` it is byte-identical except for one line, the strict-mode parse regex at `index.js:12`, which reintroduces two defects. First, its nested quantifier `(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)*` backtracks exponentially: a ~120-byte attacker-supplied SRI string parsed with `{strict: true}` blocks the event loop for seconds to minutes (measured 2.2 s at 27 `?` chars, 4x growth per added char). Second, its `[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{44,88}` digest class rejects valid short digests and accepts `=` mid-digest, which makes strict parse and strict serialization disagree and makes two of the repo's six test files fail (`test/integrity.js:75`, `test/stringify.js:110`). The remaining code matches the published release and needs no further comment; apart from that one line the change is sound.

Findings recorded: `fnd_a0e7c2a97644ba58` (medium, ReDoS) and `fnd_03057b65a34b327c` (low, strict-parse regression).

findings.title: Strict parsing drops valid short digests and accepts '=' mid-digest, breaking strict round-trips and shipped tests
findings.body:
Strict-mode parsing at `index.js:12` now rejects digest strings it used to accept, and
accepts ones it should reject, so `{strict: true}` silently throws away real integrity
metadata. This commit's own test suite fails because of it.

```js
const STRICT_SRI_REGEX = /^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{44,88})(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)*$/
```

Two problems in the digest group `[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{44,88}`:

1. The length window 44–88 is not derived from the algorithm and is shorter than
   nothing the library itself produces or accepts elsewhere. An unpadded sha256 digest
   is 43 chars; a short-but-valid entry such as `sha512-foo` is 3. Both are dropped
   without error, whereas non-strict parse keeps them.
2. `=` is allowed anywhere inside the digest, not just as trailing padding, so a
   non-base64 string is accepted as a strict digest.

**Evidence:**

```js
const sri = require('ssri')
const unpadded = require('crypto').createHash('sha256').update('x').digest('base64').replace(/=+$/, '')
sri.parse('sha512-foo', {strict: true}).toString()                     // ''
sri.parse('sha512-foo').toString()                                     // 'sha512-foo'
sri.parse('sha256-' + unpadded, {strict: true}).toString()             // '' (43 chars)
sri.parse(sri.parse('sha512-YQ==').toString({strict: true}), {strict: true}).toString() // ''
// strict serializer emits it, strict parser drops it: round-trip is lossy
const mid = 'A'.repeat(20) + '=AAAA' + 'B'.repeat(20)
sri.parse('sha512-' + mid, {strict: true}).toString()                  // accepted
sri.parse('sha512-' + mid, {strict: true}).toString({strict: true})     // '' (rejected)
```

The strict serializer validates digests with `BASE64_REGEX = /^[a-z0-9+/]+(?:=?=?)$/i`
(`index.js:10`, `index.js:53`), which has no length bound and only permits trailing
padding, so parser and serializer disagree in both directions.

The shipped tests catch this: `npx tap test/*.js` fails `test/integrity.js:75`
(`concat(..., {strict: true})` returns `''` instead of `sha512-foo`) and
`test/stringify.js:110` (strict stringify returns `''` instead of
`sha512-foo \r \n\tsha256-bar`). Two of six test files fail, so `npm test` (and the
CI config that runs it) fails on this commit.

**Impact:** Callers that pass `{strict: true}` to validate untrusted metadata get an
