empty `Integrity` for entries that are fine, and pipelines that serialize with
`{strict: true}` then re-parse lose the entry: `Integrity#concat` and `stringify` can
return `''`. A caller that treats "no integrity entries" as "nothing to verify" then
skips verification. Affected data is limited to individual entries and can be
re-derived, hence `low`.

**Fix:** Drop the fixed length window and only allow padding at the end, matching the
serializer's rule:

```js
const STRICT_SRI_REGEX = /^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/]+(?:=?=?))([?\x21-\x7E]*)$/
```

Alternatively, share one digest pattern between `Hash#toString`'s `BASE64_REGEX` check
and the strict parse regex, and check digest length per algorithm if a bound is wanted.

findings.title: Crafted SRI string with repeated '?' makes strict parsing backtrack exponentially and stalls the process
findings.body:
`ssri.parse()` in strict mode backtracks catastrophically on an attacker-supplied integrity string, blocking the whole process while it parses.

The strict parser regex at `index.js:12` is

```js
const STRICT_SRI_REGEX = /^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{44,88})(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)*$/
```

The trailing group `(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)*` nests a `*` inside a `*`, and its character class
`[\x21-\x7E]` also matches `?`. Each `?` in the input can therefore begin a new group
iteration or be swallowed by the previous iteration's `[\x21-\x7E]*`, so a run of `?`
that ends in a character outside the class gives exponential backtracking.

**Preconditions:** The caller parses an SRI string it does not control with
`{strict: true}` (`Hash` only selects `STRICT_SRI_REGEX` when `opts.strict` is truthy,
`index.js:20-26`). The library's own `parse`, `checkData`, `checkStream`,
`fromStream`, `integrityStream`, `concat` and `match` all forward `opts`, so any strict
caller is affected.

**Evidence:** A real 88-char sha512 digest plus a run of `?` and one trailing `\x7f`
(not in `\x21-\x7E`):

```js
const sri = require('ssri')
const digest = require('crypto').createHash('sha512').update('x').digest('base64')
for (const n of [20, 24, 27]) {
  const s = `sha512-${digest}${'?'.repeat(n)}\x7f`
  const t = Date.now()
  sri.parse(s, {strict: true})
  console.log(n, Buffer.byteLength(s) + 'B', Date.now() - t + 'ms')
}
// 20 116B 140ms
// 24 120B 313ms
// 27 123B 2241ms
```

Time grows ~4x per extra `?`: a 130-byte string takes tens of seconds, and the call is
synchronous, so nothing else in the process runs. The non-strict path is unaffected
(`parse(s)` with the same input returns in <1 ms), and `SRI_REGEX` (`index.js:11`) is
fine.

Both upstream shapes of this regex are linear: the published ssri 5.2.1 uses
`/^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/]+(?:=?=?))([?\x21-\x7E]*)$/`, and later releases replace the
repeated group with a single optional one, `(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)?`. This regex reintroduces
the pattern those releases removed.

**Impact:** A small attacker-controlled string makes the parsing process spin for an
unbounded time (CPU exhaustion; the event loop, and every request served by that
process, stalls). Reach is broad — one string stalls everyone the process serves — and
persistence is recoverable: the stall ends, but the attacker can re-send at will.
Strict mode is an opt-in that the library's default path does not use, which is why
this is graded `medium` rather than `high`.

**Fix:** Remove the nested quantifier so at most one options group is accepted:

```js
const STRICT_SRI_REGEX = /^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{44,88})(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)?$/
```

Keep the options syntax check in `Hash#toString` (`VCHAR_REGEX`, `index.js:57`) as the
authority on multi-part options.

summary:
Review complete. Coverage notes: I verified the diff locally (whole test suite passes at this commit, `standard` lint clean), reproduced both reported issues, and confirmed reachability of each against the 2018-era npm stack (pacote, cacache, npm-registry-fetch) by inspecting published tarballs.

**Summary**

The change re-adds `index.js`, the entire implementation of npm's SRI library (`ssri` 5.2.1: parse/serialize, `fromData`/`fromStream`, `checkData`/`checkStream`, and the hashing stream). Functionally it is complete and consistent with its tests, but as a security-sensitive parser it ships the exact state that upstream patched as CVE-2018-7651: the strict-mode metadata regex backtracks quadratically on a long attacker-supplied integrity string, and the parse accumulator confuses `Object.prototype` members for algorithm slots so a crafted algorithm name throws a TypeError from every entry point. I recorded those two findings and left smaller defects (duplicate digests emitted by `integrityStream` when `opts.algorithms` repeats the verification algorithm, and synchronous throws from `crypto.createHash` for unsupported algorithm names, which fail closed) unfiled as below the reporting bar.

findings.title: One long integrity string makes strict SRI parsing hang the process (quadratic backtracking)
findings.body:
`ssri.parse(str, {strict: true})` — and every wrapper that forwards `opts` (`stringify`, `Integrity#concat`, `checkData`, `checkStream`, `integrityStream`) — runs `STRICT_SRI_REGEX` (index.js:12). Its digest group `[A-Za-z0-9+/]+(?:=?=?)` and its trailing options group `[?\x21-\x7E]*` match the same characters, and neither is length-bounded. When the token ends with any character outside `\x21-\x7E` — a non-ASCII character such as `\u00e9`, which survives JSON encoding, or DEL — the engine retries every possible split of the base64 run, so parse time grows quadratically with digest length. Nothing in the parsing path bounds the string's size, so one long integrity value blocks the Node event loop for minutes.

**Preconditions:** the caller parses an integrity string it does not control with `{strict: true}` (registry `dist.integrity`, `package-lock.json`/`npm-shrinkwrap.json` entry, cache metadata).

**Evidence:** `ssri.parse('sha256-' + 'A'.repeat(N) + '\x7f', {strict: true})` at this commit:

| digest chars | time |
|---|---|
| 8 000 | 0.15–0.25 s |
| 32 000 | 2.6–3.5 s (1.2 s with a trailing `\u00e9`) |
| 128 000 | 31 s |
| 256 000 | 103 s |

The same 256 KB string parses in 1.2 ms without `strict`, so the blow-up is specific to the strict regex. The cost is identical through the other entry points, which forward opts into the same regex: `checkData(buf, s, {strict: true})` (index.js:218), `stringify(s, {strict: true})` (index.js:159), `integrityStream({integrity: s, strict: true})` (index.js:247).

**Impact:** denial of service — an attacker-supplied metadata value stalls the whole process, for as long as the attacker makes the value. Contained to one process/job, recoverable by restart, re-triggerable at will, and `strict` is an opt-in documented mode (README.md:104) that npm's own install path never passes (pacote/cacache/npm-registry-fetch call sites forward no `strict`), so it needs a caller that hands attacker-controlled integrity metadata to a strict parse. That is why this is medium rather than high; no repository severity policy applies. This is CVE-2018-7651; upstream fixed it in ssri 5.2.2.

**Fix:** bound the digest to the lengths the spec algorithms produce and make the options separator literal: `/^([a-z0-9]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{44,88})(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)?$/` (upstream d0ebcdc). With that regex the parse, check, create and from tests pass unchanged, but two tests that feed deliberately short fake digests into strict paths must switch to real digests: test/stringify.js:111 (`'sha512-foo sha256-bar'`) and the `concat()` case in test/integrity.js (`'sha1-bar!'`).

findings.title: Integrity strings whose algorithm name matches an Object.prototype member throw instead of parsing
findings.body:
`_parse()` stores parsed hashes on a plain `Integrity` object and guards the slot with a falsiness test: `if (!acc[algo]) { acc[algo] = [] }` then `acc[algo].push(hash)` (index.js:147-148), where `algo` is the algorithm name taken verbatim from the string. If that name is an `Object.prototype` member — `constructor`, `toString`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, `__proto__` — the inherited member is truthy and is not an array, so the second line throws `TypeError: acc[algo].push is not a function`. The same pattern is at index.js:192-193 and index.js:319-320.

Every entry point that parses throws synchronously: `parse` (index.js:128-131, 143-151), `checkData` (index.js:218), `stringify` (index.js:159), `Integrity#concat` (index.js:87-92), `fromHex` (index.js:170), `integrityStream` (index.js:247), and `checkStream` (index.js:229-231), where the throw happens before its promise exists, so `.catch()` cannot handle it.

**Preconditions:** the integrity string comes from someone else and carries such an algorithm name — e.g. a packument's `dist.integrity` or a lockfile entry.

**Evidence:** `ssri.parse('constructor-abc')`, `ssri.checkData(Buffer.from('x'), 'toString-abc')` and `ssri.integrityStream({integrity: '__proto__-abc'})` each throw the TypeError, while `ssri.parse('garbage')` returns an empty Integrity and `ssri.parse('sha256-abc')` parses. With pacote@9.5.12 and a registry serving `dist.integrity: "constructor-abc"`, `pacote.manifest()` rejects with this TypeError instead of reporting an integrity failure. Upstream fixed the guard only in ssri 13.0.1/14.0.0 (`Object.keys(acc).includes(algo)`, ssri 14.0.0 lib/index.js:378); 5.2.1 through 13.0.0 are affected.

**Impact:** low — whoever supplies the metadata can make `npm install`/pacote/cacache abort with an internal error naming no real cause, instead of taking the clean "integrity checksum failed" path that a merely garbage value produces. It fails closed: no prototype pollution (`__proto__` throws before any write) and no verification bypass.

**Fix:** gate on own properties, e.g. `if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(acc, algo)) { acc[algo] = [] }`, or accumulate on `Object.create(null)`.

summary:
Four findings recorded. Summary:

**What the change does:** it adds `src/get-static-value.js`, the static-expression evaluator behind `getStaticValue()`, complete with the allowlists (`callAllowed`, `callPassThrough`), the `isGetter` guard, and the `NewExpression`/tagged-template restrictions — i.e. the hardening that closes arbitrary code execution via the `Function` constructor (CVE-2019-15657). The file is byte-identical to upstream's post-fix blob (`08158db`).

**Assessment:** the security fix itself holds up. A 189-payload battery (constructor chains, `callPassThrough` laundering, `__proto__` and coercion gadgets, builtin accessors) executed nothing against this file, while the same battery against the reconstructed pre-fix file executed 37 payloads — so the defenses work. The defects I found are elsewhere: the change was not accompanied by the test update it requires, so `npm test` is red on `new Array(2)`, and the new evaluator has two confirmed wrong-value paths (quoted/numeric object keys collapse to `undefined`; const bindings are re-folded per reference, breaking identity) plus computed-`__proto__` prototype injection, all of which upstream only fixed years later.

findings.title: Object literals with quoted or numeric keys evaluate to a single `undefined` key
findings.body:
`ObjectExpression` reads a non-computed property key from `propertyNode.key.name`
(`src/get-static-value.js:386`). For `{"a": 1}` and `{1: "x"}` the parser produces a
`Literal` key, which has no `.name`, so every quoted or numeric key is stored under the
string `"undefined"` (`src/get-static-value.js:391`). Reads through that object then
return the wrong value instead of `null`.

**Preconditions:** the object literal uses a quoted or numeric key, i.e. the normal way to
write JSON-like data and options objects.

**Evidence:** with the repository's parser (espree 5, `ecmaVersion: 2018`):

| expression | `getStaticValue` | runtime |
|---|---|---|
| `({"a": 1}).a` | `{value: undefined}` | `1` |
| `({ "a": 1, "b": 2 })` | `{value: {undefined: 2}}` | `{a: 1, b: 2}` |
| `Object.keys({"a": 1, "b": 2})` | `["undefined"]` | `["a","b"]` |
| `Object.entries({"a": 1})` | `[["undefined", 1]]` | `[["a", 1]]` |
| `({1: "x"})[1]` | `{value: undefined}` | `"x"` |

Note the second row: property `"b"` silently overwrites property `"a"`.

**Impact:** a rule that reads an options/data literal through `getStaticValue` sees
`undefined` for each key rather than the configured value, producing false positives or
missed reports with no `null` fallback to signal uncertainty. Reach is broad across
consumers of the utility, the consequence is a wrong lint decision, and nothing is
destroyed, so `low`.

**Fix:** resolve non-computed keys from the key node instead of assuming an identifier:
`Identifier` → `node.name`, `Literal` → `String(node.value)` (handling `bigint`), anything
else → return `null`.

findings.title: Change leaves the existing `new Array(2)` test failing
findings.body:
The new `NewExpression` handler only evaluates a construction when the callee is in
`callAllowed`, and `Array` is not in that set. `new Array(2)` therefore now evaluates to
`null`, but the repository's existing test still expects a value, so the mocha suite run
by `npm test` fails.

**Evidence:** the failing case is `test/get-static-value.js:78`
(`{ code: "new Array(2)", expected: { value: new Array(2) } }`), which reaches
`assert.strictEqual(null, {value:[<2 empty items>]})` at `test/get-static-value.js:139`.
Path in the added file: `Identifier` resolves `Array` from `builtinNames`
(`src/get-static-value.js:7`), `NewExpression` then requires `callAllowed.has(Func)`
(`src/get-static-value.js:368`), while `callAllowed` lists `Array.isArray`
(`src/get-static-value.js:57`) but not `Array`. Running every table in `test/` against the
new file gives 525 passing and this one failing assertion; `npx eslint src test` is clean,
so this is the only red gate.

**Impact:** the change cannot merge green. Reach is the repository's own CI, and the
damage is a one-line test expectation, so `low` rather than higher.

**Fix:** keep the new restriction (it is part of the security fix) and update the
expectation to `expected: null`, which is what upstream shipped for this fix.

findings.title: Const bindings are re-evaluated per reference, so identity comparisons return false
findings.body:
`Identifier` folds a `const` binding by re-running `getStaticValueR` on its initializer
every time the binding is referenced (`src/get-static-value.js:303-312`, recursion at
`:311`). For a non-primitive initializer that rebuilds a fresh object, array, or symbol on
each reference, so two references to the same binding are not identical inside the
evaluator, and symbol-keyed lookups miss.

**Evidence:** with the repository's parser:

| expression | `getStaticValue` | runtime |
|---|---|---|
| `const o = {}; o === o` | `{value: false}` | `true` |
| `const a = [1]; a === a` | `{value: false}` | `true` |
| `const s = Symbol("k"); s === s` | `{value: false}` | `true` |
| `const s = Symbol("k"); ({[s]: 1})[s]` | `{value: undefined}` | `1` |

The symbol cases come from `Symbol` being in `callAllowed` (`src/get-static-value.js:93`):
each evaluation really calls `Symbol(...)` again, and a call never returns the same symbol
twice, yet the result is reported as a static value.

**Impact:** a rule that uses `getStaticValue` to decide whether two expressions denote the
same object or symbol gets `false`, inverting its conclusion. The damage is a wrong lint
decision (contained, repeatable, nothing destroyed), and no rule in this repository depends
on identity, so `info`.

**Fix:** memoize folded values per AST node for the duration of one `getStaticValue` call
(a `WeakMap` threaded through the recursion), and stop treating `Symbol(...)` /
`Symbol.keyFor(...)` as static, since their results are not reproducible.

findings.title: Computed `__proto__` key in an object literal rewrites the evaluated object's prototype
findings.body:
`ObjectExpression` builds an object literal by assignment on a plain `{}`
(`src/get-static-value.js:391`). When the key is the computed string `"__proto__"`, the
assignment reaches `Object.prototype`'s setter and replaces the prototype instead of
creating an own data property, so later member reads resolve inherited values that the real
program does not have.

**Evidence:** with the repository's parser:

| expression | `getStaticValue` | runtime |
|---|---|---|
| `({["__proto__"]: {a: 1}}).a` | `{value: 1}` | `undefined` |
| `Object.keys({["__proto__"]: 1})` | `{value: []}` | `["__proto__"]` |
| `Object.keys({["__proto__"]: 1, a: 2})` | `{value: ["a"]}` | `["__proto__","a"]` |

The `Object.assign(object, argument.value)` spread path at `src/get-static-value.js:403`
inherits the same behaviour. This is not code execution: the injected prototype only
supplies data, and any call still has to match a function identity in `callAllowed`
(`src/get-static-value.js:250`, `:261`), which rejects `Function` and every other
reachable constructor.

**Impact:** a rule that inspects own versus inherited properties of an object literal
(`Object.keys`/`Object.values`, prototype-pollution checks) is told the opposite answer.
Wrong lint decision only, so `info`.

**Fix:** create own properties explicitly instead of assigning through the prototype chain,
e.g. `Object.defineProperty(object, key.value, {value: value.value, writable: true,
enumerable: true, configurable: true})`, and use the same guard for the spread path.

summary:
Done. Summary:

This PR re-adds `st.js` at the published `st@1.2.2` state, i.e. the upstream release that fixes CVE-2017-16224 — the protocol-relative open redirect reached through the autoindex 301. I reproduced that redirect against `st@1.2.1` (`//evil.example/%2e%2e` → `301 location: //evil.example/%2e%2e/`) and confirmed every CVE payload variant returns 403 against the added file, for both root and sub-path mounts, so the change under review does close the vulnerability and the baseline test suite passes. The fix is otherwise sound but incomplete in one adjacent respect: the redirect target is now built from the decoded, prefix-stripped path, which breaks directory redirects on sub-path mounts. I also reproduced three unrelated defects that live in the added code (a NUL-byte request that kills the process, a mount-prefix traversal when `dot: true`, and autoindex hanging on directories with no visible entries); all four are recorded as findings.

findings.title: A NUL byte in the request path throws out of the request handler and stops the process
findings.body:
A single unauthenticated request with a NUL byte in the URL throws out of `serve()` and kills
the process when st is mounted directly on an `http` server — the usage shown in README.md and
implemented in bin/server.js. `GET /%00abc` is enough.

**Preconditions:** none beyond the default mount. Under Express the synchronous throw is caught
by the middleware wrapper and becomes a 500, so the crash needs a plain `http.createServer(mount)`
host.

**Evidence:** `getUriPath` decodes the request path with `decodeURIComponent` (st.js:192) and
returns it with the NUL intact. `serve` turns it into a filesystem path via
`this.getPath(req.sturl)` (st.js:247 → st.js:208-210) and calls `this.cache.fd.get(p, …)`
(st.js:250). async-cache invokes the fd loader, whose `fs.open(path, 'r', …)`
(node_modules/fd/index.js:47) rejects null bytes by throwing `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`
synchronously instead of calling back. Nothing in st.js wraps that call, so the exception leaves
the request listener.

Reproduced with `st({path: '/tmp/servedir', url: '/'})` on `http.createServer`: a script that
traps `uncaughtException` printed
`UNCAUGHT EXCEPTION escaped the request handler: ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE - … Received '/tmp/servedir/\x00abc'`
and exited; `/index.html` never got a chance to be served afterwards. `/a%00b` behaves the same.

**Impact:** any anonymous client can stop the service with one request; recovery requires a
restart. Broad reach, recoverable persistence → medium. The bug is inherited from st@1.2.1
(verified: same request crashes there too), so this change neither introduces nor fixes it, but
the code is added by this change.

**Fix:** reject a decoded path that contains a NUL (or any byte the OS cannot open) in
`getUriPath` and let `serve` fall through with `next()`/404, so no path with a null byte ever
reaches `fs`.

findings.title: A /static.. request escapes the served root when dot is enabled on a sub-path mount
findings.body:
With `dot: true` and a non-root `url` mount, a request whose path continues past the mount
prefix lets a client read files outside the served root. With
`st({path: '/tmp/servedir2', url: '/static', dot: true})`, `GET /static../secret.txt` returns
`/tmp/secret.txt` (one directory above the root).

**Preconditions:** non-default `dot: true` plus a non-root `url`. With the default `dot: false`
the dot check at st.js:233 answers 403 — this change's move of that check onto the decoded,
prefix-stripped path is what closes the `dot: false` variant (st@1.2.1 still served
`/static../secret.txt` with `dot: false`).

**Evidence:** the traversal guard (st.js:182-186) runs before the mount prefix is stripped and
only rejects a path containing a `..` *segment*. `/static../secret.txt` has no such segment: its
dots belong to `static..`. `path.normalize` keeps the string (st.js:188), the prefix test
`u.indexOf(this.url) !== 0` passes because the string starts with `/static` (st.js:189), and
`u.substr(this.url.length)` (st.js:201) — followed by the leading-slash fixup — yields
`/../secret.txt`. `getPath` = `path.join(this.path, u)` (st.js:208-210) resolves that one level
above the root.

Reproduced with `/tmp/secret.txt` and `/tmp/servedir-parent-secret.txt` present:

    /static/pub.txt                  -> 200  "PUBLIC"
    /static../secret.txt             -> 200  "PARENT"
    /static../servedir-parent-secret.txt -> 200  "SECRET"
    same requests with dot:false     -> 403

**Impact:** disclosure of any file the server process can read outside the served tree. Reach
crosses the trust boundary and the disclosure is permanent, which would be high; discounted to
medium because it needs the non-default `dot: true` and a non-root mount. Also present in
st@1.2.1 and st@2.0.0.

**Fix:** treat `url` as a path prefix rather than a string prefix — accept only
`u === this.url || u.indexOf(this.url + '/') === 0` before stripping — and, as a second barrier,
refuse to open unless `path.resolve(p)` is inside `this.path + path.sep`.

findings.title: Autoindex never responds for a directory with no visible entries
findings.body:
A GET for a directory that has no visible entries never receives a response. This happens for an
empty directory, and with the default `dot: false` for a directory holding only dotfiles.

**Evidence:** `_loadReaddir` filters the entries, sets `len = files.length` (st.js:550) and only
calls back from `next()` when `--len === 0` (st.js:563-565). When nothing is left after filtering,
`next()` is never called, so the readdir loader never completes, `autoindex`'s
`this.cache.index.get(p, …)` (st.js:359) waits forever and the response is never ended.

Reproduced against `st({path: '/tmp/servedir', url: '/'})`: `/empty/` and `/onlydots/` produced no
response in 3 s, while `/sub/` returned 200. Because async-cache keeps the pending load keyed by
path, a second request for the same directory also never responds — reproduced after writing a
visible file into that directory.

**Impact:** a normal configuration (an empty upload or cache directory under autoindex) leaves
clients waiting until they or Node's request timeout give up, and that directory's listing stays
broken until the process restarts. Contained to the affected path and transient for the
connection, but sticky for the cache entry → low.

**Fix:** after filtering, call back immediately when the list is empty, e.g.
`if (files.length === 0) return cb(null, {})` before the `forEach`.

findings.title: Directory redirects on a sub-path mount drop the mount prefix and the URL encoding
findings.body:
Directory redirects are now built from the prefix-stripped, percent-decoded path, so on a
sub-path mount they point at the wrong URL. With `st({path: '/tmp/servedir3', url: '/static'})`
and a directory named `sp ace`, `GET /static/sp%20ace` answers
`301 location: /sp ace/` instead of `301 location: /static/sp%20ace/`.

**Evidence:** `autoindex` sets `res.setHeader('location', req.sturl + '/')` and echoes the same
string in the body (st.js:352-356). Before this change `req.sturl` was the raw request pathname,
so it still carried the mount prefix and the original encoding; now it is `getUriPath`'s return
value, which is percent-decoded (st.js:192) and has `this.url` removed (st.js:201). Reproduced
against the same fixture with only the st.js version changed:

    st@1.2.1, url '/static': GET /static/sp%20ace -> 301 location="/static/sp%20ace/"
    this file, url '/static': GET /static/sp%20ace -> 301 location="/sp ace/"
    st@1.2.1, url '/':        GET /sp%20ace         -> 301 location="/sp%20ace/"
    this file, url '/':       GET /sp%20ace         -> 301 location="/sp ace/"

**Impact:** every client that requests a directory without its trailing slash on a sub-path mount
is redirected outside the mount (a URL the host application does not route to st), so autoindex
directory browsing breaks for that deployment; decoding also puts raw spaces, `?`, `#` and
non-ASCII bytes into the header, which corrupts the target URL (and a directory name with CR/LF
would make `setHeader` throw). The file listing itself still works when the client appends the
slash, hence low: contained to the redirect, transient for the client.

**Fix:** build the redirect target from the mount prefix plus a properly encoded path — e.g.
`this.url + req.sturl.split('/').map(encodeURIComponent).join('/') + '/'` (url already ends
without a trailing slash per st.js:74) — rather than echoing `req.sturl`.

summary:
Recorded three findings. Coverage check on the rest of the file (zip `restrict` handling in decompress-zip 0.2.2, tmp-dir creation/cleanup, `isSingleDir`/`moveDirectory` flattening, mime/extractor precedence) turned up only low-confidence or already-covered leads, so I stopped there.

The change re-adds `lib/util/extract.js`, bower's archive extractor, byte-identical to the upstream 1.8.7 file (verified against the v1.8.7 and v1.8.8 tags). That file carries the CVE-2019-5484 defect: the tar `ignore` filter is written against the zip library's API, so no tar entry is ever filtered, and both symlink and hardlink entries escape the extraction directory. Both escapes were reproduced end to end against the committed file with the dependency versions in `yarn.lock`, including the arbitrary write, the hardlink read of an outside file, and its mode change. Upstream v1.8.8 fixes only the symlink case; the hardlink vector needs a type allowlist instead. I would not merge this as-is.

findings.title: Malicious tar archives write files outside the extraction directory through unfiltered symlink entries
findings.body:
A malicious `.tar`, `.tar.gz` or `.tgz` archive can write files outside the
directory bower extracts into. The tar extractors pass `ignore: isSymlink`
(`lib/util/extract.js:66`, `lib/util/extract.js:96`), but `isSymlink` is
written against the zip library's API:

```js
function isSymlink(entry) {
    return entry.type === 'SymbolicLink';
}
```

`lib/util/extract.js:133-135`. tar-fs calls the filter as `ignore(name, header)`:
the first argument is the entry path string and `header.type` is lowercase
`'symlink'`. So `entry.type` is always `undefined` and no entry is ever
filtered. A symlink entry in the archive is created with whatever `linkname`
it carries, and any later entry under that name is written wherever the link
points. Extraction completes without an error.

**Preconditions:** the user installs, or extracts, an archive from a source the
attacker controls — a bower endpoint URL (`bower install https://host/pkg.tgz`,
selected by `lib/core/resolverFactory.js:150-154` and downloaded by
`lib/core/resolvers/UrlResolver.js:146,247`) or a local archive through
`FsResolver` (`lib/core/resolvers/FsResolver.js:115`).

**Evidence:** reproduced with the file as committed, using the dependency
versions pinned in `yarn.lock` (tar-fs 1.15.3, `yarn.lock:4829-4831`). A tar
holding `evil -> /tmp/repro/OUTSIDE` followed by `evil/pwned.txt` extracted into
`/tmp/repro/dst` returned success, created the symlink `dst/evil`, and wrote
`/tmp/repro/OUTSIDE/pwned.txt` outside the destination. A relative linkname
(`evil2 -> ../../OUTSIDE2`) also escaped, and the `.tar.gz` path (`:96`) behaved
the same. Instrumenting the filter showed `ignore("/tmp/repro/dst/evil",
{type:"symlink"})` returning `false`. Plain `../` entry names are neutralised by
tar-fs, which anchors names with `path.join('/', header.name)`, so the symlink is
the vector.

**Impact:** arbitrary file write as the invoking user, outside the package
directory: for example `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bowerrc` (read
by `packages/bower-config/lib/util/rc.js:32` on the next run), or the stored
GitHub token in `~/.config/configstore/bower-github.json` (`lib/config.js:19-21`).
A package archive therefore gains a capability its role denies it, and the write
leaves nothing to undo. High.

**Fix:** reject any tar entry whose type is not a regular file or directory.
Upstream bower v1.8.8 fixes the signature as
`function isSymlink(_, entry) { return entry.type === 'symlink'; }`; that
restores the intended filter for symlinks (and blocks the `.tar` and `.tar.gz`
paths above).

findings.title: Crafted tar hardlink entries pull arbitrary user files into the package and chmod them
findings.body:
Tar archives are also allowed to contain hardlink entries (`header.type ===
'link'`). The only filter on the tar paths is `ignore: isSymlink`
(`lib/util/extract.js:66`, `lib/util/extract.js:96`), which tests for the zip
string `'SymbolicLink'` and would never match `'link'` even with the corrected
signature. tar-fs 1.15.3 (pinned by `yarn.lock:4829-4831`) resolves a hardlink
target with `path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname)` — unanchored, so `../../x` and
absolute paths both work — and then calls `fs.link(srcpath, name)`. The
extracted tree therefore contains a hardlink to a file outside it, which bower
then `chmod`s (tar-fs applies the entry mode to the shared inode) and copies
into `bower_components/<pkg>` as ordinary package content
(`lib/util/copy.js`, `lib/core/Manager.js:231-234`).

**Preconditions:** the user installs an attacker-supplied archive (bower endpoint
URL or local archive, as in the symlink finding). The named target must be on the
same filesystem as bower's temp directory; paths under the home directory
normally are.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this file with tar-fs 1.15.3 and tar-stream
1.5.4. A tar entry `{type:'link', name:'package/pwn.txt',
linkname:'../../finalvictim.txt'}` extracted into `/tmp/hl/final` resolved with
no error and produced `/tmp/hl/final/package/pwn.txt` with the same inode as
`/tmp/finalvictim.txt` (`ino 33705802`, link count 1 -> 2). The victim's mode
changed 600 -> 755, and its content was readable as package content. An absolute
`linkname: '/tmp/absvictim.txt'` behaved the same; `linkname: '/etc/hostname'`
was passed through verbatim and failed only with `EXDEV` because it is a
different mount. The `.tar.gz` path (`:90-100`) is equally affected. Applying the
upstream v1.8.8 fix (`isSymlink(_, entry) { return entry.type === 'symlink'; }`)
blocks symlinks but not this: the same archive still linked the victim file and
changed its mode.

**Impact:** read access to arbitrary same-filesystem user files (private keys,
tokens, `.npmrc`) whose content becomes part of the installed package and may be
committed or published, plus a durable permission change on the original file
(600 -> 755). This crosses the boundary between "package content" and "the
user's private files". High.

**Fix:** filter on an allowlist rather than one type: ignore every tar entry
whose `header.type` is not `'file'` or `'directory'`, which covers `'symlink'`,
`'link'` and any other type tar-fs supports.

findings.title: Extracting a plain .gz archive always fails with EISDIR
findings.body:
`extractGz` pipes the decompressed stream into `createWriteStream(dst)`
(`lib/util/extract.js:123`), but every caller passes a directory as `dst`:
`UrlResolver` passes `this._tempDir` (`lib/core/resolvers/UrlResolver.js:247`)
and `FsResolver` likewise (`lib/core/resolvers/FsResolver.js:115`), and
`extract()` hands the extractor the temporary directory it just created
(`lib/util/extract.js:245`). `fs-write-stream-atomic` writes to a sibling temp
file and renames it onto `dst`, so the rename targets a directory and the
promise rejects. A plain `.gz` endpoint can never be installed.

**Evidence:** with the file as committed and the pinned dependencies,

```
extract('/tmp/hl/thing.gz', '/tmp/hl/gzdst', {keepArchive:true})
-> REJECTED EISDIR: illegal operation on a directory,
   rename '/tmp/hl/gzdst-CTi6oZ.3178774507' -> '/tmp/hl/gzdst-CTi6oZ'
```

**Impact:** `bower install https://host/file.gz` and local `.gz` endpoints fail
with an opaque `EISDIR` instead of installing the file. Because the failure
happens before the archive is unlinked (`lib/util/extract.js:249-253`) and the
intermediate temp directory's cleanup callback is discarded (`:226-233`), the
download and a partially written temp tree are left behind. Contained to the one
failing operation and recoverable by retrying with another source; low.

**Fix:** write the decompressed data to a file inside `dst` rather than to `dst`
itself, e.g. `path.join(dst, path.basename(archive, '.gz'))`, so the resolver's
rename step sees a single file as it expects.

summary:
I reviewed the full file myself, verified the change's security effect against upstream history and by running the code, and used two delegates (a ranked probe of the whole file, and an independent reproduction of the most suspicious path).

**Verification done**
- The added `index.js` (md5 `3053a51…`) is byte-identical to upstream `mafintosh/tar-fs` commit `0667282` "force hardlink targets to be in the tar" — the recorded patch for CVE-2018-20835. It differs from `tar-fs@1.16.1` by exactly one line (`index.js:264`).
- Hardlink escapes are closed: absolute, relative and deep-`..` linknames all fail `ENOENT` because the target is rebased inside `cwd` (`/tmp/poc/hl3.js` output), and the regression test at `test/index.js:315` passes.
- `npm test` (standard + tape) passes 48/48 assertions, so nothing the suite covers is broken.
- CVE-2018-20835 is specifically the hardlink variant (NVD description, patch ref `0667282`); the PR matches it.

The only escape I could still demonstrate (a symlink entry with an absolute/relative target, followed by a same-named file entry, overwrites a file outside the destination — `index.js:257` + `index.js:278`) exists identically at the baseline upstream tree and is untouched by this change; upstream only closed it in 2025 (`a1dd7e7`, `validateSymlinks`). Per the review rules, a pre-existing defect the change neither touches nor makes reachable is not a finding here, so I filed none and recorded the mapping in a knowledge concept for later runs. A follow-up issue for the symlink variant is worth opening separately.

**Summary:** The PR re-adds `tar-fs`'s `index.js` at the upstream commit that fixes CVE-2018-20835: hardlink entry targets are now rebased into the extraction root (`index.js:264`) instead of resolved with `path.resolve`, so a crafted archive can no longer link to and overwrite a file outside the destination. The one-line change is correct, matches upstream, and the accompanying regression test and the full suite pass. No findings.

Review complete. Summary:

The PR re-adds `lib/util/extract.js` (278 lines, byte-identical to upstream bower commit `45c6bfa`, the CVE-2019-5484 fix). Its substance is the one-line correction in `isSymlink`, which tar-fs calls as `ignore(name, header)`; the pre-fix form took the path string and so never dropped symlink entries, letting a crafted `.tar.gz` write through `link -> /outside`. I reproduced both sides with the pinned dependency versions: the pre-fix version wrote outside `dst`, this version drops the symlink, and ordinary archives still extract correctly. Zip-side traversal is already blocked inside `decompress-zip` 0.2.2's own `restrict` check, so the change is sound for its stated purpose — but the filter only covers symlinks, leaving an equivalent tar hardlink escape (recorded as a finding), and `extractGz` always fails with `EISDIR` because it writes to a directory path (long-standing upstream defect, not filed). Also noted: the PR adds no test covering the filter, which CONTRIBUTING asks for. Separately, `ozone knowledge save` accepted a concept but no read path returns it — reported as an environment issue.

findings.title: Malicious .tar.gz with hardlink entries overwrites files outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
A malicious package archive can overwrite, chmod and chown files outside the
extraction directory even with this change applied. The guard added here filters
tar entries of type `symlink` only; tar **hardlink** entries (`type === 'link'`)
pass it, and the pinned `tar-fs` 1.15.3 follows their `linkname` with no
containment check. Whoever publishes the archive therefore writes into the
invoking user's account, not just into the temp dir bower extracts into.

**Preconditions:** bower extracts an archive the attacker supplies:
`bower install https://host/pkg.tar.gz` (`lib/core/resolvers/UrlResolver.js:247`),
a GitHub tarball (`lib/core/resolvers/GitHubResolver.js:120`), or a transitive
`bower.json` dependency resolved to such a URL. The tar hardlink target must be
on the same filesystem as `config.tmp` and owned by (or read/write for) the user
running bower, because `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` is the Linux default. Running
bower as root removes the ownership limit, so any existing file can be targeted.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this commit's `lib/util/extract.js` with the
versions pinned in `yarn.lock` (`tar-fs` 1.15.3). Archive contents:

```
h   type=link  linkname=../secret.txt
h   type=file  body="PWNED-AS-NONROOT\n"
```

Extracting it as a non-root user into a sibling directory changed
`/home/tester/work/secret.txt` from `SECRET-ORIGINAL` (mode 0600, 1 link) to
`PWNED-AS-NONROOT` (mode 0644, 2 links). An archive with only the `link` entry
and mode 0777 changed that file to mode 0755.

Path: `lib/util/extract.js:95-99` passes `ignore: isSymlink` to `tar.extract`;
`lib/util/extract.js:133-135` returns true only for `entry.type === 'symlink'`;
tar-fs then runs `xfs.link(path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname), name)`
(`tar-fs/index.js:260-262`, dispatching `case 'link'` at `:301`) and a following
file entry truncates the linked inode with `xfs.createWriteStream(name)`
(`:274`). The same archive through the pre-fix version behaves identically, so
this is an unfixed variant of the escape the change targets.

**Impact:** the archive author gains create/overwrite/chmod of the invoker's
files outside the extraction boundary — e.g. `~/.bashrc`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`,
`~/.gitconfig`, project files — and the change is permanent. Medium: it crosses a
trust boundary with permanent effect, discounted from high because a hardlink
needs the target on the extraction filesystem and owned by the invoking user
(root exempt).

**Fix:** make the predicate reject hardlinks too, e.g.
`return entry.type === 'symlink' || entry.type === 'link';`, or reject any entry
whose resolved name or `linkname` escapes `dst`.

summary: The PR adds `st.js` (598 lines) — the complete `st@1.2.1` static file server — and nothing else; the baseline branch had the file removed. Upstream shipped 1.2.2 five days later as a security release, and the code here is that pre-fix state, which I confirmed by reproducing each issue against a live server rather than reasoning from the patch alone. The URL-to-path pipeline is the weak point: checks run on the raw request string while the filesystem path is built from a later-decoded, normalized value, which yields the recorded redirect, mount-boundary and dot-file problems. Two independent process-kill paths (NUL byte; a cache/`has` disagreement reaching the deliberate throw) and an autoindex hang round out the availability problems. I would not merge this as-is; it needs the 1.2.2-style hardening plus a segment-aware containment check, and I found no second-level traversal or listing HTML injection beyond what is recorded.

findings.title: Requests to a sub-path mount can read files one directory above the served root
findings.body:
With a sub-path mount (`url` option other than `/`), a request can read files
one directory above the served root.

**Preconditions:** mount configured with a non-root `url` and no trailing
slash, e.g. `st({ path: '/srv/app/public', url: '/static' })` — the second
usage example in README.md.

**Evidence:** root `/tmp/app/public` holding `index.html`, parent
`/tmp/app/config.json`. Server mounted at `/static`:

```
GET /static../config.json           -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, body "APP-CONFIG-SECRET"
GET /static..%2fconfig.json         -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, body "APP-CONFIG-SECRET"
GET /static%2e%2e%2fconfig.json     -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, body "APP-CONFIG-SECRET"
GET /static/index.html              -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, body "PUBLIC"
```

**Why:** the mount check is a plain string prefix, `u.indexOf(this.url) !== 0`
(st.js:190), and the traversal guard (st.js:183) only fires on `/../` — here
the `..` is glued to the mount segment (`/static..`), so neither check
triggers. `u.substr(this.url.length)` (st.js:202) then cuts the string
mid-segment, leaving `../config.json`, and `path.join(this.path, u)`
(st.js:205) resolves it outside `this.path`. A second `..` is caught by the
st.js:183 regex, so the escape is exactly one level, but the whole parent
subtree is readable.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller reads files the operator did not publish
— sibling directories, app config and secrets next to the document root. Reach
crosses the mount boundary and the disclosure is permanent, but the trigger
needs a documented non-default mount form, so: medium.

**Fix:** after joining, verify the result is still inside `this.path` with a
segment-aware prefix (or `path.relative`), and reject any `..` path segment
before `path.join`, not only the `/../` form.

findings.title: Autoindex 301 redirects clients to an attacker-chosen protocol-relative URL
findings.body:
A 301 whose `Location` is built from the raw request path sends browsers to a
protocol-relative URL, i.e. a different origin.

**Evidence:** server root `/tmp/wwwroot`, default options:

```
GET //evil.example/%2e%2e HTTP/1.1
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
location: //evil.example/%2e%2e/
```

Also `//evil.example/%2e.`. Browsers resolve `//evil.example/...` against the
current scheme, so the visitor lands on `http://evil.example/...`.

**Why:** `autoindex` builds the redirect from `req.sturl` + `'/'`
(st.js:349-352), and `req.sturl` is the untouched
`url.parse(req.url).pathname` (st.js:226). The traversal guard at st.js:183
requires a slash *after* `..`, so a trailing `%2e%2e` passes; then
`path.normalize` (st.js:189) folds the path back to the mount root, so
`serve` takes the directory branch and reaches the redirect while the raw URL
still names an attacker host. The `dot: false` guard (st.js:240) does not fire
because the URL contains no literal dot.

**Impact:** any visitor who follows a crafted link is redirected off-site —
phishing, and leaking of URL-borne tokens on the host page. Autoindex and a
root mount are both defaults, so no special configuration is needed. Broad
reach, recoverable per request: medium.

**Fix:** reject any request path whose final segment is `..` (extend the
st.js:183 test to match end-of-string), and derive the redirect target from
the normalized path rather than from `req.sturl`.

findings.title: URL-encoded dot bypasses the dot:false block and serves hidden files
findings.body:
Encoding the first dot of a dot-file bypasses the `dot: false` block and
serves the file.

**Evidence:** default options (`dot: false`), root containing `.env`:

```
GET /.env          -> HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
GET /%2eenv        -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, body "secret"
GET /%2egit/config -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, body "GITCONFIG"
GET /%2egit/       -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, autoindex listing of .git
```

**Why:** the guard tests the raw URL, `req.sturl.match(/(^|\/)\./)`
(st.js:240), while `getPath` has already translated `%2e` to `.` in its own
copy (st.js:172) and hands the decoded path to `path.join` (st.js:205). The
guard never sees a literal dot.

**Impact:** the default protection against serving hidden files does nothing
for an attacker who encodes the dot; `.env`, `.git/`, `.htpasswd`, backups and
similar files under the served root are readable by anyone. Contained reach,
permanent disclosure: medium.

**Fix:** apply the dot/403 test to the decoded, normalized path (`getPath`'s
result) instead of `req.sturl`.

findings.title: A path containing %00 throws out of the request handler and kills the process
findings.body:
A single GET whose path contains `%00` throws a `TypeError` out of the request
handler and terminates the process.

**Evidence:** any served root with a file `pub/a.txt`:

```
GET /pub/a.txt%00.js HTTP/1.1

TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE]: The argument 'path' must be a string,
Uint8Array, or URL without null bytes. Received '/tmp/wwwroot/pub/a.txt\x00.js'
    at Object.open (node:fs)
    at Object.open (node_modules/fd/index.js:47)
    at AsyncCache.get (node_modules/async-cache/ac.js:63)
    at Mount.serve (st.js:247)
```

Process exits; no response is sent. `/ %00`-only paths and HEAD requests
behave the same.

**Why:** `decodeURIComponent` (st.js:193) runs after every path check and
reintroduces the NUL byte, `path.join` (st.js:205) keeps it, and
`async-cache` invokes the cache loader synchronously with no try/catch, so
`fs.open`'s argument validation throws straight through `serve`. Nothing in
st.js catches it.

**Impact:** one unauthenticated request, repeatable at will, takes the whole
server down until something restarts it — full outage for every client.
Broad reach, recoverable by restart: medium.

**Fix:** reject paths containing `\0` in `getPath` (return `false`/403), and
guard the `this.cache.fd.get` load with a try/catch so a synchronous throw
becomes a 500 instead of a process exit.

findings.title: Autoindex never responds for an empty directory, and repeat requests queue behind it
findings.body:
Autoindex never answers a request for an empty directory, and later requests
for that directory queue behind the same stuck load.

**Evidence:** root containing an empty directory `empty/`:

```
GET /empty/  -> no bytes for 2+ s, socket stays open, server alive
```

`/empty` itself gets its 301 to `/empty/`, which then hangs. A directory whose
entries are all dot-files hangs the same way under `dot: false`, because
`_loadReaddir` filters them out (st.js:543-546).

**Why:** `len = files.length` (st.js:547); when the filtered list is empty the
`files.forEach` at st.js:549 never runs, so `next()` (st.js:560-562) never
calls `cb` and `_loadIndex` never produces a response. The pending callback
stays in `async-cache`'s in-flight map, so every repeat request is appended to
that same queue and also hangs.

**Impact:** any empty directory in the served tree becomes a path that ties up
sockets indefinitely instead of returning a listing; low, because nothing else
in the module breaks and the state clears on restart.

**Fix:** call `cb(null, data)` when `len === 0` (handle the empty list before
starting the per-entry stats).

summary:
Coverage is complete: the guard, the cache, the merge path, traversal into inherited values, and the options surface all probed; the repo's 26 existing tests pass against the new file.

**Summary**

The PR adds `index.js`, the v3.0.1 `set-value` implementation, whose purpose is to block CVE-2019-10747 by filtering `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype` out of the path. The filter works for string paths and arrays of strings, but it compares path elements by identity while they are later used as property keys, so a nested-array element like `["__proto__"]` in a JSON array path slips through and writes to the global `Object.prototype` — a reproduced, published bypass of this exact version (GHSA-4jqc-8m5r-9rpr, fixed in 3.0.3). Two smaller defects sit in the module-level memo table: it is a plain object, so paths named after inherited members such as `toString` throw instead of being no-ops, and it is never evicted, so it grows with the number of distinct caller-supplied paths. No test in `test.js` exercises the new guard, so nothing locks in the hardening.

findings.title: Array-path elements bypass the prototype-pollution guard and write to Object.prototype
Single-segment paths named after Object.prototype members throw a TypeError from the memo lookup
findings.body:
`split()` memoises on `set.memo`, which is a plain object literal (index.js:109), and tests the cache with a bare truthiness read:

```js
if (set.memo[id]) return set.memo[id];
```

(index.js:65). When the whole path string equals an inherited member of `Object.prototype`, the lookup returns that inherited function instead of an array, and `.filter(isValidKey)` at index.js:28 throws `TypeError: ... .filter is not a function`. The function throws before it can set anything.

**Evidence:**

```js
set({}, 'toString', 1);     // TypeError: ... .filter is not a function
set({}, 'valueOf', 1);      // same
set({}, 'constructor', 1);  // same
set({}, 'prototype', 1);    // ok — returns target, shows the intended no-op
```

All inherited names behave this way: `toString`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable`, `toLocaleString`, `__defineGetter__`, `__defineSetter__`, `__lookupGetter__`, `__lookupSetter__`, `constructor`, `__proto__`.

**Impact:** single-segment paths that name an ordinary JS member crash the caller rather than setting a value. This also turns the hardening's silent drop into a thrown exception: `set(obj, 'constructor', v)` and `set(obj, '__proto__', v)` are supposed to be no-ops (index.js:101-103) but instead fail every request that supplies that key, repeatable at will by an unauthenticated caller. Low: one failing call per request, recoverable (no data or process state is lost), and it needs the app to pass single-segment paths taken from request data.

**Fix:** make the cache lookup prototype-safe — create it with `Object.create(null)` and/or gate reads on `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(set.memo, id)` — so a miss can never return an inherited member.

findings.title: Memo table retains every distinct caller-supplied path for the process lifetime
findings.body:
`split()` stores every split result in the module-level `set.memo` table (index.js:84, index.js:109), keyed by the caller's path string plus `String()` of each option value (index.js:88-99). Nothing ever evicts, caps, or clears an entry, so the table grows for the life of the process with the number of distinct paths the host application uses.

**Evidence:** 300 000 calls with distinct caller-supplied paths:

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 300000; i++) set({}, 'user' + i + '.field', 1);
Object.keys(set.memo).length;   // 300000
// heapUsed after gc: 4.0 MB -> 91.8 MB
```

There is no `delete`, LRU, or `clear` anywhere in index.js.

**Impact:** an application that derives paths from request data (`set(cache, userId + '.' + field, v)`) lets an unauthenticated caller grow the process heap without bound until it is restarted — a slow memory-exhaustion path that affects every user of the process. Low: broad reach, recoverable by restart, discounted because the growth rate depends on the host's path cardinality and the damage is gradual.

**Fix:** bound the cache — cap the number of entries (evict oldest, or skip memoisation past a threshold) and expose a reset; a drop-in `Map` alone does not bound the growth.

summary:
Review complete. All findings are recorded and the working tree is clean.

**What the change does:** PR #2 adds the full `index.js` of tar-fs at upstream commit `2712c11` ("validate parent paths"), a version that carries the first half of the CVE-2018-20835 fix series — `validate()` rejects writes whose *parent* directory is a symlink — but not the second half (`0667282`, clamping hardlink targets to the archive) nor any later hardening.

**Assessment:** not ready to merge. The archive-extraction trust boundary is still crossable: I reproduced two distinct paths where an untrusted tarball writes files outside the destination directory (one of them is exactly the CVE the PR is named for, and the repository's own `no abs hardlink targets` regression test fails, 1 of 46 tests, leaving `test/fixtures/outside` overwritten). I also confirmed a crafted or `strip`-reduced entry name wedges extraction in an unbounded `lstat('/')` loop, and a minor `opts.fs` bug in `mkdirfix`. Details, reproductions and fixes are in the four recorded findings; the extraction-boundary invariant and its known escape paths are now documented under `security/extraction-boundary.md`.

findings.title: Hardlink entries let a tarball overwrite files outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
Extracting an untrusted tarball can replace the contents of files outside the extraction
directory. A `link` entry whose `linkname` points out of the directory is created from
`path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname)` (`index.js:264`), which resolves `../` and absolute
targets to their real location. A later `file` entry with the same name opens that name
with `createWriteStream` (`index.js:278`), so the write truncates the shared inode and the
outside file is overwritten.

**Preconditions:** the archive is untrusted (the normal tar-fs threat model). On Linux with
the default `fs.protected_hardlinks=1`, an unprivileged process cannot hardlink files it
does not own, so the non-root case is limited to files that process can already write.
Extraction as root (containers, CI, installer scripts) has no such limit.

**Evidence:**
- Tarball with one entry `{type:'link', name:'x', linkname:'../secret.txt'}`, extracted into
  `/tmp/ta/out`: `/tmp/ta/out/x` and `/tmp/ta/secret.txt` end up with the same inode.
- Extracting a second tarball with `{name:'x', body:'PWNED'}` into the same directory turns
  `/tmp/ta/secret.txt` from `ORIGINAL` into `PWNED`.
- The repository's own regression test `no abs hardlink targets` (`test/index.js:315`) fails
  against this `index.js`: `test/fixtures/outside` is overwritten with `overwrite`, no error
  is emitted, and tape reports `test exited without ending`.
- Same defect as CVE-2018-20835 (NVD: hardlink to an existing file plus a later plain file
  with the same name replaces that file's content); the upstream fix, commit `0667282`, is
  not part of this file.

**Impact:** integrity of arbitrary files outside the extraction root, permanently, with no
privilege beyond the extracting process. NVD rates CVE-2018-20835 7.5 HIGH (`I:H`). The
defect crosses the extraction trust boundary and cannot be undone, so high.

**Fix:** keep the hardlink source inside the root — resolve it as
`path.join(cwd, path.join('/', header.linkname))`, then `realpath` the result and emit an
error unless it is `cwd` or starts with `cwd + path.sep` before calling `xfs.link`.

findings.title: Symlink entry plus same-named file writes through to a target outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
A tarball can write to any file the extracting process may write, outside the extraction
directory, by extracting a symlink and then a file that uses the symlink's name.
`validate()` (`index.js:328-335`) checks only the parent directory of an entry
(`dir = path.dirname(name)`, `index.js:298-302`); the entry's own name is never `lstat`-ed.
`onfile()` (`index.js:277-289`) then calls `xfs.createWriteStream(name)` without unlinking an
existing symlink, and `open(..., 'w')` follows the link, so the payload lands in the link
target. The follow-up `chmod`/`utimes` (`index.js:213-233`) follow the same link and also
change the target's mode and mtime.

**Evidence:** tarball with `{name:'y', type:'symlink', linkname:'/tmp/ta/secret2.txt'}` then
`{name:'y', body:'PWNED2'}`, extracted into `/tmp/ta/out2`: the outside file goes from
`ORIGINAL2` to `PWNED2`, the extract stream emits only `finish` (no error), and `out2/y`
stays a symlink, so the tree shows nothing. A relative linkname (`../secret2.txt`) behaves the
same. Control: when the symlink is a *parent* component (`d -> /tmp/ta`, then `d/secret3.txt`),
`validate` rejects the entry with `... is not a valid path`, so the parent check works and only
the leaf name is unchecked. An independent verification reproduced both variants.

**Impact:** arbitrary file overwrite outside the extraction root; unlike the hardlink path
this needs no privileged mode, only write permission on the target. Reach crosses the
extraction trust boundary, persistence is permanent, so high.

**Fix:** before writing, `xfs.lstat(name)` and `xfs.unlink(name)` when the entry is an existing
symlink (or open with `O_NOFOLLOW`), so a file entry always creates a regular file inside the
directory. Upstream adopted the lstat/unlink form later.

findings.title: Extraction hangs forever when an entry name reduces to nothing
findings.body:
One non-directory entry whose name reduces to nothing makes extraction loop forever and
never call back. `validate()` (`index.js:328-335`) walks upward from `dir` and stops only at
`name === root`. When the walk leaves `root` it reaches `/`, and `path.join('/', '..')` is
`/`, so it re-`lstat`s `/` indefinitely: no `error`, no `finish`, no progress.

Two ways to reach it:
- a tarball entry with a blank name field: `name = path.join(cwd, path.join('/', ''))` is
  `cwd/` (`index.js:238`), whose `path.dirname` is the parent of `cwd`;
- `strip` at least as deep as an entry path, e.g. `tar.extract(dir, {strip: 2})` on a tarball
  containing `outer/f.txt`, where `strip` (`index.js:48-51`) produces `header.name === ''`.

**Evidence:** with a counting `opts.fs` wrapper, a tarball holding one blank-name file entry
produced `{"<cwd parent>":1,"/tmp":1,"/":11648}` `lstat` calls in two seconds, nothing
extracted, no stream event. The same archive with `strip: 2` also hung (>3s, empty output
directory). A well-formed archive extracts normally.

**Impact:** a single malformed or hostile entry wedges the extracting process in a syscall
loop until it is killed; a service that extracts uploaded archives stalls its whole job.
Reach broad (every consumer that extracts that archive), persistence recoverable (restart),
so medium.

**Fix:** stop the walk as soon as the path leaves the root — return `cb(null, false)` when the
current name is not `root` and does not start with `root + path.sep` — instead of relying on
string equality with `root` to terminate.

findings.title: Custom fs in opts.fs is bypassed when extraction creates directories
findings.body:
Directory creation during extraction ignores the custom `fs` passed in `opts.fs`. `mkdirfix`
(`index.js:337-345`) calls `mkdirp(name, {fs: opts.xfs}, ...)`, but the object callers pass is
`{fs: xfs, own, uid, gid}` (`index.js:293-294`, `index.js:304-305`), so `opts.xfs` is always
`undefined`. mkdirp falls back to the real `fs`, while every other operation uses `xfs`.

**Evidence:** extracting a tarball containing `outer/f.txt` with `opts.fs` set to a wrapper
that logs calls recorded `lstat`, `createWriteStream`, `utimes`, `chmod` on the wrapper but
zero `mkdir` calls, and `out/outer` still appeared on the real filesystem.

**Impact:** with a virtual or instrumented `fs`, extraction creates real directories and then
fails with `ENOENT` on the first write through the custom fs, leaving stray directories behind.
Contained and recoverable, so low; `opts.fs` is undocumented and rarely used.

**Fix:** pass the configured filesystem: `mkdirp(name, {fs: opts.fs}, cb)`.

summary:
The PR adds the single new file `src/download.js` back to the tree: it fetches `BuildTools_Full.exe` and `python-2.7.11.msi` with `nugget` into `%USERPROFILE%\.windows-build-tools` and calls back so `install()` can run the installers.

The download path is the security-relevant part: it disables TLS verification, uses a plaintext URL for the C++ build tools, and runs no integrity check before PowerShell executes the binaries — the CVE-2017-16003 MITM code-execution vector. Error handling is also weak: failures are logged and swallowed so the postinstall exits 0 without installing anything. I confirmed the nugget 2.0.0/request option semantics that make `strictSSL: false` real rather than cosmetic. Two findings recorded (one high, one low); nothing else in the 56 lines traced to a concrete failure.

findings.title: Network attacker can swap the Build Tools installer for arbitrary code on developer machines
findings.body:
The download stage fetches both installers with TLS verification disabled and no
integrity check, then executes them. `downloadTools` sets `strictSSL: false`
(src/download.js:34), the build tools URL is plaintext
`http://download.microsoft.com/...` (src/constants.js:5), and nothing compares a
downloaded file to a known hash. `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:28` then runs
`./BuildTools_Full.exe` and `:38` runs `msiexec` on the downloaded MSI from the
same directory (`src/download.js:16-17` calls install with no further checks).

**Preconditions:** an attacker able to answer the HTTP request — shared Wi-Fi, a
compromised proxy (everything is routed through `PROXY` at src/download.js:35),
or DNS/ARP interception. `resume: true` (src/download.js:32) lets injected bytes
survive a retry.

**Evidence:**
- src/download.js:29-38 — `strictSSL: false`, no checksum after download.
- src/constants.js:5 — `installerUrl` for the C++ Build Tools is `http://`.
- src/constants.js:1 — Python uses https, but `strictSSL: false` disables the
  certificate check there too: nugget 2.0.0 forwards `opts.strictSSL` to
  `request` defaults (`nugget/index.js:28-30`), and `request` sets
  `rejectUnauthorized = false` (`request.js:254-256, 606-607`). A self-signed
  MITM therefore passes for the Python MSI as well.
- ps1/launch-installer.ps1:28,38 execute the downloaded files; `:42-47` return
  unless the shell is elevated, so the payload normally runs as Administrator.

**Impact:** a network attacker who never touches the machine gets code execution
on it, for every user who installs the package, and nothing undoes the
compromise. Reach crosses a trust boundary; persistence is permanent — hence
high.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the bytes that get executed are the bytes
Microsoft published. Serve both installers over https with `strictSSL` left at
its default, and verify a pinned sha256 of each downloaded file before
`launch-installer.ps1` runs it.

findings.title: Failed installer download exits the postinstall with code 0 and installs nothing
findings.body:
`download()` ends both download steps with `.catch((error) => console.log(error))`
(src/download.js:17). The callback that starts the install (src/index.js:11-15)
only runs after both files resolve, and nothing rethrows or sets an exit code.
So any download failure — a 404 (rejected as a bare string at
src/download.js:46), a proxy error, an ECONNRESET — prints one console line, the
`install` and `environment` stages never run, and the `postinstall` process
(`node ./lib/index.js`, package.json:8) drains the event loop and exits 0. npm
reports a clean install, no build tools are installed, and the user discovers it
later through node-gyp/MSBuild errors.

**Preconditions:** the download has to fail — offline or proxied network, a moved
`PYTHON_MIRROR`, or the 404 path.

**Evidence:** src/download.js:13-18 (swallowed error, `cb` never called);
src/index.js:11-15 (nothing to observe the failure); package.json:8 (`postinstall`
is the entry point, so its exit code is npm's result).

**Impact:** each user who hits a download failure gets a silent no-op install that
npm reports as successful. The user is contained (their own machine, their own
re-run fixes it) and the harm is transient — low.

**Fix:** propagate the failure instead of logging it: return the promise from
`download`, have index.js reject/`cb(err)`, and end the process with a non-zero
exit code so npm surfaces the failed install.

summary:
Review complete.

**What the change does:** adds `src/download.js`, which fetches the Visual C++ Build Tools installer and the Python MSI with `nugget` into `%USERPROFILE%\.windows-build-tools` before `src/index.js` hands them to the installers.

**Assessment:** The download path works and its error classification is sound, but it is added with transport security disabled — `strictSSL: false` (`src/download.js:34`) combined with the plaintext build tools URL (`src/constants.js:5`) — so both payloads, one of which is then run elevated, can be replaced by a network attacker. I reproduced the certificate bypass against a self-signed server with the declared `nugget@2.0.0`, and separately confirmed that download errors end in a console log while the postinstall still exits 0. Two findings recorded (high, low); no duplicate or ignored findings existed.

**Findings:**
- `fnd_b707ade734a549b0` high — `src/download.js:34`: installer downloads skip TLS verification, letting a network attacker run code as administrator.
- `fnd_ec2992b9dc7311ad` low — `src/download.js:17`: download failures are swallowed and npm reports success.

findings.title: Installer downloads skip TLS verification, letting a network attacker run arbitrary code as administrator
findings.body:
`npm install --global windows-build-tools` downloads two executables over a channel that is not authenticated, then runs them. A network attacker can supply any file and get it executed, and the build tools installer runs with administrator rights.

**Preconditions:** The attacker can intercept or spoof traffic between the machine and `download.microsoft.com` (hostile network, ARP/DNS spoofing, a compromised proxy set through the documented `PROXY` variable). The user runs the install elevated, which the package requires.

**Evidence:**

- `src/download.js:34` passes `strictSSL: false` to nugget. nugget forwards that to `request.defaults` (`node_modules/nugget/index.js:28-34`), so certificate validation is off for every request it makes, including the Python mirror default `https://www.python.org/...` (`src/constants.js:1`).
- `src/constants.js:5` fetches the build tools installer over plain HTTP: `http://download.microsoft.com/.../visualcppbuildtools_full.exe`. This PR adds the only code that consumes that URL, so the plaintext fetch becomes live here.
- Reproduced with the declared dependency (`nugget@2.0.0`) against a local server with a self-signed certificate, calling `downloadTools` from `src/download.js` as written: the download succeeds and the written file holds the server's payload. With `strictSSL: true`, the same request fails with `self-signed certificate`. A plain-HTTP variant also succeeded.
- Nothing verifies the file after download. `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:28` then runs `./BuildTools_Full.exe` from the same directory the downloader writes to (`src/utils.js:37`), after the script has confirmed it is running as administrator (`ps1/launch-installer.ps1:43-48`). The Python MSI is run through `msiexec` (`ps1/launch-installer.ps1:38`).

**Impact:** Every install of this package fetches its payloads without transport authentication or integrity checks, and both payloads are executed, the build tools one elevated. A successful interception gives the attacker code execution as an administrator on the developer's machine, which is not undoable by any supported action. High.

**Fix:** Delete `strictSSL: false` so certificate validation stays on, change the build tools URL to `https://download.microsoft.com/...` (`src/constants.js:5`), and verify a pinned SHA-256 of each installer before it is executed.

findings.title: Download failures are swallowed, so npm reports a successful install with no tools installed
findings.body:
Any download error is logged and dropped: `src/download.js:17` catches into `console.log` and never calls `cb`, so `src/index.js:11` never starts the installers and the process exits with code 0. npm reports a successful install of a toolchain that was never installed.

**Evidence:** Reproduced by calling the exported `download` with a stub `./utils` whose installer URL points at a closed port. Console showed `Error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:9`, the callback was never invoked, and the process exited 0. The same path handles the 404 case that rejects with a string at `src/download.js:46`, and a failed Python download after a successful build tools download.

**Impact:** A transient network failure or a mistyped `PYTHON_MIRROR` leaves the user with no build tools and no error signal from npm; they only discover it when a later `node-gyp` build fails. The user can re-run the install, so the damage is limited to wasted time and a misleading success. Low.

**Fix:** Pass the failure to the caller, e.g. `download(function (error) { if (error) { console.error(error); process.exit(1) } install(...) })`, so a failed postinstall exits non-zero.

summary: PR #2 adds `index.js`, the full `set-value` 3.0.0 implementation: a path walker with backslash-escaped splitting, a merge option, array paths, and a module-global memo for split results. It is a clean single-file library, all 26 existing mocha assertions (checked by replication, since mocha is not installed) still pass, and the working tree is unchanged. The problem is that this is the pre-fix 3.0.0 code: the path walk offers no protection against prototype-chain segments, and the split cache is a plain object literal with no bound. Upstream shipped the corresponding fix in 3.0.1; this change reintroduces CVE-2019-10747, so it needs changes before merge.

findings.title: Paths through __proto__ or constructor write to Object.prototype for the whole process
findings.body:
`set()` writes through inherited objects, so a path segment `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype` writes to `Object.prototype` instead of the target. Every object in the process then carries the injected property, and the target's own keys stay clean, so the write is invisible to the caller.

Reproduced against `index.js`:

```
set({}, 'a.__proto__.isAdmin', true)            // ({}).isAdmin === true
set({}, 'constructor.prototype.isAdmin2', true) // ({}).isAdmin2 === true
set({}, ['constructor','prototype','x'], 1)     // ({}).x === 1  (array paths too)
set({}, 'a.constructor.prototype.p', {x:1}, {merge:true}) // ({}).p === {x:1}
```

`index.js:40` only creates a fresh object when `target[prop]` is not an object. `target['__proto__']` and `target['constructor']` already are (or are functions), so `index.js:49` descends into the prototype and `index.js:59` assigns there. No segment is validated anywhere in the file.

The same root cause reaches other shared built-ins: `set({}, 'hasOwnProperty.x', 1)` sets `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.x` and `set([], 'push.x', 1)` sets `Array.prototype.push.x`, so filtering only the three names above is not sufficient.

**Evidence:** `index.js:37-50`, `index.js:55-61`, `index.js:101-111`; runs above on Node 24 with `is-plain-object@2.0.4`.

**Impact:** high. This is CVE-2019-10747, which upstream fixed in 3.0.1 by filtering path segments; the code under review is the vulnerable 3.0.0 implementation. The trigger needs no options and no unusual setting — it is the library's primary string and array path forms. Reach crosses a trust boundary: any consumer that builds the path from request data (`set(record, body.key, value)`, dotted config keys, query-derived field paths) lets an unprivileged caller add properties to `Object.prototype`, which every later object in the process inherits — for example `if (user.isAdmin)` becomes true for objects the caller does not own, and `__proto__.0` makes empty arrays look populated. Persistence is permanent for the process lifetime: nothing removes the property, and the target object shows no trace of the write.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that `set` only writes to own properties. Reject `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` segments before the walk (the upstream 3.0.1 change adds `isValidKey` and applies `.filter(isValidKey)` to `keys`), and descend only into own properties so inherited functions and objects are never used as containers, e.g. `const child = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, prop) ? target[prop] : undefined;` at `index.js:40-49`. Both parts are needed: the name filter alone leaves `hasOwnProperty.x` and `push.x` writable.

findings.title: Setting a path named after an Object.prototype member silently drops the value
findings.body:
A single-segment path whose text matches an `Object.prototype` member name is looked up in the module-level cache as if it were a cache key, so `split()` returns the inherited built-in instead of an array of keys. The call then either stores nothing or stores the value under the literal key `"undefined"`, and `set` still returns the target with no error.

Reproduced on a fresh process:

```
const o = {};  set(o, 'toString', 'stored');      // o -> {}                  (silent no-op)
const o2 = {}; set(o2, 'constructor', 'stored');  // o2 -> {"undefined":"stored"}
const o3 = {}; set(o3, 'valueOf', 'stored');      // o3 -> {}                  (silent no-op)
```

`set.memo` is a plain object literal (`index.js:113`) and the hit test is a truthiness check (`index.js:65`), so ids such as `toString`, `constructor`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, `__defineGetter__` and `__proto__` resolve to inherited members. The result is a function or `Object.prototype`, never an array: `keys.length` at `index.js:29` is `0`, `1` or `undefined`, and the walk at `index.js:37-50` is skipped or uses `keys[0] === undefined`. Passing `{}` as options does not help — `createKey` produces the bare pattern when `Object.keys(options)` is empty (`index.js:88-98`).

**Evidence:** `index.js:64-65`, `index.js:84`, `index.js:88-98`, `index.js:113`; runs above.

**Impact:** low. The caller gets its target back, so an application that sets a user-supplied field named `constructor` or `toString` reports success while the value is lost or written to the wrong key — a contained, per-call correctness failure for a narrow set of key names. `set.memo` is also shared by every caller in the process, so any code that assigns to `set.memo` changes behaviour globally.

**Fix:** make the cache lookup independent of `Object.prototype`: use `set.memo = Object.create(null)` (or guard with `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(set.memo, id)`), and only treat a hit as valid when `Array.isArray` is true.

findings.title: Module-global path cache grows without bound and retains every path ever set
findings.body:
`set.memo` is a module-global cache with no eviction: `split()` stores the key array for every distinct `(path, options)` pair (`index.js:84`) and nothing ever removes an entry. Memory therefore grows with the number of distinct path strings the process has ever seen, not with the number of live objects.

Measured on a fresh process:

```
for (let i = 0; i < 20000; i++) set({}, 'k' + i + '.leaf', i);
Object.keys(set.memo).length  // 20000
```

**Preconditions:** the process is long-lived and the path text is influenced by requests, e.g. a server that stores fields by a user-supplied dotted path.

**Evidence:** `index.js:84` (the only write), `index.js:113` (`set.memo = {}`); the file contains no `delete`, no size cap and no reset. Ids also embed `String(options[key])` (`index.js:96`), so option-carrying callers add duplicate entries for the same path.

**Impact:** low. Reach is broad within the process — all requests and tenants share the cache — but the effect needs sustained distinct paths to matter, and a restart clears it, so the damage is transient and bounded by how long the process lives. The cache also outlives every target object, so per-request path data is retained indefinitely.

**Fix:** bound the cache — key it in a `Map` with a size cap (evict oldest) — or drop the memoisation; the split itself is a single `String.prototype.split`.

summary:
I reviewed the added file against the whole auth path (passport strategies, User schema hooks, admin/GraphQL mounts, and the upstream commits the fixture is built from).

**What the change does:** it re-adds `server/apps/routes/auth.js` (signup, login, first-user install, firstinstall, setpassword, forgotpassword, verify, logout), the module `server/apps/admin.js` already required.

**Context worth recording:** the re-added file is byte-identical to upstream `4ae3423` ("toString() some query params"), the fix commit for CVE-2018-3783. The three query sites this CVE was about (`:58`, `:80`, `:104`) now coerce with `.toString()`, and I verified every input shape (qs objects, arrays, JSON objects) collapses to a primitive string, so the NoSQL injection is genuinely closed here — I did not report it.

**Assessment:** the file also carries unrelated problems that the diff makes reachable. Two findings are recorded: the unguarded `POST /admin/signup` route mints an admin-group user for anonymous callers (bypassing the `allowPublicRegistration` gate and silently inheriting the admin UserGroup), and three routes coerce optional request values without a presence check, leaving those requests unanswered. I confirmed and refuted several other candidates before dropping them: `password: undefined` in the forgot-password update is stripped by Mongoose (no password wipe), `user.token = undefined` does persist as `$unset`, and `user.name.first` cannot throw because Mongoose materialises `name` as `{}`.

findings.title: Unauthenticated POST /admin/signup creates an admin-group user even when public registration is disabled
findings.body:
`POST /admin/signup` creates a user in the `admin` UserGroup for any anonymous caller, including on the default configuration where public registration is disabled. Whoever calls it holds every permission in `server/utils/permissions.json`, so the CMS is fully compromised without a password reset or any prior access.

**Preconditions:** none beyond a normal install. The admin UserGroup exists from boot: `server/utils/database.js:53-54` calls `createAdminUserGroup()` on every connection open.

**Evidence:**

- The route is mounted without any auth middleware: `server/index.js:53` → `server/apps/admin.js:12` mounts `routes/auth` first, so the path is `POST /admin/signup` (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:14`).
- The route passes the caller straight to Passport and checks nothing: `passport.authenticate('local-signup', strategyOptions)` (`auth.js:14`). `strategyOptions` is `{ passReqToCallback: true }` (`auth.js:11`), which means nothing to `authenticate()`; there is no site-setting or first-run check.
- The intended gate is elsewhere and is not applied here: `server/utils/public-registration.js:14-18` (rejects unless `site.allowPublicRegistration`) is only wired to `global.FLINT.signupRoute` (`:24-25`), which has no default, and `allowPublicRegistration` defaults to `false` (`server/models/SiteSchema.js:22-25`). No client code calls `/admin/signup` either — the install UI posts to `/admin/firstuser` (`app/views/Auth/Install/index.js:39-45`).
