- The new user lands in the admin group by schema default: `server/utils/passport.js:30` builds `new User(req.body)`, and `server/models/UserSchema.js:39-48` assigns the UserGroup with `slug: 'admin'` whenever `usergroup` is absent (`:43-45`). That group has every permission set to `true` (`server/utils/create-admin-usergroup.js:11` against `permissions.json`).
- Session and escalation: Passport logs the user in on strategy success (`req.logIn`), `server/apps/graphql.js:14` admits any authenticated request via `helpers.js:9`, and `graphql.js:23` loads the caller's permissions, so every `perms.*` check in `server/graphql/mutations/**` passes (for example `mutations/users/deleteUser.js:19`, `mutations/sections/removeSection.js:18`, `mutations/site/updateSite.js:16`).
- Reproduction: `curl -i -X POST https://host/admin/signup -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"a@evil.tld","username":"a","password":"p"}'`, then reuse the returned session cookie against `/graphql`. The route has no success handler, so Passport calls `next()` and the client sees the SPA 404 — the account is already saved and the session established, so the failure status hides nothing.

**Impact:** unauthenticated caller gains capability its role denies (crosses the trust boundary) and the created account plus any content it deletes or edits persists (permanent), so this is `high`. No discount applies: no non-default setting, no prior capability, and the site owner cannot notice it from the response. The gate that exists in `public-registration.js` shows the project intends this endpoint to be closed by default.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — user creation by an anonymous caller must respect the site's registration setting, and a self-registered user must not inherit the admin group. Smallest change: drop the `/signup` route from `auth.js` (no client uses it), or mount it behind the same `publicMiddleware` from `server/utils/public-registration.js`; separately have the `UserSchema` `pre('validate')` fall back to `Site.defaultUserGroup` or a non-privileged group instead of `slug: 'admin'`.

findings.title: Missing token, email or query parameter leaves auth requests unanswered (unguarded .toString())
findings.body:
Three auth routes call `.toString()` on a request value before checking it exists, so a request that omits the value throws inside an `async` handler. Express 4 does not observe returned promises, and this server installs no error middleware and no `unhandledRejection` handler, so the request never receives a response and the socket stays open until the server timeout.

Triggers, all unauthenticated:

- `GET /admin/verify` with no `t` — `req.query.t.toString()` at `server/apps/routes/auth.js:104` (`req.query.t` is `undefined`).
- `POST /admin/forgotpassword` with `{}` or `{"email":null}` — `email.toString()` at `auth.js:80`.
- `POST /admin/setpassword` with `{"password":"x"}` and no `token` — `token.toString()` at `auth.js:58`. The missing-password case is handled explicitly at `auth.js:53-56`, which makes the missing-token case easy to miss.

**Evidence:** the three call sites above; no `app.use((err, req, res, ...))` and no `process.on('unhandledRejection')` anywhere in `server/`, `index.js` or `dev.js`. The routes are mounted with no auth middleware (`server/apps/admin.js:12`), so all three paths are reachable anonymously.

**Impact:** each request parks a connection for the duration of the server timeout while returning nothing, so an anonymous caller can cheaply hold many sockets open, and legitimate callers get a hung request instead of a 400. Under the declared runtime (`package.json` engines `node: ^8.0.0`) the promise rejection is only logged, so the consequence is availability and diagnosability, not data loss — `low`. On newer Node the same rejection terminates the process, which the site owner would see as a crash loop.

**Fix:** validate the parameter before coercing it — return `400` when `token`, `email` or `req.query.t` is missing or not a string — or reject early with a shared guard so the coercion at `:58`, `:80` and `:104` only ever sees a present value.

summary:
The change restores `server/apps/routes/auth.js`, which mounts the unauthenticated `/admin` auth endpoints (signup, login, first-user install, password reset, verify, logout). I reviewed the whole file, traced it into the router mounting, passport strategies, the user model and the GraphQL authorization layer, and ran the routes against a real MongoDB 4.4 + mongoose 4.11.13 harness built from the repository's own files to confirm or refute each suspicion.

The main risk is that every request value goes straight into a Mongoose filter, and the body parsers accept nested objects, so operator injection is live and I reproduced full account takeover with it; a second reproduced issue is that `/admin/signup` hands out a working admin account to anyone. Two lower-severity reliability issues (an attacker-triggered login lockout and hanging requests from unhandled rejections) are also recorded. The logout, verify redirect, token clearing and first-install flows behaved correctly in testing.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can take over any account through the password-reset token lookup
findings.body:
`POST /admin/setpassword` passes `req.body.token` straight into a Mongoose filter
(`server/apps/routes/auth.js:58`). Both body parsers accept nested objects
(`bodyParser.urlencoded({ extended: true })` and `bodyParser.json()`,
`server/index.js:30-31`), so a caller can send `{"token": {"$gt": ""}}`. Mongoose
keeps the operator (it only casts the operand, not the key) and the query matches the
first user that has any token set. The handler then overwrites that user's password
(`:64`), clears the token (`:65`), saves (`:67`) and calls `req.login(user)` (`:73`),
which returns a signed session cookie. No reset email, token value, or credentials are
needed.

**Preconditions:** one user must have a `token`. The attacker can create that state for
any address they know through the unauthenticated `POST /admin/forgotpassword`
(`:78-101`), which writes a token unconditionally; `{"email": {"$ne": null}}` there
also works against an arbitrary account.

**Evidence:** reproduced with MongoDB 4.4, mongoose 4.11.13 and the repository's own
`UserSchema`, passport strategies and `server/apps/routes/auth.js`:

```
POST /admin/forgotpassword {"email":"victim@example.com"} -> 200 {"success":true}
victim token after forgotpassword: 0123456789abcdef
POST /admin/setpassword {"token":{"$gt":""},"password":"pwned"}
    -> 200 {"success":true}   set-cookie: present
victim password changed? true   token cleared? true
GET /admin/whoami with that agent's cookie: {"email":"victim@example.com"}
form-encoded variant token[$gt]=&password=... -> 200 {"success":true}
```

Both routes are mounted before any guard (`server/apps/admin.js:12`,
`server/index.js:53`), so the request needs no session. The same unvalidated-value
pattern appears at `:80` (`{ email }` in `/forgotpassword`) and `:105`
(`{ token: req.query.t }` in `/verify`); their impact is smaller but one fix covers
all three.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated attacker sets any token-bearing account's password and
receives an authenticated session, so they can use the admin API as that user.
Every account created by this file lands in the admin usergroup, so the reachable
accounts include site administrators. The write is permanent and the token owner also
loses their pending reset link. Graded high under the review severity policy: the
change crosses a trust boundary and the effect persists.

**Fix:** restore one invariant: every value placed in these Mongoose filters is a
string. Reject non-string `token` (and `email`, `req.query.t`) with 400 before
querying, e.g. `if (typeof token !== 'string') return res.status(400).json({ message:
'Cannot find user.' })`.

findings.title: Unauthenticated POST /admin/signup creates a working admin account
findings.body:
`router.post('/signup', passport.authenticate('local-signup', strategyOptions))`
(`server/apps/routes/auth.js:14`) is mounted on the admin router before any
authentication (`server/apps/admin.js:12`, `server/index.js:53`), so an unauthenticated
request creates a user. The intended public signup path checks
`site.allowPublicRegistration` (`server/utils/public-registration.js:13-27`), which
defaults to `false` (`server/models/SiteSchema.js:22-25`); `/admin/signup` bypasses
that check. The created user is also privileged: `UserSchema.pre('validate')`
(`server/models/UserSchema.js:39-48`) always overwrites `usergroup` with the admin
group (the `if (this.usergroup) next()` at `:40` has no `return`, so the assignment at
`:46` runs regardless), and the admin group carries every permission
(`server/utils/create-admin-usergroup.js:11`). GraphQL authorizes from that usergroup
(`server/apps/graphql.js:18-29`, `server/utils/get-user-permissions.js`).

**Evidence:** reproduced with the repository's `UserSchema`, passport strategies and
`server/apps/routes/auth.js` against MongoDB 4.4:

```
POST /admin/signup {"email":"attacker@evil.com","username":"attacker","password":"hunter2"}
    -> 404 (no handler after passport.authenticate, so no body is sent)
user created? true   usergroup == admin group? true
POST /admin/login {"email":"attacker@evil.com","password":"hunter2"}
    -> 200 {"success":true}   set-cookie: present
```

The 404 does not mean the request failed: the account exists and can log in.

**Impact:** anyone who can reach the site gets a persistent admin account with write
access to pages, entries, users, plugins and site settings, on any installation —
including the default one, where public registration is disabled. This crosses a trust
boundary with a permanent effect, hence high.

**Fix:** remove the route or put it behind the same gate the public signup uses
(`allowPublicRegistration`) plus an authenticated-admin check. The admin-group
defaulting in `UserSchema.js:39-48` is pre-existing and needs its own fix so new
self-registered users do not become administrators.

findings.title: Invalid input to /admin/firstuser leaves the request hanging with an unhandled rejection
findings.body:
None of the async handlers in `server/apps/routes/auth.js` catch rejections (`:20-39`,
`:50-76`, `:78-101`, `:103-113`), and Express 4 does not catch a rejected handler
promise. On an empty database, `POST /admin/firstuser` with a body that fails
validation (`server/models/UserSchema.js:12-22` requires `email` and `username`) makes
`save()` reject at `:33`; the client never gets a response and the process emits an
unhandled rejection. The same applies to the explicit `throw` at `:34`, to a missing
admin usergroup at `:30-31`, and to database errors in the other handlers.

**Evidence:** reproduced against MongoDB 4.4:

```
POST /admin/firstuser {} -> request times out after 3s (no response)
UNHANDLED REJECTION: User validation failed: username: Path `username` is required.,
                     email: Path `email` is required.
```

**Impact:** an unauthenticated request can leave connections open and, on Node 15 and
later where an unhandled rejection is fatal by default, terminate the server; on the
Node 8 runtime `package.json` targets it only logs and hangs the request. Low: the
damage depends on the runtime version, and the trigger on a populated database returns
early at `:22`.

**Fix:** wrap each handler in try/catch (or an async wrapper) and answer 400/500 instead
of leaving the promise unhandled.

findings.title: Anyone can lock an account out of password login by requesting a reset
findings.body:
`POST /admin/forgotpassword` (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:78-101`) writes a fresh random
token to the account with the supplied email (`:87-90`) and mails it. Any login for a
user who has a token is rejected (`server/utils/passport.js:43`), so an unauthenticated
caller who knows an address can turn off password login for that account, as often as
they like, without any secret.

**Preconditions:** the caller knows the victim's email address; the request needs no
session (`server/apps/admin.js:12`).

**Evidence:** reproduced with the repository's user model and passport strategies:

```
attacker: POST /admin/forgotpassword {"email":"admin@site.com"} -> 200
victim:   POST /admin/login {"email":"admin@site.com","password":"secret"} -> 401
```

Recovery depends entirely on the reset email arriving. Mail is optional: the server
logs a nodemailer failure and keeps running (`index.js:117-121`), so on an install
without SMTP the admin stays locked out with no supported way to clear the token.

**Impact:** denial of login for one account per request, repeatable against any account
whose address is known. Contained and normally recoverable through the emailed reset
link, which is why this is low rather than higher; the unconfigured-mail case is
permanent but needs that non-default setting.

**Fix:** do not make a pending reset change login eligibility. Track "must set
password" (account activation) separately from "reset requested", or require the
caller to prove control of the address before writing the token.

summary:
**Summary.** The PR adds `index.js` to a tree whose other files are the published 2.1.1 sources, and the file it adds is byte-identical to upstream 2.2.0. Its one security-relevant change is `index.js:207`, where `new Buffer(proxy.auth)` became `Buffer.from(proxy.auth)`, closing the uninitialized-memory leak/DoS on typed-in `auth` (CVE-2018-3739, the published record that superseded CVE-2018-3736). That fix is correct and matches what upstream shipped.

One regression comes with it: `Buffer.from` only accepts strings from Node v4.5.0 / v5.10.0, so on Node 4.0–4.4 and 5.0–5.9 — still inside the range `.travis.yml` exercises and undeclared in `package.json` (no `engines`) — every authenticated proxy request throws `TypeError: this is not a typed array.`, which I reproduced on v4.1.0 and v5.9.0. The added file otherwise passes the suite on Node 4.9.1 and 8.17 (14 passing); it cannot run on Node 24 because the fixture's snakeoil key is rejected by modern OpenSSL, which is unrelated to the change. Other failure modes I found in the file (unbounded CONNECT-response buffering, hang when the proxy closes without a full response, proxy TLS options leaking into the endpoint connection, unbracketed IPv6 CONNECT authority) are unchanged from the shipped 2.1.1 module, so I left them out of scope.

findings.title: Requests with proxy auth throw on Node 4.0–4.4 and 5.0–5.9, which the package still claims to support
findings.body:
Requests that use an authenticated proxy fail on Node 4.0–4.4 and 5.0–5.9. On those
runtimes `Buffer.from` is still `Uint8Array.from` (`Buffer` extends `Uint8Array`
there), so it does not accept a string and throws. The change at `index.js:207`
calls it for every request that has `proxy.auth` set:

```js
headers['Proxy-Authorization'] =
  'Basic ' + Buffer.from(proxy.auth).toString('base64');
```

The string-capable `Buffer.from` shipped in Node v4.5.0 / v5.10.0. `package.json`
has no `engines` field and `.travis.yml` lists `node_js: 4` and `5`, so those
ranges are still within the stated support window; CI resolves `4`/`5` to the
latest patch release and cannot catch this.

**Preconditions:** runtime is Node 4.0–4.4 or 5.0–5.9, and the agent is
constructed with `auth` (proxy credentials).

**Evidence:** ran the reviewed file with `agent-base@4.1.0`:

```
$ node -v                      # v4.1.0
$ node repro.js                # new HttpsProxyAgent({host,port,auth:'user:pass'})
THREW: TypeError - this is not a typed array.

$ node -v                      # v5.9.0
$ node -e "Buffer.from('user:pass').toString('base64')"
THREW this is not a typed array.
$ node -e "new Buffer('user:pass').toString('base64')"
dXNlcjpwYXNz
```

The previous form (`new Buffer(proxy.auth)`) works on those runtimes, so this is
a regression for them. `agent-base` catches the synchronous throw and turns it
into `req.emit('error')` (`node_modules/agent-base/index.js:154-160`); the proxy
socket opened at `index.js:76` is never destroyed on that path, so each failed
request also leaks a connection.

**Impact:** every proxied request with credentials fails immediately instead of
going through the proxy. The affected runtimes are a narrow slice of the Node 4/5
lines, the failure is loud rather than silent, and upgrading the runtime clears
it — low. The upstream release that introduced this line added the missing floor
in the same release (`History.md` for 2.2.0: "Add `engines` to package.json -
requires Node.js >= 4.5.0"), which confirms the requirement is real and was meant
to be declared.

**Fix:** declare the floor the code now assumes, e.g. `"engines": { "node": ">= 4.5.0" }`
in `package.json`, or keep a path that does not depend on the newer API. Restore one
invariant: the module must never call an API that its declared support range lacks.

summary:
Verification complete. I ran the jsdom reproduction myself: with the pre-fix form (`$("
" + msg + "
")`) the live region ends up containing a real `IMG` element; with the form in this PR (`$container.text(msg)` then `.html($container)`) every payload stays escaped text. **Summary** This PR adds `selectize-plugin-a11y.js` (141 lines), a jQuery plugin that gives Selectize.js combobox roles, an assertive live region, and `aria-*` state tracking. The one security-relevant write is `speak()` at `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:27-31`, which builds a text-only node and hands a jQuery object to `.html()` — jQuery treats a non-string value as `empty().append(node)`, so no HTML is ever parsed; the only caller (line 53) passes `$target.text()`. I verified this against jQuery 1.7.2–3.7.1 semantics and reproduced it in jsdom with ``, `

Verification complete. No findings to record.

**What the change does:** PR #1 adds `xmpp/util.js` (158 lines) to the dojox tree — XMPP helpers for XML escaping (`xmlEncode`), JID escaping, stanza building (`createElement`), HTML-to-text conversion, and Base64.

**Assessment:** This is the security fix, not the regression. The baseline tree (`d6b93d9e`, upstream `1.17.0-pre`) carries the vulnerable `xmlEncode` — `str.replace("&","&").replace(">",">")…` at `xmpp/util.js:8` in upstream, which encodes only the first occurrence of each character (CVE-2019-10785). The added file replaces it with a single-pass `/g` callback over a 5-entry map (`xmpp/util.js:5-21`); I ran that implementation in Node and every occurrence of `&`, `>`, `<`, `'`, `"` is escaped, with no re-scan of replacement text (`"<<<<"` → `"<<<<"`, `<script>` → `&lt;script&gt;`). The file's blob hash (`1cf54413`) matches the upstream fix commit `6eb27835` ("fixes potential xss by properly encoding xml") byte for byte, syntax-checks clean, and requires nothing beyond its declared `dojox.string.Builder` / `dojox.encoding.base64` dependencies.

Residual weaknesses I traced but did **not** file, because they are unchanged upstream code this change only restores, not defects it introduces: `createElement` (`xmpp/util.js:92-108`) never escapes attribute values, so callers such as `PresenceService.js:275` and `xmppSession.js:361` can inject markup if a peer-supplied `from`/`id` reaches them unescaped; `stripHtml`/`htmlToPlain` are lossy rather than sanitizing; `Base64.encode` truncates non-ASCII characters (`sasl.js:57`); and `decodeJid` returns a literal `"ARG"` for escapes outside its switch (`xmpp/util.js:85`). All of these are identical in upstream dojox master, so they belong in a separate issue, not on this fix.

The PR re-adds `xmpp/util.js` (147 lines) to a baseline that had it deleted, restoring the `dojox.xmpp.util` module that `TransportSession`/`sasl` require and the rest of the XMPP stack calls transitively. The added content is the genuine pre-fix upstream file: it differs from npm dojox 1.15.3 only in whitespace, and from every fixed release (1.14.6 through 1.16.3) only in `xmlEncode`. That function is the CVE-2019-10785 defect — single-string `replace` calls escape only the first occurrence of each special character — and I reproduced the consequence: a roster name yields an emitted `item` with an attacker-chosen extra attribute, while a benign name like `Bob & Sons & Co` produces a non-well-formed stanza. I recorded one medium finding; the remaining helpers in the file (`createElement`, `stripHtml`, `decodeJid`, Base64, and the dead loop in `stripHtml`) have no clear in-repo path to a worse outcome than a malformed stanza, so I left them unreported.

findings.title: xmlEncode escapes only the first special character, letting a roster contact name inject attributes into outbound XMPP stanzas
findings.body:
`dojox.xmpp.util.xmlEncode` (xmpp/util.js:5-10) escapes each special character with a
plain-string `String.prototype.replace` pattern:

```js
str.replace("&", "&").replace(">", ">").replace("<", "<").replace("'", "'").replace('"', """)
```

A string pattern replaces only the **first** match, so any input with a second `"`,
`<`, `>` or `&` keeps raw markup characters. Both callers
(xmpp/RosterService.js:33 and :78-80) pass the result into
`createElement`, which wraps attribute values in quotes with no escaping
(xmpp/util.js:86-88), so a surviving `"` closes the `name` attribute early and the
rest of the value becomes attacker-chosen attributes.

**Preconditions:** the victim's server routes an `<iq type="set">` carrying a roster
`<query xmlns="jabber:iq:roster">` whose item `name` holds the payload.
`iqSetHandler` (xmpp/xmppSession.js:344-352) accepts it without checking `from`, and
`rosterSetHandler` stores the name verbatim (xmpp/xmppSession.js:403-406, and for new
entries :432-436 via `createRosterEntry` :529). The payload reaches the wire when the
app next mutates that entry, e.g. `addRosterItemToGroup` / `rosterItemRenameGroup` /
`removeRosterItemFromGroup`, which call `updateRosterItem` (xmpp/RosterService.js:109-223).
`addRosterItem` (:33) reaches it whenever the app passes an attacker-influenced alias.

**Evidence:** running the exact function and `createElement` bodies in node:

```
payload : a"" onmouseover="alert(1)
encoded : a"" onmouseover="alert(1)          (only the first quote escaped)
emitted : <item jid="victim@example.com" name="a"" onmouseover="alert(1)" >
parsed by expat: {'jid': 'victim@example.com', 'name': 'a"', 'onmouseover': 'alert(1)'}
```

The same function breaks legitimate data: `Bob & Sons & Co` encodes to
`Bob & Sons & Co`, whose bare `&` makes the stanza non-well-formed, so the server
rejects the roster operation.

Upstream fixed exactly this line by delegating to `dojo.string.escape`
(npm dojox 1.14.6 / 1.15.4 / 1.16.2 / 1.16.3 `xmpp/util.js:5-7`), which uses global
regexes; the added file matches the pre-fix content. CVE-2019-10785 describes this
function: "vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting ... due to
dojox.xmpp.util.xmlEncode only encoding the first occurrence of each character".

**Impact:** Attacker text from a routed roster stanza ends up as markup in stanzas
the victim's client sends to its server, crossing a trust boundary. The injected
attributes change roster semantics (for example `subscription="remove"` deletes the
contact, and injected handler attributes follow the value into any client that
renders roster names as HTML, the outcome the CVE records). The change is
recoverable — the user can re-add the contact — and it needs the local roster
mutation as a trigger, so per the reach x persistence policy this is medium.

**Fix:** escape every occurrence. Smallest change:
`str.replace(/&/g,"&").replace(/</g,"<").replace(/>/g,">").replace(/"/g,""").replace(/'/g,"'")`
(escape `&` first), or call `dojo.string.escape(str)` as upstream does.

summary: The PR adds a 228-line `index.js` that is byte-identical to upstream `https-proxy-agent` v2.1.1 — the version covered by GHSA-8g7p-74h8-hg48 (CVE-2018-3739, duplicate CVE-2018-3736) — so it re-introduces a file with two known advisories rather than shipping the fixed code that landed in 2.2.0/2.2.3. I reproduced both: a non-string `auth` reaching `new Buffer()` (uninitialized heap bytes into the `Proxy-Authorization` header on Node ≤7, crash or attacker-sized allocation on any version) and a failed CONNECT handing the live proxy socket to node's HTTP client, which then writes the destination's `Authorization`, `Cookie` and body in cleartext to the proxy. A third reproduced issue is that proxy-scoped TLS options are merged into the destination handshake, so `rejectUnauthorized: false` set for a self-signed proxy silently disables origin certificate verification. Other probed leads — hangs with no timeout, unbounded pre-CONNECT buffering, CRLF injection through `proxy.headers`, missing `defaultPort`, and proxy `auth` leaking to the origin — were either refuted by testing (agent-base sets `port = 443` and `auth` never reaches the origin request) or bounded enough to leave unreported.

findings.title: Numeric or object proxy auth reaches new Buffer(), leaking uninitialized heap and allowing DoS
findings.body:
The CONNECT request builder passes `proxy.auth` straight to the deprecated `new Buffer()`
constructor without a type check (index.js:205-208). `auth` is copied verbatim from the
caller's options at index.js:35/58 and the module accepts any options object, so a
non-string value is treated as a Buffer constructor argument rather than as credentials.

**Preconditions:** the application supplies `auth` from typed/untrusted input (the
advisory's own example: JSON config), or simply forwards a parsed config where `auth`
ended up numeric. Reaching the line needs only the public API:
`new HttpsProxyAgent({ host, port, auth })` plus any request using the agent; no special
node version or flag.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this tree (`agent-base@4.3.0`).
- Numeric `auth: 512` produces `Proxy-Authorization: Basic <base64 of 512 bytes of process
  heap>` in the CONNECT request captured by a raw `net.Server` on the proxy port. On Node
  <= 7 (in this release's supported range — `.travis.yml` tests Node 4-8, `package.json`
  has no `engines` field) `new Buffer(n)` is `Buffer.allocUnsafe(n)`: a run on Node
  v7.10.1 yielded 229 of 512 nonzero bytes, including leftover V8 heap strings and
  pointers. On Node >= 8 the memory is zero-filled, so only the DoS half survives.
- `auth: { user: 'x' }` or `auth: true` throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` from index.js:207
  after `net.connect(proxy)` has already opened the proxy socket (index.js:76); the throw
  escapes `callback`, the `ClientRequest` emits `'error'`, and with no listener installed
  by the caller the process exits (observed exit code 1). The proxy connection is left
  open (one dangling socket per failed request).
- Large numeric values amplify memory before any network work: `auth: 268435456` raised
  RSS from 55 MB to 1054 MB in 767 ms; `402653166` fails with `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG`.
- The upstream fix for this exact line (2.2.0, commit "Use `Buffer.from()`") makes
  `Buffer.from(proxy.auth)` throw before allocating for both the numeric and object cases.
  Advisories: GHSA-8g7p-74h8-hg48 / CVE-2018-3739 (CVE-2018-3736 is its rejected
  duplicate), hackerone.com/reports/319532, vulnerable range `<2.2.0`.

**Impact:** uninitialized process memory (V8 heap fragments, pointers, other requests'
data) is base64-encoded and written to the proxy server, on the Node versions this
release supports. Who triggers it: whoever controls the `auth` value; who is harmed: the
client process's confidentiality, plus availability because a non-string `auth` crashes
the request/process and a numeric `auth` gives an attacker-controlled allocation size.
Severity: the disclosure crosses a trust boundary to the proxy and is permanent, dropped
one tier because it requires the caller to forward untrusted non-string input as `auth`
(not the documented string form). Policy: no repository severity policy exists, so the
matrix tops out at `high`.

**Fix:** never pass a caller value to a size-taking constructor. Coerce once:
`headers['Proxy-Authorization'] = 'Basic ' + Buffer.from(String(proxy.auth)).toString('base64')`
(or upstream's `Buffer.from(proxy.auth)`, which rejects non-strings), and validate
`proxy.auth` in the constructor so a bad value fails before any socket is opened.

findings.title: Failed CONNECT hands the live proxy socket to the HTTP client, sending credentials in cleartext to the proxy
findings.body:
When the proxy answers the CONNECT with any status other than 200, the agent removes its
own listeners and then returns the still-connected proxy socket to node's HTTP client
(index.js:158-170, `fn(null, socket)` at :169). The buffered status line is replayed onto
that socket (:173-189), so the caller sees an ordinary 407/403 response and nothing
signals that the socket is the real proxy connection. Node's client then flushes the
serialized request — headers and body — to the proxy in cleartext: no tunnel was
established, and the `secureEndpoint` TLS upgrade at :141-154 only runs in the 200 branch.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this tree. A raw `net.Server` on the proxy port answers
the CONNECT with `HTTP/1.1 407 Proxy Authentication Required` and keeps the connection
open; with `http.get({ host: 'example.com', port: 80, path: '/', headers: { Authorization:
'Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_123', Cookie: 'sid=abc' }, agent })` the proxy receives, after its
407, `"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nAuthorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_123\r\nCookie: sid=abc\r\n
Host: example.com:80\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n"`. Same result for an `https://` target
against a `403`-answering proxy, and for a POST — the body (`TOP_SECRET_POST_BODY`) leaks
too. The client still reports `statusCode 407`, so applications treat it as a handled
proxy-auth failure. With upstream's fixed file (2.2.4) the proxy receives zero bytes after
its 407.

**Impact:** the destination's credentials and request body are handed to an intermediary
that was never supposed to see them — a rejecting proxy, or any attacker who can answer
the CONNECT (a MITM'd or hostile proxy just replies 407 and harvests). Severity: crosses
a trust boundary with a permanent disclosure (credentials are out; nothing undoes it),
dropped one tier because it needs the proxy to answer non-200 rather than tunnel. Policy:
no repository severity policy exists, so the matrix tops out at `high`. Advisories:
GHSA-pc5p-h8pf-mvwp (CWE-300, `<2.2.3`), hackerone.com/reports/541502, fixed upstream in
2.2.3/3.0.0.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — after a failed CONNECT the client must never be able to
write to the proxy connection. Destroy the socket and hand back a detached stub that only
replays the buffered response, as upstream does:
`socket.destroy(); socket = new net.Socket(); socket.readable = true;` then
`socket.push(buffers)` in `onsocket` instead of `socket.emit('data', buffers)`.

findings.title: Proxy TLS options leak into the destination handshake and disable certificate verification
findings.body:
Proxy options are stored on the agent (`Agent.call(this, opts)` at index.js:33) and
`agent-base` merges them into every request's options — `Object.assign({}, this.options,
ownOpts)` in agent-base index.js:73 (identical in 4.1.0 at index.js:79). The endpoint TLS
upgrade then hands that merged object straight to `tls.connect(opts)` (index.js:141-154),
so TLS settings the caller intended for the proxy connection — `rejectUnauthorized`,
`ca`, `checkServerIdentity`, `pfx` — also apply to the destination. Setting
`rejectUnauthorized: false` for a proxy with a self-signed certificate therefore turns off
certificate verification for every HTTPS origin reached through that agent, silently.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes `rejectUnauthorized: false` (or a private `ca`, or
any `checkServerIdentity`) in the proxy options — the standard workaround for a corporate
proxy with an internal CA — and does not set its own TLS options on each request.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this tree with a self-signed origin (`CN=localhost`,
rejecting otherwise with `DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT`) behind a plain tunnelling proxy:

- agent `new HttpsProxyAgent({host, port, protocol:'http:'})`, request without TLS options
  -> `https.get` fails with `DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT` (verification works).
- agent `new HttpsProxyAgent({host, port, protocol:'http:', rejectUnauthorized:false})`,
  same request without TLS options -> request succeeds and reads the origin body, i.e. the
  origin certificate was never verified. The request options win when both are set
  (`ownOpts` overrides `this.options`), so the failure is the inherited default.

**Impact:** certificate verification for the destination is disabled without the caller
asking for it, so any party able to intercept the tunneled connection can present its own
certificate and read or alter the request while the client sees success. Severity: crosses
a trust boundary with a permanent disclosure, dropped one tier because it needs the
non-default `rejectUnauthorized`/`ca` setting on the proxy options. This is not covered by
the two upstream advisories for this version, so it remains unfixed upstream; no
repository severity policy exists, so the matrix tops out at `high`.

**Fix:** do not let proxy-scoped options reach the endpoint handshake. Build the endpoint
TLS options explicitly from the request's own options (host/servername/port plus the
caller's per-request TLS settings), and keep the proxy options separate for the
`net.connect`/`tls.connect` call that opens the proxy connection.

summary:
Review complete. Summary:

This PR adds `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js` (300 lines), the liblinear wrapper, re-adding it from upstream commit `92c045d3` — the pre-0.9.5 version, even though the tree's `package.json` already declares 0.9.5. The file's training and test paths build shell command lines from constructor options and execute them with `child_process.execSync`, reintroducing the command-execution vulnerability fixed upstream in 0.9.5 (CVE-2020-4066 / GHSA-77qv-gh6f-pgh4); I reproduced the injection for `learn_args`, `train_command`, `test_command`, and a slash-free `model_file_prefix` using stub binaries, with a benign control creating no marker. The correct change is the upstream fix: `execFileSync` with argument arrays, and `learn_args` as an array. The file also remains an outdated copy with unrelated functional defects (serialization and retraining), so it should be reconciled with the current version rather than merged as-is.

findings.title: SvmLinear options are interpolated into shell commands, executing arbitrary commands
findings.body:
`SvmLinear.trainBatch` and `SvmLinear.classifyBatch` assemble shell command lines by string concatenation and run them through `child_process.execSync`, which invokes `/bin/sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in the `learn_args`, `train_command`, `test_command`, or `model_file_prefix` constructor options therefore run as commands with the Node process's privileges.

**Preconditions:** The calling application puts attacker-influenced text into one of those constructor options (for example, training arguments or a model file prefix taken from config or a request). Dataset entries are not injectable: labels and feature values are only serialized into the `.learn` file (`formats/svmlight.js:15-26`). `model_file_prefix` only injects when the value has no path separator, because the dataset file is opened with that string before the shell runs (`classifiers/svm/svmcommon.js:15-18`); a value containing `/` fails there first.

**Evidence:** `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:100` builds `this.train_command+" "+this.learn_args+" "+learnFile+" "+modelFile` and passes it to `execSync` at `:103`; `:146` does the same with `this.test_command`, `this.modelFileString`, and `/tmp/out_<timestamp>`, executed at `:148`. With a stub `liblinear_train`/`liblinear_test` on `PATH` and `learn_args: "; touch /tmp/PWN_args; #"`, `trainBatch` ran `liblinear_train ; touch /tmp/PWN_args; # ...` and created the marker; `train_command: "liblinear_train; touch /tmp/PWN_traincmd;"` and `test_command: "liblinear_test; touch /tmp/PWN_testcmd;"` did the same. A benign run created no marker. This is CVE-2020-4066 (GHSA-77qv-gh6f-pgh4); upstream fixed it in 0.9.5 by switching to `execFileSync` with argument arrays (commit 03475a6a), and this PR re-adds the pre-fix file.

**Impact:** Arbitrary command execution on the host running the classifier, as the Node process. Reach crosses a trust boundary and the effect is permanent, but the attacker must control a value the library's caller supplies as configuration (dataset contents cannot inject), so this is `medium` rather than `high`; the upstream CVSS 3.8 reflects the same privilege requirement.

**Fix:** Never join arguments into a shell string. Make `learn_args` an array and call `child_process.execFileSync(this.train_command, this.learn_args.concat([learnFile, modelFile]))`; call `execFileSync(this.test_command, [testFile, this.modelFileString, "/tmp/out_"+this.timestamp])` in `classifyBatch`; and use `execFileSync('liblinear_train', ['.'])` in `isInstalled`.

Review complete. The PR adds `selectize-plugin-a11y.js` (140 lines) — an a11y plugin for Selectize 0.12.4 that adds ARIA attributes, an assertive live region and a MutationObserver to announce option changes; the tree is byte-identical to upstream 1.0.4 (`0824359781`). The main problem is DOM XSS, reproduced end-to-end: line 52 hands the active option's label to `speak()`, line 28 parses `"
" + msg + "
"` as HTML, and line 29 inserts the result into a region attached to `document.body` (line 97). Because `.text()` decodes entities and jQuery evaluates inline `

findings.title: A crafted option label runs arbitrary script in the page through the live region
findings.body:
Option label text is re-parsed as HTML when it is announced, so a label containing markup runs script in the page. `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:28` builds `$("
" + msg + "
")`, which makes jQuery parse `msg` as HTML, and line 29 inserts the result into the live region. Line 52 passes `$target.text()` — the active option's label — as `msg`, and line 97 attaches that region to `document.body`. jQuery 3.3.1 `.html()` falls through to `this.empty().append(value)` for a non-string argument, and `domManip` then evaluates inline `" region html after : "
" globalThis.PWNED : 1 The same sink with an `img` payload leaves a live, body-attached `
` (region children `[DIV, IMG]`), which fires `onerror` in a real browser. This is CVE-2019-15482; upstream fixed it in 1.1.0. **Impact:** an actor who supplies an option label gets script execution in the origin of the page that renders the widget, against every user who opens that dropdown — a trust boundary crossing that repeats on each page load for as long as the stored label exists. Hence high. **Fix:** announce text, never markup. Build the node from text and let the message be inserted as text content: speak: function (msg) { var $container = $("
"); $container.text(msg); this.$region.html($container); } (what upstream 1.1.0 ships). A plain `this.$region.text(msg)` also works.

findings.title: Combobox never gets aria-haspopup because the attribute is spelled haspopup
findings.body:
The combobox is left without `aria-haspopup`, because line 118 spells the
attribute `haspopup`. jQuery passes unknown names straight to `setAttribute`, so
the element gets a meaningless `haspopup="listbox"` and assistive technology is
never told that the combobox opens a listbox — the one piece of state this plugin
adds for the popup.

**Evidence:** initialised jQuery 3.3.1 + selectize 0.12.4 + this file in jsdom and
read the attributes of `[role=combobox]`:

    haspopup attr      : "listbox"
    aria-haspopup attr : null

`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:115-123` is the only place the attribute is written, and
nothing else in the repo sets it.

**Impact:** every instance the plugin serves (broad, permanent for the life of the
page) loses the popup hint, so screen-reader users are not told that the field
expands. Discounted to low because the worst outcome is a missing hint: `role`,
`aria-expanded`, `aria-owns` and `aria-activedescendant` still work, and no data or
capability is exposed.

**Fix:** rename the key to `"aria-haspopup": "listbox"` in the `.attr({...})` call
at line 115.

findings.title: destroy() removes the live region but leaves its MutationObserver attached
findings.body:
`destroy()` removes the live region but never disconnects the MutationObserver, so
a destroyed widget keeps observing its own detached DOM.

Line 32 keeps the observer in a function-local `observer`, so no other code can
reach it; the destroy hook at lines 133-139 only runs
`self.accessibility.liveRegion.$region.remove()` and then the original `destroy`.
After teardown the observer stays registered on `$dropdown`, `$control` and
`$control_input` (lines 58-73) and its callback closes over `self`. Two
consequences:

- the closure holds the instance and its detached wrapper/dropdown subtree alive,
  so `destroy()` does not free the widget the way selectize's own docblock
  promises;
- any later mutation of those nodes re-enters the callback and writes into the
  already-removed region, where the announcement is silently dropped.

Line 97 also appends an assertive `role="log"` region to `document.body` per
instance, and only `destroy` removes it — an init path that disposes the element
without calling `destroy` leaves the region in `body` for the life of the page.

**Evidence:** code reading of lines 32, 58-73, 97 and 133-139. Measured that one
instance appends exactly one body-level `[aria-live]` region and that `destroy()`
removes it (`regions on body: 2` for two selects, `1` after destroying one), while
no code path reaches `observer.disconnect()`.

**Impact:** memory and DOM retained per destroyed widget on long-lived pages, plus
a stale writer. Contained to the page's own memory and cleared by a reload, so
info.

**Fix:** keep the observer on the instance (for example
`self.accessibility.liveRegion.observer`) and call `observer.disconnect()` in the
destroy hook before removing the region.

summary:
**Summary:** PR #2 adds `lib/linux.js`, the Linux backend that reads a MAC address from `/sys/class/net/<iface>/address`. It does so by concatenating the caller-supplied interface name into a string handed to `child_process.exec`, so the value is interpreted by the shell. I reproduced command execution through the public `one(iface, callback)` API and confirmed a second, narrower vector through `all()` with a kernel-reported interface name; the fix is to drop the shell (`execFile`/`fs.readFile`) and allow-list the interface name.

The rest of the change is benign: the file is wired in at `index.js:62-64`, and the `.trim().toLowerCase()` result is stable. One high-severity finding recorded; no other issues met the reporting bar.

findings.title: Interface name is interpolated into a shell command, so callers' iface input runs as OS commands
findings.body:
`lib/linux.js:4` builds a shell command by concatenating the caller's `iface`
argument: `exec("cat /sys/class/net/" + iface + "/address", ...)`. On Linux,
`macaddress.one(iface, callback)` passes a string `iface` unchanged to this sink
(`index.js:109`; the `typeof iface === 'function'` branch at `index.js:79` only
covers the no-`iface` form), so any metacharacter in that value is run by
`/bin/sh -c` with the application's privileges. `macaddress.all()` reaches the
same sink with kernel-reported interface names (`index.js:121`).

**Preconditions:** the consuming application forwards untrusted data as `iface`
to `macaddress.one(string, callback)` on Linux, and passes a callback
(`index.js:108`). `all()` needs an interface name containing shell
metacharacters to exist in the process's network namespace, which requires
`CAP_NET_ADMIN` or a container runtime that names interfaces from user config.

**Evidence:** calling `one('lo; touch /tmp/inv/marker; #', cb)` builds
`cat /sys/class/net/lo; touch /tmp/inv/marker; #/address` and the marker file is
created; the `#` comments out the appended `/address`. `one('lo', cb)` still
returns `00:00:00:00:00:00` and `one('nope0', cb)` returns the benign `cat`
error, so the injection is distinguishable from normal failures. Backtick and
`$()` payloads execute the same way. No escaping exists anywhere on the path:
the only `escape()` in the tree (`lib/windows.js:3-7`) escapes for a `RegExp`,
while the command it runs is the constant `ipconfig /all`. Linux interface names
may legally contain `;`, `#`, `$`, backticks and `>`, so the `all()` vector is
real even though it is narrower.

**Impact:** arbitrary OS command execution as the host process. The library
crosses a trust boundary — data the caller may have received from a remote
actor becomes shell code — and the effect is permanent (secrets read, data
destroyed, no supported undo). Per the severity policy in
`.ozone/skills/code-review` (reach × persistence), this grades high; the repo
defines no `critical` tier.

**Fix:** stop invoking a shell. Use
`execFile('cat', ['/sys/class/net/' + iface + '/address'])`, or read the file
with `fs.readFile`, and validate `iface` against `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,15}$` before
use.

summary:
Review complete. Findings recorded (1 medium, 3 low), working tree clean.

**Summary:** The PR adds `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js`, a wrapper that shells out to the LibLinear binaries. Its previous form built a command string and ran it through `execSync`; this version passes the program and its arguments separately to `execFileSync` (`SvmLinear.js:97`, `:143`), so the shell-injection issue that motivated the change is gone — all paths, including `model_file_prefix` and the learn/test file names, now travel as argv elements.

The rewrite has real defects of its own. The installation probe at `:46` hands a whole command line to `execFileSync` as the executable path, so `isInstalled()` is false for everyone and the classifier cannot be constructed at all; the shipped tests gate on that same probe and skip silently. Behind that blocker sit three further functional bugs that each need their own fix: a changed `learn_args` type that every in-repo caller still uses as a string, a serialization pair reading a field that never exists, and a model cache that is not invalidated on retrain. Overall: the security fix is correct, but the component ships unusable and I would not merge without the probe fix.

findings.title: SvmLinear cannot be constructed: installation probe looks for a file named 'liblinear_train .'
findings.body:
`new SvmLinear(opts)` always throws "Cannot find the executable 'liblinear_train'" — even when `liblinear_train` is on `PATH`. The installation probe passes the whole command line `'liblinear_train .'` as the *executable path*; `execFileSync` does no shell word-splitting, so the lookup is for a PATH entry literally named `liblinear_train .` (with a space and a dot). No such file exists in any normal install, the `ENOENT` is caught, `isInstalled()` returns false, and the constructor at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:37-41` throws. The classifier is therefore unusable for every caller, and with it the `trainBatch`/`classify` path this file exists to provide.

**Evidence:** with a stub `liblinear_train` on `PATH` (Node v24):

```
execFileSync('liblinear_train .')        -> ENOENT          // SvmLinear.js:46
execFileSync('liblinear_train', ['.'])   -> runs the stub
execSync('liblinear_train .')            -> runs the stub    // the form this commit replaced
SvmLinear.isInstalled()                  -> false
node classifiers/svm/SvmLinearDemo.js    -> Error ... at new SvmLinear (SvmLinear.js:40)
```

The unchanged sibling answers the same question correctly with a shell (`classifiers/svm/SvmPerf.js:44`, `execSync("svm_perf_learn")`). The regression does not surface in tests because `test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:90`, `test/classifiersTest/SvmMulticlassTest.js:12` and `test/classifiersTest/multilabel/MetaLabelerSvmTest.js:95` all gate on the same probe: mocha reports "SvmLinear tests skipped", 0 passing, with the binary present.

**Impact:** functional break, not a security one: every consumer of the added classifier fails at construction, so the feature ships dead and its whole test suite is silently skipped. Reach is broad (all users of `SvmLinear`); the effect is a thrown error rather than data loss, so `medium`.

**Fix:** restore an argv probe and stop treating a non-zero exit as "missing" — real `liblinear_train` exits non-zero for the bogus `.` argument, so `execFileSync('liblinear_train', ['.'])` alone still returns false. Either catch only `ENOENT` (`if (err.code !== 'ENOENT') return true`) or probe with `which`/`where`, and use `this.train_command` rather than the hardcoded name.

findings.title: Trained SvmLinear models serialize to undefined, and restored models classify with no model
findings.body:
A trained `SvmLinear` model is not serializable: `toJSON()` returns `undefined` because it reads `this.mapFeatureToWeight`, a property no code in this file ever assigns. The model lives in `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` (set at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:112-113`, read at `:117-120` and `:153-171`). `fromJSON` writes back into the same unused field (`:226-228`).

**Evidence:** the round trip through the library's own wrappers — `EnhancedClassifier.toJSON` delegates at `classifiers/EnhancedClassifier.js:493`, `fromJSON` at `:505`; `BinaryRelevance` delegates at `classifiers/multilabel/BinaryRelevance.js:225` and `:231-234`:

```
trained instance: getModelWeights() = {"0":-5,"1":5}   toJSON() = undefined
JSON.stringify(enhanced)  = {"pastTrainingSamples":[]}          // classifier key dropped
after fromJSON: classify() -> TypeError ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE: The "path" argument must be of type
                            string ... Received undefined        // setModel(undefined) -> readFileSync, :111
multilabel (BinaryRelevance): toJSON -> {} ; restored getAllClasses() = [] , classify() = []   // no error
```

Even a correct payload is not enough: `fromJSON` must write `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` *and* repopulate `allLabels`, which `classify` reads at line 156. The sibling `SvmPerf` does the round trip correctly with the same field name throughout (`classifiers/svm/SvmPerf.js:84,113,125-131`).

**Impact:** saving and reloading an `SvmLinear`-backed classifier loses the model; the single-label path then throws, and the multi-label path silently returns no labels at all — wrong answers for every restored model. Contained to the caller's own model and recoverable by retraining, so `low`.

**Fix:** serialize the field that is actually used — `toJSON: return this.mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` and `fromJSON: set it and refresh this.allLabels = Object.keys(...)`, mirroring `SvmPerf`.

findings.title: String learn_args (used by every shipped caller) crashes trainBatch with TypeError
findings.body:
The `learn_args` option now has to be an array, but every caller shipped in this repository passes a string, so `trainBatch` dies with `TypeError: args.join is not a function` before any process is spawned.

`this.learn_args = opts.learn_args || []` (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:28`) accepts a string, and `String.prototype.concat` at line 94 turns the string plus the two paths into one string (`"-c 20" + "/x.learn,/x.model"`), so line 95 calls `.join` on a string. If line 95 were passed, line 97 would then throw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` because `execFileSync` rejects a string for its `args` parameter.

**Evidence:** string callers in the tree: `classifiers/svm/SvmLinearDemo.js:18` (`learn_args: "-c 20"`), `classifiers/svm/SvmLinearMulticlassDemo.js:27`, `test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:91`, `test/classifiersTest/SvmMulticlassTest.js:18`, `test/classifiersTest/multilabel/MetaLabelerSvmTest.js:96` (`"-c 20.0"`). `README.md:442` shows the same string form (there bound to `SvmPerf`, which still documents a string at `classifiers/svm/SvmPerf.js:13`).

```
"-c 20".concat(['/a.learn','/a.model'])  -> "-c 20/a.learn,/a.model"   (a string)
args.join(...)                           -> TypeError: args.join is not a function   (SvmLinear.js:95)
execFileSync(cmd, "-c 20")               -> ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE: The "args" argument must be of type object
```

**Preconditions:** reachable once the construction bug is fixed; `trainBatch` is the first code that touches `learn_args`, so callers currently stop earlier, in the constructor.

**Impact:** the change silently alters a public option's type and leaves every in-repo call site broken, including the two demos and three test files. Contained to one library API and recoverable by fixing the call sites, so `low`.

**Fix:** normalize in the constructor so both shapes work — `this.learn_args = _.isArray(opts.learn_args) ? opts.learn_args : String(opts.learn_args || '').split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean)`. Passing the result as argv elements keeps the shell-injection fix intact.

findings.title: Retraining an SvmLinear instance keeps classifying with the previous model's weights
findings.body:
Retraining an instance keeps answering with the first model. `trainBatch` writes a new model path (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:104`) and refreshes `allLabels` (`:83-84`), but never clears `this.mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight`; the lazy load in `classify` only runs when that property is falsy (`:153-154`). Every `classify` after a second `trainBatch` therefore scores against model #1 while the label list comes from model #2.

**Evidence:** two model files for the same two labels, the second with the sign flipped (weights rows `0`, `5` vs `0`, `-5`):

```
model A                -> classify([1]) = 0   weights {"0":{"1":5},"1":{"1":-5}}
retrain to model B     -> classify([1]) = 0   weights {"0":{"1":5},"1":{"1":-5}}   // stale
fresh instance, model B-> classify([1]) = 1   weights {"0":{"1":-5},"1":{"1":5}}
```

This is the normal path, not an edge case: `classifiers/svm/SvmLinearDemo.js:34-44` calls `trainBatch` once per partition and classifies the fold with the same instance, and `classifiers/multilabel/BinaryRelevance.js` retrains its per-label classifiers. The shipped tests do not catch it because `test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:90` and friends skip whenever `isInstalled()` is false.

**Impact:** silently wrong classifications on every retrained instance — cross-validation folds, incremental workflows and multi-label retraining all score against a stale model, with no error and no warning. Contained to the process's own results and recoverable by constructing a fresh instance, so `low`.

**Fix:** invalidate the cache whenever a new model is trained — `this.mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight = null` (and `this.allLabels = ...`) at the top of `trainBatch`, or store the loaded model keyed by `this.modelFileString` and reload when it changes.

summary:
Coverage is complete: I reproduced the injection fix, the traversal surface, the integration with `index.js`, and the baseline load failure, on six Node runtimes.

**Summary**

The PR re-adds `lib/linux.js`, the Linux backend that `index.js:63` already required, so `require('macaddress')` no longer throws `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on Linux (verified against the parent commit). It switches from `exec` to `execFile` with an argument array, which does close the shell-injection vector of CVE-2018-13797 — `$(id)` and backtick payloads are not executed, and `test.js` and `one()`/`all()` work on this host. Two residual weaknesses remain: `iface` is still concatenated into the `cat` path (`lib/linux.js:4`), which on Node below 18 lets a NUL byte truncate the argument and read arbitrary files, and the result is returned without the MAC validation the other backends perform; I recorded the first as a medium finding. The fix as a whole is a clear improvement, so the change is approvable with that follow-up.

findings.title: Untrusted iface lets callers read arbitrary files as the MAC address on Node below 18
findings.body:
`macaddress.one(iface, cb)` passes `iface` unvalidated into the `cat` argument in
`lib/linux.js:4`. A caller that forwards untrusted input (the threat model of
CVE-2018-13797) can therefore choose the file that `cat` reads, and whatever the file
contains comes back as the "MAC address" string.

The switch to `execFile` closes shell metacharacter injection — `$(id)` and backticks
are not executed — but the path is still built by string concatenation, and the
mandatory trailing `/address` segment is not a constraint on Node runtimes that do
not validate NUL bytes in `spawn` arguments: the kernel truncates the argument at the
first NUL, dropping `/address` and everything after it.

**Preconditions:** the embedding application passes an untrusted value as `iface`
(same assumption as the CVE this change fixes) and runs Node that accepts NUL bytes in
child arguments — verified on 0.12.18, 6.17.1, 12.22.12 and 16.20.2, which covers the
versions `.travis.yml` tests. Node 18.20.4, 20.19.0 and 24.22.0 reject the call with
`ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`; on those runtimes only a directory traversal that lands on a
file literally named `address` still works (`one("../../../../../tmp/adtest/address")`
returned that file's contents), which bounds the damage there.

**Evidence:** end-to-end through the public API on Node 16.20.2:

    node -e 'require("./index.js").one("../../../etc/hostname\u0000", function(e,m){console.log(e, m)})'
    -> 71d4426ba9fc              (host hostname; /etc/passwd likewise returned in full)

Direct backend call, same runtime: `require("./lib/linux.js")("../../../../etc/passwd\u0000x", cb)`
yields the passwd contents. `lib/linux.js:4` builds the argument; `index.js:109` forwards
`iface` from the caller without any check.

**Impact:** an untrusted actor who controls `iface` reads any file the host process can
read, and the content is returned through the documented `(err, mac)` callback, so it
usually lands in the application's log, telemetry, or UI. Reach crosses a trust
boundary and the disclosure is permanent, but it needs a runtime below Node 18 and a
caller that forwards untrusted input, so I grade it one tier down from high: **medium**
(repo instructions define no `critical` policy).

**Fix:** reject `iface` before building the path — Linux interface names are at most 15
characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]`, so `/^[\w.:-]{1,15}$/.test(iface)` is sufficient, and
an invalid name should call back with an error. Replacing `execFile("cat", ...)` with
`fs.readFile("/sys/class/net/" + iface + "/address", "utf8", ...)` removes the child
process entirely; parsing the result against a MAC regex, as `lib/unix.js:9-13` does,
keeps malformed content out of the caller's value.

summary: The change adds `lib/formats/ssh.js` (114 lines) back to the tree, restoring SSH-format public/private key parsing that `lib/formats/auto.js` and `lib/key.js` already require. The added file is byte-identical to the sshpk 1.13.1 release — I confirmed this against the upstream tarballs and against upstream commit `4d01aede`, from which the rest of the checkout is unchanged — so the parser works, `npm test` runs 536/537 (the one failure is a pre-existing Node-version issue in `test/fingerprint.js`), and both defects that upstream fixed in 1.13.2 (commit `46065d3`) are carried along with it. I reproduced both through the public API: a quadratic regex stall on crafted key input and a bogus `"undefined"` comment on ordinary comment-less keys. Two findings are recorded; a knowledge note on keeping the 1.13.2 regexes and the `m[3]` guard could not be published because `ozone knowledge save` acknowledges writes it never stores (reported).

findings.title: Crafted SSH public key stalls the parser quadratically (CVE-2018-3737 ReDoS)
findings.body:
`Key.parse()` runs a quadratic regular-expression scan on attacker-supplied SSH
public keys, blocking the Node.js event loop. A ~14 KB string stalls the process
for most of a second; the cost grows with the square of the input, so repeated
requests exhaust the single thread that serves every concurrent caller.

**Evidence:** both regexes in the new format parser backtrack catastrophically
when the key line is invalid in a particular way. `SSHKEY_RE` (`lib/formats/ssh.js:17`)
is quadratic on a long space/tab run followed by a non-space character and a
newline; `SSHKEY_RE2` (`lib/formats/ssh.js:19`) is quadratic on a long base64 run
followed by `=\n`, because `[a-zA-Z0-9+\/ \t\n]+[=]*` of length *m* is retried
against `(.*)$`, which cannot cross the newline, giving O(m²) work. The second
regex runs again on the retry path at `lib/formats/ssh.js:51`.

Measured through the public API (node v24.22.2, default arguments):

```
parseKey('ssh-rsa A' + ' '.repeat(n) + '=\nB')
  n=4000  ->   73 ms
  n=8000  ->  308 ms
  n=16000 -> 1450 ms      (4x input, ~20x time)

parseKey('ssh-rsa ' + 'A'.repeat(n) + '=\nB')
  n=8000  ->   79 ms
  n=32000 -> 1141 ms
  n=64000 -> 4802 ms
```

The same `Buffer` input takes the same time. No option or explicit format is
needed: `lib/index.js:14` → `lib/key.js:216-238` (format defaults to `'auto'`,
`lib/key.js:219`) → `lib/formats/auto.js:24-27` (string) and `:33-36` (Buffer) →
`lib/formats/ssh.js:28,30,51`. `PrivateKey.parse()` (`lib/private-key.js:32`) and
`bin/sshpk-conv` take the same path. Neither this file nor `lib/formats/auto.js`
bounds the input length before the regex pass; the length checks in
`lib/formats/rfc4253.js:79` and `lib/ssh-buffer.js:90,103,144` only run after the
bytes are decoded.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes untrusted data to `parseKey`/`Key.parse`
(the normal reason to use this library, e.g. an "add your SSH key" endpoint that
accepts a few KB or more from an unauthenticated client).

**Impact:** this file is byte-identical to the sshpk 1.13.1 release; upstream
replaced both regexes in 1.13.2 (commit 46065d3) for this reason, published as
CVE-2018-3737. Availability only — any parsing service blocks all of its
concurrent work for the duration of the scan, and an unprivileged caller can
re-trigger it at will. Reach is broad (every request handled by the stalled
process) and persistence is recoverable (the stall ends, then repeats), so
**medium** under this run's scale.

**Fix:** use the upstream 1.13.2 patterns, which remove the ambiguity:

```js
var SSHKEY_RE = /^([a-z0-9-]+)[ \t]+([a-zA-Z0-9+\/]+[=]*)([ \t]+([^ \t][^\n]*[\n]*)?)?$/;
var SSHKEY_RE2 = /^([a-z0-9-]+)[ \t\n]+([a-zA-Z0-9+\/][a-zA-Z0-9+\/ \t\n=]*)([^a-zA-Z0-9+\/ \t\n=].*)?$/;
```

and, independently, reject inputs above a sane length before matching.

findings.title: Comment-less public keys parse with comment "undefined" and re-serialize with a bogus trailing comment
findings.body:
Parsing an SSH public key that has no comment returns a key whose `comment` is
the literal string `"undefined"`. Serializing the key then appends ` undefined`
to the line, and the documented `'(unnamed)'` default plus any `options.filename`
provenance are both lost.

**Evidence:** when the key line has no comment, `SSHKEY_RE` matches with its
optional group 3 absent, so `m[3]` is `undefined` (`lib/formats/ssh.js:17`).
`rfc4253.readInternal` always sets `ret.consumed` (`lib/formats/rfc4253.js:128-131`),
so the comment-recovery block at `lib/formats/ssh.js:65` always runs for a
comment-less key, and line 74 concatenates the missing group:

```js
var data = m[2] + m[3];        // "AAAA...c=" + undefined  ->  "AAAA...c=undefined"
```

`realOffset` lands exactly at the end of the base64 body, so the trailer sliced at
`lib/formats/ssh.js:89` is `"undefined"`, and it is assigned as the comment at
`:91-92`. `lib/key.js:237-238` then skips the `options.filename` fallback because
a non-empty string is truthy.

Reproduced with the ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 test key from `test/horrors.js` and with an
RSA key:

```
parseKey(key, 'ssh').comment                -> "undefined"   (expected "(unnamed)")
parseKey(key, 'ssh').toString('ssh')        -> "ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 AAAA...c= undefined"
parseKey(key, 'ssh', '/home/u/id.pub')      -> "undefined"   (expected "/home/u/id.pub")
```

A key that does have a comment is parsed correctly, so the defect hits the most
common input shape (a bare `.pub` line) and is silent — `npm test` is 536 pass /
1 fail, and the failure (`test/fingerprint.js:117`) is unrelated and pre-existing.
No test covers a comment-less key that matches `SSHKEY_RE`.

**Impact:** wrong metadata travels into anything written from the key
(`key.toString('ssh')`, `bin/sshpk-conv` output, `authorized_keys` lines, comment-
based labels). Fingerprints and signatures are unaffected, so keys still work;
the damage is a wrong, invented label that cannot be distinguished from a real
comment afterwards. Contained to the parsed key and recoverable by the caller, so
**low**.

**Fix:** one line, as upstream 1.13.2 did:

```js
var data = m[2] + (m[3] ? m[3] : '');
```

summary:
Reviewed the single added file and the code around it. No findings to record.

**What the change does:** it adds `lib/formats/ssh.js` (114 lines), the `ssh` public-key reader/writer that the rest of this tree already expects (`lib/key.js:31` requires it, `lib/formats/auto.js:9` routes `ssh-`/`ecdsa-` strings to it).

**Assessment:** the added file is byte-identical (blob `7f88ceb`) to `sshpk` 1.13.2, i.e. the upstream fix for CVE-2018-3737 (fixed by commit `46065d3`), not the pre-fix code from the baseline's parent commit. I confirmed this empirically: an adversarial timing sweep against the pre-fix regexes is quadratic (`'ssh-rsa AAAA' + '='*64000 + '\nZ'` takes seconds), while the added regexes and the full `parseKey(..., 'ssh')` path, including the comment-recovery loop at `lib/formats/ssh.js:74-92`, stay linear from 8 KB to 2 MB. The file's API calls match this commit's `rfc4253` (`readInternal(ret, 'public', kbuf)`, `consumed` at `lib/formats/rfc4253.js:130`), and the suite passes 536/537 — the one failure (`test/fingerprint.js:117`) also fails on the pristine upstream tree and never touches this file. Minor upstream quirks in the restored file (comment recovery for line-wrapped keys, deprecated `new Buffer`, lenient trailing-garbage parsing) are pre-existing 1.13.2 behaviour with no meaningful impact path, so I left them unreported.

The PR adds only `src/run.js`, the two async process helpers (`run` via `exec`, `runWithSpawn` via `spawn`) that every other module in the tree already requires — without it the package cannot even be loaded. The code is the pre-fix upstream file and works, but its `exec`-based default export puts caller-built command strings through `/bin/sh`, and the existing clone, tag and ignored-file call sites paste raw values into those strings; I reproduced command execution through both `--remote-url` and `--start-tag` against the real CLI. One high finding is recorded; the remaining rough edges (no `error` listener on the spawned child, per-chunk string conversion of stdout) only bite on paths where the tool is already unusable, so I did not file them.

findings.title: run() executes command strings through a shell, so remoteUrl, tags and ignoredFiles can inject commands
findings.body:
`src/run.js:10` sends its command string to `child_process.exec`, which runs it through `/bin/sh`. Every call site builds that string by pasting in a value with no quoting, so any value containing `;`, `&&`, `$(...)` or backticks runs as an extra command with the tool's privileges. The reachable sinks are:

- `src/index.js:225` — `git clone ${remoteUrl} ${_tmpDir}`
- `src/index.js:116` and `src/index.js:118` — `git ls-files ${ignoredFile}`, `git checkout -- ${ignoredFile}`
- `src/index.js:127` — `git diff ${startTag} ${endTag} --binary > ${patchFile}`
- `src/check-out-tag.js:6` — `git rev-parse ${tag}` (called with `startTag`/`endTag` from `src/index.js:64, 69, 89, 97, 102, 141, 158`)
- `src/commit-and-tag.js:8` — `git tag ${tag}`

Nothing in the repo quotes or validates these values; `git-status.js` and `git-remove-all.js` already avoid the shell by using `runWithSpawn`, but the clone and tag paths do not.

**Preconditions:** The caller controls one of those values. Typed on the CLI by the same person (`bin/git-diff-apply.js:8-20` passes yargs values straight through) this is self-injection. It becomes a trust-boundary crossing for library consumers: `ember-cli-update` 1.0.0 passes `remoteUrl: blueprint.outputRepo` (`src/compare.js:79`), and `outputRepo` is read from `.ember-cli-update.json` in the checked-out project (`src/load-safe-blueprint-file.js`, which copies unknown blueprint keys through). A malicious repository therefore controls `remoteUrl` and runs commands on a maintainer's machine or in CI.

**Evidence:** Reproduced against the checked-out tree after `npm install`:

```
$ node bin/git-diff-apply.js --remote-url 'x; touch /tmp/pwned-remote; #' --start-tag v1 --end-tag v3
...
$ ls /tmp/pwned-remote
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 ...            # payload ran even though `git clone x` failed
```

Tag path, with a valid remote so the clone succeeds:

```
$ node bin/git-diff-apply.js --remote-url /tmp/remote2 --start-tag 'v1; touch /tmp/pwned-tag; #' --end-tag v3
...
$ ls /tmp/pwned-tag
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 ...
```

**Impact:** Arbitrary command execution as the user or CI job running git-diff-apply, escalating to whatever credentials that context holds. The same root cause also breaks legitimate values (a remote path or tag containing a space is split into extra shell words). This is CVE-2019-10776; the repo defines no `critical` tier, so it is graded `high`: reach crosses a trust boundary and the effect is permanent.

**Fix:** Restore one invariant — no caller-supplied value is ever parsed by a shell. Pass argument arrays to `spawn` (the existing `runWithSpawn`, `src/run.js:15`) instead of building strings: `runWithSpawn('git', ['clone', remoteUrl, _tmpDir])` for `src/index.js:225` (the upstream 0.22.2 fix), plus the tag, ignored-file and `git diff` sinks, piping `git diff` stdout to the patch file instead of using `>`. Keep `startCommand`/`endCommand` (`src/create-custom-remote.js:25, 38`) as shell strings — running an arbitrary command there is the documented `--create-custom-diff` feature, not an injection.

summary:
The change adds a single new file, `src/run.js`, restoring the command runner that every other module in the tree imports: a `run()` that executes a command string via `child_process.exec`, and a `runWithSpawn()` that spawns argv arrays. Ship it as is and the package works again, but `run()` reintroduces the shell sink that CVE-2019-10776 / GHSA-84cm-v6jp-gjmr describes: callers concatenate `remoteUrl` (src/index.js:225), tag names (src/check-out-tag.js:6, src/commit-and-tag.js:8), and ignored-file paths (src/index.js:116-118) into that string, and I reproduced arbitrary command execution from a crafted URL — including a silent variant that completes with "success". Making the runner shell-free, as the sibling `runWithSpawn` already is, closes it.

Beyond that, the spawn path lacks an `error` listener, so a spawn failure crashes the process and leaves its promise pending; other robustness gaps I found (signal handling, buffer decoding, unbounded stderr) are speculative for git's actual output and were left unreported. Two findings recorded; repo left clean.

findings.title: Shell command injection: run() executes interpolated remoteUrl and tag names through /bin/sh
findings.body:
`run()` hands its argument string to `child_process.exec`, which runs it through `/bin/sh -c`. Callers build that string by interpolating values that come from outside the process, so a `;`, `$()` or backtick in `remoteUrl`, a tag name, or an ignored file path runs as a separate shell command with the developer's privileges. This is CVE-2019-10776 / GHSA-84cm-v6jp-gjmr (rated critical upstream).

**Evidence:**

The sink — src/run.js:6,10:

```js
const execPromise = promisify(exec);
...
let { stdout } = await execPromise(command, options);
```

The unescaped callers — src/index.js:225 `` `git clone ${remoteUrl} ${_tmpDir}` ``, src/index.js:116,118 (`${ignoredFile}`), src/index.js:127 (`${startTag} ${endTag}`), src/check-out-tag.js:6 (`git rev-parse ${tag}`), src/commit-and-tag.js:8 (`git tag ${tag}`).

Reproduced against a clean local repo and a local remote repo:

```
$ node bin/git-diff-apply.js --remote-url='/tmp/repro/remote; touch /tmp/repro/PWNED; #' \
    --start-tag=v1 --end-tag=v2
$ ls /tmp/repro/PWNED      # created, before the clone could fail
```

The `$()` form is silent — the tool reports `success` and exits 0 while the payload runs:

```
--remote-url='/tmp/repro/remote$(touch${IFS}/tmp/repro/PWNED2)'
```

Git accepts shell metacharacters in ref names (`git tag 'ev;id;'` succeeds; only space, `~^:?*[\`, `..`, `@{` are rejected), so a tag name read from an untrusted remote repo (`git ls-remote --tags`) and passed as `--start-tag`/`--end-tag` also injects at src/check-out-tag.js:6 and src/commit-and-tag.js:8. The same file already shows the safe pattern: `runWithSpawn` at src/run.js:15-23 spawns without a shell and is used at src/git-remove-all.js:11,61.

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution in the caller's shell for anyone who can influence a `remoteUrl`, tag name, or ignored-file argument — including a repository owner whose tag names a wrapper passes through, or a shared/CI-config URL. Reach crosses a trust boundary and the result is permanent (attacker code can read keys, credentials, and the working tree). Upstream rates it critical; per this review's policy the finding stops at high.

**Fix:** keep one invariant — no untrusted value is ever parsed by a shell. Either replace `run()` with `execFile`/`spawn` plus an argv array, or move the interpolating call sites to `runWithSpawn`, e.g. `runWithSpawn('git', ['clone', remoteUrl, _tmpDir])` (the upstream 0.22.2 fix), `['rev-parse', tag]`, `['tag', tag]`, `['ls-files', '--', ignoredFile]`, and write the patch file with `git diff` stdout instead of a `>` redirection.

findings.title: runWithSpawn has no 'error' listener, so a failed spawn kills the process and leaves its promise pending
findings.body:
`runWithSpawn` listens for `stdout`, `stderr` and `close` only (src/run.js:24,27,30) — never `error`. When the command cannot start (git not on PATH, a `cwd` that no longer exists, a missing `.cmd` shim on Windows), Node emits `error` on the child process with no listener, which becomes an uncaught exception, and the promise returned at src/run.js:16 never settles.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e "
const { runWithSpawn } = require('./src/run');
runWithSpawn('definitely-not-a-real-binary', ['x']).catch(e => console.log('rejected', e.message));
process.on('uncaughtException', e => { console.log('UNCAUGHT:', e.code); process.exit(7); });
setTimeout(() => console.log('promise never settled'), 1500);"
UNCAUGHT: ENOENT
```

**Impact:** the first call in a run is `git status --porcelain` at src/git-status.js:6, made from src/index.js:200 inside a `try/catch` meant to report `'Not a git repository'`. That catch never runs because the throw happens outside the promise, so the CLI dies with a raw Node stack trace instead of a useful error, and a host that installs its own `uncaughtException` handler hangs instead. Contained to the machine running the tool, and a retry after fixing the environment succeeds, so this is informational.

**Fix:** attach `child.on('error', reject)` next to the stdio handlers so a spawn failure rejects the promise and callers' existing `try/catch` handles it.

summary:
The change re-adds the CLI entry point `angular-http-server.js` for the SPA dev server, with request URL → filesystem path mapping delegated to a new `lib/get-file-path-from-url` helper and `--path` handling consolidated into one `basePath` (`angular-http-server.js:20`, `:68`, `:101`). Read as the upstream path-traversal fix (CVE-2018-3713), the logic at the call site is sound: rejected requests resolve to `dummy`, which fails `fs.stat` and falls back to `index.html`, and no containment check is done locally but none is needed given the helper's `startsWith(basePath)` and `../` rejection.

The problem is that this PR ships only the entry point: `lib/get-file-path-from-url.js` exists in no commit of this repository, so `node angular-http-server.js` aborts at line 12 with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` and the traversal protection the change is meant to add is absent from the diff. Everything else in the file (port parsing, silent `pem` errors, `returnDistFile` calling `process.exit` inside a request, 200-for-everything) is either upstream behaviour unchanged by this diff or not reachable through normal use, so I filed nothing on it.

findings.title: Entry point requires ./lib/get-file-path-from-url, which this change does not add, so the server cannot start
findings.body:
The added entry point imports a helper that does not exist in this repository:
`const getFileNameFromUrl = require('./lib/get-file-path-from-url')`
(`angular-http-server.js:12`). Node resolves that require at module load, so
`node angular-http-server.js` — and the `angular-http-server` bin declared in
`package.json` — dies with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` before the index.html check or
`server.listen` ever run.

**Evidence:**

- `git ls-tree -r HEAD --name-only` lists no `lib/` directory, and
  `git log --all -- lib` has no commits: the module was never in this tree.
- `cd example && node ../angular-http-server.js` →
  `Error: Cannot find module './lib/get-file-path-from-url'` with the require
  stack pointing at `angular-http-server.js:12`.
- `test/mocha.opts:2` targets `lib/**/*.spec.js`, which also matches nothing.
- The missing module is where the whole URL → filesystem-path mapping lives.
  `requestListener` passes `req.url` and `basePath` straight to it
  (`angular-http-server.js:68`) and hands the result to
  `fs.stat`/`fs.readFileSync` (`:70`, `:73`) with no containment check of its
  own. So the directory-traversal protection this change exists to introduce is
  not part of the change at all.

**Impact:** Every documented use of the package fails immediately (README quick
start, `--path`, `--ssl`, `--cors`); the release is unusable, and the path
traversal fix cannot be evaluated because none of it shipped. The failure is
loud and at startup, with no data or state affected, so this is a release
blocker rather than a security exposure.

**Fix:** Ship `lib/get-file-path-from-url.js` (and its spec) in this change.
If the helper is not ready, keep path resolution inside `angular-http-server.js`
so the entry point never requires a module the package does not contain.

summary:
**What the change does:** it adds `lib/conversion.js`, the module `index.js` already requires — the factory that defaults global options, writes html/header/footer temp files, and dispatches to the `phantom-server` or `dedicated-process` strategy. The file is byte-identical to upstream `phantom-html-to-pdf@0.6.0`, so this is a restoration of the library's entry point rather than a hand-written patch, and the review centres on the behaviour it introduces.

**Assessment:** the change is functionally sound and matches upstream, but the path handling it introduces is unsafe: the caller-supplied `tmpId` is joined into filesystem paths unchecked, which I reproduced as a write outside `tmpDir` with attacker content. A second, smaller defect is that all converter instances share one process-wide options object. Both are recorded as findings; the rest of the file (option defaulting, the `waitForJS` guard, the `file:///` URL default) raised only hypotheses I could not turn into a failure path, so I left them unreported.

findings.title: Unvalidated tmpId writes HTML and PDF files outside tmpDir
findings.body:
