Grade `medium`: it crosses a trust boundary (uninitialized heap bytes into application output) and is re-triggerable by an unprivileged caller, discounted because it needs a non-integer bound and leaks roughly one byte per call.

**Fix:** normalize the range before it reaches `Buffer#copy` - after the clamps at `bl.js:138-145`, truncate `srcStart` and `srcEnd` to integers, and advance `bufoff` by the byte count returned by `Buffer#copy` instead of by `l`.

findings.title: `slice()` with an inverted range returns bytes instead of an empty buffer
findings.body:
`slice()` and `copy()` return real data when `start` is greater than `end`. `new BufferList(['AAAAA','BBBBB']).slice(-5, 1)` returns `'B'` and `.slice(-5, -6)` returns `'BBBB'`; `Buffer#slice` on the concatenated bytes returns an empty buffer for both.

**Why:** after the negative adjustment, `srcStart` is 5 and `srcEnd` is 1, so `len`/`bytes` are `-4` (`bl.js:149-150`). The single-buffer fast-path test `bytes <= this._bufs[off[0]].length - start` (`bl.js:174`) is trivially true for a negative `bytes`, so `Buffer#slice(start, start + bytes)` (`bl.js:177`) is called with `slice(0, -4)`, and a negative end is read as "4 bytes before the end of the buffer". With `dst` supplied, `bl.js:176` copies those bytes and returns the count.

**Evidence:**

```js
const two = new BufferList(['AAAAA','BBBBB'])
two.slice(-5, 1)     // 'B'   (native: '')
two.slice(-5, -6)    // 'BBBB' (native: '')
two.slice(3, 1)      // ''    (correct, because start 3 is not on a buffer boundary)
two.toString('utf8', -5, 1)  // 'B'
```

The fast path is reached whenever the negative `bytes` is still smaller than the remaining length of the first buffer (`bl.js:174`), which covers the boundary cases and every case with a negative `bytes` where `start` is at or past the buffer start; the result is always a reinterpretation of a negative `Buffer#slice` end.

**Impact:** the caller receives bytes it asked to exclude - a range computed from user input that ends up inverted discloses the tail of an internal buffer instead of returning empty, and any length check on the result sees a non-empty buffer. Grade `low`: one call site, wrong data returned rather than memory disclosure, and the trigger is a caller-side inverted range.

**Fix:** treat an empty or inverted range as empty - return `dst || Buffer.alloc(0)` when `srcEnd <= srcStart`, next to the existing early returns at `bl.js:142-145`.

findings.title: `indexOf()` and `shallowSlice()` throw TypeError when the buffer list is empty
findings.body:
`indexOf()`, `shallowSlice()` and `get()` throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` when the list has no internal buffers, instead of returning `-1`, an empty list or `undefined`. The empty state is normal, not an edge case: `_read()` calls `consume(size)` (`bl.js:104-105`), so any list that has been read from or drained ends up with zero buffers while `length` is 0.

**Why:** `_offset(offset)` returns `undefined` when `this._bufs` is empty and `offset !== 0` (`bl.js:41-48`: the loop body never runs). The callers dereference the result without a guard: `bl.js:311-312` in `indexOf`, `bl.js:219-220` in `shallowSlice`, and `bl.js:123-124` in `get` (which also lets `get(0)` through because its bound check is `index > this.length`).

**Evidence:**

```js
const bl = new BufferList(); bl.append(Buffer.from('abcdef')); bl.consume(6)
bl.indexOf('a', 3)              // THROW TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0')   (native: -1)
new BufferList().indexOf('a', 1)   // same THROW
new BufferList().shallowSlice(2, 3) // same THROW   (expected: empty BufferList)
new BufferList().get(0)            // same THROW   (expected: undefined)
new BufferList().indexOf('a', 0)   // -1, only offset 0 is safe
```

**Impact:** an unhandled exception where the documented contract is a `-1` return (`README.md:140`). In a stream parser that reads and then searches with a non-zero offset, a fully drained list turns a normal miss into a thrown error; if the offset comes from the request (e.g. a resume position) the process can be crashed. Grade `low`: one request is affected and the thrown error is recoverable unless the caller leaves it unhandled.

**Fix:** make `_offset` total - return `[0, 0]` when `this._bufs.length === 0` - or guard the three callers so an empty list yields `-1` / an empty `BufferList` / `undefined`.

findings.title: `end()` drops the encoding and callback arguments of the stream end() signature
findings.body:
`BufferList#end()` declares a single parameter and forwards only the chunk, so the `encoding` and callback arguments of the standard `Writable#end(chunk[, encoding][, callback])` signature are dropped. `bl.end('ff', 'hex', cb)` stores the three ASCII bytes `6666` instead of the byte `0xff`, and `cb` is never called, so code waiting for stream completion hangs.

**Why:** `bl.js:109-110` overrides the inherited method:

```js
BufferList.prototype.end = function end (chunk) {
  DuplexStream.prototype.end.call(this, chunk)
```

`encoding` and `callback` are not declared, so JavaScript discards them before the call. The method also returns `undefined`, so `bl.end('x').slice()` throws, unlike the rest of the API, which returns `this`.

**Evidence:**

```js
const bl = new BufferList()
bl.on('error', () => {})
bl.end('ff', 'hex', () => { console.log('done') })
// bl.toString('hex') === '6666'   (expected 'ff')
// 'done' is never printed; the callback is collected by nothing
bl.end('68656c6c6f', 'hex')        // stores '68656c6c6f', not 'hello'
```

**Impact:** a caller that uses the documented stream signature gets wrong bytes written and a completion callback that never fires - a silent hang in the cleanup path rather than an error. Grade `low`: contained to one caller, and only reachable when an `encoding` or callback argument is passed.

**Fix:** match the inherited signature and pass everything through - `function end (chunk, encoding, callback) { DuplexStream.prototype.end.call(this, chunk, encoding, callback) ... }` - and return `this`.

findings.title: Generated `read*` methods throw instead of defaulting the offset to 0
findings.body:
The generated `read*` methods reject a call without an explicit offset, although `README.md:190-194` presents them as "all of the standard byte-reading methods of the `Buffer` interface", whose offsets default to 0. `bl.readUInt8()` and `bl.readUInt16BE()` throw `RangeError: The value of "size" is out of range`, while `Buffer.from('a').readUInt8()` returns the byte.

**Why:** the generator at `bl.js:382-383` forwards the caller's `offset` unchanged:

```js
BufferList.prototype[m] = function (offset) {
  return this.slice(offset, offset + methods[m])[m](0)
}
```

With `offset` undefined, `slice(undefined, undefined + 1)` evaluates to `slice(undefined, NaN)`; `copy()` keeps `srcEnd = NaN` (`bl.js:140` only replaces non-numbers) and `Buffer.allocUnsafe(NaN)` at `bl.js:181` throws. The variable-width family has the same gap one argument further along: `readIntBE(0)`/`readUIntLE(0)` (`bl.js:377-378`) throw when `byteLength` is omitted.

**Evidence:**

```js
const bl = new BufferList(Buffer.from('abcdefgh'))
bl.readUInt8()        // THROW RangeError: The value of "size" is out of range. It must be >= 0 && <= 9
bl.readUInt16BE()     // same THROW
bl.readDoubleBE()     // same THROW
bl.readIntBE(0)       // same THROW (byteLength is undefined)
bl.readUInt16BE(0)    // works: 25185
Buffer.from('abcdefgh').readUInt8()   // 97 - the Buffer behaviour bl claims to mirror
```

**Impact:** code written against the `Buffer` interface - including the argument-less forms the README lists at `README.md:99` - gets a `RangeError` instead of a value, so a drop-in replacement for `Buffer` fails on the default-offset call; an uncaught error crashes the request. Grade `low`: contained to the caller, deterministic, and trivially worked around by passing `0`.

**Fix:** default both parameters where the methods are generated - `function (offset = 0)` at `bl.js:377` and `bl.js:382`, and `byteLength` defaulted or validated in the variable-width branch.

summary:
**Summary**

The PR re-adds `lib/parser.js` (the `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` parser that the baseline fixture had removed) to `lib/websocket_extensions.js`. It is a verbatim copy of the published websocket-extensions 0.1.3 release — I diffed it against the npm tarballs of 0.1.3 and 0.1.4, and the only substantive difference from 0.1.4 is the missing backslash exclusion in the `QUOTED` character class, i.e. the CVE-2020-7662 fix is absent. A 46-byte header of 40 backslashes blocks the event loop for ~11.6 s through the public `generateResponse` path that `websocket-driver` feeds from the client's request header, and cost grows ~100× per 10 bytes.

Coverage beyond that: the spec suite passes (79 tests, 97 assertions), the parser/consumer contract (`Offers`, `serializeParams`, `SyntaxError`) is honoured, and valid headers up to the 16 KB Node header limit parse in a few milliseconds with no other polynomial blowup. One serializer defect is real and reproduced — a stateful `/g` regex makes values needing quotes emit unquoted, producing headers this parser rejects. Other candidates from the scan (`__proto__`/`constructor` name handling, non-string input, CRLF in values) need contrived or trusted-caller preconditions and were not filed.

findings.title: Crafted Sec-WebSocket-Extensions header hangs the process (exponential backtracking in QUOTED)
findings.body:
`Parser.parseHeader` takes exponential time on a short, attacker-supplied
`Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` header, blocking the Node event loop and denying service to every
client of the process.

**Evidence:** In `lib/parser.js:5` the quoted-string pattern is

```js
QUOTED = /"((?:\\[\x00-\x7f]|[^\x00-\x08\x0a-\x1f\x7f"])*)"/,
```

The negated class still accepts `\` (`\x5c`), so each backslash in a quoted string can be
consumed either as an escape pair (`\\[\x00-\x7f]`) or as an ordinary character. When the
closing quote never arrives the two alternatives are tried in every combination, so the work
doubles with each backslash:

```
$ node -e "require('./lib/parser').parseHeader('a; b=\"' + '\\\\'.repeat(40))"
30 backslashes (36 bytes) ->    22 ms
40 backslashes (46 bytes) ->  2285 ms
```

Reachable from the wire: `websocket-driver` passes the client's own request header to
`generateResponse` (`lib/websocket/driver/hybi.js:289` in websocket-driver 0.7.5) and the
server's header to `activate` (`client.js:132`). Through that path a 46-byte header
(`permessage-deflate; b="` followed by 40 backslashes) held the event loop for 11.6 s before
throwing `SyntaxError`:

```
$ node -e "...new Extensions().generateResponse('permessage-deflate; b=\"' + '\\\\'.repeat(40))"
threw: SyntaxError: Invalid Sec-WebSocket-Extensions header: permessage-deflate;
generateResponse with 46-byte header blocked the event loop for 11664 ms
```

The cost grows ~100x per 10 bytes added, and Node's default 16 KB header limit leaves room
for thousands of them, so a single handshake can hang the process effectively forever.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated remote peer gains the capability to stop a Node server that
uses `websocket-extensions` (directly, or through `websocket-driver`/`faye-websocket`) from
serving anyone, so reach crosses a trust boundary; the damage is undone by a restart, which
makes persistence recoverable. Cross a trust boundary x recoverable = `high` under the
severity policy. This is the flaw tracked as CVE-2020-7662.

**Fix:** Remove the ambiguity by excluding the backslash from the negated class:

```js
QUOTED = /"((?:\\[\x00-\x7f]|[^\x00-\x08\x0a-\x1f\x7f"\\])*)"/,
```

Then every backslash can only start an escape pair. That one-character change is what
upstream 0.1.4 shipped; with it, 40 backslashes parse in 0.2 ms and 4000 in 0.03 ms. The rest
of the added file matches the published 0.1.3 release, so this is the only missing part of the
fix.

findings.title: Param values needing quotes are serialized unquoted after the first such param
findings.body:
`serializeParams` decides whether to quote a parameter value using a module-level regex that
carries `lastIndex`, so after the first value that contains a non-token character, later
values are written unquoted. The resulting `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` string cannot be parsed
back — even by this library's own parser.

**Preconditions:** an extension session emits a param value containing a space, comma, quote
or similar character (for example the `'hi, there'` value in `spec/parser_spec.js:66`).

**Evidence:** `NOTOKEN` is declared with the `g` flag (`lib/parser.js:4`) and used with
`RegExp.prototype.test` (`lib/parser.js:63`), which leaves `lastIndex` set after a match:

```
$ node -e "var P=require('./lib/parser');
  console.log(P.serializeParams('x', {a:'p q', b:'r s', c:'t u'}))"
x; a="p q"; b=r s; c="t u"        <- b and c must be quoted

$ node -e "var P=require('./lib/parser'); P.parseHeader(P.serializeParams('x',{a:'p q',b:'r s'}))"
SyntaxError: Invalid Sec-WebSocket-Extensions header: x; a="p q"; b=r s
```

The same input serialized twice in one process produces two different strings
(`x; a="p q"; b=r s; c="t u"` then `x; a=p q; b="r s"; c=t u`), so the output depends on
unrelated earlier calls. `lib/websocket_extensions.js:50` and `:105` splice this string into
the handshake header.

**Impact:** One handshake ends in a rejected header or a wrong offer list: the peer sees a
malformed or truncated extension list instead of the intended parameters. Reach is contained
(one connection) and a retry restarts the cycle, so the severity is `low`
(contained x recoverable).

**Fix:** Make the quoting test independent of call history — test against a non-global regex,
or reset `NOTOKEN.lastIndex = 0` before use. The same round-trip invariant is broken for an
empty string (`{a: ''}` serializes to the unparseable `x; a=`) and for a value ending in a
backslash (only `"` is escaped at `lib/parser.js:64`, so the closing quote is escaped away),
so quote or escape every value that is not a bare token.

summary:
## Summary

The change re-adds `lib/parser.js` at the upstream 0.1.4 revision: the `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` header parser, whose only material difference from the vulnerable 0.1.3 is the `QUOTED` character class now excluding `\` (`lib/parser.js:5`). I confirmed the fix is the correct one for CVE-2020-7662 — the 0.1.3 backslash kernel costs ~2.4 ms at 26 characters and grows ~2.7× per two characters, while this revision stays flat at ~0.002 ms, and a probe of 74 adversarial header families plus 40k fuzz cases (up to 256 KB inputs) found no remaining superlinear regex behaviour; the existing suite passes (79 tests). Three defects remain in the new file and are recorded: quadratic work merging duplicate params with a valid, attacker-supplied header, a stateful global `NOTOKEN` regex that emits unquoted values, and inconsistent backslash escaping between serializer and parser. The security fix itself is sound; the residual issues are low/info and none reopen the ReDoS.

findings.title: Valid headers with many duplicate params cost quadratic time in parseHeader
findings.body:
`Parser.parseHeader` merges duplicate params by rebuilding the array on every repeat
(`lib/parser.js:41`: `offer[key] = [].concat(offer[key]); offer[key].push(data)`), which
copies the whole array each time, so a param repeated k times costs O(k²) time and
allocation. Cost tracks the duplicate count, not the header size.

**Preconditions:** the header passes `EXT_LIST` — this is a *valid* header, so validation
does not stop it. The header is supplied by the remote peer during the handshake:
`lib/websocket_extensions.js:94` (server, `generateResponse`) and `:61` (client, `activate`).

**Evidence:** measured on this checkout (Node 24, min of 3 runs), header
`'a' + ';b'.repeat(k)`:

| header bytes | duplicates | time |
|---|---|---|
| 8 001 | 4 000 | 16.6 ms |
| 16 001 | 8 000 | 80.4 ms |
| 32 001 | 16 000 | 797 ms |
| 64 001 | 32 000 | 5 856 ms |

Control with distinct param names, 22 891 bytes → 3.3 ms and 100 891 bytes → 11.9 ms
(linear), so the growth comes from the rebuild at `lib/parser.js:41`. Replacing the concat
with an in-place push makes the same inputs linear.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated client can block the process's event loop, stalling every
connection that process serves, from one syntactically valid handshake header. Reach is
broad, but the HTTP layer's header-size limit bounds it: Node's default
`http.maxHeaderSize` is 16 384 bytes, which caps one request at about 80 ms; front ends that
allow 64 KB headers (common for proxies) reach about 6 s per request. Because that existing
limit bounds the damage, this is filed as low, not medium.

**Fix:** append in place instead of rebuilding:
`if (hasOwnProperty.call(offer, key)) { if (!Array.isArray(offer[key])) offer[key] = [offer[key]]; offer[key].push(data); }`.

findings.title: Stateful NOTOKEN regex emits unquoted values, so serialized headers fail to parse
findings.body:
`NOTOKEN` is declared with the `g` flag (`lib/parser.js:4`) and used with `.test()`
(`lib/parser.js:63`). `RegExp.prototype.test` on a global regex starts at `lastIndex` and
sets it to `matchIndex + 1` on success, so a value whose only non-token character sits
before that offset is reported as token-safe and emitted unquoted at `lib/parser.js:63-66`.
The result is a serialized header that violates the grammar its own parser enforces, or a
silently different parameter set.

**Evidence** (fresh process, one call each, this checkout):

```
Parser.serializeParams('x', {a: 'p q', b: 'r s'})
  -> x; a="p q"; b=r s
  -> Parser.parseHeader(...) throws SyntaxError: Invalid Sec-WebSocket-Extensions header

Parser.serializeParams('x', {a: ['hi, there', 'ab,cd']})
  -> x; a="hi, there"; a=ab,cd
  -> parseHeader -> [{name:"x",params:{a:["hi, there","ab"]}}, {name:"cd",params:{}}]
```

The first call leaves `lastIndex` at 2, so `"r s"` is scanned from offset 2 and the space at
offset 1 is invisible (`/[^...]/g` statefulness: `test('p q') -> true, lastIndex 2;
test('r s') -> false, lastIndex 0`). In the array case the short value splits at its comma,
which invents a phantom offer named `cd` — the peer receives a different extension/
parameter set than the caller sent. The state also survives between calls, so one
connection can corrupt the header generated for a later one.

**Impact:** any caller that passes a parameter value containing a space, comma or other
non-token character — including the second such value in a single call — gets a header that
peers reject (handshake failure) or misparse. `spec/parser_spec.js` misses it because it
only ever serializes one quoted value per test. The trigger is local extension code, not a
remote actor, and nothing is lost beyond one failed or malformed handshake, so severity is
low.

**Fix:** remove the `g` flag from `NOTOKEN` at `lib/parser.js:4`; it is a pure predicate and
the flag has no other use.

findings.title: Param values containing a backslash are corrupted or rejected on round-trip
findings.body:
`serializeParams` escapes only `"` when quoting a value (`lib/parser.js:64`), while
`parseHeader` deletes every backslash from a quoted value (`lib/parser.js:34`). The tightened
`QUOTED` in this change (`lib/parser.js:5`, the CVE-2020-7662 fix) now also *requires* every
`\` to be followed by an ASCII character, so a value that ends in a backslash is serialized
into a header this parser rejects.

**Evidence** (fresh process per case, this checkout):

```
serializeParams('a', {b: 'x\\'})  -> a; b="x\"
  parseHeader -> SyntaxError: Invalid Sec-WebSocket-Extensions header: a; b="x\"

serializeParams('a', {b: 'x\\y'}) -> a; b="x\y"
  parseHeader -> [{name:"a", params:{b:"xy"}}]      (backslash dropped)
```

Before the fix the same first header parsed as `x`; it now throws, because `\"` is consumed
as an escaped quote and no closing quote follows. The second case shows the older defect that
survives the fix: `replace(/\\/g, '')` at `lib/parser.js:34` cannot tell an escape from a
literal backslash.

**Impact:** an extension whose offer/response parameter value contains a backslash produces a
`Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` header that a conforming peer rejects (failed handshake), or a
value the peer reads with backslashes stripped. Extension parameters in practice are tokens
or numbers, and the values come from local extension code rather than a remote actor, so
this is filed as info.

**Fix:** make the serializer and parser agree on escaping: escape `\` before `"` at
`lib/parser.js:64` (`value.replace(/\\/g, '\\\\').replace(/"/g, '\\"')`) and unescape
`\\`/`\"` at `lib/parser.js:34` instead of deleting every backslash.

summary: ## Summary The PR adds one new file, `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts` (534 lines), the HTML tokenizer/sanitizer that TinyMCE's `DomParser` uses for `setContent`, `load`, paste and `getContent` round-trips. It is byte-identical to TinyMCE's pre-patch 4.9.9 source for CVE-2019-1010091, so the change re-introduces the known flaw rather than fixing it. The comment/CDATA emission path is the weak spot: CDATA text, comment text and `srcdoc`-style attributes all leave the parser less escaped than they arrived, and the parser's output is assigned to `innerHTML`. The most serious case reproduces end-to-end against this tree — a crafted CDATA section becomes a live `` — and two further validation gaps are confirmed in the same file. Overall: the change should not be merged as-is; the parser needs the CDATA sanitization loop and stricter comment padding/attribute-name checks before it re-enters the build.

findings.title: Single-pass CDATA sanitization lets crafted CDATA inject live markup (mXSS)
findings.body: CDATA content is sanitized with a single `String.replace` pass, so removing one comment marker can create another. A crafted CDATA section therefore reaches the editor DOM as live markup, and its contents never pass element or attribute validation. **Preconditions:** Attacker-controlled HTML reaches `editor.setContent()`, `editor.load()`, `insertContent`/paste, or any consumer that round-trips content through `tinymce.html.DomParser` + `Serializer`. Default settings suffice (`validate: true` does not help, because the payload is plain text inside a CDATA token). **Evidence:** - `trimComments` (SaxParser.ts:59-61) does `text.replace(/` becomes `-->`. - `SaxParser.ts:499-500` runs that result through `cdata(...)`; `DomParser.ts:433-434` stores it as a `#cdata` node. - `InitContentBody.ts:97-106` rewrites `#cdata` to `#comment` with value `'[CDATA[' + value + ']]'`; `Writer.ts:133-135` emits `''` with no escaping; `SetContent.ts:82-90` assigns the serialized string to the body via `editor.dom.setHTML` (`innerHTML`). - Reproduced against this tree (real `DomParser` + `Serializer` + the `InitContentBody` filter copy, output parsed by parse5/jsdom): input `]]>` → serialized `]]-->` → `innerHTML` contains `` followed by a live ``. - The `` is never tokenized as an element, so `parseAttribute` (SaxParser.ts:198-268) never sees `onerror`; the payload also survives `valid_elements: 'p'`. **Impact:** Untrusted content that goes through TinyMCE's parser escapes as live HTML and executes script in the origin that renders the editor or its stored output — the mXSS class this parser's comment/cdata filtering exists to prevent. Severity: reach crosses a trust boundary (attacker content runs script in a victim's page), permanent when content is stored, so high. **Fix:** Restore the invariant "the emitted comment/CDATA text contains no comment delimiters": repeat the strip until it is stable (upstream TINY-4669 does exactly this), i.e. `let out = text; while (/

findings.title: Comment values starting with '-' are emitted as an abruptly closed comment, exposing the rest as live markup
findings.body: The comment branch only neutralizes values that start with `>`. A comment value starting with `-` is written back as `…`, which the HTML parser treats as an abruptly closed empty comment, so the rest of the comment value becomes live markup. **Preconditions:** Attacker-controlled HTML reaches `editor.setContent()`, `editor.load()`, `insertContent`/paste, or a `DomParser` + `Serializer` round-trip; default settings. **Evidence:** - `SaxParser.ts:488-498` captures the comment body and pads only `value.charAt(0) === '>'` (line 490); `Writer.ts:138-140` then emits `''` verbatim. - Reproduced against this tree (real `DomParser` + `Serializer`, output parsed by parse5/jsdom): input `-->` is emitted unchanged, and the browser parses it as an empty comment (``) followed by a live ``. - Attribute validation never runs on the payload: the `` sits inside the comment token, so `parseAttribute` (SaxParser.ts:198-268) never sees it and `onerror` is not stripped. **Impact:** Stored or pasted comment markup that a browser would otherwise treat as inert (or that TinyMCE is expected to neutralize) becomes executable markup in the page that renders the editor content. Severity: crosses a trust boundary and persists in stored content, but the escape depends on the browser's abrupt-comment-close rule and was verified with parse5 rather than a physical browser, so medium. **Fix:** Pad every comment value that can form an abrupt close — not just a leading `>` — e.g. emit `' ' + value` unless the value starts with a character that cannot close the comment, or escape `-` at the start of the value.

findings.title: Attribute value containing 'data-mce-type' disables schema validation and lets srcdoc survive
findings.body:
`isInternalElement` is decided by a substring search over the whole attribute
string, so any attribute *value* containing `data-mce-type` marks the element as
"internal". Internal elements skip the schema whitelist entirely
(`SaxParser.ts:206`, `SaxParser.ts:371`), and the only residual filter
(`SaxParser.ts:258`) checks exact URL attribute names and `on*`. `srcdoc`, which
the schema deliberately excludes from `iframe` (`Schema.ts:328`), is neither, so it
survives.

**Preconditions:** Attacker-controlled HTML reaches `editor.setContent()`,
`editor.load()`, `insertContent`/paste, or a `DomParser` + `Serializer` round-trip;
default schema and settings.

**Evidence:**
- `SaxParser.ts:353-354`: `isInternalElement = attribsValue.indexOf('data-mce-type') !== -1`.
- Reproduced against this tree (real `DomParser` + `Serializer`):
  `<iframe srcdoc="<script>alert(1)</script>"></iframe>` is reduced to
  `<iframe></iframe>` (schema drops `srcdoc`), but
  `<iframe title="data-mce-type" srcdoc="<script>alert(1)</script>"></iframe>`
  or `<iframe data-mce-type="x" srcdoc="...">` is emitted with `srcdoc` intact and
  is assigned to the editor body via `innerHTML` (`SetContent.ts:82-90`).

**Impact:** A deliberate schema exclusion can be bypassed with a decoy attribute,
putting an `srcdoc` iframe into the page. Browsers parse `srcdoc` as HTML in an
iframe that inherits the parent origin, so script inside it runs in that origin;
that execution step was not reproduced here (no browser in this environment), so
this is filed as medium rather than high. It also persists: serialization only
drops the `data-mce-type` attribute, not `srcdoc`.

**Fix:** Decide internal-ness from attribute *names*, e.g. test
`/(^|\s)data-mce-type\s*=/` against `attribsValue`, or check
`attrList.map['data-mce-type']` after parsing attributes, so a value can never
flip the flag.
